Pair it with voice traits named in real-estate language rather than adjectives, so the traits are memorable enough to check against.

entries.tagline: A global architecture practice whose main navigation is a type list — project names in near-black with their one-line descriptors set in grey on the same line, no thumbnails at all.
entries.summary: Snøhetta opens with no hero image: a single two-line sentence ("Snøhetta is a global transdisciplinary practice, working on projects of all scales.") sits alone on warm off-white, and the first photographs arrive below it as a strip that bleeds off both edges. From there every section runs on the same editorial spine — a small grey label in the left column, the content in the right, hairline rules as the only dividers, and zero accent colour, so all colour comes from the buildings. The page's centrepiece is a text index of highlighted projects where the name is near-black and its descriptive subtitle is grey on the same line, which makes a navigation list double as copy. It is a deliberately quiet page for a practice whose work is anything but, and the restraint is what makes 40 years of wildly different projects read as one body.
whatWorks: No hero image at all: one two-line sentence in a light weight at display size defines the practice, so the promise is read before anything is looked at — the images arrive second, as a strip.
The project filmstrip bleeds off both edges at varied heights and scales rather than sitting in a tidy carousel of equal cards, so it reads as a working contact sheet instead of a slideshow.

A label-left / content-right spine (Disciplines, Latest News, Upcoming Events, Highlighted Projects) means the page needs no section headings, no cards and no boxes — just a grey label, a hairline rule and the content.

The Highlighted Projects index sets the name in near-black and its descriptor in mid-grey on the SAME line ("Under — Europe's First Underwater Restaurant"), and lets the grey clause overrun the right edge instead of truncating it.
Upcoming Events is an actual table with Event / Location / Date column heads and a real dated lecture in it — a checkable, current section rather than a rotating news tile.

The two mid-page blocks (Our process / Sustainability and Responsibility) are deliberately unequal in size and vertically staggered, so a two-item row reads as an editorial spread rather than two matching cards.

The footer carries display controls — dark mode, a simplified view and low-resolution imagery — alongside the legal and transparency links, treating bandwidth and reading comfort as brand features rather than settings.

sections.name: Header & hero statement
sections.notes: The header is three items with no plate behind them: the wordmark left, the word "Menu", and a small mountain glyph right — no category words, no CTA, no search box. The hero is text only: one sentence broken over two lines in a light weight at roughly 48px, left-aligned on warm off-white, with nothing else on the first screen. For a practice whose work is intensely photographic, choosing to open on a sentence is a confidence move — it says the ideas come first and the pictures will keep.

sections.name: Project filmstrip
sections.notes: Immediately below the sentence, a horizontal strip of project images bleeds off both the left and right edges, with the images at different heights and one scaled up and pushed lower than its neighbours. Because it is clipped rather than contained, the eye registers "there is much more of this" without a counter or a "view all" button, and the ragged top and bottom edges keep it from reading as a stock carousel.

sections.name: Disciplines
sections.notes: The first labelled section: "Disciplines" in small grey type in the left column, and in the right column four rows separated by hairline rules — Architecture, Landscape Architecture, Interior Architecture, Product Design. It is the whole service offer in four words per line, set at heading scale with no icons and no descriptions. This is where the page establishes the label-left / content-right grammar that every following section reuses.

sections.name: Latest News & Upcoming Events
sections.notes: News is a horizontal carousel of three story cards, each with a dateline above the headline and images cropped to different heights, with prev/next arrows below rather than overlaid. Events is not a carousel at all but a table — Event / Location / Date column heads, hairline rules, the lecture title in black and the speakers in grey. Putting a real dated table on the homepage is the cheapest possible proof that the practice is currently active.

sections.name: Process & Sustainability blocks
sections.notes: Two prose blocks with images, but pointedly not a 2-up card row: "Our process" gets a small square image in the left column, "Sustainability and Responsibility" gets a much wider landscape image in the right column and sits lower on the page. Each has a plain bold label, three lines of body copy, and no button. The asymmetry is what makes it read as a spread instead of a component.

sections.name: Highlighted Projects index
sections.notes: The page's best section and its real navigation: nine projects as lines of type, each with the name in near-black at heading scale followed inline, on the same line, by its descriptive subtitle in mid-grey — "Norwegian National Opera and Ballet | Giving...", "Times Square | Putting the 'square' back in T...", "Under | Europe's First Underwater Restaurant". The grey clause deliberately runs past the right edge rather than being truncated with an ellipsis, which reads as abundance rather than as a bug. It closes with a single "→ See all of our projects". No thumbnails, no cards — you navigate by reading.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Opens with two plain text columns — "Get in touch" and "Policies and Governance" — with no cards, buttons or forms, then the footer proper: the mountain mark, four link columns (General / Disciplines / More), an inline search field with a "+" affordance, and a bottom rule carrying © Snøhetta 2026, Current Openings, Legal Documents, Transparency Act, Cookies & Tracking and the social links. Sitting with them are display controls for dark mode, a simplified view and low-resolution imagery — an unusually generous, and unusually honest, thing to publish for an image-heavy site.

principle.title: Let the index be a sentence, not a thumbnail
principle.explanation: A grid of image cards forces every item to compete on its photograph, hides what the thing actually IS behind a title, and needs a new card style the moment the content types diverge. Setting the same list as type — name in near-black, one grey clause naming what it is, on the same line — makes the index readable at a glance, scannable by keyword, honest about items with weak photography, and free of layout debt. It also flatters the copy: the descriptor has to be written well because there is nothing else to look at.
principle.howToApply: On the next project, neighbourhood or listing index, build the primary list as type before you build a grid: address or name in near-black at heading scale, one mid-grey clause on the same line naming what it actually is ("A 1920s Craftsman two blocks from the lake"), hairline rules only, no cards. Let the grey clause overrun the container rather than truncating with an ellipsis. Keep photography in a separate edge-bleeding strip above the list, so the pictures set the mood and the type does the navigating.

site.name: StreetEasy — Reddit promoted post (free-form in-feed ad)

entries.category: Reddit promoted post (free-form in-feed single-image ad)
entries.tagline: A real-estate ad that opens with a market statistic and says "YMMV" — written in the platform's own register, and selling a decision guide rather than listings.
entries.when: Reddit in-feed, ~2025–26 (documented in Reddit's own advertiser case study)
entries.summary: The unit is a single-image promoted post from StreetEasy, Zillow's New York City listings brand, running in the Reddit feed against zip-code, community and keyword targeting. Everything unusual about it is in the copy: the primary text opens with a fact about the reader's own city ("Two-thirds of New Yorkers rent while the remainder buys"), uses Reddit's own shorthand "YMMV", and offers a rent-vs-buy guide rather than a listings search — an offer aimed one step upstream of the transaction, at someone still deciding. The creative splits rather than overlays: a flat brand-blue field carries the logo and a two-line question, and a documentary photograph of a brownstone sidewalk is inset beneath it, so no type ever sits on the image. Reddit reports the campaign ran 20% above CTR benchmark, 11% under its CPC goal, and 15% more efficient cost per incremental visit than other social platforms, with longer average session times.
whatWorks: Opens with a number instead of a pitch: "Two-thirds of New Yorkers rent while the remainder buys" enters the feed as information about the reader's city, so the first line earns attention before any brand claim is made.
Written in the platform's register — "YMMV" is Reddit's own idiom, and the sentence structure reads like a comment; the "Promoted" label ends up being the only thing marking it as an ad.

Sells the decision aid, not the inventory: the offer is a guide that helps you choose rent vs buy "which option fits your budget, goals, and lifestyle" — correctly matched to a feed audience that is deliberating, not shopping.
The creative is split, not overlaid: brand-blue upper field for the logo and headline, photograph inset below it, so nothing competes with type and both survive at feed scale on a phone.
The headline is a question answered by its own second line — "Rent or buy in NYC?" / "We'll help you decide" — staggered right so the two lines read in sequence rather than as one block.

Honest, unstyled location photography: a real brownstone sidewalk with a green awning numbered 71, shot at eye level with a person walking through it. No rendered interior, no stock couple with keys — the street does the aspirational work.
CTA restraint: one outline "Learn More" pill in Reddit's own chrome plus the bare domain "streeteasy.com" in a white footer bar. No urgency copy, no badge, no second ask.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The u/StreetEasy handle and "Promoted" label sit above three lines of primary text whose first clause is a statistic, not a slogan. Because the number is about the reader's own market and the phrasing concedes uncertainty ("YMMV"), the unit reads as a contribution to the feed rather than an interruption of it — which is exactly the register Reddit punishes brands for missing.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: Inside the creative, white type on flat brand blue asks "Rent or buy in NYC?" and answers itself on the next line, "We'll help you decide" — both right-staggered so the eye steps down and right. It is a two-beat structure: name the reader's live question, then position the brand as the referee rather than the seller. No price, no inventory count, no feature.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: The frame is split horizontally: the top third is a saturated brand-blue field holding the speech-bubble building logomark and wordmark plus the headline; below it an inset documentary photograph of a tree-lined NYC block — brownstone, iron railings, green awning, a pedestrian mid-stride — offset right so the blue field frames it on the left. Insetting rather than full-bleeding the photo is what keeps the type clean and keeps the brand colour, not the picture, as the first thing recognised in the scroll.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: A white bar under the creative with "streeteasy.com" small and grey on the left and a single outline-pill "Learn More" on the right — Reddit's native ad chrome, unmodified. The restraint is deliberate: the persuasion has already happened in the primary text, so the button only has to be the obvious next step, not a second argument.

principle.title: Write the ad in the platform's own register, and offer the guide rather than the listing
principle.explanation: On a community platform, the format that converts is the one that survives being read as a normal post — a checkable local number, ordinary sentence rhythm, and the site's own shorthand do more for credibility than any amount of polish. Pairing that voice with an upstream offer (a guide, a calculator, an explainer) also matches feed intent: people scrolling a city subreddit are deciding whether to move, not choosing between two addresses. Ask for the smaller, earlier commitment and you get the click, the longer session, and the audience before your competitors are even in the consideration set.
principle.howToApply: For a Lofty or 35353 paid-social unit, open the copy with one checkable local number you actually have ("62% of Rowlett listings closed under ask last quarter"), write it in the register of the place it will run — plain sentences, no exclamation marks, concede what you don't know — and make the offer a guide or calculator rather than "browse homes". Build the creative as a flat brand-colour panel carrying the logo and a two-line question-and-answer, with an honest street or exterior photo inset beneath it so no type sits on the image, and leave the platform's own CTA chrome untouched.

entries.tagline: Translated the European avant-garde into plain American — then invented the standards manual so it would still be plain American after he left the room.
entries.summary: Beall came to design sideways, with an art-history degree from the University of Chicago and no design training, and spent the 1930s converting Constructivist and Bauhaus grammar — asymmetric layering, flat colour planes, block type, photomontage — into something a farmer in Indiana would read without hesitation. His posters for the Rural Electrification Administration are the proof: a giant white bulb on a field split red and blue, a black farmhouse silhouette, thin rays doing the work of invisible current, and the single word LIGHT. In 1937 he became the first designer given a one-man show at the Museum of Modern Art. Then he did the less glamorous and more consequential thing: from the mid-1950s he built full identity programmes for Connecticut General, International Paper, Caterpillar and Martin Marietta, and documented them in style books and graphics standards manuals — among the first fully articulated in America — because he defined the designer's job as pre-creative, creative and post-creative, and refused to stop at the mark.
whatWorks: Split the job into three named phases — pre-creative (research and audit), creative (design), post-creative (documentation and enforcement) — and quote all three, so the standards document is scope rather than unbilled goodwill.

Write the standards deliberately loose: the Connecticut General style book fixed trademark, typeface and colour policy but left layout to judgement with limited formal rules — a rulebook people can follow beats one they route around.

Design for the room, not the desk: the REA posters had to land across a barn or a general store on a reader with no prior interest, so they were built from one symbol, two flat colours and a five-word slogan.
Draw the invisible. When the benefit cannot be photographed — current, flow, connection, reach — invent a device (arrow, ray, line) that shows it moving from A to B.

Keep the imported form, localise the words: he held on to Constructivist structure but wrote the copy in American vernacular ("When I think back…", "It's fine for us"), so a modern layout never read as foreign.
Raid a discipline outside design for your reference library — art history, in his case — and mine it for structure the trained designers around you have not already used.

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: With the audience's ignorance, not the brief's wish list. For the REA he was designing for households that had never had electricity, so he started from one concrete benefit at a time — light, running water, a better home, farm work — rather than from a layout or a slogan. And before form on the corporate work came what he called the pre-creative phase: understanding the company, its documents and its people well enough to know what the mark would have to survive.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Import a foreign visual language and re-say it in the local vernacular. Beall took the European avant-garde's asymmetric layering of word and image, flat colour planes, block type and experimental photography, and paired them with plainspoken American slogans and an unmistakably patriotic red-white-blue — so the poster felt like a familiar object using an unfamiliar grammar. He ran the REA work as three successive series, moving from pure flat symbol (1937) to photomontage bonded onto those same flat planes with colloquial captions (1939, 1941), refining rather than restarting.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: The arrow and the flat field. A page split into two or three flat colour fields gives a silhouette or a photograph a stage and does the work a border would do, without a border; thin rays and arrows carry the eye and stand in for a thing that has no shape — current running from the pole to the farmhouse. Later he layered documentary photography onto those same planes, so the photomontage inherited the poster's structure instead of dissolving it.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: "The designer's role in the development, application and protection of the trademark may be described as pre-creative, creative and post-creative." The mark is not finished when it is drawn — it is finished when it is documented and defensible, which is why the Connecticut General style book (1958, 500 copies, bound with his own notes on typographic design) and the International Paper standards manual (1960) exist at all. His counter-instinct is the interesting part: the standards were kept informal and few on purpose, betting on trained judgement over an exhaustive rulebook.

principle.title: Budget the pre-creative and post-creative phases, not just the design
principle.explanation: Most identity and template work is priced as if the deliverable were the artwork, so the research that makes it right and the documentation that makes it last both get done for free or not at all — and the thing degrades the first time someone else uses it. Beall's three-phase framing turns those into named, quotable phases with their own outputs: an audit before, a standards document after. It also changes what "finished" means, from "the file is approved" to "someone who has never met me can apply this correctly next year."
principle.howToApply: On the next identity, template or section-block system, write the estimate in three lines — pre-creative (audit what exists, where it will be used, what it must survive), creative (design), post-creative (a short standards page plus the master files). Keep the standards deliberately short and enforceable, Beall-style: fix the mark, the typeface and the colour roles, then leave layout to judgement. Anything you would not be willing to enforce should not be in the document.

entries.category: Public brand guidelines hub (museum / cultural institution)
entries.tagline: Nine web tiles, each illustrated with a live specimen of the component it documents — and a typographic underline specified down to the stroke weight.
entries.summary: The Australian Museum publishes its brand system as a public hub of nine tiles — Logo, Typography, Colour, Pattern, Descriptor, Motion, Photography, Brand Voice, Terms of Use — sitting on a page that is itself set in the brand, chevron watermark and all. What lifts it above the usual press-kit page is that every tile is illustrated with a rendered sample of the thing behind it: the logo on its construction grid, a giant orange "Aa", the colour bars with tints, the chevron pattern, and the word "Descriptor" underlined above a real headline. The specs behind those tiles are unusually exact for a public guide — clearspace of more than half the width of the "A" in AM, a 30mm / 100px minimum, pattern scaled so 6–8 peaks fit the longest edge, a rule that only two to three colours may be combined, and a heading underline set at 10% of font size with a 20–30% offset on the last line only. Its weak spot is the opposite of vagueness: the palette is named and downloadable but no hex, RGB, CMYK or Pantone value appears on the page, and there is no numeric contrast standard behind a five-colour secondary palette.
whatWorks: The index teaches before you click: each of the nine tiles renders a live specimen of its component (logo on its grid, a display-scale "Aa", colour bars with tints, the pattern, the underlined Descriptor over a real headline) instead of an icon or a word.
The guide is set in its own system — orange and red, chevron pattern watermark behind the grid — so the page doubles as the largest application example in the document.

Small type devices are specified with numbers, not adjectives: main-heading underline at 10% of font size weight, 20–30% offset, last line only; descriptors underlined at 15%; credits all-caps at a 5.5pt floor, 120% leading, 75 tracking.

The pattern has a scale rule rather than a vibe: size it so 6–8 peaks fit the longest edge of the media, rotate only in 90° steps, crop sections rather than showing the whole thing, and never use transparency over solid colour (which would invent off-brand hues).

Colour is governed by role and count, not just by swatch — organisational communications may use only the core and neutral palettes, promotional work unlocks the secondary palette, and no more than two to three colours may be combined in any piece.

The "Descriptor" is an unusual and very copyable idea: a documented brand device — top-left, four words maximum, drawn from a list of 40+ approved terms, never a call to action or a URL — that tells the reader what kind of thing they are looking at before the headline does.

Brand Voice is a four-trait model (Expert, Wonder, Progressive, Specific) with explicit modulation guidance — a science strategy dials Expert and Progressive up and Wonder down — and worked examples across strategy documents, social posts, brochures, fundraising ads and education materials.

sections.name: Identity system index
sections.notes: A nine-tile grid titled "Our Identity System", each tile a rendered specimen plus a one-line description and a "See more" link, over a chevron watermark. Below it, governance is a person rather than a process: a "Request a job" block naming the Design Coordinator with a direct email and phone number, plus a separate Terms of Use covering IP. Warm and answerable — but there is no version number, date or changelog anywhere on the hub.

sections.name: Logo
sections.notes: Print pack (PDF/EPS/JPEG, CMYK) and screen pack (PDF/SVG/PNG, RGB), each bundled with guidelines. Two mono versions with a stated rule — black against light colours and imagery, white reversed out of dark. Clearspace is expressed in the mark's own anatomy: spacing greater than half the width of the "A" in AM. Minimum size is given in both media — never smaller than 30mm or 100 pixels wide. Placement is tied to the grid (top-right or bottom-right, three columns wide), and co-branding is specified properly: a full "A" width between partner logos, equal heights where possible, half an "A" width either side of a divider.

sections.name: Typography
sections.notes: Apercu is the marketing typeface, Arial the internal system fallback, with the hard line that all external communications must use Apercu. The hierarchy is spelled out level by level with real values: main headings in Apercu Black at 110% leading, title case or all caps with 100 tracking; subhead 1 at 2× body size; subhead 2 / CTA at body size; long-form print body at 8.5pt on 11.5pt; short-form body at 130% leading; credits all-caps Apercu Bold with a 5.5pt floor. The underline treatment — last line only, 10% of font size, 20–30% offset — is the brand's signature typographic device and it is specified as tightly as the logo.

sections.name: Colour
sections.notes: Three palettes with defined jobs: Core (preferred, for anything from the museum as an organisation), Neutral (to unify and complement), Secondary (promotional latitude for exhibitions, programs and events) with nature-derived names — Cockatoo Yellow, Eucalyptus Green, Saltwater Aqua, Bluebottle Blue, Amethyst Purple. Combination guidance covers tone, contrast versus monotone, and legibility ("consider using tints"), capped at two to three colours per piece. An Adobe .ase/.ai swatch file is the deliverable — and, notably, the only way to get an actual value.

sections.name: Pattern & Descriptor
sections.notes: The pattern is built from elements of the logomark itself, extended and repeated into a master pattern, so the identity scales from a 100px mark to a full-bleed field without a second asset. Rules are quantified (6–8 units along the longest edge, 90° rotation only, crop rather than tile the whole thing, any brand colour including tints, no transparency over solids, sits behind or in front but never competes with content). The Descriptor is the other half of the layout system: top-left, four words maximum, from an approved list of 40+ terms across Groups / Content / Activity, never a CTA or a web address, never too vague or too specific, and explicitly not for space-constrained formats like banner ads.

sections.name: Photography & Motion
sections.notes: Photography is split into four named categories with distinct direction — Engagement (candid, fly-on-the-wall, subjects not facing camera, faces showing awe or wonder), Objects (white/grey/black backdrops, evenly lit, a soft cast shadow preferred; in-situ shots shallow depth of field), Portraits (natural light matched to the message; moody shadow used sparingly), Events (interaction and emotion, and explicitly not lots of backs of heads). It asks for visible diversity including people with disability, negative space in wide shots for text overlay, and a neutral grey card on shoot for colour reference. Motion has its own section plus a dedicated logo-animation guideline and downloadable resources — which most guides this size still omit entirely.

sections.name: Brand Voice
sections.notes: Four traits, each with do's and don'ts: Expert (reference qualifications, let the reader infer authority, never boast), Wonder (show what is rare, never exaggerate or overstate or deceive), Progressive (real-world societal impact, don't confuse institutional progress with societal progress), Specific (name the actual specimen or statistic, don't bury the reader in jargon). Crucially it documents modulation — which traits to dial up or down per context — and shows the same voice across five channels rather than presenting one exemplary paragraph.

needs: Actual colour values. The palette is named and downloadable as an Adobe swatch, but no hex, RGB, CMYK or Pantone appears on the page — so anyone building a web page, a slide or an email has to open Illustrator to get a number they could have copied.

A numeric contrast standard. "Ensure sufficient tonal contrast" and "consider using tints" is guidance, not a rule; a five-colour secondary palette needs a per-background legibility table (permitted heading colour, body colour, treatment on white) or stated WCAG ratios.

A digital layer. Every spec is print-first — 8.5pt on 11.5pt, 30mm, tracking in thousandths. There is no px/rem type scale, no web font licensing note beyond "Apercu or Arial", no link, button or form guidance, no responsive rules and no dark mode.

Iconography. There is no icon section at all, which is a conspicuous hole for an institution running gallery wayfinding, ticketing and accessibility symbols; without one, every project invents its own set.

An applications gallery. The tiles document components beautifully but nothing shows them assembled — no finished poster, banner, social post, exhibition wall, email or slide — and the grid is referenced ("three columns wide") without ever being drawn.

A version stamp and changelog. Governance is a named Design Coordinator with a phone number, which is warm but unversioned: nobody can tell whether the pack they downloaded last year is still current, or what changed.

Cultural protocols for imagery. The site carries an Acknowledgement of Country and the collection holds extensive First Nations material, but the brand pages surface no protocol for that imagery — consent, attribution, restricted or secret-sacred material, deceased persons — beyond a general IP Terms of Use and a casting-diversity note in Photography.

principle.title: Make the contents page teach — every tile a live specimen
principle.explanation: Most guides index themselves with icons, or with words on flat colour, so the reader has to open nine pages to discover which one they actually needed — and the people most likely to bounce are the occasional users the guide exists for. Rendering each tile as a real sample of its component (the logo on its construction grid, type at display scale, the actual colour bars, the pattern, the device in situ) turns the index into the fastest lesson in the document: you learn the system's flavour in one screen and you click already knowing what you will find. It also forces honesty, because a component with nothing worth showing gets exposed immediately.
principle.howToApply: On the next brand or block-library index, replace icon tiles with rendered specimens at real fidelity: set the type sample in the actual typeface at display size, show the palette as its real bars including tints, put the logo on its clearspace grid, and show any signature device applied to a real headline rather than described. Keep one line of plain-language description and one link per tile, set the index page itself in the system it documents, and if a tile has no specimen worth rendering, that is the signal the component is underspecified.

entries.tagline: A marketing page where every feature section is a working demo of itself, so the product is proved rather than described.
entries.summary: Tailwind's homepage is one very long, very disciplined proof sequence: an almost bare hero, then a run of feature blocks where each claim (responsive design, dark mode, container queries, 3D transforms, gradients) is shown as a live rendered specimen sitting beside the exact utility classes that produced it. The page is built in the thing it sells, so its own typography — huge tracking-tighter headings, balanced text, a restrained gray-950/white core — doubles as the sample. It ends on the commercial layer (Tailwind Plus) only after the free product has been demonstrated a dozen times over.
whatWorks: Hero does almost nothing: one long headline set tracking-tighter at display size, one explanatory sentence naming real utilities (flex, pt-4, text-center, rotate-90), and a single 'Get started' link — no product screenshot, no gradient hero art
Every feature block is a two-part unit: the rendered result and the code that produced it, side by side, so the reader never has to trust a claim
Demos use one consistent fake subject (a 'Beach House on Lake Huron' listing, a property grid) so you compare the technique, not the content
Abstract capabilities get concrete specimens — the P3 palette shipped as the full 50→950 ramp, easing shown as four cards running linear / ease-out / ease-in-out / ease-in at the same duration
Social proof is a grid of sites you already know (OpenAI, Reddit, Rivian, Shopify, The Verge, NASA/JPL) under the line 'you probably had no idea' — proof of range, not of popularity
The paid product appears once, late, as three named tiers (Templates / UI Blocks / UI Kit) rather than being braided through the free content

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Type-only: one headline at text-6xl→8xl with tight tracking and balanced line breaks, a single subhead sentence that lists actual class names, and one CTA to /docs/installation. The restraint is the credibility play — a CSS framework that needed a decorated hero would be arguing against itself.

sections.name: Sponsors
sections.notes: A logo grid immediately after the hero, framed as 'what pays for full-time maintenance'. For an open-source project this is the trust section, and putting it above the features says the project is funded and alive.

sections.name: Why Tailwind CSS? — the demo run
sections.notes: A dozen feature blocks in sequence: responsive design (one card at five breakpoints), filters stacked on one image, dark mode as a side-by-side pair, @theme CSS variables, the P3 colour ramp, CSS grid, transitions with four easings, cascade layers, logical properties shown as an LTR/RTL flip, container queries, gradients, 3D transforms. Each is result + code, never prose alone.

sections.name: Ship faster and smaller
sections.notes: An editor mockup showing index.html next to the generated build.css — the payoff section that turns 'utility classes' from a stylistic argument into a shipped-bytes one (<10kB typical).

sections.name: Tailwind in the wild
sections.notes: Twelve familiar brand cards under 'Build whatever you want, without touching your CSS file.' Because the demos above all look like Tailwind's own aesthetic, this section exists to disprove that the framework has a look.

sections.name: Tailwind Plus
sections.notes: The single commercial block: three products with one image each and one 'Explore' link, priced nowhere on this page. It reads as an upgrade path, not a paywall.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Four plain columns (Tailwind CSS / Tailwind Plus / Resources / Community), no newsletter capture, no repeated CTA — plus a link to the trademark policy, which is where the brand rules actually live.

principle.title: Prove each claim with a rendered specimen and the code beside it
principle.explanation: A feature list asks for trust; a specimen earns it. When the result and the exact source sit side by side in the same block, the reader verifies the claim in one glance and simultaneously learns how to reproduce it — the marketing copy and the documentation become the same artifact, which also means the page cannot drift from the product without visibly breaking.
principle.howToApply: On the next feature section, kill the paragraph and build a two-column unit: left, the thing actually rendered at real fidelity (component, listing row, map card, form state); right, the eight-to-twelve lines that produce it, copyable. Hold one fake subject constant across every block so the technique is the only variable, and if a claim has no renderable specimen, treat that as evidence the feature isn't ready to lead.

site.name: Armor All — 'Skin Care' portrait digital unit

entries.category: Static digital unit (portrait ~3:4, also run in print)
entries.tagline: A macro photograph of a cracked dashboard reframed as ageing skin, with a two-word headline doing all the work.
entries.when: Digital + print, Peru, July 2026 — agency Fiasco, Lima
entries.summary: The whole unit is one extreme close-up of a sun-cracked leather dashboard, lit so the crazing reads exactly like dry skin under a beauty-ad light. Copy is four words in two lines — 'Your car deserves / Skincare' — set small, low-left, in white, with the weight shift doing the emphasis instead of a size jump. Brand and payoff sit bottom-right at badge scale. Nothing is explained; the photograph carries the analogy and the copy just names it.
whatWorks: One focal point: a single texture at macro scale, cropped so no car is recognisable — the subject becomes 'surface', which is what the product actually treats
Headline is four words and set at maybe 4% of the frame height; the confidence of small type on a big image is the tone of the ad
Emphasis by weight, not size — 'Your car deserves' in light, 'Skincare' in semibold on the next line, same size, so the analogy lands on one word
Type sits in the darkest, least-detailed part of the photograph, so no scrim, box or stroke is needed for legibility
Brand lockup and tagline ('Protect what moves you.') are parked in the opposite corner at small scale, letting the image own the middle third
No product shot at all — the category cue is borrowed from beauty advertising, which is the entire idea

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The texture reads as skin for a beat before you resolve it as a dashboard. That one-beat delay is the whole stopping mechanism, and it works because the crop removes every car cue (no wheel, no badge, only a vent edge).

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'Your car deserves Skincare' — a category swap in four words. The line does not explain the product, the finish or the SPF equivalence; it trusts the picture to have already made the argument.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Warm brown monochrome, single raking light down the crazed leather, deep falloff to near-black at the left where the type sits. Shot like cosmetics packaging rather than like automotive: soft, tactile, dermatological.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: There isn't one, and that is the honest read: this is an awareness unit ending on brand + tagline. The unit's job is the analogy; the omission of a button is a deliberate cost, and would need adding for any performance placement.

principle.title: Borrow the visual grammar of the category you're comparing yourself to
principle.explanation: When the selling idea is an analogy ('this is skincare for your car'), the fastest way to transmit it is to shoot the ad the way that other category shoots its own — lighting, crop, colour, restrained type. The audience decodes genre before it reads words, so the borrowed grammar does the argument in a pre-verbal instant and the headline only has to confirm it.
principle.howToApply: Write the analogy as a sentence first ('a listing page is a magazine feature', 'title insurance is a seatbelt'), then art-direct the unit in the borrowed category's conventions rather than your own: light and crop like the reference, cap the copy at a headline that merely names the swap, place type in the frame's darkest quiet zone so it needs no box, and keep brand assets at badge scale in a corner.

entries.tagline: The architect who called himself a 'typotekt' and built advertising pages like structures — from the printer's actual inventory of parts.
entries.summary: Zwart came to graphic design from architecture and interiors, and never stopped working like a builder: he composed pages from the material the print shop already owned — rules, bars, wooden display letters, the typewriter, photostats — arranged on diagonals and axes that route the eye like circulation through a plan. His long run of NKF cable advertisements and his PTT work are the canonical demonstration; he later designed the Bruynzeel kitchen, which tells you how little he separated 'graphic' from 'product'. Voted Dutch designer of the century in 1999.
whatWorks: Design from the available inventory: rules, dots, bars and existing type instead of custom-drawn ornament — constraints of the shop become the visual language
Route the reader deliberately: one dominant diagonal or axis, then a clear second and third stop, rather than a symmetrical block of text
Repetition as illustration — a cable cross-section or a single letter repeated in a receding series to explain a product property without a picture of it
Use scale contrast violently and colour sparingly: one huge element, one red, everything else black on white
Treat white space as structural, not leftover — the void holds the composition apart the way a courtyard holds a plan
Cross-train on purpose: he moved between typography, interiors, photography and product, and each discipline supplied moves to the others

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: With the physical constraints, not a concept: what does this printer have, what does the press allow, what must this page do for the client's product. Because he learned in architecture, the brief arrives as a problem of structure and circulation rather than of decoration.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Compose with found parts on an asymmetric axis. Bars and rules divide the field, type sizes step in large jumps, and the diagonal creates a reading path with a first, second and third stop. Everything present must be doing structural work — nothing is placed for balance alone.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Making the product's property the picture: repeating a form in series, sectioning a cable, letting a photomontage collide with letterforms. Also the deliberately 'unartistic' toolkit — typewriter type, photostats, elementary shapes — which reads as engineering rather than styling.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Function first: a page is judged by whether it delivers the message quickly, not by whether it is beautiful. He rejected fixed styles and centred symmetry as inherited habits, and considered the designer's job to be organising information for a modern reader in a hurry.

principle.title: Design from the inventory you actually have, and let the constraint become the style
principle.explanation: Zwart's pages look invented because they were assembled from a strictly limited kit — the shop's rules, bars and type — rather than from an unlimited imagination. A closed kit forces structural decisions (scale, position, axis, repetition) to carry the expression, which is why the work still reads as designed rather than decorated a century later.
principle.howToApply: Before designing a page or a set of ads, write down the kit: two type sizes and two weights, one rule thickness, one accent colour, the components the CMS already ships. Then make the composition do the work — one dominant diagonal or axis, big scale jumps, a repeated element that explains a product property — and ban any new ornament that isn't already in the kit.

entries.category: Public press kit / newsroom brand-assets page
entries.tagline: A famously well-designed company publishes a deliberately tiny asset page — three wordmark colours, a checkout badge, executive portraits, and a licence.
entries.summary: Stripe's public brand page is not a brand guide and does not pretend to be one: it exists inside the newsroom to serve journalists and integrators. It gives the wordmark in exactly three colours with a one-line rule about which goes on which background, the 'Powered by Stripe' badge with a suggestion to link it to stripe.com, downloadable ZIPs, a press-photo gallery of founders and leadership, and a pointer to the Marks Usage Agreement that carries the real legal force. Everything a designer would want — hex values, clearspace, the typeface — is withheld, which is itself the position.
whatWorks: Scope is honest: it sits under /newsroom, so the artifact announces its own job (press and integration) instead of masquerading as guidelines
The wordmark rule is one sentence a non-designer can obey: slate and blurple on light, white on dark, and nothing else
Ships the thing integrators actually need — the 'Powered by Stripe' badge as a downloadable kit, with the recommendation to link it back to stripe.com
Press imagery is treated as a brand asset: leadership and founder portraits, pre-cleared, in a gallery, so publications don't scrape screenshots
The enforceable layer is separated out and linked (Marks Usage Agreement), keeping the page short while leaving the rules legally binding
Assets are ZIPs, not per-file downloads — one click and the requester has every variant

sections.name: Wordmark
sections.notes: Three colour versions (slate, blurple, white) with the light/dark background rule stated in a single line, plus a download for the logo kit. No mark-only version is offered, because the wordmark IS the identity.

sections.name: 'Powered by Stripe' badge
sections.notes: The co-branding layer, aimed at merchants: badge files plus the recommendation to hyperlink to stripe.com. This is the section doing the most work in the wild — it appears on thousands of checkouts.

sections.name: Press imagery
sections.notes: Photographs and short bios for ten-plus executives and board members, plus a Collison cofounder portrait, all downloadable. It is the newsroom's real payload.

sections.name: Legal
sections.notes: One paragraph pointing every asset at the Marks Usage Agreement — the page's only hard governance, deliberately kept off the visual layer.

sections.name: Downloads
sections.notes: Two ZIPs (logo kit, badge kit) and a media gallery; no Figma file, no tokens, no per-platform exports.

needs: Colour VALUES — 'slate' and 'blurple' are named but no hex, RGB, CMYK or Pantone appears anywhere, so a partner cannot match the wordmark's own colours
Clearspace and minimum-size diagrams for both the wordmark and the badge — the two assets most likely to be crushed into a checkout footer
Misuse examples shown, not implied: the wrong colours, the stretched wordmark, the badge on a busy background, captioned with the tell
Typography: Stripe's type system is one of the most imitated on the web and is entirely absent, even as a 'use your own type' instruction
A screenshot / product-imagery rule — press will illustrate stories with Dashboard UI, and nothing here says which states are approved
A version number and date, plus a named contact route for approvals beyond the legal agreement

principle.title: Name the audience in the URL, then give that audience only what it needs
principle.explanation: Stripe's page is short because it lives in the newsroom: journalists need portraits and a wordmark, integrators need a badge, and neither needs a type scale. Filing the asset page under the audience it serves prevents the two failure modes of brand pages — a press kit bloated into a half-guide, or a full guide gutted to protect secrets — because the scope question is answered before the first asset is chosen.
principle.howToApply: Split brand publishing by requester: a /press page (portraits, logo ZIP, boilerplate, one-line colour rule, legal link), a /brand or partner page (lockups, clearspace, colour values, co-brand geometry, misuse pairs), and an internal guide (strategy, voice, type, applications). Say at the top of each which one it is and where the other two live — and even in the shortest version, publish the hex values, because a colour with a name and no number cannot be reproduced.

entries.tagline: A homepage that argues its product's philosophy in plain sentences and near-zero imagery, and lets a custom typeface carry the entire brand.
entries.summary: Are.na sells a paid research tool with a page built almost entirely from left-aligned text: two framing sentences, five one-word steps, a short manifesto against ads and algorithms, real tag examples from members' collections, a plain statement about the size of the team and where the money comes from, and four principles headed 'The Secret'. There is no hero image, no dashboard screenshot, no gradient. The only styling gestures are the measure, the vertical rhythm and Areal, the custom typeface credited in the footer's colophon — the design equivalent of the product's own no-algorithm stance.
whatWorks: Dual positioning in two sentences: the literal ('software for saving and organizing content that is important to you') above the poetic ('a toolkit for assembling new worlds from the scraps of the old')
The process is five single words — Capture, Arrange, Search, Connect, Network — each with one line of explanation, which is faster to absorb than any diagram
Positioning by negation: an explicit 'no ads, no algorithms' block that tells you what the product refuses, not what it features
Real member tags used as the sample content ('spatial discontinuity', '1980s advertisements', 'early internet') — the taste of the community IS the product demo
Business-model transparency as trust: a five-person team, member-funded, with the subscriber count stated in the open (20,516 supporters)
A colophon crediting the custom typeface (Areal by Dinamo) — a one-line signal to exactly the audience it wants, doing the work a logo usually does

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Logo, two links (Sign up / Log in) and two sentences of positioning. No image and no product shot: the restraint filters the audience and matches a tool whose value is quiet, long-term collection.

sections.name: How it works
sections.notes: Five sequential single-word steps with one-line definitions. Because the words are the product's own vocabulary (blocks, channels, connections), reading the section teaches the interface's model before you sign up.

sections.name: No ads, no algorithms
sections.notes: A short manifesto block. This is the actual conversion argument for the target user — the section exists to be quoted, not skimmed.

sections.name: Search examples
sections.notes: A row of genuine, weird member tags standing in for screenshots. It shows what lives inside without a single UI frame, and self-selects people who find those tags appealing.

sections.name: Long-term / API
sections.notes: A plainly written note on the team's size and funding, then a developer section for the API. Together they read as durability: small, paid-for, extensible.

sections.name: The Secret + Editorial
sections.notes: Four philosophical principles, then a grid of Are.na Editorial articles — the page closes on the culture rather than a pricing table, with membership mentioned only in passing.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Dense but ordered columns (Discover, Product, Company, Support), apps, socials, legal — and the typeface colophon, which is the site's only self-conscious flourish.

principle.title: Let the sample content be your screenshot
principle.explanation: Interface screenshots show the container; the container is rarely the reason anyone joins. Showing the actual weird, specific things members have collected communicates the culture, the depth and the use case simultaneously, and it self-selects the audience — people who like the tags will like the tool, and people who don't will bounce before signing up, which is a feature for a paid product.
principle.howToApply: On the next product or listings page, replace at least one UI screenshot with a set of ten to twenty real specimens rendered as plain text at reading size — actual saved searches, actual neighbourhood names, actual client questions — chosen for character rather than coverage. Set them in the brand typeface, left-aligned, no cards, and let the specificity do the persuading.

site.name: Heymondo — 'You travel with insurance, not superpowers' wide digital unit

entries.category: Static digital unit (wide ~16:9, part of a 220-asset global set)
entries.tagline: A bulleted list of absurd travel risks set in acid green over an unretouched hostel photograph — insurance sold as comedy, not fear.
entries.when: Digital + film + static, France / Romania / UK, July 2026 — agency TURBO, photography Yosigo
entries.summary: The unit is a documentary-flat photograph of a chaotic hostel bunkroom with a traveller asleep mid-shoe, overlaid with a four-item checklist in the brand's acid green: 'snake bite / scorpion sting / extra life / Heymondo travel insurance', the third item's bullet drawn as an empty circle so you register that one is not covered. The tagline sits underneath in small caps. The brand logotype floats right at the same weight as the list. The insight (the Peltzman effect — people take more risks when they feel protected) is delivered as a joke rather than a warning.
whatWorks: Reframes the category away from fear: no accident imagery, no hospital, no worried faces — the risk is played for comedy so the brand becomes likeable at the moment of consideration
The list is the layout: four short lines with dot bullets create the hierarchy and the punchline order, no headline block needed
One filled/unfilled bullet does the argument — 'extra life' is the unchecked item, so the visual system carries the gag without extra copy
Type is set in the brand's single loud green at heavy weight over a mid-tone photo; the colour is the identity element and it never appears anywhere else in the frame
The photograph is deliberately unglamorous and unretouched (clutter on the floor, sagging bunks) — honest imagery makes the joke land as recognition, not as advertising
Built as a flexible global platform: the same construction survives translation across six European markets and 220 assets, because the mechanic is a list rather than a crafted sentence

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The photo reads as a real snapshot for a beat — cluttered floor, fluorescent light, someone asleep in their clothes — so it stops the scroll by not looking like an ad, then the green list detonates on top of it.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: A four-line checklist escalating from plausible (snake bite, scorpion sting) to impossible (extra life) to the product. The tagline 'You travel with insurance, not superpowers' is set small beneath, functioning as the caption to the joke rather than as the headline.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Documentary travel photography, natural light, no colour grade beyond what the room gave; teal curtains and warm wood already sit under the green type, and the type is placed across the darkest, least busy third on the left.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: No button — the brand logotype at right closes the unit. For a feed placement the platform's own CTA chrome carries the click, which is why the creative can spend its whole surface on the joke; a display placement would need a button added in the same green.

principle.title: Sell protection with a joke about the risk, not a picture of it
principle.explanation: Fear-based creative in insurance, security or real-estate categories triggers avoidance: people scroll past the thing they don't want to think about. Comedy about the same risk keeps attention on the frame long enough to name the product, and it flatters the audience by assuming they already know the risk — which is the actual state of a traveller who is already searching for cover.
principle.howToApply: Write the risk list literally, then push the last item past plausibility until it's funny, and let one visual device (an unchecked bullet, a struck-through line, a missing item) carry the punchline instead of a second sentence. Shoot or source honest, unstyled photography of the real situation, put the type in one brand colour that appears nowhere else in the frame, and keep the tagline small — the list is the headline.

entries.category: Constructive graphic design / German post-war modernism
entries.tagline: Made a career of drawing invisible processes — growth, connection, rotation — and turned the results into corporate marks like Deutsche Bank's slash-in-a-square.
entries.summary: Stankowski trained as a painter, worked as a photographer and advertising designer in Zürich, and after the war built Stankowski + Duschek in Stuttgart on a single idea he called constructive graphic art: that a mark or diagram should express a *process* rather than depict an object. He drew systematic series — permutations of a form under one rule — as free art, then drafted from those series when a client needed an identity, which is how the 1974 Deutsche Bank mark (a rising diagonal enclosed in a square, read as growth within a stable frame) came out of decades of studio experiments.
whatWorks: Name the invisible thing the brand does (growth, exchange, flow, connection) and draw that, instead of drawing what the company sells
Work in series: make twenty permutations of one form under a single rule, then choose — the range is the research, and it survives to become other projects
Keep the mark to a geometry a hand can redraw from memory — a diagonal, a square, a dot — so it holds at any size and in any medium
Refuse the art/design boundary: paintings and studies feed identity work, and identity constraints sharpen the paintings
Design the whole system, not the logo: signage, forms, print and colour rules shipped as one programme from the studio
Keep a personal archive of forms; the answer to a new brief is often an old study, already resolved

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: By converting the brief into a process word. Not 'a bank' but 'growth inside stability'; not 'a utility' but 'distribution'. The word becomes the drawing problem, which is why his marks tend to look like diagrams of behaviour rather than pictures of things.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Systematic variation. Fix one rule (rotate this element by 15°, halve the interval each step, mirror on one axis), then execute the whole series on a grid and judge the family together. The chosen mark is the strongest member of a set, not a one-off sketch.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Constructive reduction to two elements in tension — a moving form and a containing form — with flat colour and no illustrative detail. The Deutsche Bank mark is the canonical case: a slash for movement, a square for security, nothing else.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: A mark must be functional first: reproducible in one colour, redrawable, legible small, and expressive of the company's activity rather than of a designer's taste. He judged work by whether the underlying idea could be stated in a sentence and seen in the geometry.

principle.title: Draw the verb, not the noun
principle.explanation: Marks that depict what a company owns (a building, a key, a house) age badly and collide with every competitor in the category, because the noun is shared. A mark that encodes what the company *does* — grow, connect, move, protect — is unique to the business model and stays true through product changes, and it forces the geometry to stay simple because a process has to be legible as a relationship between two elements.
principle.howToApply: At the start of an identity or icon set, write the verb: 'we route', 'we verify', 'we hold'. Then run a real series — at least fifteen permutations under one stated rule — before choosing, and test the survivor at 16px, in one colour, and hand-drawn from memory. Keep the rejected variations in a studio file; the next brief in the same family usually already has its answer there.

entries.tagline: A design system whose brand job is the opposite of most: make hundreds of different agencies look unmistakably, verifiably governmental.
entries.summary: USWDS documents design principles, 40+ components, patterns, templates, utilities and a full design-token layer for federal websites, versioned in the open (currently 3.x) with v1/v2 archives and a migration guide. Its brand contribution is unusual and worth stealing: instead of protecting one organisation's mark, it standardises the *proof of identity* — the .gov banner with the flag, the 'official website of the United States government' language, and the HTTPS/lock explanation — so that trust is a component rather than a design decision. Agency-specific identity (each department's own seal, palette, typography) is left deliberately outside the system.
whatWorks: Trust is shipped as a component: the government banner, the flag icon, the 'Official websites use .gov' expandable copy — identical everywhere, so citizens learn one signal
Tokens are the brand layer — colour, typography, spacing, shadow, opacity and z-index are published as named tokens rather than as a swatch page
Theming is built into the token system, so an agency customises within a bounded palette rather than overriding CSS
Patterns are documented as whole user journeys (create a profile, complete a complex form, choose a language), not just components — guidance at the altitude where public services actually fail
Accessibility and Section 508 are structural, not an appendix: they appear inside each component's guidance and as a top-level page
Real governance: semantic versions, release notes, legacy docs for v1 and v2, and a published migration path for upgrading

sections.name: Design principles
sections.notes: A short set of principles ('start with real user needs', 'earn trust', 'embrace accessibility', 'promote continuity') that every later rule references. They function as the strategy layer a brand guide would open with.

sections.name: Design tokens
sections.notes: The system's foundation: colour, typography, spacing, shadow, opacity, z-index published as named tokens with a documented scale. This is where an agency's visual latitude is defined and bounded.

sections.name: Components
sections.notes: 40+ documented UI elements from buttons and inputs to date pickers, modals and identifier/footer blocks, each with usage guidance, accessibility notes and code. The identifier and banner components are the identity-bearing ones.

sections.name: Patterns
sections.notes: Journey-level guidance for common government tasks — complex forms, name and address entry, language selection — with the reasoning for each recommendation.

sections.name: Templates
sections.notes: Ready page-level layouts (landing, documentation, authentication, 404, forms) so a small agency team ships a compliant page without designing structure.

sections.name: Utilities
sections.notes: Utility classes for adapting layouts and prototyping quickly 'without touching a line of CSS' — the pragmatic escape hatch that keeps teams inside the system.

sections.name: Governance / releases
sections.notes: Version 3.x with release notes, archived v1 and v2 documentation, and a dedicated migration guide — a living system with a stated upgrade route.

needs: An explicit identity layer for the thing it standardises: the banner and identifier are components, but there is no page explaining the *brand* logic of federal trust signals as a system others could extend
Verbal identity — voice and tone with do/don't rewrites; government copy is the highest-stakes writing in the system and lives in a separate plain-language handbook
Logo and seal guidance for agencies (clearspace, minimum size, how a departmental seal co-exists with the .gov banner) — currently every agency invents this
Photography and illustration art direction, so agency sites stop reaching for stock imagery that undermines the trust the banner just established
Motion principles for the interactive components (accordion, modal, in-page navigation), including reduced-motion behaviour
A worked co-branding example for the very common case of two agencies or an agency plus a contractor appearing on one page

principle.title: Turn your trust signal into a component nobody may redesign
principle.explanation: Citizens learn to recognise legitimacy from a repeated visual pattern, not from individual sites' craft. By fixing the banner, its language and its security explanation as an unmodifiable component while leaving each agency's own look flexible, USWDS makes trust portable across hundreds of independently built sites — and removes the temptation for a designer to make the one element whose value is its sameness look 'better'.
principle.howToApply: Identify the element on your product or client sites whose whole job is recognisability — licence and disclosure block, agent identity, brokerage lockup, security/compliance strip — and ship it as one locked component with fixed copy, fixed spacing and no theming hooks. Document what may vary around it, and put the reasoning next to the lock so teams stop trying to restyle it.

entries.tagline: A homepage that refuses to sell anything: one line, two doors, and a footer — the audience router as a design decision.
entries.summary: Herman Miller's front page is three elements tall. The logo, the sentence 'Designed for everybody' set as the only heading, and two equal blocks — 'Shop for home' and 'Plan for workplaces' — each a room photograph over a short question that identifies the visitor to themselves ('Are you shopping for your own home?' / 'Are you a designer or architect specifying for a workplace?'). Then the footer, and the 'Part of the MillerKnoll collective' bar. For a brand with sixty years of icons to flash, choosing to route rather than merchandise is the whole idea: the two audiences need completely different sites, so the homepage's job is to send you to the right one before a single price appears.
whatWorks: One heading, no subhead, no hero carousel — 'Designed for everybody' is both the brand line and the justification for the split that follows
The two doors are given exactly equal visual weight (same image size, same type, same arrow link), so neither audience is treated as the secondary one
Each door is labelled by the visitor's own task and verified with a question — 'Shop' vs 'Plan' is the actual difference between a consumer and a specifier
Photography does the qualifying: a lived-in room with Eames, Nelson and Noguchi pieces on one side; a real workplace floorplate with Sayl/Cosm chairs and monitors on the other
Set in the brand's own grotesque with tight, dark headings on plain white — the interiors supply every colour on the page
Zero promotional furniture: no email capture, no banner, no 'new arrivals'; the page ends after it has done its one job

sections.name: Header
sections.notes: Just the red-dot Herman Miller mark, top left. No global nav, no search, no cart — the page deliberately cannot be browsed, only chosen from.

sections.name: Statement
sections.notes: 'Designed for everybody' at heading scale, left aligned, in near-black. It reads as brand philosophy and simultaneously licenses the two-audience split beneath it.

sections.name: Door 1 — Shop for home
sections.notes: A styled but plausible living room: leather sofa, yellow moulded chair, pleated Nelson pendant, art on the wall. Caption is a question, then one sentence promising 'everything you need—from living spaces to home offices'. The arrow link is the only affordance.

sections.name: Door 2 — Plan for workplaces
sections.notes: An office floor shot with height-adjustable desks and task chairs. Its sentence promises product models and a materials library — the specifier's vocabulary, which is how the door filters correctly without saying 'trade'.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Region selector, copyright, and a tight row of legal/accessibility links, then a full-width 'Part of the MillerKnoll collective' bar — corporate structure disclosed at the bottom rather than confusing the split above.

principle.title: When two audiences need different sites, make the homepage a router — and give both doors equal weight
principle.explanation: Trying to serve a consumer and a professional on one merchandised homepage produces a page that half-serves both: the specifier scrolls past sale pricing, the shopper scrolls past spec sheets. A two-door page costs one extra click and buys a correctly segmented journey — and equal treatment of the doors is what keeps the professional audience from feeling like an afterthought, which matters most when they place the largest orders.
principle.howToApply: For a site with genuinely split audiences (buyers vs sellers, residents vs investors, consumers vs agents), build a routing page: one brand sentence, two or three equal blocks, each with a real photograph of that audience's context, a label naming their task as a verb, and a question they can answer 'yes' to. Ban every other module from the page — no offers, no email capture — and let the destination sites carry the merchandising.

entries.category: Static social feed unit (4:5, 2160×2700) — self-initiated concept
entries.tagline: One absent-minded mistake per frame, staged as a 3D miniature on flat brand red, with Arabic lettering as the only headline.
entries.when: Self-initiated / student concept for the Egyptian market, published August 2026 — creative direction and design by Mohamed Abd El-Aziz
entries.summary: A five-unit set where each frame shows a single lapse of concentration — throwing the phone in the bin instead of the paper, ironing inside the washing machine, the remote in the fridge — built as a CG miniature diorama on saturated NESCAFÉ red, shot from a high three-quarter angle. The type is a two-line piece of Arabic brush lettering ('Need focus, need NESCAFÉ') in white, and the only other elements are the logo top-left and a red mug bottom-right. It's a spec/self-initiated concept rather than a bought placement, but as a unit it is a clean lesson in single-idea construction: one behaviour, one colour field, one line, one product cue.
whatWorks: One frame, one mistake: the set varies the situation and never the layout, so a scroller who sees two of them recognises the mechanic instantly
Flat brand red as the entire environment — no location, no background detail — makes a busy 3D scene read as a single silhouette in feed
The figure is posed mid-error with the wrong object leaving the hand, so the story resolves without a caption
Headline is hand-lettered in the market's own script and sized to a compact two-line block, treated as a graphic mass rather than a line of copy
Product cue is one spilling mug in the bottom corner at small scale — present but not competing with the gag
4:5 portrait with the action stacked centre-frame and generous top margin, so the platform's own copy and CTA chrome never crop the joke

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The wrong-object gesture: a hand about to drop a phone into the wastebasket. It reads at thumbnail size because the two objects are silhouetted against flat red with nothing else in the frame.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: Two lines of brush-lettered Arabic — 'Need focus' / 'Need NESCAFÉ' — locked as one block at upper right, white on red. Because it's lettering rather than a typeface, it carries warmth and a hand-made cadence that a corporate grotesque wouldn't.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: CG miniature diorama: desk, chair, laptop, bin, all in a pale palette so the red field and the white shirt dominate. High camera angle, hard shadows, exaggerated hand reaching toward the lens for depth — a poster construction, not a product shot.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: None in the creative; the mug and the logo are the only brand furniture. The set was designed to run in feed and on mall digital screens, where the environment supplies context — an honest limitation of a concept piece rather than a performance unit.

principle.title: Fix the layout, vary only the incident
principle.explanation: A set of ads whose composition, colour field, type block and product cue never move turns repetition into recognition: each new frame costs the viewer no decoding effort and adds one more piece of evidence for the same idea. It also makes production scalable and briefable — the only creative question per unit becomes 'what is the incident?', which is the part an audience actually finds funny or true.
principle.howToApply: Build a template with the four fixed slots (ground colour, subject position, headline block, product cue), then write ten incidents on one line each and produce the best five without touching the template. In a listings or brokerage context the incident is the specific detail — the odd staircase, the wrong-sized fridge, the 3am price drop — and the frame around it never changes.

entries.tagline: Built a lifetime practice on hand-lettering and a personal archive of European ephemera — and deliberately kept the studio small enough to draw everything herself.
entries.summary: Fili art-directed Pantheon Books for eleven years, producing around two thousand jackets that broke American publishing's habit of photographic covers by putting drawn letterforms first. Since 1989 her own studio has specialised in food, restaurant and packaging identities — the work most people know without knowing the name. Her method is unusually documentable: she collects European (mostly Italian) signage, packaging and menus obsessively, sketches letterforms by hand before any software, and works from a narrow, historically informed palette. She has also co-authored a shelf of books with Steven Heller that are effectively her research published as reference.
whatWorks: Keep a personal reference archive organised by letterform and period, not by project — the archive, not the brief, is where solutions come from
Draw the words first: the identity is a piece of lettering, so type selection never becomes the whole design decision
Design custom letterforms per project instead of licensing a display face, so the mark cannot be copied by buying a font
Constrain the palette to a handful of historically coherent colours and hold it across every touchpoint (menu, tin, awning, bag)
Publish the research: turning the archive into books makes the influences legible and brings in clients who want exactly that
Stay small on purpose — a two-to-three person studio keeps the principal's hand on every drawn curve

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: In the archive and on paper. She looks for period and place first — which decade, which country, which trade the piece should feel like it came from — then pulls physical references and starts drawing letters, before any layout or software decision.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Lettering-led identity: the name is drawn, refined through many pencil passes, then vectorised and tuned. Everything else (palette, ornament, secondary type, packaging) is derived from the letterforms rather than chosen alongside them.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: European vernacular filtered rather than copied — Art Deco and early-20th-century Italian signage cues, subtle borders and ornament, tight and elegant spacing, one restrained accent colour. The result reads authentically old without being pastiche because it is drawn fresh at the correct proportions.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Elegance and appetite over novelty; a food identity must make you hungry and must survive being printed on a paper bag. She judges work by whether the letterforms could plausibly have existed in the period they evoke, and rejects anything that depends on a trend to look good.

principle.title: Build a reference archive, then draw from it — never search for style at the start of a project
principle.explanation: Searching for a look mid-brief produces whatever the internet is currently promoting, which is why so much work converges. A curated personal archive collected over years is a competitive asset: it is unique to you, it is organised by the thing you actually need (letterform, period, colour pairing), and it lets a project begin with a specific historical reference rather than a mood board of other people's finished work.
principle.howToApply: Start a filed archive of photographed lettering, signage, packaging and print — sorted by letterform type and period, not by client — and add to it weekly. On the next identity or campaign, choose the period and place before the layout, pull three physical references, and hand-draw the wordmark on paper first; let the palette, ornament and secondary type be derived from that drawing rather than chosen in parallel.

site.name: Python Software Foundation — The Python Logo

entries.tagline: One of the world's most-used logos is governed by a single page of prose, a pile of file formats, and an invitation to 'ask first'.
entries.summary: The PSF's logo page is a permissive, deliberately non-designed artifact: it states that projects and companies are *encouraged* to use the logo to indicate they work with Python, permits the two-snakes device alone on the same terms as the combined lockup, lists every available file format (PNG, flattened PNG, Photoshop, three SVG variants, a 269×326 device-only PNG), documents the 'Python Powered' logo in wide and tall forms at named pixel sizes (200×80, 140×56, 100×40, 70×28 / 140×182, 100×130, 70×91), admits the logo font is 'Flux Regular' which it owns but cannot redistribute, and routes everything contestable to the PSF Trademark Usage Policy. Its governing sentence is the opposite of most brand pages: 'we want the logo to be used as widely as possible'.
whatWorks: The intent is stated before the rules: wide adoption is the goal, so the page reads as an invitation rather than a warning — correct for an open-source ecosystem
The lockup and the mark-only device are explicitly granted the same permissions, removing the most common real-world question in one sentence
Formats are exhaustive and honest, including the editable Photoshop file and multiple SVG exports (generic vs Inkscape-specific) rather than one 'official' asset
The 'Python Powered' badge is published at named pixel sizes, which is the practical substitute for a minimum-size rule in a web-first ecosystem
The type is disclosed with its licensing constraint ('the PSF owns a copy but we cannot distribute it'), which is more useful than silence
Escalation is human and low-friction: derived versions and edge cases are covered by 'please ask first' plus a link to the trademark policy

sections.name: The Python logo
sections.notes: The combined logo and the two-snakes device shown at small scale, with the permission statement and the format list beneath. The whole visual specification of the identity lives in these two images.

sections.name: Logo files
sections.notes: Seven download links covering PNG, flattened PNG, PSD and three SVG variants plus a device-only PNG at a stated pixel size — the page's most substantial contribution.

sections.name: The Python Powered logo
sections.notes: The community badge in wide and tall lockups, each offered at four fixed pixel sizes plus SVG. Fixed sizes act as de-facto minimum-size governance.

sections.name: Guidelines for use
sections.notes: Three short paragraphs: the logo is a PSF trademark, the PSF defends it against damaging or confusing use, adoption is encouraged, and derived versions require asking first — with a link to the formal Trademark Usage Policy.

sections.name: T-shirts and merchandise
sections.notes: Merch is explicitly allowed for personal use, with permission required for selling — the single most common community question, answered in two sentences.

needs: Colour values: the yellow and blue are the most recognisable part of the identity and no hex, RGB, CMYK or Pantone appears anywhere on the page
Clearspace and minimum-size diagrams for the primary lockup (only the badge gets sizes, by accident of being offered at fixed dimensions)
Misuse examples shown side by side — recoloured snakes, stretched lockup, device on a busy photograph — captioned with the tell, in the style of WordPress's 'fauxgo' section
A dark-background version and a rule for which asset to use on dark surfaces; nothing here addresses inverse use
A substitute-typeface instruction: since Flux Regular cannot be distributed, the page should name what to set adjacent wordmarks in
Version, date and owner — the page reads as static and undated, while the trademark policy it depends on lives elsewhere and evolves

principle.title: State the permission posture in the first paragraph
principle.explanation: Most usage pages open with prohibition and leave the reader guessing whether their honest, well-meant use is allowed — so they either don't use the mark or use it wrongly and quietly. Declaring the posture up front ('we want this used as widely as possible, here is the line') turns the page into a decision tool: the reader knows within one sentence whether they are inside the intended use, and only edge cases consume anyone's time.
