principle.howToApply: Open any brand-assets or partner page with one sentence naming who the assets are FOR and what outcome you want (wide co-branding, strict protection, credit only), then the two or three hard limits, then the files. Grant the obvious cases explicitly — mark-only use, credit lines, personal merch, linking — so the inbox only receives the genuinely ambiguous requests, and pair it with a named human route for those.

entries.tagline: Sells a sale from a navy panel next to a real photograph, then closes the page with five sentences about responsibility instead of a promo block.
entries.summary: The page is honest about being a shop and unembarrassed about being an argument. The hero is a split: a genuine expedition photograph on the left (a rider on a glacial shoreline, with a photo-credit button on the image) and a flat navy panel on the right carrying 'Need Clothes?' plus four sale pills. Beneath it, category carousels use in-situ athlete photography instead of studio product shots, a full-bleed 'Let it go' band promotes Worn Wear trade-in *before* any new-product push, stories follow, and the page ends on five plain promises — guarantee, footprint, grassroots activism, gear kept in play, profits to the planet — each linking to the programme that backs it. Commerce comes first in sequence; the values row is what you leave on.
whatWorks: Hero split of photograph + flat colour panel: the photo never has type burned into it, so imagery stays honest and the offer stays legible
Every image carries a photo-credit affordance (a small camera button) — the brand treats photography as authored work, which is itself a trust signal
Category tiles are shot in the field with the product being used at distance, not on a model against seamless; you're buying the activity
Resale is merchandised like a product ('Let it go — trade in your used Patagonia gear for credit', one white pill CTA on a full-bleed image) rather than buried in the footer
The closing row is five one-sentence commitments, each an explicit link to proof (Ironclad Guarantee, Our Footprint, Action Works, Worn Wear, profit commitment) — claims with receipts
Sale is handled with restraint: a small top ribbon, one hero panel, and one red 'Sale' nav item, with no countdowns or percentage badges on tiles

sections.name: Utility bar + nav
sections.notes: Activism, Stories and Worn Wear sit to the LEFT of the logo in the utility row — before commerce navigation — while the main nav is a plain category list with only 'Sale' in red. Ordering is the argument.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Left: full-bleed documentary photograph with a photo-credit button. Right: flat navy panel with 'Need Clothes?' at display scale, one line of terms, and four outlined pills for Men's / Women's / Kids' & Baby / Packs & Gear. Two audiences of shopper routed in one screen.

sections.name: Category carousel
sections.notes: New Arrivals, Daypacks, Rainwear, Capilene tees, Kids' — each tile a landscape action photograph with a plain bold label and two or three sub-links, arrow-advanced. No prices, no badges.

sections.name: Worn Wear band
sections.notes: Full-bleed image of a trail runner mid-scree with 'Let it go.' in white and a single 'Get Started' pill. Placing the resale programme at mid-page, at hero scale, is the most quietly radical layout decision on the site.

sections.name: Latest Stories
sections.notes: A row of editorial cards (film and long-form) with the same photographic treatment as commerce tiles, so content and product read as one publication rather than a blog bolted on.

sections.name: Five commitments
sections.notes: 'We guarantee everything we make. / We take responsibility for our impact. / We support grassroots activism. / We keep your gear in play. / We give our profits to the planet.' Each is a link. This replaces the conventional newsletter-and-promo footer stack.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Newsletter signup with an explicit privacy and financial-incentive notice, a Need Help column that leads with repair and trade-in, then dense company links including the Progress Report and climate risk disclosures.

principle.title: Put the offer on a colour panel beside the photograph, never on top of it
principle.explanation: Burning promotional type into a photograph forces you to grade, darken or scrim the image until it stops being a real picture, and it guarantees the crop breaks on mobile. A split of full-bleed image and flat brand panel keeps the photography honest and authored, gives the offer perfect contrast at any size, and lets the two halves be re-ordered or stacked responsively without re-exporting art.
principle.howToApply: Build hero and campaign bands as a two-cell layout: one cell is an uncropped photograph credited to its photographer, the other a flat brand colour holding the headline, one line of terms and the CTAs as outlined pills. Keep every promotional word inside the panel, keep type off the image entirely, and reserve full-bleed image-with-type for a single mid-page band where the message is three words or fewer.

site.name: Thank You Farmer — 'Sun Cover' wide digital unit

entries.category: Static digital unit (wide ~16:9, also run in print)
entries.tagline: A car under a white cover in an empty summer car park, captioned in two half-sentences that meet across the frame.
entries.when: Digital + print, Greece, July 2026 — agency 'maybe,', photography Iason Pachos
entries.summary: One photograph, shot flat and dry in real Mediterranean midday light: a sedan wrapped in a white cover in an empty parking lot, mountains behind, fence and cranes in the distance. The copy is split — 'We protect' floats at the left edge of the car, 'what we want to last.' at the right — so reading the line requires crossing the whole image, which is also how long it takes to notice the cover is doing sunscreen's job. The product (an SPF 50+ sun stick) sits bottom-left at thumbnail scale with three lines of name, and the wordmark closes bottom-right. The insight is stated in the campaign notes and never in the ad: you already cover your car; your skin gets the same sun every day.
whatWorks: The analogy is a found behaviour, not an invented metaphor — covering a parked car is a real habit in hot countries, so the ad feels observed rather than concocted
Copy split across the frame turns reading into looking; the two fragments only resolve as a sentence once your eye has travelled the length of the car
Type is small, white, unstyled and placed on the pale sky/asphalt boundary — no scrim, no box, no drop shadow
Real location photography with the ugly bits left in (chain-link fence, shipping containers, faded parking lines) buys the credibility the idea needs
The product appears once, tiny, with the actual SKU name and 'SPF 50+' in the only saturated colour in the frame (a red accent), so the offer is unmistakable without competing
Wide 16:9 crop with the subject dead centre and empty margins — the composition survives being letterboxed into a banner or cropped to 4:5

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The white shrouded car in an otherwise empty lot: a familiar object made slightly strange. It works because the shape is ambiguous for a half-second before it resolves as a covered car.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'We protect … what we want to last.' Split across the image, set in a plain light sans at maybe 2% of frame height. The restraint implies confidence and forces engagement; the line also does double duty as a brand statement about preservation rather than sunburn.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Documentary-flat colour photography — hard overhead sun, pale blue sky, bleached asphalt, no grade or glamour. The whiteness of the cover is the only bright value in the frame, which is what pulls the eye to the centre.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: None; the unit closes on a product thumbnail with its name and SPF, plus the wordmark. For a performance placement it would need a button, but the product lockup functions as the recognition cue in a category where the pack is the CTA.

principle.title: Find an existing behaviour that already proves your point, then just photograph it
principle.explanation: Invented metaphors have to be explained; observed behaviours only have to be pointed at. Using a habit the audience already performs (covering the car, double-locking the door, checking the school district) makes the argument feel like recognition rather than persuasion — and it lets the creative be a single honest photograph, which is cheaper to produce and far harder to disbelieve than a constructed illustration.
principle.howToApply: Before art-directing, list the protective or preparatory habits your audience already has in the situation you're selling into, and pick the one that is visually specific. Shoot it in real light, on a real location, with the unflattering context left in; split a short line of copy across the frame so reading it takes the eye across the evidence, and keep the product to a corner thumbnail carrying the one spec that matters.

entries.tagline: Turned a paper company's promotional magazine into a 61-issue laboratory, designing with the printing process itself as his medium.
entries.summary: Thompson designed Westvaco Inspirations for Printers from 1939 to 1962 — a free magazine sent to printers and designers that existed to show what paper and presses could do, and which he used as an open-ended experiment in colour separation, overprinting and type-as-image. His most famous move was to build spreads from engravings and process plates the printer already owned, re-inking and re-registering them into new images; his most radical was Alphabet 26, a proposal for a single unified alphabet that replaced the dual upper/lowercase system. He later art-directed for major magazines, taught at Yale for decades, and designed the Washburn College Bible with line breaks set to speech phrasing.
whatWorks: Get yourself a recurring vehicle with a real audience and use it to experiment — a house publication beats a portfolio because it has a deadline and a print run
Design with the production process as material: separations, overprints, misregistration and screens become the visual idea rather than defects
Mine existing assets — old engravings, stock plates, previously used art — and recompose them instead of commissioning new imagery
Let type be the picture: enormous letterforms, cropped characters and colour-separated words carry the page where an illustration would normally sit
Test the alphabet's rules themselves (Alphabet 26) — sometimes the deepest craft question is the convention, not the layout
Set line breaks for the reading voice, not for the measure — the Washburn Bible breaks lines on phrases, which is a typographic decision about speech

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: From the manufacturing constraint outward: which papers, how many inks, which plates exist, what the press can hold in register. The brief for Inspirations was literally 'demonstrate the material', so the medium was always the starting subject.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Systematic experiment inside a fixed format. Each issue tackled one idea — a colour-separation trick, a scale contrast, an alphabet study — executed with the printer's real constraints, so every experiment was also a usable specimen for the sales rep who delivered it.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Re-using and re-registering existing engravings and process plates, deliberately shifting the separations to make new colour images; combined with type at poster scale, tightly cropped, integrated into the artwork rather than sitting above it.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Clarity is the point of the experiment, not the casualty of it: a spread has to be legible and printable at scale. He judged typography by how it reads aloud and how it survives the press, and he treated design education and practice as the same activity.

principle.title: Make the production constraint the creative material
principle.explanation: Constraints from the medium — ink limits, register tolerance, compression artefacts, email-client CSS, ad-unit weight caps — are usually treated as taxes to be minimised. Designing *with* them produces work that could not have been made another way and that is guaranteed to survive production, because the effect and the limitation are the same thing. It also gives a series its identity: the constraint is the family resemblance.
principle.howToApply: On the next constrained deliverable, write the limit down as an ingredient and build the idea from it: a 150KB banner becomes a two-colour flat-vector unit, a 1x email header becomes a type-only lockup, a compression-heavy platform becomes an excuse for hard-edged flat colour. Then run a short series of experiments inside one fixed format — same size, same grid, one variable per piece — and publish them, so the experiments accumulate into a recognisable body of work.

entries.category: Licensee brand guide (thousands of independent organisers)
entries.tagline: A guide written for volunteers who will build their own logo tonight — so it ships a generator, one mandatory typeface, and a hex value.
entries.summary: TEDx has to keep tens of thousands of independently organised events recognisable as TED without any of them having a designer. The guide answers that by making the logo constructible: 'TEDx + your unique event name + when applicable, the event type modifier', Helvetica mandatory with Inter Light as the open-source substitute, tracking locked at 0 (kerning allowed), TEDx always red at #EB0028 / Pantone 185, location name only black or white, backgrounds only solid white or black, event name left-aligned and matched to the height of 'TEDx', maximum four lines at roughly 22 characters, modifiers (Women, Youth, Salon, Studio) in bold — plus a hosted Logo Generator that outputs the correct file, and .eps templates for print. The 2023 revision is versioned by licence date: new events must follow it, pre-2023 events may keep their old logo.
whatWorks: The rules are all decidable numbers or binaries — one hex, one Pantone, tracking 0, four lines max, ~22 characters, two permitted background colours — so a volunteer cannot 'interpret' them
It ships a tool, not just a spec: the Logo Generator builds the lockup from the licensed event name, which removes the single biggest source of drift
The typeface problem is solved twice — Helvetica ('comes pre-installed on most computers') with Inter Light named as the open-source fallback, so nobody substitutes Arial by default
Naming is governed with the logo, because for TEDx the name IS the lockup: single-word locations set solid (TEDxBoston), multi-word locations break to lines with spaces

Prohibitions are concrete and cover the actual failure modes: never 'TEDx' or 'TED' alone, never all-caps or equal-size location names, never recolour the red or the x, never place on colour, photographic or patterned backgrounds

Governance by licence generation — 'mandatory for events licensed from 1 January 2023, optional for earlier ones' — which is how you version a rule across a volunteer network without invalidating existing assets

sections.name: Lockup construction
sections.notes: The anatomy: TEDx + event name (+ optional modifier). Rules for one-word vs multi-word locations, line breaks, four-line maximum and the ~22-character measure, with the event name left-aligned and cap-height matched to 'TEDx'.

sections.name: Typeface
sections.notes: Helvetica required ('an integral part of our visual identity'), Regular weight for Neue-family users, Inter Light as the open-source alternative, tracking fixed at 0 with individual kerning permitted.

sections.name: Colour
sections.notes: TEDx always red — #EB0028, Pantone 185 — with spot colour preferred in print and 4-colour process accepted; location name only black or white; backgrounds only solid white or black.

sections.name: Clear space & placement
sections.notes: A required buffer around the whole lockup that no other graphic or logo may enter, stated in prose rather than as a measured diagram.

sections.name: The Logo Generator
sections.notes: A hosted tool that takes the licensed event name and modifiers and returns a correctly constructed PNG in Inter; .eps templates are provided via Dropbox for high-resolution and print adaptation.

sections.name: Prohibitions
sections.notes: An explicit never-list: no TEDx or TED alone, no all-caps or equal-sized event names, no colour changes to the red or the x, no other typefaces, no logos on colour/photo/pattern grounds, no unnecessary multi-line layouts.

sections.name: Version & tagline change
sections.notes: Guidelines mandatory for events licensed on or after 1 January 2023; the old 'x = independently organized TED event' tagline is no longer required in the logo.

needs: Measured clearspace and minimum-size diagrams — the buffer is described in words while every other rule is a number, which is the one gap a volunteer will fill by guessing

A dark-mode / photographic-background solution: banning photo backgrounds is realistic for the logo but leaves organisers with no sanctioned lockup for the poster they will inevitably make over an image
A secondary palette and type scale for everything that is NOT the logo — signage, slides, tickets, social — so the surrounding design has rules rather than only prohibitions
Worked co-branding geometry for local sponsors, the most common organiser problem after the logo itself
Accessibility guidance: #EB0028 on white and on black both need stated contrast behaviour at title and body sizes
A visible version number and changelog on the page itself, rather than versioning implicitly by licence date

principle.title: If non-designers must build the asset, ship a generator — not a spec
principle.explanation: Every rule you write is a chance for a volunteer to improvise. A tool that takes their inputs and emits the correct artwork converts an entire class of judgement calls into a form field, which is why TEDx logos are consistent across tens of thousands of events run by people who have never opened Illustrator. The written spec then only has to serve the rare high-resolution or print case.
principle.howToApply: Wherever the same lockup or template will be assembled repeatedly by people outside the design team (agent cards, listing banners, event or office sub-brands), build the smallest possible generator — a form or a Figma template with locked layers that outputs correct PNG/SVG — and reserve the written guidance for the print exceptions. Pair it with a hard never-list aimed at the four or five ways it will actually be broken.

entries.tagline: Black, white and one acid yellow, with live counters instead of adjectives — the whole page argues in numbers.
entries.summary: Ramp's homepage is a very long proof stack held together by extreme colour discipline: near-black type on white, product UI in greyscale, and a single acid yellow reserved for primary buttons and nothing else. The hero is four words ('Time is money. Save both.'), one clarifying line, and an inline email field where a hero image would normally go; above it a live ticker states the share of US corporate payments processed by Ramp, and below the hero a second strip counts what its agents did today (receipts processed, accounting fields coded, expenses reviewed, invoices processed). Every section after that is a claim attached to a figure — 70,000 customers growing 3.2x faster than average, 27M hours saved, 75% faster close, a Notion tile reading '$1M+ saved on global spend' — before the page finally lands on three plain pricing tiers and an implementation checklist.
whatWorks: One accent colour, used only for the primary action: with black/white/grey everywhere else, the yellow button is unmissable without any size or motion trick
Live counters instead of adjectives — a running percentage of US corporate payments and a real-time 'agents at work today' strip make scale feel observed rather than claimed
The hero's conversion element replaces the hero image: email field plus 'Get started for free' inline, so the first screen is a form, not a poster
Product UI is shown as overlapping real panels (invoice, bill details, approvals, a physical card) rather than one flat screenshot — it reads as a working system mid-task
Logo grid earns its place by including one tile that is a case study (Notion, '$1M+ saved on global spend') so proof-of-logo becomes proof-of-outcome
Every product section names the mechanism, not the benefit — OCR extraction, policy enforcement, contract parsing, ERP sync — which is what a finance buyer needs to evaluate
Type is a single tight grotesque at two or three sizes; hierarchy comes from weight and colour (black statement + grey continuation on the same line), never from a second typeface

sections.name: Announcement + nav
sections.notes: A thin dark bar carrying one genuinely new thing ('AI Token Spend Management') with a 'Learn more' link, then a plain nav with two CTAs — outlined 'See a demo' and yellow 'Get started' — establishing the colour rule in the first 60px.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: A small all-caps kicker holding the live payments-processed figure, then 'Time is money. Save both.' at display scale, one line of product scope ('Cards, expenses, bill payments, and banking – in the blink of AI'), and the inline email + yellow button. No hero art above the fold except the form.

sections.name: Product collage + agent ticker
sections.notes: Overlapping greyscale UI panels and a black card, overlaid by a live ticker of today's agent activity with six counters. It answers 'what is it' and 'is it real' in one band.

sections.name: Customer proof
sections.notes: 'Join 70,000 of the world's most ambitious companies growing 3.2x faster than the average American business' with a Read-the-report link, then a bordered logo grid (Visa, Stripe, Perplexity, Anduril, CBRE, Discord, Twilio, Webflow, Glossier, Shopify) where one cell is a photographed customer story with a dollar figure.

sections.name: Platform / product run
sections.notes: 'One platform for all of finance. Agents for every workflow, working 24/7.' followed by eight product sections in order — cards, expenses, AP, travel, procurement, Ramp Intelligence, accounting automation, banking — each with its mechanism and a metric.

sections.name: Outcome metrics + case studies
sections.notes: 27M+ hours saved, 75% faster close, 3x more efficient intake-to-pay, a 30-day implementation guarantee, then named customers with specific savings (Poshmark's 50% faster month-end close, Advisor360°'s $80K+).

sections.name: Pricing + implementation
sections.notes: Three tiers stated plainly (Free $0, Plus $15/user, Enterprise custom), 200+ integrations, and an administrator setup checklist — unusually, the page teaches the switch before asking for it.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Dense but ordered: products, solutions, resources, customers, legal, plus Docs / Help Center / Trust Center links that were also surfaced at the very top for evaluators.

principle.title: Spend your only saturated colour on the action, and let live numbers do the adjectives
principle.explanation: A monochrome page with one reserved accent removes the need for badges, glows or size escalation to signal the primary action — attention goes where the colour is, every time. And a counter that moves converts a marketing claim into an observation: the reader isn't asked to believe 'we process a lot', they watch it happen, which is far harder to discount than a superlative.
principle.howToApply: Pick one accent and forbid it everywhere except primary buttons and one kicker; build every other element from near-black, grey and white so product screenshots sit in the palette naturally. Then replace at least two adjectives on the page with a live or dated figure — properties listed this week, average days on market, closings this month — displayed as a small all-caps kicker above the headline rather than in a stat card.

site.name: Gozo — 'Routes of Reverence' 4:5 festive social unit

entries.category: Static social feed unit (4:5, 1080×1350), 3-part festive series
entries.tagline: City road geometry redrawn as a Durga Puja symbol, with a single car as the moving dot — a mobility brand whose map becomes the icon.
entries.when: Digital, India, September 2025 — agency Three Fourth Solutions
entries.summary: Each unit in this three-part set takes the visual language of a navigation map — white route lines, black cross-streets, a car glyph, a circular waypoint — and bends it into an icon associated with a specific day of Durga Puja; in this frame the routes trace a ceremonial mace/weapon form, with the car sitting at the base of it as though it drew the shape. The field is a single flat festive orange with a woven-texture fill, edged by a narrow lotus-motif border; the wordmark sits top-right and a two-part headline ('This Ashtami / Courage, devotion, and joy guide you.') anchors the lower left in a warm display serif above a plain sans line. It is a clean lesson in making a brand's own functional vocabulary do the festive work instead of dropping in generic celebration graphics.
whatWorks: The metaphor is built from the product's own UI vocabulary — route lines, waypoint circles, a car glyph — so the greeting is unmistakably from a mobility brand
One flat culturally coded colour field with a subtle woven texture keeps the frame readable at thumbnail size while avoiding the flat-vector sterility of most festive posts
A thin lotus-motif border does all the 'festival' signalling, leaving the centre free for the idea (far better than gold gradients and diyas over everything)
Typographic pairing carries the tone shift: a warm high-contrast display serif for the occasion name, a neutral sans for the wish — two voices, two jobs
Composition is diagonal and off-centre with real empty space, so the eye travels the route lines from the car up to the symbol before reading the copy
The series varies only the symbol and the day name, which makes a multi-day festival calendar producible without a new concept each time

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The recognisable map abstraction on a saturated orange field stops the scroll, and then the second read — that the roads form a ceremonial symbol — is the reward. Two-stage recognition inside one static frame.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'This Ashtami' in a display serif with 'Courage, devotion, and joy guide you.' beneath in sans. The word 'guide' is the hinge that ties a devotional wish to a navigation product without a sales line.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Flat festive orange with woven texture, white route strokes with rounded caps, thin black cross-streets, one small white car in plan view, circular waypoints. Lotus border framing. No photography, no gradient, no drop shadows.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: None inside the creative — brand mark only. Correct for a festive-greeting placement where the goal is affinity; the platform copy field carries any offer, and the unit stays a greeting rather than a promotion.

principle.title: Make festive and seasonal posts from your own functional vocabulary
principle.explanation: Seasonal creative is where brands lose their identity fastest: everyone reaches for the same stock symbols and the post could belong to any company. Constructing the seasonal image out of the elements your product already owns — routes, pins, floor plans, keys, price graphs, contract lines — means the greeting still performs brand recognition while it performs the sentiment, and it forces a real idea instead of decoration.
principle.howToApply: List the graphic primitives your product genuinely owns (map routes and pins, floorplan walls, key silhouettes, chart lines, signature lines). For the next holiday or milestone post, draw the occasion's symbol using only those primitives on one flat culturally appropriate colour, signal the occasion with a narrow motif border rather than an overlay, and pair a display serif occasion name with a plain sans wish — then vary only the symbol across the series.

entries.when: Founded 1957 (as Brownjohn, Chermayeff & Geismar); Chermayeff & Geismar & Haviv since 2013 · New York
entries.tagline: Six decades of marks that are still in service — Chase, Mobil, NBC, National Geographic, PBS — produced by a studio that deliberately never grew.
entries.summary: The studio's operating model is the lesson: a tiny partnership where the principals do the drawing, no account layer, no house style, and one obsessive standard — a mark must be simple, appropriate and distinctive enough to survive fifty years. Ivan Chermayeff and Tom Geismar's 1960 Chase Manhattan mark was effectively the first abstract corporate symbol in America, and the pattern repeated: Mobil's circle-in-'o', the NBC peacock, the National Geographic yellow rectangle, PBS, Pan Am, Barneys, Smithsonian, Library of Congress. Sagi Haviv joined as partner in 2013 on the same terms — partners work on the work.
whatWorks: Keep the studio small enough that the person who signs the work draws the work; no pyramid of juniors, no account managers between the client and the designer
Judge every mark against three words — appropriate, distinctive, simple — and use them as the review vocabulary rather than personal taste
Design in one colour, at small size, first: if the mark fails as a black shape at 12mm, it fails, regardless of how it looks on a presentation board
Refuse a house style: each identity should look like the client, which is only possible if the studio has no signature to protect
Aim explicitly for longevity — draw for fifty years of service, which rules out anything dependent on a current effect or trend
Sell the reasoning, not the reveal: the presentation explains why the geometry is right for this business, so the client can defend it internally for decades

sections.name: How it's structured
sections.notes: A partnership of two, later three, with a handful of designers. Partners lead their own projects end to end and present their own work. The deliberate absence of scale is what protects the standard — there is no capacity to take on work the partners can't personally draw.

sections.name: How it takes on work
sections.notes: Long-horizon identity problems for institutions that will keep a mark for decades — banks, broadcasters, museums, publishers. The engagement is framed as designing a system that outlives the current management, not as a campaign.

sections.name: Signature method
sections.notes: Abstract reduction: find the one geometric relationship that encodes the business (interlocking segments for a merged bank, a circle inside a letter for a fuel brand, a fanned spectrum for colour television), then refine it until nothing can be removed. Everything is tested small, in one colour, and in motion where relevant.

sections.name: What holds it together
sections.notes: The three-word test (appropriate, distinctive, simple), the insistence that partners execute, and an institutional memory of what has actually survived in the wild — the studio can point to sixty years of marks still in use as evidence for its own rules.

principle.title: Test the mark as a small black shape before you test it as a design
principle.explanation: Most identity failures are not aesthetic, they are dimensional: the mark dies as a favicon, on an embroidered polo, in a fax-quality contract header, or in a single-colour sign. Judging the shape in one colour at tiny size first eliminates those failures while they are cheap to fix, and it forces the geometry to carry the meaning — which is exactly what makes a mark last fifty years.
principle.howToApply: Before any colour, gradient or lockup work, print the candidate marks as black shapes at 12mm and 24px, photograph them on a phone screen at arm's length, and try drawing each from memory after ten seconds. Kill anything that needs colour, detail or explanation to be recognised, and review the survivors out loud against three words — appropriate, distinctive, simple — with the client in the room.

entries.category: Trademark / fair-use guidance for fans and third parties
entries.tagline: The famous grammar rules — LEGO is an adjective, never a noun, never a plural — published as brand governance for a fan economy.
entries.summary: Fair Play is not a visual guide; it is a written-language and trademark artifact aimed at the millions of people who talk about LEGO online. Its rules are unusually quotable: say 'models built of LEGO bricks', never 'LEGOs'; set the word in the same typeface as the surrounding text and never isolate or emphasise it; attach the ® symbol; never place the red logo on an unofficial site; never build the trademark into a domain name because a domain implies source; carry a disclaimer such as 'LEGO® is a trademark of the LEGO Group of companies which does not sponsor, authorize or endorse this site.' It then permits non-commercial fan use of the word marks and limited excerpts of copyrighted material with attribution — a permission structure designed to keep an enormous fan-content economy legal without policing it.
whatWorks: Governs the brand where it actually lives — in sentences typed by other people — which no logo-clearspace diagram can reach
Rules are memorable and testable: adjective not noun, no plural, no possessive, same typeface as body text, ® present
The reasoning is stated ('a domain name identifies source', 'the logo must stay distinctive'), so fans can extend the rule to cases the page never lists
Draws a bright line where confusion actually happens — the logo and the domain — while being permissive about the word mark in fan discussion
Supplies the exact disclaimer sentence to copy, which is the single highest-compliance move on the page
Distinguishes clearly between non-commercial fan use, which is broadly allowed, and commercial use, which is not — the distinction fan creators most need

sections.name: Using the LEGO name in text
sections.notes: The core rules: adjective only ('LEGO bricks', 'LEGO set'), never a noun or plural, never possessive; typeset in the same face as surrounding text with no isolation, highlighting or special treatment; ® on use.

sections.name: The logo
sections.notes: An absolute prohibition on the red logo appearing on unofficial sites, framed by the argument that its distinctiveness is the asset being protected.

sections.name: Domain names
sections.notes: The trademark may not be incorporated into an internet address, because a domain reads as source identification and therefore implies sponsorship.

sections.name: Attribution / disclaimer
sections.notes: A supplied sentence for unofficial sites to carry, naming the LEGO Group and explicitly disclaiming sponsorship, authorisation and endorsement.

sections.name: Permitted non-commercial use
sections.notes: Fan sites may use the word marks (not the logo) to discuss products so long as the use is not 'unduly emphasized' and cannot mislead a viewer about sponsorship; limited excerpts of copyrighted material are allowed for non-commercial information exchange with a copyright notice.

needs: Shown do/don't pairs: every rule here is prose, and 'LEGOs' beside 'LEGO bricks' — or the logo on a fan page beside a compliant text credit — would teach faster than a paragraph
Colour, typography and any visual specification at all: there is no hex for LEGO red, no typeface, no clearspace, so a licensed partner learns nothing about making something look right
A sanctioned asset for fan creators — a small 'built with LEGO bricks' text lockup or badge would channel the demand the logo ban creates (Blender and Python both solve this with community badges)
Platform-specific guidance for where fan content actually lives: YouTube thumbnails, marketplace listings, print-on-demand, app names
AI-era clauses: prompt-generated LEGO-style imagery and model renders are now the most common trademark collision and are unaddressed
A version number and revision date, plus a named contact route for permission requests rather than only prohibition

principle.title: Write the rules for the sentence, not just the logo
principle.explanation: For most brands the mark appears in third-party text far more often than in third-party artwork, and the damage from a genericised name (a trademark used as a plural noun) is permanent in a way a squashed logo never is. Codifying grammar — part of speech, plurality, capitalisation, typeface parity, the ® — gives partners, journalists and fans a rule they can actually follow while typing, with no design tool involved.
principle.howToApply: Add a 'writing the name' page to the brand guide with five lines: the part of speech ('Ridgeline is a proper adjective — Ridgeline listings, not Ridgelines'), never plural or possessive, always sentence-consistent typeface with no bold or caps treatment, the ® or ™ placement, and one supplied disclaimer sentence partners can paste. Then show one wrong-and-right pair per rule, and name a human to ask.

entries.tagline: Navigates by intent instead of category — 'Get organized with Transit', 'Market runs to beach days, sorted' — so the shopper picks a situation, not a SKU.
entries.summary: Bellroy opens on a full-bleed action photograph (a man mid-leap between a concrete wall and blank blue sky, bag on back) carrying three heavy condensed lines — CARRY SMART. MOVE FREE. GO FAR. — and one small orange Bestsellers button. What follows is the interesting part: instead of a category grid, a row of eight thumbnail tiles captioned as intents and situations ('Keep things Lite', 'Get organized with Transit', 'Gear up for travel season', 'Duffels for plans big or small', 'Market runs to beach days, sorted'), then Trending now, then collection families each with a personality descriptor, then a values block leading with B Corp certification and hard numbers (25M bottles upcycled, 100% Gold-rated leather sourcing) and the durability argument 'Better with age'. The search field sits above the hero, acknowledging that many visitors arrive knowing the product name.
whatWorks: Intent-first navigation: tiles are labelled by the situation and the outcome ('Market runs to beach days, sorted') rather than by product type, which is how people actually shop for carry
Hero photography shows the product in motion and mid-use at distance — the bag is on a body doing something, never floating on seamless
Type does the brand voice: heavy condensed caps for the manifesto lines, a light humanist sans for everything functional, so the loud voice appears exactly once per screen
One orange accent for CTAs and the promo bar, against greys and photographic colour — the same discipline Ramp uses, applied to retail
Collections are given personalities rather than specs (Transit, Lite, Venture, Cinch, Tokyo, Classic, Laneway), turning a large range into a set of characters a shopper can identify with
Sustainability leads with certification and countable facts (B Corp, 25M bottles) plus 'Better with age', tying environmental claim to the product's actual value proposition — durability
Search is placed above the fold and phrased as a question ('What are you looking for?'), respecting the large share of visitors who arrive with a known model in mind

sections.name: Promo bar + minimal header
sections.notes: A thin orange bar with one offer and an email-capture link, then just the wordmark, a mail icon and a cart — the nav itself is a mega-menu that stays out of the way until asked for.

sections.name: Search
sections.notes: A wide plain search field directly above the hero. Unusual placement, and a correct read of a catalogue where product names (Transit Workpack, Lite Sling) are the actual search terms.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Full-bleed photograph split by a hard vertical edge — grey wall against blue sky — with three condensed white lines set in the flat grey half and one small orange Bestsellers button. Type sits entirely on the quiet side of the frame.

sections.name: Intent tiles
sections.notes: Eight small image tiles with two-line captions written as jobs and occasions rather than categories, each linking into a filtered range. This row replaces the conventional 'Shop by category' block.

sections.name: Trending now / featured
sections.notes: A carousel of current products and new releases with minimal copy, letting the intent row above do the qualifying and this row do the merchandising.

sections.name: Collection families
sections.notes: Six or seven ranges presented with short personality descriptors, so a repeat customer can navigate by the family they already own.

sections.name: Values / B Corp
sections.notes: A dedicated block with certification, upcycled-bottle and leather-sourcing figures, and the 'Better with age' durability argument — claims that are countable rather than atmospheric.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Four ordered columns (Help, Shop, About, Company) with warranty and repair links prominent, socials and an email signup — the after-sale promise placed where a carry buyer looks for it.

principle.title: Label the entry points by the situation, not the category
principle.explanation: Category labels ('Bags', 'Wallets', 'Tech') ask the visitor to translate their problem into your taxonomy, and a shopper who can't translate leaves. Situation labels ('Get organized with Transit', 'Market runs to beach days, sorted') let them recognise themselves in one read, and they carry merchandising intelligence — the tile can point at a curated filtered set rather than a whole department.
principle.howToApply: Rewrite the primary entry tiles as five to eight situations your audience will recognise, each phrased as an outcome and pointing at a pre-filtered set — for property, that means 'First place, walkable, under $500k' or 'Room for a workshop' instead of 'Single family / Condo / Land'. Keep the taxonomy in the nav for people who want it, put the situations on the page, and give each tile one honest photograph of that situation.

entries.category: Static social feed unit (4:5, 1080×1350), topical/occasion post
entries.tagline: A double meaning of 'power' staged as a flat-lay: earbuds beside a ballot paper on a green-white-green ground.
entries.summary: For Nigeria's Democracy Day, oraimo built a top-down flat-lay on three vertical bands of dark green, grey and green — the national flag rotated into a background texture — with its Spacebuds 2 case open on the left and an illustrated ballot paper on the right, three empty boxes beside three illustrated candidate portraits. Two half-lines of copy sit either side of the gap ('You can choose immersive Sound…' / '…& choose immersive peace.'), and the payoff runs along the bottom: 'The power is in your hands. Happy Democracy Day.' with the product name and an 'AI-Powered' chip at right. It's a clean example of an occasion post that earns its place by finding a genuine pun in the product's core benefit rather than pasting a flag over a product shot.
whatWorks: The pun is in the product truth: a power bank / audio brand talking about civic 'power' is a real double meaning, not a borrowed sentiment
National colours are used as an abstract striped ground with visible grain texture, so the flag is present without being a flag graphic pasted on top
Copy is split across the two objects so the sentence structure mirrors the choice being described — two halves, one decision
Green highlight applied only to the two words that carry the pun ('immersive Sound', 'Happy Democracy Day'), with everything else in white — colour as emphasis, not decoration
The illustrated ballot avoids photographic realism, which keeps the unit from reading as political material while still being instantly legible
Product is shown open and lit as the hero object at flat-lay scale, with the model name and one feature chip ('AI-Powered') as the only spec — enough to make the post shoppable later

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A top-down flat-lay on a hard green/grey/green split reads instantly in feed, and the ballot paper is the unexpected object that makes you stop on a consumer-electronics post.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: Split copy across the two objects, then the payoff line 'The power is in your hands.' The construction lets the pun land twice — once as product benefit, once as civic message — without a single explanatory sentence.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Studio flat-lay: open charging case with green-marbled lid and earbuds, illustrated ballot card with three portraits in traditional dress, textured concrete-and-green ground, soft top light with contact shadows so both objects sit on the same surface.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: None; the brand mark sits top-left and the product name plus feature chip bottom-right. Correct for an occasion post, where a hard CTA would read as trading on a national holiday.

principle.title: Earn an occasion post by finding the pun inside your product's core benefit
principle.explanation: Most holiday posts are brand tax: a logo over a flag, no idea, no memory. A genuine double meaning between the occasion's language and the product's actual function ('power', 'connection', 'moving', 'closing', 'home') gives the post a reason to exist and makes it recognisably yours — and it disciplines the layout, because a pun needs exactly two objects and one line.
principle.howToApply: List the words your product owns literally (power, signal, keys, close, move, home, cover) and check them against the occasion's vocabulary before designing anything; if no honest overlap exists, skip the occasion. When one does, stage exactly two objects — one product, one occasion object, illustrated rather than photographed if the subject is sensitive — split the line across them, and use the accent colour only on the two words carrying the pun.

entries.when: 1900–1988 · German (worked in Vienna and The Hague)
entries.tagline: Drew about 4,000 pictograms for Isotype and set the rule that made data pictures honest: repeat the symbol, never resize it.
entries.summary: Arntz was the draughtsman of the Vienna Method of pictorial statistics, working with Otto Neurath from 1928 and later in The Hague, producing the roughly 4,000 signs that became Isotype — the direct ancestor of every wayfinding and interface pictogram in use today. His achievement is as much systemic as graphic: a closed vocabulary of silhouettes, each reduced to an outline that stays unambiguous at any size, plus a strict grammar for combining them (a base figure plus attributes; one symbol equals a fixed quantity, so more means more symbols, never a bigger symbol). He came to it from politically committed woodcut printmaking, which is why the figures have weight and stance rather than the blandness of later icon sets.
whatWorks: Repeat units to show quantity instead of scaling one symbol — the rule that keeps a chart from lying about area
Build a closed vocabulary first, then compose from it: a base figure plus a small set of attributes covers thousands of specific cases
Reduce to a silhouette that survives without interior detail, and test recognition at the smallest size the system will ever print
Keep style constant across the whole set so differences in a chart read as data, not as drawing variation
Design for translation: pictures carry meaning across languages and literacy levels, which was the entire political point of the project
Bring a craft discipline with you — woodcut training gave the figures their stance, weight and confident negative space

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: From the statement the data has to make, agreed with the statistician before drawing: what is being counted, in what unit, and what comparison the reader must be able to make. The visual work starts only once the unit is fixed.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Build the sign as a flat black silhouette on a strict shared baseline and proportion, with no interior modelling; then extend the vocabulary combinatorially — the same worker figure gains a tool, a hat, a colour to become a specific occupation — so the set grows without new drawing conventions.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Countable rows: quantities expressed as repeated identical signs on a grid, with a stated key ('one figure = 1 million'). Where a partial unit is needed, the sign is cut, not shrunk. Colour is flat and used categorically.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Clarity over expression, and honesty over impact: the chart exists to make an ordinary reader see a social fact, so any device that flatters the designer or exaggerates the comparison is disqualified. Ambiguity in a silhouette is a defect, not a style.

principle.title: Show quantity by repeating the unit, never by scaling the symbol
principle.explanation: Scaling a symbol to represent a bigger number distorts perception, because the reader judges area while the data encodes length — a house drawn twice as tall reads as four times as much. Repeating an identical unit keeps the comparison countable and exact, and it forces you to declare the unit itself, which is the discipline that makes an infographic trustworthy rather than merely attractive.
principle.howToApply: For the next stat block or market-data graphic, pick one unit (one house = 10 sales, one figure = 100 residents), state the key on the graphic, and show quantities as repeated identical glyphs on a shared baseline — cutting a glyph for partial units instead of scaling it. Draw the glyph set as flat silhouettes from one closed vocabulary so every future chart reuses the same parts, and check each at 16px before it enters the set.

entries.category: Open-source logo page with an explicit fan-art carve-out
entries.tagline: Publishes hard rules for credit and prominence — then says modifying the logo is 'part of your own artistic freedom' and it will never act against tributes.
entries.summary: Blender's logo page does three things well and unusually. It gives real values (PMS 716 / #e87d0d, PMS 647 / #265787, white) and a downloadable logo kit. It states five numbered usage conditions for third parties — the logo may only point to Blender or give credit; your own branding must be more prominent; promotional merchandise is fine only as a secondary brand; the logo must be used unaltered, in original colours, original typography and always complete; commercial use requires explicit written permission with a picture of the intended use. Then it draws a deliberate line between rules and tolerance: an 'On artwork and community websites' section acknowledges the logo has been reworked hundreds of times as tribute, calls that artistic freedom, and promises the Foundation will never act against it — 'just don't expect us to officially approve of it'. Finally it ships a separate Community Badge (PNG and SVG) for tutorial makers, with its own three rules.
whatWorks: Colour is actually specified — two Pantones with hex equivalents plus white — which most open-source logo pages omit entirely
The prominence rule is written as an outcome test, not a measurement: 'it has to be clear for an average viewer that this is not an official Blender website, publication or product'
Rules are numbered and short (general usage, prominence, products, modification, commercial use), so a community member can cite '#4' in a discussion

Ships a purpose-built Community Badge for exactly the use the logo rules would otherwise block — crediting Blender in tutorials, videos and books — in PNG and SVG with its own three rules and a shown in-context example
Credit guidance distinguishes two cases with named examples: type the words out (not the logo) when saying a project was made with Blender, or place the logo among other logos, never in isolation
It states its own legal footing plainly — the logo and the name are trademarks and are NOT covered by the GNU GPL, the single most misunderstood fact about the project

The fan-art carve-out is honest governance: it separates what the Foundation will enforce from what it merely won't endorse, which stops a rule nobody can enforce from undermining the rules that matter

sections.name: Logo & permitted purpose
sections.notes: The mark shown with its one-line purpose — official Foundation projects and content; third parties may use it only to credit Blender or to link to blender.org — plus the Download Logo Kit button and a pointer to the trademark policy.

sections.name: Colour
sections.notes: Three chips with real values: PMS 716 / #e87d0d, PMS 647 / #265787, WHITE / #ffffff, with a note that the variations are for simple or plain-colour backgrounds.

sections.name: Usage guidelines (1–5)
sections.notes: General usage (link must point to blender.org), Prominence (Blender only ever a secondary brand), Products (merch allowed as secondary brand), Modification (unaltered, original colours and typography, always complete: mark + wordmark), Commercial use (explicit permission, with a picture of the intended use; film credits are not commercial).

sections.name: On artwork and community websites
sections.notes: The tolerance clause: hundreds of reworkings are treated as honest tribute, modification is 'part of your own artistic freedom', the Foundation will never act against it, and no official approval is implied.

sections.name: Usage in credits
sections.notes: Two worked cases with linked examples (Spring, Sintel): type the credit as words rather than using the logo, or include the logo alongside other logos — never in isolation.

sections.name: Community Badge
sections.notes: A separate badge for content creators in PNG and SVG, with three rules (indicate Blender was used, never use as your own logo, use as-is unaltered and complete) and an example of it applied to a video thumbnail.

sections.name: History
sections.notes: A closing link to an Internet Archive history of the logo — small, but it frames the identity as something that has evolved and will again.

needs: Clearspace and minimum-size diagrams: 'always complete' and 'unaltered' are stated, but nothing tells a user how much air the lockup needs or how small it may go
Misuse examples shown at the same size as the correct mark, captioned with the tell — the page describes modification bans in prose while cheerfully linking to a gallery of modifications
Typography: the wordmark's typeface is never named, and there is no guidance for setting 'Blender' in adjacent text
A dark-background rule beyond 'simple or plain colour' — which of the three variants belongs on dark UI, and what happens on photographic grounds
A version number, revision date and owner for the page; the trademark policy it defers to lives elsewhere and changes independently
Contrast and legibility guidance for #e87d0d, which fails as small text on white and is the colour most likely to be reused by the community

principle.title: Separate what you will enforce from what you merely won't endorse
principle.explanation: A brand page that forbids everything gets ignored wholesale, because the community can see that most of it is unenforceable. Naming the small set of rules you will actually defend (never as a primary brand, never for commercial products, never altered in official credit contexts) and explicitly tolerating the rest converts the page from a bluff into a working agreement — and it protects the rules that matter by not spending credibility on the ones that don't.
principle.howToApply: In the next brand or partner page, split usage into three named tiers: Required (the two or three rules you will chase — prominence, no commercial resale, no implied endorsement), Provided (the sanctioned asset for the most common community use — a 'built with' badge, a co-brand lockup, a credit line to type out), and Tolerated (what you won't police but won't approve). Say which tier each rule belongs to, and give the tolerated tier a sentence in plain language.

entries.title: Build a three-frame 300×250 animated banner in pure CSS
entries.tool: CSS (HTML + CSS only, no JS, no libraries)
entries.skill: Frame timing and hold discipline in a fixed ad unit: sequencing three messages with correct dwell times, one shared easing, and a final frame that holds with the CTA visible
entries.brief: Build a single 300×250 medium-rectangle banner that plays three frames — hook, benefit, offer + CTA — and then stops on frame three. All animation in CSS keyframes, total runtime under 15 seconds, last frame holds forever (animation-fill-mode: forwards), and the CTA is visible in the final state without any hover.
steps: Set a 300×250 container with overflow:hidden and position:relative; stack three absolutely positioned .frame divs inside it.
Give every frame the same animation duration (e.g. 12s) and use percentage keyframes to schedule each one: frame 1 visible 0–30%, frame 2 30–60%, frame 3 60–100% and held.
Animate only opacity and a small translateY (8–12px) — no scale, no blur — with one shared easing (cubic-bezier(.2,.7,.2,1)) so all three frames move with the same personality.
Overlap each transition by about 4% so a frame starts appearing just before the previous one is gone; hard cuts look broken at banner scale.
Put the CTA button in frame 3 only, and confirm the final state after the animation ends still shows logo + offer + button (no element left at opacity 0).
Wrap the animation rules in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference), and make the default state frame 3 fully visible so a reduced-motion user sees the complete offer immediately.

assets.label: Frame 2 (benefit)
assets.value: See what your monthly payment could buy.

assets.label: Frame 3 (offer + CTA)
assets.value: Free 10-minute buying-power check  ·  CTA: Check my number

assets.label: Starter code (fix and finish this)
assets.code:
Still paying rent in 2026?

See what your monthly payment could buy.

Free 10-minute buying-power check

Check my number

entries.successLooksLike: The banner plays hook → benefit → offer in under 15 seconds, never loops, and the resting state is a complete, readable offer with the CTA button visible. Transitions feel like one system (same easing, same distance). With reduced motion enabled, the final frame is shown immediately and nothing moves.
entries.stretch: Duplicate the markup and re-time the same three frames for a 728×90 leaderboard: the copy must be trimmed, not just resized, and the frames will need shorter dwell times because a leaderboard is read in passing.

entries.tagline: A twelve-site restaurant group whose homepage is genuinely written — Bombay-cafe prose in every section — while the only two things a guest actually needs stay one tap away.
entries.summary: Dishoom's site reads like a piece of writing that happens to take bookings. Each block opens with narrative copy in the brand's Bombay Irani-cafe voice (“Each Dishoom is a love letter to Bombay”), set warm cream-on-dark with a serif display face over sans body, and illustrated with a deliberate mix of heritage reference photography and hot, close food shots. The utility never gets buried underneath the romance: View Menus and Book a Table sit in the hero, a three-tile hub repeats them mid-page, and the cafe list is a plain scannable set of place names rather than a map widget. The page is long, but almost none of it is scaffolding — recipes, the store, awards and the meal-donation count each give a non-booking visitor a reason to be there.
whatWorks: The hero carries exactly two CTAs — View Menus and Book a Table — which are the only two jobs a restaurant visitor arrives with; everything else on the page is discovery.
Copy does the branding work: period-accurate, warm, specific prose (dish names, a 1914 cafe, chai rituals) instead of adjectives about authentic dining.
Heritage and archive imagery sits beside appetite photography, so provenance and hunger are argued in the same eyeline rather than in a separate About page.

Twelve-plus locations are published as a horizontally scanning list of plain place names (with Permit Rooms as their own category) — faster than a map for a group whose guests already know their city.
Recipe and store carousels use one fixed card grammar (category badge, dish image, title, arrow), so heterogeneous content still reads as one system.
The proof block states facts with issuers attached — Sunday Times Best Places to Work 2025, 25 million meals donated, B-Corp — rather than unattributed superlatives.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Full-width band with a Hindi welcome and an illustrated SVG device over a warm ground; one line of scene-setting prose, then the two CTAs (View Menus / Book a Table). The sticky header repeats the Book button so the booking door never leaves the screen.

sections.name: Mission — a love letter to Bombay
sections.notes: Large display type states the brand idea in one sentence, illustrated with heritage photography (B. Merwan, 1914; bun maska). This is where the brand argues for itself, and it sits above the commerce rather than hidden in an About page.

sections.name: Three-tile hub — Menus / Reservations / Store
sections.notes: A three-column grid of image tiles with arrow affordances repeats the primary tasks mid-scroll, so a reader who came for the story can convert at the moment the story lands.

sections.name: Cafe explorer
sections.notes: A prose lead-in (“Take refuge with a warming cup of chai…”) then a plain horizontal list of the twelve-plus cafes and the Permit Rooms. No map, no cards — names as links, which is the shortest path when the visitor already knows their neighbourhood.

sections.name: Bombay comfort food + recipes
sections.notes: Descriptive copy walks breakfast through to dinner naming real dishes, backed by a four-image carousel; below it a recipe carousel with a fixed card grammar turns the brand into something you use at home, not only visit.

sections.name: Store, awards & impact
sections.notes: “For all persons and purses” sells gifts in the same voice, then a plain bulleted awards list, the 25-million-meals figure and the B-Corp badge supply checkable proof without a testimonial slider.

sections.name: Newsletter & footer
sections.notes: Signup asks for name, email, optional birthday and home cafe — each field earns its place — under casual copy (“First-dibs on new launches”). The six-column footer separates Visit Us / Explore / Shop / Cafe Support / Store Support so the two businesses, restaurants and retail, never tangle.

principle.title: Write the site in the brand's own voice — and never let the story bury the two doors
principle.explanation: Most hospitality and property sites split into a beautiful brand page nobody converts on and a utilitarian booking page with no voice. Dishoom refuses the split: every section is written prose in a specific period voice, and the two utility actions are repeated at the top, in the middle and in the sticky header. The narrative is what makes the brand worth choosing; the always-visible doors mean choosing costs one tap.
principle.howToApply: On the next hospitality or listing-group page, write each section's lead as a sentence a person would actually say (name the street, the year, the dish, the neighbourhood) instead of a feature label — then pick exactly two actions for the whole page, put both in the hero, repeat them once mid-scroll as an image-tile hub, and keep one of them in the sticky header. Publish locations as a plain list of names before reaching for a map.

site.name: Samsung — Google Display Network banner set (160×600 / 300×600 / 728×90 / 300×250)

entries.category: Display banner set — Google Display Network, multi-format (skyscraper, half-page, leaderboard, medium rectangle)
entries.tagline: One product idea rebuilt — not rescaled — for every slot in the GDN size matrix, with the CTA pill held at a constant size so the click target reads identically everywhere.
entries.when: Google Display Network, Spanish-language (Samsung LatAm), c. 2022 — presented by designer Carolina Kis on Behance
entries.summary: Three Samsung product lines (premium monitors, gaming monitors, the Flip 2 board) run across the standard IAB display sizes, and the craft is in what changes between formats. The verticals stack logo, product photograph, headline, CTA; the leaderboards run the same four elements left to right with the photograph cropped to a strip; the medium rectangle overlaps a black copy panel onto the image. Copy never exceeds a product name plus a three-word benefit fragment, and the only theming is a black/white inversion — a white card for the gaming line, black for premium and Flip 2. Because the source is a designer's portfolio presentation, treat the browser mockup as packaging; the units inside it are the real artefact.
whatWorks: The composition is re-laid per aspect ratio rather than scaled: verticals stack the four elements, horizontals sequence them, so nothing lands at an unreadable size in the narrow slots.
The MÁS INFO pill keeps a near-constant height across every format, so the click target has the same visual weight in a 728×90 as in a 300×600.
Copy is capped at a product name plus a benefit fragment (“Monitores Premium / Trabajo optimizado.”), which is what survives being read in passing.
One inversion is the entire theming system — white ground for the gaming line, black for premium and Flip 2 — so the set reads as a family without a second palette.
The SAMSUNG wordmark is locked to the same corner in every size, giving the set a fixed anchor before the eye reaches the message.
Photography shows the monitors in real workspaces and in use — a designer at the Flip board, a retail floor on screen — rather than floating renders on a gradient.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The wordmark plus a full-bleed product photograph carries the first read; no headline competes at the top of the unit, so the eye lands on the hardware before the words.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: Two lines maximum, always in the same order: product name at display weight, then a lowercase benefit fragment at roughly half the size. The line break is deliberate (“Trabajo en equipo, / simplificado.”), not a wrap.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: One monitor or board, photographed in a working environment, cropped to whatever the format allows — a full scene in the 300×600, a strip in the leaderboard, a corner overlap in the 300×250. The subject stays the same; only the crop changes.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: An outlined pill reading MÁS INFO, white on black or black on white, placed at the end of the reading path in every format — bottom in the verticals, right in the horizontals — and held at a consistent size across the whole set.

principle.title: Re-compose per format, never rescale — and hold the CTA at a constant size
principle.explanation: A banner set fails when one master artwork is squeezed into every slot: type drops below reading size in the leaderboard and the CTA becomes a target only a mouse could hit. Rebuilding the same four elements per aspect ratio keeps each unit legible on its own terms, while pinning the CTA's physical size and the mark's corner position makes the set read as one campaign even though no two units share a layout.
principle.howToApply: For the next ad set across the six standard sizes (768×1024, 1024×768, 480×320, 970×250, 320×480, 300×600): define four elements only — mark, photograph, two-line message, pill CTA — then lay out each size from scratch, stacking in the portraits and sequencing left-to-right in the landscapes. Fix the pill height and the mark's corner across all six, cap the message at a name plus a three-word fragment, and use a single black/white inversion instead of a second colourway.

entries.tagline: The Swiss designer who stopped designing artefacts and started designing the programme that produces them.
entries.summary: Gerstner trained as a typographer in Basel, worked for Geigy, and in 1958 co-founded Gerstner+Kutter — which became GGK, one of Europe's most influential agencies. His 1964 book Designing Programmes argued that a designer's real output is a rule-set: define the parameters of the problem, generate the family of solutions those rules allow, then choose. He proved it with the mobile grid for Capital magazine, a field system that resolves into several different column counts, and with Gerstner-Programm, a typeface generated as a systematic matrix of widths and weights rather than drawn one style at a time. Not every brief wants this much machinery, but for anything that must keep producing work after you leave, it is the most transferable method in this journal.
whatWorks: Restate the brief as parameters before sketching: which variables actually move, and what values each may take.
Build a morphological box — list every variable with its options, then work through the combinations — so the range gets explored systematically instead of by inspiration.
Design a grid that is mobile: one field system that legitimately resolves into two, three, four or more column arrangements, so variety comes from the system rather than from breaking it.
Treat type and layout as one matrix, deriving weights, widths and sizes from a stated procedure so the family is consistent by construction, not by eye.
Judge a programme by whether another designer can operate it correctly without you in the room.
Prefer the solution that answers the whole family of problems over the one that answers today's instance beautifully.

sections.name: How he begins
sections.notes: By describing the problem rather than picturing the answer — for Gerstner the description of the problem is already part of its solution. The first work on a brief is enumerating its parameters and constraints (formats, languages, quantities, who will operate it) until the brief is a set of variables rather than an adjective.

sections.name: Core method — the design programme
sections.notes: Instead of producing one artefact he defines the rules that generate the permissible artefacts: a morphological box of variables and their options, combined systematically, from which a solution is selected. The programme, not the poster, is the deliverable — which is why the work survived being made by an agency of other hands.

sections.name: Signature technique — the mobile grid and the type matrix
sections.notes: His grid for Capital divides the page into a field system readable as several different column counts, so an editor can run a wide photograph, a dense table and a narrow column in one issue without leaving the system. Gerstner-Programm applied the same thinking to type: a matrix of related widths and weights generated by procedure rather than drawn ad hoc.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Integral, not intuitive: a solution is right when it follows from the stated rules, and a rule earns its place when it produces good results in hands other than yours. Where a purely intuitive designer asks whether this is beautiful, Gerstner asks whether the programme still holds at the next instance, in the next language, at the next size.

principle.title: Design the rule, then run it — the deliverable is the programme, not the artefact
principle.explanation: Anything that has to keep being produced — listing collateral, an ad set, a template library, a magazine — will eventually be made by someone other than its designer. If the output is a beautiful one-off it decays on the second use; if the output is a stated rule-set with its variables named, every later instance is a run of the programme rather than a fresh act of taste.
principle.howToApply: Before designing the next recurring deliverable, write the programme on one page: the variables (format, photo count, headline length, price present or not, language), the permitted values of each, and the composition rule that maps them to a layout. Build one grid that resolves into two, three and four columns so long copy, galleries and data can all sit in it. Then produce three instances from the rules alone — if you have to break a rule to make instance three look right, fix the programme, not the instance.

entries.category: Public brand hub — national tourism brand, partner- and agency-facing
entries.tagline: A national tourism brand that governs its tagline market by market — including which countries are legally required to run it in the local language — and bans AI-generated imagery outright.
entries.summary: Destination Canada publishes its “Canada, naturally” platform openly: strategy first (belief, ambition, promise, two realness pillars, a voice called Canadian Candour), then a full identity section covering the consumer logo, the corporate logo and the federal Canada wordmark, colour, typography and imagery, followed by real applications, an events chapter, a visual library and downloads. It is unusually decidable for a tourism brand — clearspace measured in units of the logo's own letterforms, ten named misuse cases, horizontal and vertical tagline lockups with different tolerances, and partner co-branding stated as parity (“our logo must match the size and visual impact of all other logos”). Its most distinctive chapter is the market-by-market tagline table, which names the approved wording per country and whether English or the local language leads, with China flagged as a legal requirement. Where it stops short is the digital layer: no contrast numbers, no tokens, no version stamp.
whatWorks: Strategy is published before assets — belief, ambition, promise, the Human and Physical realness pillars and the audience — so a partner can tell what the rules are for.

Tagline governance runs per market with the reason attached: Mandarin required by law in China, French only in France, English preferred in Japan, Korea and Mexico, each with approved wording supplied.

Clearspace is expressed in the logo's own geometry (one and a half squares above and below, two either side; corporate protection based on the height of the C) rather than in millimetres that break on rescale.
Co-branding is stated as parity plus a colour rule — match size and visual impact, keep red primary, use Suisse Int'l where possible — which a partner with no design training can check.
Colour is named and valued (Canadian Flag Red #E60013, PMS 032, C0 M100 Y100 K0) with a hard ratio rule: red always leads, and never more than two secondary colours at once.
Art direction takes a 2026 position and writes it as a rule: candid over staged, people in frame even at landscape scale, dusk and dawn light, subtle pops of red — and no AI-generated images.

sections.name: Brand Story
sections.notes: Belief (“travel is a force for good”), ambition, and the promise “Canada connects you with what is real”, with two pillars — Human Realness and Physical Realness — and the audience named. The platform line “Canada, naturally” is explained rather than merely displayed.

sections.name: Logo
sections.notes: Three marks governed together: the consumer logo (type forming a heart with the maple leaf), the corporate logo, and the federal Canada wordmark. Reverse version specified, clearspace in letterform units, corporate minimum 25 mm / 1 in, and ten explicit misuse cases — distort, angle, drop shadow, reproportion, rearrange, outline, clashing or patterned grounds, boxing, busy photographs.

sections.name: Tagline lockups & markets
sections.notes: The horizontal lockup (preferred) requires at least one logo-width of separation with no maximum; the vertical lockup is fixed and may not be adjusted at all. Then the market table: approved tagline wording per country with the language rule for each, including the Chinese legal requirement.

sections.name: Tone & Manner
sections.notes: “Canadian Candour” — refreshingly real, down-to-earth, conversational — defined as much by what it is not: not too try-hard, too earnest, too folksy or too slapstick. Useful because the failure modes named are the ones this brand actually risks.

sections.name: Colour
sections.notes: Canadian Flag Red #E60013 / PMS 032C-032U / C0 M100 Y100 K0 / RGB 230-0-19 leads everything, flagged by black and white. Seven named secondaries (Prairies Yellow #FADA46, Great Lakes Blue #B9DDF5, Maple Red #500603, Aurora Purple #D5D8EF, Forest Green #062F23, Sunset Pink #F4D2D8, Pacific Teal #AADACA) with a hard cap of two at a time, used as minor accents.

sections.name: Typography
sections.notes: Canada Bold for headlines — uppercase, single weight, leading at 90% of font size, primarily left-aligned to a margin with centring allowed only in portrait or vertical formats — and Suisse Int'l for body copy and data visualisation, chosen for long passages.

sections.name: Imagery
sections.notes: A real art-direction chapter: what to shoot (people and Indigenous communities, natural wonders, wildlife, landmarks from unexpected angles, shared meals, cities), how to shoot it (dusk and dawn, close framing, camera inside the action, people even as small figures), and the don'ts — nothing staged, no heavy filtering, no posed eye contact, no clichés, no AI-generated images, and don't overuse the red.

sections.name: Brand Examples, Events, Visual Library & Downloads
sections.notes: Applications across print, digital and video; a dedicated events chapter; and a separate visual library plus downloads section so partners leave with assets rather than screenshots.

needs: No numeric contrast pairings — a #E60013 red and seven pastel secondaries are published with no ratios and no per-background legibility table.
No digital layer: no px/rem type scale, no spacing system, no buttons or components, no dark-mode transformation, despite the brand living mostly in feeds and on screens.
No font licensing or fallback guidance — Suisse Int'l is a commercial licence and Canada Bold is bespoke, so a partner has no legal route to set the brand correctly and no named substitute.
No motion principles, even though video applications are shown and the events chapter implies screen work.
No iconography section — a system this heavy on wayfinding-style applications will grow icons whether or not they are governed.
No version number, date or changelog and no named approval route, so partners cannot tell whether they hold the current rules.

principle.title: Govern the brand line market by market — and attach the reason, especially when it's legal
principle.explanation: A tagline is the one asset that gets translated by people who will never read the guide. Publishing approved wording per market, plus whether English or the local language leads and why — a legal requirement in China, cultural preference elsewhere — converts an endless approval queue into a lookup, and stops well-meaning local teams inventing a translation the brand then has to live with.
principle.howToApply: In the next brand guide or partner kit, add a one-row-per-market table before the applications chapter: market, approved wording, which language leads, and the reason in four words (“required by law”, “local preference”, “English tested better”). Apply the same pattern to any phrase that must not be improvised — a compliance line, a licence disclosure, a bilingual property descriptor — and pair it with a clearspace rule expressed in the logo's own letterforms so it survives every rescale.

entries.tagline: Three products sold on one page, each given its own colour chapter — and every screenshot caught mid-action rather than sitting at rest.
