entries.summary: Superhuman has to pitch three things (Go, Mail, Docs) on one homepage, and it solves that with a repeated chapter template: product lockup, a headline that mixes light and bold weight in a single line, a one-sentence subhead, a purple pill CTA beside a quiet 'Learn more ›', then a bento of product-UI cards on a tinted panel. The whole page runs on a warm off-white ground so the tinted chapters — dark teal for Go, purple for Mail, warm sand for Docs — act as wayfinding: you know which product you're in from the hue alone. The strongest move is the imagery: none of the screenshots show a resting interface, they all show the product doing something (the hero has Go flagging '14 months → 16 months' with 'Knowledge Checker · 3 sources' inside a real Google Doc). One honest weak spot: five different primary CTA verbs (Try Go / Get Mail / Try Docs / Request a demo / Get started), and the marquee testimonial is attributed to 'Enterprise Retail Company' rather than a named brand — the proof softens exactly where it should harden.
whatWorks: Every product shot is caught mid-action, not at rest: the hero shows Go correcting a claim inside a live Google Doc — '…pays for itself in 14 months. 16 months.' with 'Knowledge Checker · 3 sources' — so the mechanic is visible instead of described

Headline emphasis carried by weight, not colour or a second size: 'Bring AI inside every app and tab with Superhuman Go' runs light-then-bold on one line, so claim and product name share a single type size
Each product owns a hue — Go dark teal, Mail purple, Docs warm sand, enterprise deep aubergine — so scroll position tells you which pitch you are reading without a sticky label

Card copy is two-part: a small quiet eyebrow that names the feature ('Inline suggestions', 'Split Inbox', 'Docs MCP') over a full benefit sentence — the label is scannable, the sentence does the selling
Fragment copy where a sentence would flatten: 'As you type, your agents underline what needs your attention. Mid-sentence. Mid-argument. Mid-mistake.' — three beats, decreasing length
Logo bar sits in a hairline-ruled six-cell grid with every mark flattened to black (OpenAI, Figma, Rivian, Brex, Zapier, DoorDash), so credibility arrives without importing six brand palettes
Small brand warmth in structural places: a nav item literally called 'Love' for customer stories, and a huge low-contrast SUPERHUMAN watermark closing the footer

sections.name: Announcement bar + hero
sections.notes: A lavender strip ('Looking for Superhuman Mail? Learn more →') catches the legacy-product visitor before the hero can confuse them. The hero itself is a split: left is a dark teal panel holding a three-row product switcher — Go / Mail / Docs, each an icon plus a one-line descriptor ('The agent that works everywhere you work') — with the headline and 'Try Go' pill anchored at the bottom; right is a browser-framed Google Doc with Go's sidebar and a live correction popover. The switcher doubles as the page's table of contents, so the hero explains the product family and the lead product at once.

sections.name: Trust bar
sections.notes: 'Trusted by the most innovative organizations in the world' over six logos in a bordered grid, hairline dividers between cells, all marks reduced to flat black. Placed immediately under the hero so the abstract 'agent' claim gets grounded before any feature talk.

sections.name: Chapter I — Superhuman Go
sections.notes: Opens with the lockup, a centred two-weight headline ('Get help from agents right where you work'), one subhead line, then the CTA pair. Below it a bento: one wide card for 'Inline suggestions' with the doc screenshot bleeding off the right edge, then two half-width cards ('Context-aware chat', 'Go app'). A tab row (Featured / Prep for meetings / Write and edit / Automate your emails / Build agents) then swaps in three integration cards with pastel rounded-square icon tiles — the tabs let a long use-case list occupy one screenful instead of five.

sections.name: Proof band
sections.notes: A full-bleed lavender band with one large quote set in the same headline face, the payoff clause bolded inside the sentence — 'Go helps me stay in one tab and actually finish things.' — followed by name, role and a 'View all customer stories ›' link. Bolding the clause rather than pull-quoting it keeps the testimonial conversational; the anonymised company is the weak link.

sections.name: Chapters II & III — Mail and Docs
sections.notes: The exact same template re-runs twice, which is what makes a very long page feel short. Mail leads with a number ('Save 4+ hours every week on email and scheduling') and cards for Auto Drafts, Share Availability and Split Inbox; Docs leads with 'Align your team with collaborative AI documents' and cards for Docs, Docs AI and Docs MCP. Behind the UI panels sit soft mesh gradients and one cloud photograph — decoration is confined to the backdrop, never on the interface itself.

sections.name: Enterprise + final CTA
sections.notes: The enterprise block breaks the centred rhythm deliberately: deep purple, left-aligned, small eyebrow ('Superhuman for enterprise'), 'Designed for humans, built for enterprise', a white ghost button, and a screenshot showing a red strikethrough rewriting vague copy into '$2.1M in net-new ARR' — the one place the page argues in numbers. Then a full-bleed blurred blue-green gradient band with 'Make it your best workday yet' left and an outlined 'Get started' right: one line, one button, no form.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Deep aubergine, wordmark plus a positioning line ('Builders of Superhuman Platform apps'), then five link columns split Products / Company / Legal / Connect — with Trust, Status and Community given the same weight as marketing pages. Closed by an oversized SUPERHUMAN watermark at maybe 8% contrast, which fills dead footer space with brand instead of padding.

principle.title: Screenshot the mechanic, not the resting state
principle.explanation: A clean screenshot of an idle interface proves only that the thing exists. A screenshot caught mid-action — the suggestion being accepted, the wrong number struck through and replaced, the source count showing — proves the thing works, and it does it faster than the paragraph next to it. It also forces honesty: you cannot fake a mid-action frame without inventing the behaviour behind it.
principle.howToApply: Before shipping any product or process section, ask of each image: 'what is happening in this frame?' If the answer is 'nothing', reshoot it at the moment of change — cursor placed, popover open, before-and-after visible in the same crop, the real number showing. On a listing or service page the equivalent is the same: show the search returning results, the form mid-fill, the annotated floorplan — not the empty state.

site.name: Hinge — 'No Ordinary Love' social / OOH key visual

entries.category: Social / OOH campaign key visual (documentary portrait)
entries.tagline: An ad with no headline, no logo and no CTA in frame — the casting is the whole hook.
entries.when: Launched August 2026 — third chapter of Hinge's 'No Ordinary Love' campaign, this year built around a free audiobook of five real couples' stories, with OOH in New York and London and social on TikTok/Instagram
entries.summary: This is the key visual for Hinge's 2026 chapter of 'No Ordinary Love': a documentary portrait of a real couple who met on the app, photographed side-on at eye level in flat overcast daylight on a park bridge. There is no type, no lockup and no CTA anywhere in the frame — every conversion element is deferred to the caption and the audio. What stops the scroll is specificity: black leather, studs and fishnet against soft green willow and weathered stone, chipped nail polish, a scuffed olive shoulder bag, a tartan skirt. No stock couple can fake that, which is exactly the point for a category drowning in idealised pairs.
whatWorks: Cast for specificity, not aspiration — subculture styling makes this couple unmistakably these two people, which is the one thing a generic 'happy couple' shot can never buy
Flat overcast daylight and no retouching: shine on skin, a crumpled jacket and wind-flat hair read as documentary rather than campaign
The wardrobe-versus-setting contrast does the concept work (black leather in a manicured English park), so the picture says 'unlikely, and real' with zero copy
The stone balustrade runs as a hard horizontal band across the lower third, pinning the figures so the busy foliage cannot swallow them
Subjects sit left of centre with the river receding through the middle, leaving the right third empty — deliberate room for a headline or lockup in OOH and 1:1 crops
Zero brand furniture in frame: the ad earns attention as a photograph first and is identified second, which is what lets it live as editorial across feed, OOH and a Substack

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: Pure casting and colour clash. In a feed of soft-lit, colour-graded couples, a goth pair in a National-Trust-looking park reads as a mistake for half a second — and that half second is the stop. Eye-level, side-on framing puts the viewer beside them rather than looking at them.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: Withheld on purpose. The image asserts only 'these are two real people, and this actually happened'; the claim about expressing feelings early lives in the caption, the audiobook and the couple's own recorded voiceover. Restraint like this only works when the picture is specific enough to carry the burden alone.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Composition is doing quiet work: hands are the emotional focus (her palm flat on his chest, his hand at her waist), placed almost dead centre where the eye lands after the faces. Cool greens and greys everywhere except the one saturated magenta dress, which becomes the only colour accent in the frame.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: None in the creative. The ask — listen free on Spotify or Libby — sits entirely in caption and audio, so the unit behaves like a photo essay and the conversion step arrives after interest rather than before it. Honest caveat: without the caption this frame is unattributable, so it depends completely on placement.

principle.title: Cast for specificity, not aspiration
principle.explanation: Idealised imagery is instantly legible as advertising, and the brain discounts it on sight. A subject with odd, true, un-art-directed detail — a worn bag, chipped polish, a wardrobe nobody would have chosen for a brand deck — reads as evidence instead of claim, and evidence is what a sceptical category actually needs.
principle.howToApply: When choosing between shots, pick the frame with the one true detail rather than the flawless one: the owner's dog in the doorway, the worn reading chair, the actual mug on the counter. Shoot in flat daylight, skip the retouch pass, and compose with one third left empty so the headline or logo can drop in later without recropping.

entries.category: Industrial & graphic design, visual research and design education · Milan
entries.tagline: Wrote design down as a repeatable method — and turned play into a research tool rather than a warm-up.
entries.summary: Munari worked across almost every surface a designer can touch: Futurist collage in the 1920s, the hanging 'useless machines', products for Danese (the Cubo ashtray, the Falkland lamp), sixty-odd children's books, the wordless Libri illeggibili (1949–95), and decades of teaching. What holds it together is not a look — it is a method. In 'Da cosa nasce cosa' (1981) he wrote the design process out as an ordinary sequence of steps and illustrated it with a recipe for green rice, deliberately deflating inspiration into procedure. He is the rare great whose actual legacy is transferable process rather than a signature style.
whatWorks: Restate the brief as a written problem before touching form — if your sentence already names a solution, it is the wrong sentence
Break the problem into sub-problems small enough that each one has an obvious answer, solve them separately, and treat the recomposition as the creative act
Gather data before ideas: what already exists, what the material and budget permit, what has been tried and failed
Run material experiments with no deliverable attached — and keep the results; the accident you file today is the technique you use next year
Exhaust the variations of one primitive (square, circle, triangle; one grid; one crop ratio) before choosing which to keep
Prototype with your hands to test rather than to present — 'understanding through the hands' applied to yourself, not just to children

sections.name: How he begins
sections.notes: Not with form, and never with a style reference. The first move is to write the problem down and interrogate whether it is the real problem — for Munari the problem contains the elements of its own solution, so a badly stated brief guarantees a badly formed answer. Only then does he collect data: precedents, materials, production constraints, what has already been attempted.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: The 'metodo progettuale' from 'Da cosa nasce cosa' (1981): problem → definition → break into components → gather data → analyse data → creativity → materials and technology → experiment → model → verify → drawings → solution. The point of the decomposition is that sub-problems have answers where the whole problem only has opinions. He illustrated the sequence with a cooking recipe on purpose: the method is meant to be dull, repeatable and teachable, with creativity operating inside the constraints rather than arriving from outside them.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Play as research. The Libri illeggibili carry no text at all, so paper weight, cut, fold and colour have to do the narrating — a self-imposed constraint that turns into a discovery machine. He treated the photocopier the same way in the 'Giocare con la fotocopiatrice' workshops (1991), dragging originals across the glass mid-scan to produce marks the machine was never built for, and his 'Giocare con l'arte' children's workshops from the late 1970s were structured as guided material experiments, not craft lessons. The output of play is a catalogue of techniques, kept for later.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: 'Complicating is easy, simplifying is difficult' — the test applied to every version is whether anything can come out. He rejected personal style outright: the solution should emerge from the problem, which is why his lamp, his books and his teaching materials look unrelated to each other. And the ethical floor: things that are good to look at and bad to use should not exist, so beauty never excuses a thing that fails in the hand.

principle.title: Decompose the brief until every piece has an obvious answer
principle.explanation: Most design paralysis is a scoping error, not a talent error: 'make this beautiful' has no decidable answer, so you circle it. Split it into components — type scale, crop ratio, legible price at arm's length, where the legal line sits — and each one becomes a question you can actually settle, often in minutes. The creativity moves into how you recompose the settled pieces, which is a far more reliable place to keep it than at the blank page.
principle.howToApply: On the next template or page, spend the first ten minutes writing the problem as one sentence and listing its sub-problems as a checklist, before opening any tool. For an Aperture listing layout that reads: photo aspect ratios, headline character ceiling, price legibility at arm's length, fair-housing line placement, what happens when the description runs long. Settle each in isolation, then assemble — and keep the checklist as the template's spec sheet for the next listing.

entries.tagline: A vacation-rental marketplace that answers the price objection inside every card — total for the stay, plus how much less it is than other sites.
entries.summary: Wander sells stays the way a storefront sells goods: one full-bleed photograph of a real property, the entire search form folded into the nav bar above it, and then row after row of named, editorialised inventory instead of one undifferentiated grid. The card is where the design thinking is — name and rating, then "4 beds · $2,502 for 3 nights" (total, not per night), then a green "~$220 less than other sites" that is the only saturated colour in the whole card set. A single black "Wander difference" band interrupts the browsing to make six one-sentence promises, and the footer registers the tagline itself as a mark. Honest caveat: the rows get dense fast, and the whole first screen rests on one photograph being good enough to carry it.
whatWorks: The search form lives inside the nav bar (Where / When / Who + a black "Search" pill), so it never sits on top of the hero photo; the rest of the nav is reduced to a wordmark, "List on Wander", and a hamburger.
The hero occupies roughly the top 45% of the viewport, so the first row of properties peeks above the fold — the page reads as browsable inventory rather than a brochure.
The subhead does a bullet list's job in one line by stacking period-separated fragments: "Guest-first travel. Only the best homes. 24/7 concierge. No fees or markups."

Rows are named like an editor's picks — "Lakefront life", "Mountain adventures" — and the first row is geolocated ("Stay near Clifton"), so the same inventory reads as curation rather than search results.

Every card follows a strict three-line hierarchy: name + star rating / beds · total price for N nights / the green savings delta. Total-stay pricing removes the per-night-plus-fees surprise before the click.

The dark band uses a two-tone headline at one size — "The way travel should be." in white, "Great homes, service and prices." in grey — then breaks its own polish with three loose, un-art-directed snapshots (a door numbered 0175, a desert plant) as texture against the glossy listing photography.
Browsing ends with one quiet "See more properties" pill instead of pagination, so the page has a clear bottom rather than an endless tail.

sections.name: Nav + hero
sections.notes: A full-bleed dusk photograph of an actual Wander home (lit cabin, pool, forest) with the booking form docked in the nav strip above it. The headline "Find your happy place" sits centred and low in a warm geometric sans, over the naturally dark bottom third of the photo rather than a heavy scrim, with the four-claim subhead beneath. Nothing competes: no badges, no secondary CTA.

sections.name: Curated inventory rows
sections.notes: Five-up horizontally scrollable rows, each with a plain-language title and a pair of small arrows at the right of the row header. "Stay near Clifton" personalises the first row by location; "Lakefront life" and "Mountain adventures" turn the rest into moods. This is the same catalogue three ways — the naming, not the layout, is what makes it feel curated.

sections.name: The listing card
sections.notes: 4:3 photo with a glassy "Luxury" badge top-left and a heart top-right, then three tightly ranked lines of copy. The savings line ("~$310 less than other sites") is the only green on the page, so the eye lands on the differentiator last and remembers it. Ratings are shown as a single number next to a star rather than a five-star row, which keeps the line short.

sections.name: "The Wander difference" (black band)
sections.notes: A full-width dark break after the browsing: eyebrow, two-tone headline, and a 2×3 grid of rounded icon tiles with a title and one sentence of proof each (Only the best homes, Exceptional amenities, 24/7 Concierge service, Meticulous cleaning, Stunning views, Safety and security). Every claim is answered in one sentence — no expandable copy — and the colour inversion gives the long page a spine.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: A social row that spells out platform names as text links ("Follow us @wander · X (Twitter) · Instagram · TikTok · LinkedIn · YouTube") instead of icon-only buttons, then four columns split by audience: Company, Resources, Operators, Partners — with a small "New" chip beside "Get WanderOS". The bottom bar reads "Find your happy place ® © 2026 Wander.com, Inc.", treating the tagline as the trademark.

principle.title: Answer the price objection inside the card, not in the hero
principle.explanation: A trust claim in a hero is read as marketing and forgotten by the time someone is choosing; the same claim printed in the decision unit is read as information. Wander does two things at once — prices the whole stay for the real dates instead of a per-night teaser, and prints the delta against other sites in the single accent colour on the page — so the "could I get this cheaper elsewhere" doubt is settled at the moment of the click rather than banked in a promise at the top.
principle.howToApply: On the next listing or service card, move the reassurance down to the unit being chosen: show the all-in number for the real period (total for the stay, total for the package, not a per-night or per-month hook), and put one short differentiator under it in a colour used nowhere else — "~$310 less than comparable listings", "includes photography + floorplan". Keep that accent reserved for the money line so it reads as fact, not decoration.

site.name: KFC Myanmar — "No Other Crunch Is Needed"

entries.category: Social / digital key visual (portrait feed unit, ~10:11)
entries.tagline: The whole idea is one strikethrough: the Burmese word for “toppings” crossed out at headline scale, with a single bowl proving why.
entries.when: Launched August 2026 (Myanmar) — the unit dates itself “AVAILABLE ON AUG 6”; posted to Ads of the World in August 2026
entries.summary: KFC Myanmar dropped popcorn chicken onto lahpet htamin, the national tea-leaf rice dish whose convention is that the more toppings you pile on, the better. Rather than claim superiority, the layout crosses the convention out: the word for the usual assortment of toppings is set large and struck through in one red rule, so the argument is won before you read a word. Beneath it, one branded bowl shot straight on, chicken heaped above the rim, with a basket of raw tea leaves at the corner doing the work of an explanatory sentence. It is a crowded frame — safety certification, a “Global Quality” seal, a limited-time flag and the price all fight for room — and it holds together only because the struck-out headline outweighs everything else in the composition.
whatWorks: The claim is executed rather than stated: the category's default (“all the usual toppings”) is set at headline size and struck through with a single red rule — a negation legible in under a second, in any language.

Colour codes the multilingual headline instead of a second type size: “GLOBAL QUALITY” in red, the dish name in green, connective Burmese in black, so a three-part lockup still resolves in one glance.
One hero object, shot at eye level: the KFC bowl dead-centre and nearly full-frame, chicken piled above the rim so the topping — the whole point of the ad — is unmistakable at thumbnail size.
Proof props replace copy: the bamboo basket of raw tea leaves at the lower left certifies the base is real lahpet without a line of explanation.
The offer is pushed into the corners — “8,800 KS”, “AVAILABLE ON AUG 6”, the limited-time flag — keeping the centre for product and idea. In a feed post the offer, not a button, is the CTA.

Branding is structural, not decorative: the KFC red stripes bleed off the top edge and the bucket logotype rides on the bowl itself, so the frame is unmistakably KFC even with no logo in the headline zone.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: Red bars bleeding off the top edge pull the eye up, then the struck-through word stops it. The strike is a graphic event, not typography — it reads as a gesture (someone crossed this out) which is why it survives being scrolled past at speed.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: “No other crunch is needed”, staged as negation: name the convention, kill it, then name the replacement (“GLOBAL QUALITY” + the dish). Framing the product as a substitution rather than an addition also makes it culturally polite — it respects the traditional dish instead of claiming to improve on it.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Clean studio lighting, white ground, no steam or gloss tricks; the bowl is centred with the chicken breaking the rim silhouette so the crunch reads as texture. Scattered lime and chilli and the tea-leaf basket frame the bowl without crossing in front of it.

sections.name: CTA / offer
sections.notes: Price in heavy red numerals with the currency as a superscript, a launch date top-right, and a limited-time flag near the product — an offer stack that gives the post a reason to be acted on today, kept out of the idea's way. The weak spot: four badges (FSSC 22000, Global Quality seal, limited-time, price) is one or two too many for a single frame.

principle.title: Cross out the category's assumption instead of arguing with it
principle.explanation: A superiority claim reads as advertising; a struck-out convention reads as an argument already settled, and it works pre-literately — the eye registers the negation before it decodes the words, which matters most in a feed and in any market where your reader's first language isn't the headline's. It also forces a sharper brief: you have to name the exact default you are replacing, which is harder and more useful than “we're better”.
principle.howToApply: When an offer beats a default, set that default in type at headline size and strike it — “no staging fee”, “no 6-month lock-in”, “no per-night teaser price” — then show one image that proves the replacement. One strike per frame; if it needs two, the idea isn't sharp yet. Works on a hero headline as readily as on a social unit.

entries.tagline: Ran the Stedelijk Museum and designed its 300-plus catalogues himself — in the evenings, on the cheapest paper he could find.
entries.summary: Willem Sandberg was director of Amsterdam's Stedelijk Museum from 1945 to 1962 and, at the same time, its designer: he laid out some 320 catalogues, posters and invitations, mostly at night after the museum day was over. His vocabulary was forged in hiding during the war, in the nineteen booklets of the Experimenta Typographica, and it never lost that origin — torn paper letterforms, lowercase asymmetry, one loud flat colour on brown wrapping stock, and the misregistrations of cheap printing left visible. “I don't like luxury in typography,” he said, and he meant it as a working rule, not a slogan. The lesson is the loop he built: he chose the exhibitions, wrote the point of view, and made the artefacts, so nothing was translated through a brief.
whatWorks: Keep a body of unbriefed work. The Experimenta Typographica booklets had no client and no deadline; they became the vocabulary he then spent across three hundred real jobs. Practice first, apply later — the opposite of inventing a look under deadline.

Choose the material before the layout. He picked the stock — unbleached kraft, whatever scarcity allowed — and let its coarseness set the register, so the design started from a physical fact rather than a blank artboard.
Tear instead of draw. Hand-torn letters and shapes put a human hand inside a modernist composition and produce a form that polish cannot imitate.
Treat the press's limitations as the aesthetic: coarse screens, one flat spot colour, visible misregistration — designed with, never designed around.
Work in series. A continuous, recognisable catalogue format across hundreds of pieces built consistency out of volume, without a brand manual to enforce it.
Shorten the loop between point of view and artefact — he was curator, client and designer at once — and protect the making time by defending a fixed slot for it (his was every evening).

sections.name: How he begins
sections.notes: From the exhibition and the paper, not the page. Because he was also the curator, the brief started as an argument about the work being shown; the first design decision was material — which cheap stock, how many inks, what the press could actually hold — and the layout followed from that constraint rather than preceding it.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: A private R&D practice feeding a public production line. The Experimenta Typographica (19 booklets, made while in hiding, 1943–45) were experiments in letterform, tearing, layering and text-as-image with nothing to sell; the museum's 320-odd catalogues were where those findings got spent. He kept the two separate but connected: no experiments on a client's deadline, no blank-page starts on a real job.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Torn-paper collage typography: lowercase, asymmetric, hand-torn letters and shapes over brown wrapping paper, one saturated colour, occasionally a photograph half-hidden behind translucent tracing stock. The rough edge is the identity — it carries warmth into otherwise austere modernist composition, and it dates the work to a moment when materials were scarce.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: “I don't like luxury in typography” — polish that costs directness is a downgrade, so he judged by warmth and immediacy rather than finish. Imperfection in printing was a motivation, not a defect. And the institution had one voice: posters, catalogues, labels, invitations and the galleries themselves were all treated as the same designed object, which is why a Sandberg Stedelijk piece is recognisable across two decades.

principle.title: Pick the humblest material first and let its flaws carry the identity
principle.explanation: Deciding the ground, the ink limit and the reproduction method before any layout gives a piece a spine that styling cannot supply afterwards, and it makes the work hard to copy: gloss is available to everyone, a specific rough edge is not. It also converts constraints from a problem into the design's most memorable feature, which is the cheapest kind of distinctiveness there is.
principle.howToApply: On the next piece, set the ground before the type: choose one honest material or limitation — an uncoated/kraft texture, a single spot colour, a hand-torn or hand-scanned element, photography with its grain left in — and design so that one imperfection is the thing people remember, instead of reaching for gradients, glows and drop shadows. On a print listing piece that means one warm uncoated stock, one accent, a torn-edge photo crop; on screen, one textured ground and one colour that does all the emphasis.

entries.tagline: A very long product page that earns its length by letting you hear, watch and jump to every feature instead of just reading about it.
entries.summary: Ableton sells a music-making tool, and the Live 12 page behaves like one: nearly every feature block carries an embedded audio demo or a short film of someone actually using the software at a real desk. The visual system is unusually disciplined for a page this long — paper white and a pale sage green alternate as section panels, photography is honest lived-in studio clutter (cables, drum kits, tape), and one blue is reserved exclusively for links and CTAs. An in-page 'Jump to:' table of contents names the three feature chapters up front, so a 40,000-pixel scroll never feels unmapped. Caveat: the page is heavy, and on slow connections the lazy-loaded media makes the tail of the scroll pop in late.
whatWorks: Hero headline with one rotating word in a white pill — 'Find your rhythm / thing / spark again and again in Ableton Live' — the variable word IS the value prop, and the pill makes the mechanic visible
Audio demos embedded beside each new instrument (Meld, Roar, Granulator III): proof in the product's own medium, not adjectives about sound
One interactive colour: a single blue used only for links and the Buy button, so every affordance is findable on white or sage panels
Honest studio photography — real desks, coiled cables, a mug on a book stack — the product shown inside a musician's actual mess, not a rendered void
'Jump to:' mini table of contents under the highlights film names the three chapters (Play freely / Surprise yourself / Work more intuitively) before asking you to scroll them
The 12.4 free-update banner sits on its own green panel directly under the hero — existing customers get their news without diluting the buy pitch

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Full-bleed photo of a modest home studio, headline set over it with the rotating word in a white pill, single blue 'Buy now', plus a corner tab for rent-to-own — the financing objection handled in the hero without a second CTA competing.

sections.name: Live 12.4 update banner
sections.notes: Pale green panel: 'Live 12.4 is here. A free update for all Live 12 users…' with one 'See what's new' link. Serves current owners in one stripe so the rest of the page can sell to newcomers.

sections.name: Highlights film + jump links
sections.notes: A captioned overview video, then 'Find out what's possible in Live 12' with a 'Jump to:' row naming the three feature chapters — an in-page TOC that maps the long scroll before it starts.

sections.name: Play freely with ideas
sections.notes: Sage panel, giant geometric-sans chapter title, then MIDI Transformations/Generators shown as two-column text blocks under a demonstration film; UI screenshots appear only after the environment photo establishes context.

sections.name: Surprise yourself with sounds
sections.notes: New instruments and packs, each with an inline audio player — you audition Meld and Roar on the page. Pack cards sit in a responsive grid with consistent 'Go to pack' links.

sections.name: Work more intuitively
sections.notes: Workflow improvements (stacked views, browser tagging, Sound Similarity Search) shown as before/after style UI captures with short captions; ends with 'See all new features' as the bridge for people who want the exhaustive list elsewhere.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Newsletter capture, education/community columns, socials, language and location selectors, and 'Made in Berlin' as the sign-off — the brand's provenance used as the closing line.

principle.title: Prove the feature in the product's own medium
principle.explanation: A screenshot only proves a feature exists; a demo in the medium the product actually outputs proves what it does. Ableton doesn't describe what Roar sounds like — it plays it. The claim and the evidence collapse into one element, which is why the page can run this long without feeling like marketing.
principle.howToApply: Match the proof format to the deliverable: selling print collateral, embed a page-flip or a zoomable PDF spread; selling video tours, autoplay a muted 5-second loop; selling a workflow, show the before/after in one crop. If the proof isn't in the output medium, it's an adjective.

entries.category: OOH / DOOH billboard (integrated TV + digital campaign)
entries.tagline: A two-colour sentence template where the brand name is always the punchline: '[your tedious habit] … oder aber — Uber.'
entries.when: Launched May 18, 2026 in Germany — Serviceplan's first campaign as Uber's new lead agency; posted on Ads of the World August 2026
entries.summary: Serviceplan built Uber Germany's whole platform out of one grammatical joke: 'oder aber' is a redundant German connector meaning 'or alternatively', and it almost rhymes with Uber. Each execution sets the tedious status quo in green ('Hop on hop off hop on hop off hop on…'), then resolves in white: 'oder aber — Uber.' The billboard shown was placed where actual hop-on-hop-off sightseeing buses pass, so the context supplies the first half of the argument. No photography, no product shot — black field, two type colours, and a sentence structure that can generate a new ad for any situation and any city.
whatWorks: The line is a template, not a slogan — swap the green half ('Late to the game…', 'Hop on hop off…') and the campaign scales infinitely without redesign
Colour does the argument's work: green = the painful habit, white = the resolution, so the structure reads before the German does
The brand name is the last word and the answer — you can't remember the joke without remembering the product
Contextual placement completes the ad: the billboard sits beside the real sightseeing bus it mocks, letting the street be the visual
Total restraint — black background, one typeface (Uber Move), no imagery, one tiny legal line — nothing competes with the sentence
The em-dash pause ('oder aber — Uber') builds in the comic beat; the typography times the delivery

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The green first line names a tedious routine in its own droning rhythm — 'Hop on hop off hop on hop off' literally loops like the bus ride does — and the real bus driving past the billboard is the co-star.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'oder aber' — a deliberately redundant German connector — sets up the alternative; the redundancy itself mirrors the wasted effort of the habit being replaced.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: There is no hero image: black field, Uber Move type in green and white, generous bottom whitespace. The sentence IS the visual, and the two-colour split is the layout.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: No button, no URL — the brand name in white functions as the call to action, with only a small legal disclaimer beneath. On DOOH the resolution lands as the loop's final frame.

principle.title: Write one sentence template where the brand is always the punchline
principle.explanation: A slogan is one ad; a sentence structure is an ad factory. By fixing the second half ('oder aber — Uber') and leaving the first half as a fill-in-the-blank for any tedious situation, the campaign gets endless executions, contextual placements, and a mnemonic that ends on the product's name every single time.
principle.howToApply: For a brand line, build the format '[the painful default] … or — [brand/offer]' with a fixed colour split: muted colour for the problem clause, brand colour or white for the resolution. Test it by writing ten first-halves in ten minutes — if they all work without touching the layout, the template holds.

entries.tagline: The pop-art nun who turned supermarket slogans into serigraphs — and turned looking itself into a teachable method.
entries.summary: Sister Mary Corita Kent ran the art department at Immaculate Heart College in Los Angeles, where her classroom became an avant-garde magnet (John Cage and the Eameses passed through). Self-taught in screenprinting from a mail-order kit, she appropriated vernacular advertising — Wonder Bread dots, General Mills' 'the big G stands for goodness' — and recombined it with scripture and poetry until the slogans meant something else entirely. Her fluorescent serigraphs were printed cheap and sold cheap on principle. The image here is her 1971 Rainbow Swash on a Boston gas tank — still the largest copyrighted artwork in the world — since no freely licensed portrait of her exists.
whatWorks: Carry a 'finder' — an empty cardboard frame or slide mount — and crop the ordinary world into compositions before ever sitting down to design
Assign volume before quality: 200 drawings, or hours of drawing without looking down — quantity is the price of one good eye
Physically maul the source material: tear, crumple, and re-photograph found type so it stops being a logo and becomes a shape with a history
Recontextualize instead of inventing — put an ad slogan next to a scripture line and let the collision produce the meaning
Separate making from judging as a scheduled discipline, not a mood — create first, analyze in a different session
Choose media that keep the work cheap to multiply; accessibility is a design decision, not a distribution afterthought

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: Not at the desk — on the street with a finder. Kent and her students cropped billboards, gas-station signage and grocery lettering through a small empty frame, harvesting fragments of the vernacular as raw compositional material before any brief-specific work started.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Appropriation and recombination: take commercial language everyone already knows, physically manipulate it (tear, warp, re-photograph), then splice it with scripture, Rilke or newspaper text so the familiar words are forced to carry a second meaning. The audience's existing memory of the slogan does half the communicative work.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Flat fluorescent serigraphs with hand-wrenched type — colour laid in saturated unmixed fields, letterforms bent and crowded until they read as image first, text second. Screenprinting kept editions cheap, fast to iterate, and affordable to own.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Codified in the famous Immaculate Heart Art Department Rules: 'The only rule is work — if you work it will lead to something,' 'Consider everything an experiment,' and the crucial Rule 8 — 'Don't try to create and analyze at the same time. They're different processes.' Judgment is real but scheduled; it never sits in the room while the making happens.

principle.title: Crop the world with a finder before you design
principle.explanation: Kent's compositions started as acts of looking, not drawing: a cheap cardboard frame isolated fragments of the everyday until they became layout. Sourcing raw material from the environment — cropped, decontextualized, collected in volume — means you never start a layout from a blank artboard or a stock-asset search.
principle.howToApply: Build a fragment library the way Kent did: crop tight, fixed-ratio details out of your own project photography — door hardware, tile joints, signage letters, fabric edges — and keep them as a swipe file. When a page needs texture or a hero needs a graphic element, pull from the cropped fragments of the actual subject instead of decoration invented from nothing.

entries.tagline: A property agency homepage that opens with today's story instead of a search box, and lets four facts and one photograph sell each house.
entries.summary: The Modern House sells design-led UK homes, and the site is built like a magazine that happens to transact. There is no search bar, no map, no filter panel above the fold — the fold is a single dated editorial slot ('Today at The Modern House') pointing at one hand-picked house. Below it, three galleries (Prime, New, Featured) present properties as photograph plus four data points — house name, place, price, tenure — with no badges, no agent headshots and no 'Enquire' buttons on the cards, so the photography and the naming carry all the persuasion. The whole palette is paper white, warm cream and black; every drop of colour in the page comes from the property photography itself. Caveat: buyers who arrive knowing they want three beds in Hackney under £1m have to go hunting — the search affordance is a single word in the top-right corner.
whatWorks: The homepage hero is a dated editorial slot, not a search box: eyebrow 'TODAY AT THE MODERN HOUSE' over one serif headline ('Tale of Two: an exceptional house beside Highgate Cemetery in north London') and a single outlined 'VIEW SALES LISTING' button — one house, chosen today, treated as news

Listing cards carry exactly four facts in two lines — name + place on the left, price + tenure right-aligned opposite them ('Heriot / Haslemere, Surrey' → '£2,650,000 / Freehold') — no badges, no beds/baths icon row, no CTA; the restraint is what makes them read as objects rather than inventory
Every house has a NAME set in serif above its location — Seven Whistlers, Chestnut Cottage II, The Old Vicarage — so the grid scans as a collection of characters instead of addresses

Two type roles only, used with total discipline: a transitional serif for names, prices, headlines and press quotes; widely letterspaced sans small caps for nav, section labels ('PRIME', 'NEW', 'FEATURED', 'PAST SALES') and every button

Zero brand accent colour — paper white, warm cream panels and black. Section changes are signalled by swapping the ground, and one band's edge is cut on a diagonal, so the page has rhythm without a single tinted button

The seller pitch is interleaved between buyer galleries as full-width black quote bands — '“One of the 100 Best Things in the World” — GQ' above 'HOW MUCH IS MY HOME WORTH?' — borrowing press credibility to ask for the appraisal instead of asserting it themselves
Sold work is shown, not hidden: a 'PAST SALES' gallery with a SOLD corner label where the price would be, which turns the archive into proof of the kind of house they get

sections.name: Nav
sections.notes: Three intents on the left (BUY / SELL / PRIME), centred letterspaced wordmark, and JOURNAL / NEWSLETTER / ALERTS / SEARCH on the right. The editorial arm sits at the same level as the transactional one, and 'ALERTS' quietly does the lead capture that a filter panel would.

sections.name: Hero — today's house
sections.notes: Split layout: a full-bleed interior photograph (a dark reflective splashback, bookshelves, tulips — a detail, not a wide-angle room) occupies about two thirds, with a cream panel beside it holding the dated eyebrow, a three-line serif headline and one outlined button. Choosing a house per day makes the homepage worth revisiting and signals curation before any copy claims it.

sections.name: Prime / New / Featured galleries
sections.notes: Three near-identical three-up rows, each with a small centred label and a right-aligned outlined 'VIEW ALL …' button. Same card template throughout, so the only variables are the photograph and the four facts — the segmentation (Prime = top of market, New = fresh, Featured = editor's pick) is doing merchandising work that filters would otherwise have to do.

sections.name: Black press band + seller CTA
sections.notes: A full-width black stripe with a one-line press quote in serif and an outlined 'HOW MUCH IS MY HOME WORTH?' button, its lower edge sliced on a diagonal into the next cream section. The tonal flip plus the angled cut makes the one commercial ask on the page impossible to scroll past without registering it.

sections.name: Past sales
sections.notes: Same card grid, images tagged SOLD in the top-left, and the word 'Sold' replacing the price in the right-hand column — no numbers, no bragging. It reads as portfolio, and it's the strongest argument to a seller on the page.

sections.name: Testimonial stack over full-bleed photography
sections.notes: Two press quotes with attributions in italic (Evening Standard, then Gentleman's Journal) — the second set in white over a full-bleed kitchen photograph with 'ABOUT US' beneath. Quote → CTA, quote → CTA: proof and ask are paired rather than pooled in a logo strip.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Black, four columns — ABOUT, CONTACT, newsletter subscribe with an explicit consent checkbox, and FOLLOW US icons. Trust marks (The Property Ombudsman, Trading Standards Approved Code, Zoopla, Rightmove) sit on the bottom line, and a link points to their sister brand Inigo for period houses — regulated-industry credentials and portfolio cross-sell handled without disturbing the editorial tone above.

principle.title: Open the homepage with today's pick, not the search box
principle.explanation: A search field says 'we have inventory, go dig.' A dated editorial slot — one property, chosen today, written up like a story — says someone with taste has already done the digging, and it makes the homepage worth returning to tomorrow. Curation is claimed by every agency and proved by almost none; a visible date is the cheapest proof there is.
principle.howToApply: On the Aperture homepage, give the fold a single dated slot — eyebrow 'Today at Aperture', one photograph, the house's name and a one-line reason it's worth seeing, one outlined button to the listing — and push search to a word in the top-right nav. Rotate it on a weekday cadence you can actually sustain, and keep the collection grids beneath it on one card template: name, place, price, one fact, nothing else.

site.name: Etagi — 'Go home!' (branded red cards in live football)

entries.category: Ambient media / branded content inside a live sports broadcast (+ social amplification)
entries.tagline: The real-estate brand printed its message on the referee's red card — an object whose existing meaning is already 'go home'.
entries.when: Launched May 2026 in Russia, during the WINLINE Media League football season; posted to Ads of the World in August 2026
entries.summary: Agency Soda found a piece of media nobody was selling: in football, a red card sends a player home, and 'home' is the product of the real estate agency Etagi. They partnered with the WINLINE Media League and reprinted the referees' red cards with 'GO HOME!' plus the Etagi logo and etagi.com — so every send-off, and then every highlight reel, commentary clip and outraged fan post about it, carried the ad. The case board claims over 6,000,000 views, 30+ media and Telegram mentions and 5,000+ reactions on a 500,000₽ production budget, with no media buy at all. The honest caveat: the frequency is in the referees' hands, so this is a stunt that borrows attention rather than a channel you can plan.
whatWorks: The medium already carries the message: the raised-card gesture means 'you're going home' before a single word is read, so the brand line needs no set-up
Two words do everything — 'GO HOME!' is simultaneously the referee's ruling and a property ad, and the pun only works on this exact object
The buy is a prop, not an impression: money went into printing cards instead of buying the commercial break, and the placement is unskippable because it's inside the play
It lands at peak attention — a send-off is the loudest moment in a match, when every camera and every phone is already pointed at the card
It self-distributes: highlights, screenshots and arguments about the decision re-run the ad for free, which is why 6M views cost 500,000₽
The creative is one flat red field, condensed white caps and the logo with the URL under it — anything more would be illegible at broadcast distance

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The referee's arm goes up. The stadium and the broadcast are already staring at the card — the campaign didn't create the attention moment, it rented one that recurs a few times a night and never gets skipped.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'GO HOME!' — the sport's meaning and the advertiser's offer are the same two words, which is the whole idea. The case film stretches it into a chant ('GO HOOOME!'), matching how the crowd actually says it.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: There is no layout to speak of: the standard-issue red rectangle, white condensed caps, the etagi wordmark and etagi.com beneath. Held at arm's length on a 4K broadcast, legibility is the only design requirement, and the familiar red is the brand recognition.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: Just the URL on the card. The real call to action is the gesture itself — the recall device is a thing viewers will see again next match, with or without the brand present.

principle.title: Brand the object that already means your message
principle.explanation: Most ads have to build the meaning they need before they can sell against it, which is what the first three seconds are usually spent on. If you can find an object or ritual already inside your audience's attention whose meaning IS your pitch, the set-up is free — and because the object is part of the event rather than a break in it, nobody can skip it or scroll past.
principle.howToApply: List the physical objects already present at the moment your buyer decides — the open-house sign-in card, the key tag, the SOLD rider, the lockbox, the champagne label at closing — and pick the one whose existing meaning is your offer. Brand that object with two words and a URL, at a size that reads in a phone photo, before commissioning any new creative.

entries.category: Branding studio network — studio operating model (Studio Monday)
entries.when: Founded 1993 · Brussels — now New York, Brussels, Geneva, Melbourne and Saigon
entries.tagline: A studio that refused to become one big studio — five small ones instead — and that redesigned its own company the way it redesigns a client's.
entries.summary: Base was started in Brussels in 1993 by Thierry Brunfaut, Dimitri Jeurissen and Juliette Cavenaile, and grew into what it calls 'one network, five studios, a company of cultures' — Brussels, New York, Geneva, Melbourne, Saigon, plus a digital team — doing cultural and commercial identity work with a stated bias toward substance: 'less decoration, more meaning', brands built as 'living systems: resilient, adaptive'. The part worth stealing is not the work but the operating model. Brunfaut is candid that the partners 'made ALL the possible mistakes you can make while running a creative business' before deciding to redesign Base itself, installing deliberate processes and rituals; his 5-Minute Poster series — roughly fifty typographic maxims, each made in a maximum of 300 seconds — is the same instinct at personal scale. Their public homepage is a live FEED that mixes client work, unfinished internal 'BASE_TEST' experiments and press clippings in one grid.
whatWorks: Treat your own practice as a client: write the brief for how the studio works (rituals, hand-offs, who talks to the client) and redesign it deliberately instead of letting it accrete
Timebox the idea before you craft it — 300 seconds, type only, one thought per poster — so weak concepts die cheap and the good one has to survive without technique
Keep a running public feed where tests and unfinished experiments sit beside finished projects; the archive becomes the marketing and the studio's thinking stays visible
Put the makers in the room: 'You work directly with the makers — strategists, designers, technologists. No middle layers'
Stay small on purpose and multiply instead of scaling — several small studios that learn from each other beat one large one that averages out
Design identities as adaptive systems with rules for change, not a locked logo sheet — the deliverable is behaviour under new conditions
Collect the maxims as you work: Brunfaut jots the lines that surface in meetings and while designing, and those notes become the posters

sections.name: How it's structured
sections.notes: Five permanent studios plus a digital team, each partner-led and culturally local, described as 'a network that learns from itself' rather than head office and branches. Growth happened by opening another small studio instead of enlarging the first one, which keeps every office at a size where the partners still touch the work.

sections.name: How they take on work
sections.notes: Direct contact between client and makers — no account layer between the brief and the people executing it — and a strategy step framed as cultural reading: get 'to what makes it real, then give it form with honesty and personality'. Cultural clients (museums, festivals, institutions) sit deliberately alongside commercial ones, and each keeps the other honest.

sections.name: Signature method
sections.notes: Reduction under a clock. The 5-Minute Poster series is the purest form: a hard 300-second limit, black type on white, one piece of design wisdom per sheet. Working that fast forces the concept to carry the piece, and the constraint makes producing fifty of them possible — volume and reduction from the same rule.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: 'Less decoration, more meaning' is used as a test, not a slogan — if an element is not carrying meaning it comes off. Identities are judged on whether they stay iconic while adapting, so the question at review is 'does this survive being stretched, animated, translated and handed to someone else?' rather than 'is this beautiful today?'. And when the studio itself stops working, that's a design problem with a brief.

principle.title: Timebox the concept, then judge it before you craft it
principle.explanation: Craft hides weak ideas — an hour of typesetting can make an empty thought look considered, and then you're attached to it. A hard five-minute limit produces something honest: black type, one thought, no technique to hide behind. It also makes volume possible, and volume is what lets you throw the first six away.
principle.howToApply: Before designing any page or piece of collateral, set a 5-minute timer and make one type-only slide stating the single idea — no images, no colour, one line of copy. Do five, pin them side by side, and only start real layout on the one that still reads as an idea at that size. Keep a running note of the sharp lines that come out of client calls; they're the next batch of prompts.

entries.tagline: A paint shop that sells colour by showing other people's real, half-finished rooms — and puts the exact shade name on a little tab over every single photograph.
entries.summary: Backdrop runs a black-and-white typographic chassis (letterspaced all-caps grotesque, square black buttons, hairline rules, zero brand colour) so that every colour on the page comes from the product itself. The whole page is built as one loop — choose a colour, stick a sample on the wall, get the box delivered — and it closes that loop by tagging each room photograph with the shade in it, from a small pill on editorial images (a dot of the colour plus 'SELF-PORTRAIT', 'ROAD TO TODOS SANTOS') to white tabs across the customer gallery ('DISCO NAP', 'DARK ARTS', 'CHAMPAGNE BONFIRE'). The imagery is unusually honest for the category: macro shots of the actual wallcovering curling off a cobalt ground, a hand re-sticking a 12×12" swatch, and a wall mid-job with branded blue tape, plywood and a dust sheet still down. Honest caveat: the review block is the one place proof is only asserted — a headline, four adjectives and a 'SEE REVIEWS' button, with not one review or rating on the page — and the long gallery lazy-loads slowly enough that grey tiles are visible on first scroll.
whatWorks: Every photograph names its product: a colour dot + shade name in a small pill on editorial shots, a white tab on each customer-room tile — inspiration and catalogue are the same layout
Zero brand accent colour. Nav, buttons, rules and type are black on white, so the only saturated things on screen are paint, wallpaper and rooms

The hero is split 50/50 between an extreme macro of the material (terracotta wallcovering curling over cobalt) and a product still-life on a plinth — texture first, then the object, with no lifestyle model in sight

A three-panel numbered path (1 FIND YOUR COLOR / 2 TRY THE SAMPLES / 3 MAKE IT YOURS), each panel one image plus three lines that name the mechanic — '12×12" adhesive swatches stick and re-stick' rather than 'easy sampling'
In-progress imagery: taped-off walls, plywood, dust sheets, a hand holding a swatch. The mess is shown rather than styled away, which makes the finished rooms believable

Collaborations are pitched by naming the four SKUs outright (IRISH GREEN, RIVIERA BLUE, SPEED YELLOW, RUBY STAR) instead of describing the partnership, and the rug editorial credits its photographer in 6pt inside the image
Copy voice does the differentiating where the layout stays neutral — 'DO YOU HAPPEN TO HAVE ANY WALLS?' as a section headline, 'Guess work free. Hassle free.'

sections.name: Utility bar + nav
sections.notes: A single black strip carries one rotating message ('Enjoy fast standard shipping and easy returns', 'Now shipping to Canada!') with a dismiss ×. The nav is six words — PAINT, WALLCOVERINGS, RUGS, RESOURCES, INSPO, REVIEWS — in letterspaced caps, with search and a cart count right-aligned. Behind it a repeating BACKDROP wordmark marquee runs as a graphic band, so the header does branding without a logo lockup taking vertical space. The mega-menus are where the real depth sits (paint by colour, wallcoverings by style, by designer, by scale, by application), which keeps a 13,000-word catalogue out of the homepage.

sections.name: Hero (split material / product)
sections.notes: Left half is a full-bleed macro: a sheet of terracotta wallcovering curling off a cobalt field, lit so you can read the weave. Right half is white, with a small still-life of three paint cans on a plinth against an oxblood wall flecked with painted confetti, then 'PREMIUM PAINT & WALLCOVERINGS' in two lines of caps, one subhead sentence that ends on a place ('handcrafted artwork in our studio in Downtown LA'), and two equally weighted black buttons — SHOP PAINT / SHOP WALLCOVERINGS. No price, no email capture, no offer. The fold's job is to state the two categories and show what the goods physically look like.

sections.name: 1–2–3 how it works
sections.notes: Three equal columns divided by hairlines, each headed by a numbered black disc: FIND YOUR COLOR shows a 12-dot swatch grid with the shade name typeset under each dot; TRY THE SAMPLES shows a hand pressing a 12×12" peel-and-stick swatch onto a blue wall; MAKE IT YOURS shows the branded box being carried. Copy under each is three short lines naming the mechanic and the objection it kills (waste, mess, guesswork). This is the whole business model as one scannable row, sitting immediately under the fold.

sections.name: Collections & collaborations
sections.notes: Three stacked editorial blocks in the same template — big room photograph one side, headline + paragraph + one black button the other, alternating sides. ARCHIVE opens with a question ('DO YOU HAPPEN TO HAVE ANY WALLS?') and earns credibility by sourcing the designs from F. Schumacher & Co.'s 135-year archive; PORSCHE X BACKDROP names its four limited colours; RUGS ARE HERE explains the Charlap Hyman & Herrero collection and its material (100% Abaca). Each block has exactly one CTA, and the room photos carry the colour-name pill in the top corner.

sections.name: Brand statement + proof
sections.notes: A type-only panel — 'IT'S NOT JUST PAINT, IT'S YOUR BACKDROP' set left on white — pairs with a full-bleed portrait: a woman in red on an oxblood wall holding the paint box, clothing tuned to the wall so the colour reads twice. Then the reviews block, 'DON'T TAKE OUR WORD FOR IT, TAKE THEIRS', and a row of press mastheads (AD, Vogue, The New York Times, Dwell, The Cut) set in their own logotypes, black on white, evenly spaced. The mastheads do the trust work here; the review block itself only points at proof rather than showing any.

sections.name: Customer gallery grid
sections.notes: A dense masonry grid of real rooms — a green Calder-ish living room, a yellow kitchen, a striped bedroom, a near-black hallway — each tile wearing a small white tab naming the shade (SURF CAMP, PALINDROME – SKY, DISCO NAP, GAMBIT PANEL – TEAL & EARTHY BROWN). It reads as an Instagram feed and functions as a product index, and it ends with a single centred EXPLORE THE GALLERY button rather than a CTA per tile.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Black, five columns — SHOP / INFORMATION / COMPANY / TRADE / COMMUNITY — where COMMUNITY links out to sister brands (Schumacher, Patterson Flynn, Frederic Magazine) and INFORMATION quietly carries the practical tools (Paint Calculator, How To's, Fan Decks). 'Stay in the loop.' is an underline-only input with no incentive attached, the Climate Label certification appears as a lockup, and the copyright discloses the parent ('a division of F. Schumacher & Co.') instead of hiding it.

principle.title: Put the product's name on every photograph
principle.explanation: Inspiration imagery normally dead-ends: a viewer falls for a room, a wall colour or a styled shot and has no way to act on it without a search. Backdrop closes that gap with the cheapest possible component — a small tab or a dot-plus-name pill over the corner of each image — which turns a scroll-through gallery into a browsable catalogue and quietly proves that every photo on the site is of a real product in a real room, not stock.
principle.howToApply: On listing and collection pages, give every image a small caption chip naming the specific thing it shows — the finish, the shade, the fabric, the neighbourhood, the unit number — and make the chip the link to that item. For Aperture: tag gallery shots with the actual room or material ('Primary bath — honed Carrara', 'Unit 401D — terrace'), and let the collection grid double as the index instead of adding a separate list.

site.name: Tesco Ireland — 'That's Every Little Helps' (OOH / social key visuals)

entries.category: OOH & social key visual (illustrated badge series)
entries.tagline: A 30-year-old slogan re-earned by turning it into a pile of hand-drawn enamel badges, each one crediting a specific project, colleague or number.
entries.when: Launched August 2026 · Ireland (BBH Dublin; integrated across TV, OOH incl. a Luas wrap, cinema, radio, social, Clubcard and in-store)
entries.summary: Instead of restating 'Every little helps', BBH Dublin made the slogan additive: each key visual is a cluster of illustrated pin badges — 'COOL TO BE IN COOLMINE SC', 'ADOPT A FRIEND IN CORK DAWG', 'ABACAS SCHOOL SENSORY GARDEN', a hand-lettered '27,000 IRISH COMMUNITY PROJECTS AND COUNTING', a colleague badge simply reading 'Peadar' — piled on a plain white ground beside one plain-spoken blue headline ('27,000 Irish projects supported. Not bad for a little blue token.'). Because the badges are visibly drawn by different hands, the proof looks collected rather than art-directed, and the format scales: one badge per fact means a new execution is a new pile, not a new idea. The strapline is demoted to a small handwritten 'THAT'S Every little helps' above the logo, so the claim arrives before the brand does.
whatWorks: One badge = one verifiable fact, named: a club, a school garden, a colleague's first name, a number with 'and counting' after it — specificity is the whole creative device
A number in the headline paired with a self-deprecating second sentence ('Not bad for a little blue token') — the brag is offset by a joke about its own currency
Illustration by many different hands (commissioned Irish illustrators), so the cluster reads as evidence collected over time rather than one designer's set
White ground, no photography, no gradient: the badges are the only colour, which is why they survive being a bus shelter, a 48-sheet and a 1:1 feed crop
The strapline is the smallest type in the layout, set in a handwritten script and used as a caption to the proof rather than the headline
One composition template — badge pile left, three-line headline right, script line + logo bottom-right — that stretches to a long wall wrap by simply spacing the pile out along it

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A heap of badges with the tactile specificity of a jacket lapel — smiley faces, kids' drawings, hand-lettering, a rainbow, a Tesco Community Fund star. At bus-shelter distance it reads as one colourful blob against white; at arm's length it rewards you with individual names, which is exactly the right two-speed read for OOH that gets re-photographed for social.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: Three short lines in Tesco blue, left-aligned in the white space beside the pile: '27,000 Irish projects supported. Not bad for a little blue token.' A hard number does the persuading and the second sentence does the tone; the sister execution swaps in a different pairing ('We all love Irish apples, so we've backed Irish orchards') on the same grid, proving the template.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: The badges themselves are the hero — photographed or rendered with soft drop shadows so they read as physical objects sitting on the poster, not as flat vector stickers. No shopper, no store, no product shot. Each badge is a different illustrator's mark, so the visual variety is the argument: many small helps from many different people.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: There isn't one, and that's the point — no offer, no URL, no QR. Bottom right sits the handwritten 'THAT'S Every little helps' and the Tesco logo in a white rounded panel; the ask is brand memory, and the proof (a number you can check) is what's supposed to stick instead of a click.

principle.title: Make the slogan additive: one proof object per fact
principle.explanation: A brand promise that has been repeated for decades stops being read. Re-earning it works better than restating it, and the cheapest way is to design a repeatable proof unit — a badge, a stamp, a tag, a card — where each instance carries one named, checkable specific. The unit gives you infinite executions on one layout, and the visible variety (many hands, many names) does the persuading that a single polished asset can't.
principle.howToApply: Pick the vaguest claim in your marketing ('local expertise', 'full-service', 'we care about the neighbourhood') and turn it into a series of small badge-like objects, one per verifiable specific — a street sold, a school district, a vendor you use by name, a number with a date on it. Design one composition (object cluster left, three-line headline right, brand small and bottom-right) and generate new units by swapping the pile, not the layout. For Aperture, that's a proof chip set — '48 sales in Chapel Hill since 2019', 'photography by Ana', 'staged by …' — reusable across postcards, story ads and the listing page.

entries.category: Poster design / wartime & public information graphics
entries.tagline: Britain's official war poster designer, who built a career on one working rule: maximum meaning, minimum means — and tested every idea at the size of a postage stamp.
entries.summary: Games designed roughly a hundred posters as the British War Office's official poster designer, then the 1951 Festival of Britain emblem, the BBC's first moving television symbol (1954), and campaigns for El Al, Guinness and BEA. His method was ruthlessly compressive: fuse two images into a single symbol the viewer has to complete themselves — 'I wind the spring and the public, in looking at the poster, will have that spring released in its mind.' He worked alone, without assistants or a studio to delegate to, taught at the Royal College of Art from 1946 to 1953, and would resign a job and recommend another designer rather than dilute a solution he believed in.
whatWorks: Work small first: 20–30 stamp-sized roughs before anything is drawn at size, on the rule that if it doesn't work an inch high it will never work
Synthesise rather than pick — take the two or three strongest roughs and fuse them into one image, instead of choosing a favourite and polishing it
Build the idea as a single fused symbol (two things becoming one) so the viewer completes the thought and remembers doing it
Keep a reference library of your own photographs and clippings, so the raw material for a compression is already on hand when the brief lands
Budget the means, not just the meaning: few colours, flat planes, one geometric transition doing the work — 'maximum meaning, minimum means'
Own the standard: be willing to hand the job to someone else rather than execute a compromised version of it

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: Not with layout but with volume at miniature scale. Games would produce up to thirty small pencil roughs for a single poster, working postage-stamp size deliberately so that composition, contrast and the idea itself had to survive without detail. His test was brutal and useful: designs that 'don't work an inch high will never work'. He drew on an accumulated stock of his own photographic reference rather than hunting for imagery after the brief arrived.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Compression by fusion. Rather than illustrate a message, he looked for two images that could become one — a soldier and his own shadow, a profile and a helmet, a compass point and Britannia's head for the Festival of Britain — so a single mark carried the whole argument. He then synthesised the final design out of two or three of his roughs, treating them as parts rather than candidates. His stated aim was to wind a spring in the image so the release happens in the viewer's mind, which means deliberately leaving the last step of the thought for them to take.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Airbrush and gouache, flat planes, hard-edged geometric transitions and dramatic figure/ground reversals, with colour rationed to a few flats — partly a wartime printing constraint that he turned into a house style. He executed everything himself, alone: no assistants, no studio machine, which kept the compression discipline intact from thumbnail through to finished art, and made a hundred wartime posters a matter of sustained personal craft rather than delegation.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: 'Maximum meaning, minimum means' was the working test applied to every element: anything that didn't add meaning had to justify its cost in attention. One poster carried one thought. If a client wanted the solution weakened, he would step aside and recommend another designer rather than execute it — his standard sat above the individual commission. Teaching at the RCA (1946–53) forced the method into transmissible rules, which is why it still reads as a process rather than a style.

principle.title: Judge the idea at an inch, then fuse the best two
principle.explanation: Working small strips away everything a design can hide behind — detail, texture, gradient, clever type — and leaves only composition and idea. Twenty or thirty thumbnails cost minutes each, so the format encourages quantity, and the inch-high test kills anything that needs size to make sense. Fusing the two strongest roughs (rather than picking a winner and refining it) forces the compression that makes an image memorable, because a fused symbol asks the viewer to complete it.
principle.howToApply: Before opening the artboard for a cover, flyer or hero, fill one sheet with 20–30 boxes an inch wide and draw a different composition in each — greyscale, no type smaller than a headline. Photograph the sheet, look at it on your phone, and delete anything you can't read. Then take the two best and force them into one image (the pool becoming the floorplan, the key becoming the front door) rather than refining the favourite. Same test at the end: shrink the finished piece to an inch — if the idea disappears, the idea was the detail.

entries.tagline: An ad-free ecology magazine that files its homepage under the reader's verbs — Read: / Listen: / Watch: — and keeps the deks in the empty left margin until you hover.
entries.summary: Emergence Magazine publishes essays, audio and film about ecology, culture and spirituality, and the homepage is organised the way a reader behaves rather than the way a CMS stores things. Three registers run down the page, each announced by a two-word verb in the left margin — 'Read:', 'Listen:', 'Watch:' — with a 3-up grid of cards hugged to the right two-thirds; the enormous left column is not empty decoration, it is where a card's one-sentence description appears when you hover it. Everything else is held to almost nothing: one type family (GT America, with its mono cut for the tiny letterspaced labels), no brand accent colour, no ads, and section breaks signalled only by swapping the ground from white to near-black to warm bone. The one honest caveat is that the discipline costs discovery — a first-time visitor sees eighteen cards and no way to browse by subject, and the hover-only deks mean a phone reader gets titles and bylines alone.
whatWorks: Sections are labelled with the reader's verb, not the content type: 'Read:', 'Listen:', 'Watch:' set small in the left margin — the taxonomy is what you'll be doing, so essays, interviews and films can all use one card template

The empty left third is a working component, not air: hovering any card writes that story's one-sentence dek into the margin, so the grid stays three quiet images and three titles until you ask for more
Every card declares its medium before its title with a mono, letterspaced ~10px eyebrow — ESSAY / POEM / CONVERSATION / FILM / FEATURE — in a grey that sits below the title in contrast
The byline is part of the title line, not a metadata row: 'Five Hundred Words by Marie Mutsuki Mockett', with the author's name in mid-grey so credit is given without a second element

The hero has no photograph at all — an audio feature ('50 Seasonal Meditations') gets a grainy iridescent field of silver, cyan, periwinkle and mint, because there is nothing honest to photograph about listening
Section breaks are ground swaps, not rules or headings: white → near-black for the print edition → white for the editorial statement → warm bone (#F4F2ED) for Engage
Commerce is quarantined into one small grey card beside the photograph of the actual printed book — title, '$40.00', 'PRE-ORDER NOW' — and nothing else on the page sells anything

One family does the whole page (GT America, plus GT America Mono for labels); the Bradford serif is held back for the reading pages and the print edition, so the homepage reads as an index and the article reads as a magazine

sections.name: Masthead / nav
sections.notes: Centred wordmark with the mission line 'Connecting the threads between ecology, culture, and spirituality' sitting directly under it, four destinations to one side (Engage / Print / Podcast / Store) and 'Stories' plus 'Menu' to the other. The tagline in the masthead does the work an about page usually does — by the time you scroll you already know the subject.

sections.name: Hero — the feature slot
sections.notes: A full-bleed grainy gradient field with a small 'FEATURE' chip, the title '50 Seasonal Meditations', the line 'An Emergence Magazine Production', a three-line dek and one ghost button, 'Open Feature'. It's a fold given to a single made thing rather than to the newest story, and the abstract field signals 'this is audio' without a stock photo of headphones.

sections.name: Print edition
sections.notes: A near-black band holding a photograph of the actual book — open spread, pages curling, shot on a dark ground so the paper glows — with 'VOLUME 7: SEEDS AND STRUCTURES' and a three-line description at top left, and a small grey commerce card at right ($40.00 / PRE-ORDER NOW). Photographing the object rather than rendering a mockup is the whole argument for buying it.

sections.name: Editorial statement
sections.notes: White, one tiny label ('EDITORIAL STATEMENT') and roughly forty words set at the same size as everything else: 'We believe it has always been a radical act to share stories during dark times…' No pull-quote styling, no oversized display type — the mission is stated at body size, which reads as conviction rather than marketing.

sections.name: Read: / Listen: / Watch:
sections.notes: Three near-identical registers, each a two-word verb in the left margin and a 3-up card grid on the right (six essays and a poem; three audio conversations with Terry Tempest Williams, Suzanne Simard and a three-way; three films). Hover a card and its dek is written into the margin beside the verb. Because the eyebrow declares the medium, the same card serves an essay, an interview and a film — one component, three registers.

sections.name: Engage
