sections.notes: A warm bone band with 'E N G A G E' widely letterspaced in the left margin and the event centred: title, venue on its own line ('Whidbey Institute, Washington State, US'), a hairline rule, then the date. The image card wears two pills — 'IN-PERSON RETREAT' and 'REGISTRATION OPEN' with a green dot — plus a 'DETAILS' button, and a 'NEXT' control steps through seven events from September to October 2026. Status as a pill on the card is how one carousel handles sold-out, open and announced without three layouts.

sections.name: Closing feature + footer
sections.notes: One more full-bleed feature ('Seasoning a Kid — A Search for a Practice of Place' by adam amir) with 'OPEN FEATURE', then a quiet footer: About, Pitches & Submissions, Engage, Newsletter, two social links, Terms / Privacy / Accessibility, and the line 'Emergence Magazine is an initiative of Kalliopeia Foundation.' The newsletter block states the funding model as a fact — 'We are an ad and subscription-free magazine' — which is the strongest trust signal on the page and costs one sentence.

principle.title: Label sections with the reader's verb, not your content type
principle.explanation: 'Articles', 'Videos', 'Podcasts', 'Case studies' are names for how you store things; 'Read:', 'Listen:', 'Watch:' are names for what the visitor is about to do. Verbs let a single card template carry every format (the small eyebrow does the format-declaring), they read in two words at the left edge of a wide layout, and they quietly promise a time commitment instead of a taxonomy. It also forces an honest question about each section: if you can't name the verb, the section may not be for the reader.
principle.howToApply: On an Aperture collection or journal page, replace the noun headings with verbs and keep one card template beneath each: 'Tour:' for the film and 3D walkthroughs, 'Read:' for the neighbourhood essays and press, 'See:' for the photography sets. Put the verb small in the left margin, let the grid sit in the right two-thirds, and use the empty margin for the hovered card's one-line dek so the grid itself stays photograph-plus-title. Give every card a mono eyebrow naming the format (FILM / ESSAY / FLOORPLAN / PRESS) and append the byline or agent name inline in grey rather than adding a metadata row.

site.name: Back Market — 'Downgrade Now' (digital OOH screens + social)

entries.category: Digital OOH (JCDecaux screens, Underground panels) + social, inside an integrated TV / VOD / audio campaign
entries.tagline: Sells refurbished tech by naming the stupidly ordinary thing you actually do with it — 'Your boss can't ping you here.' — and turns the category's verb upside down for the CTA.
entries.when: The 'Downgrade Now' platform launched globally in September 2024; this UK spring wave — six rotating executions across London and Birmingham — launched April 2026, alongside a wider push in the US, France, Spain and Germany
entries.summary: Back Market's in-house team under ECD Daniel Brill built a unit with three fixed parts: an absurdly specific human benefit as the headline, the product photographed dead centre, and one line of proof naming the exact model. 'Sprain your ankle in 5K' sits over a GoPro HERO11; 'Your boss can't ping you here' over a PlayStation 5; 'Fact check your mum, for less' over a MacBook Air M3 whose screen is showing a graduation-capped dog being solemnly verified. Everything is on one acid-highlighter yellow field with a serif headline, the italic landing on the price clause, and the lockup 'Downgrade now. ◁ Back Market' — so the call to action is also the positioning, in one word against a category that only ever says 'upgrade'. The honest caveat: the saving is a claim in a footnote ('based on the average selling price set by sellers…'), so the units ask you to take the money on trust while the joke does the selling.
whatWorks: The headline is a benefit no spec sheet would ever print — 'Your boss can't ping you here' for a console, 'Do hand stuff' for an iPad and Pencil — so the ad sells the ordinary act rather than the hardware

One acid yellow field does the media buying: a bus-shelter screen, a station totem and an Underground cross-track panel all read as the same brand at any distance, with no photography or texture competing

Three fixed parts, one variable: headline → product on plain ground → one proof line naming the model ('The PlayStation 5, refurbished by professionals, for way less than new.'). Six executions run without the layout moving
A serif headline with the italic falling on the offer clause ('for less.') marks the turn from joke to proposition inside one sentence
The category's verb is inverted and promoted to the CTA — 'Downgrade now.' — which makes the instruction and the positioning the same two words

The argument happens inside the screen of the device being sold: an AI-generated muscular frog on the iPhone, a fact-checked dog on the MacBook — the anti-slop point is demonstrated on the product, not asserted next to it
Products are shot centred with no props, no hands and no lifestyle set, so the copy carries all the personality and the exact model stays unambiguous

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A flat field of highlighter yellow with a large serif line and one object floating in it. At a station or across a platform the yellow registers as brand before the words resolve — the colour is the reach, and it is the only colour in the campaign.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: An everyday, faintly ridiculous use of the product, written as an imperative or a boast: 'Sprain your ankle in 5K.' / 'Fact check your mum, for less.' / 'Scroll past the slop, for less.' The joke is only funny if the use is true, which is exactly why it works as an argument for buying last year's model.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: The product dead centre, lit plainly, at a size where the model is recognisable — and where it has a screen, the screen is running the punchline. Nothing else is in the frame, so the reader's eye goes headline → object → proof line without a decision.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: Two lines at the bottom: the plain-English proof ('The MacBook Air M3, refurbished. Up to 50% less than new.') and then 'Downgrade now.' locked up with the Back Market mark, with the pricing basis in legal-size type beneath. The CTA is a verb the category treats as an insult, which is the whole brand in two words.

principle.title: Name the ordinary act, not the feature
principle.explanation: Specs and adjectives ask the reader to convert a number into a life ('5K video', 'M3 chip', 'chef's kitchen'). Naming the small, unglamorous act the thing actually enables skips that conversion and proves you know the buyer — and because the acts are absurdly specific, they are impossible for a competitor to have written first. It also generates work: one true mundane use per product is an endless supply of headlines on a layout that never changes.
principle.howToApply: For a listing or a collateral set, write ten ordinary acts the property makes possible before writing any copy — 'Take the call outside', 'Park both cars without negotiating', 'Read until the light goes at 8', 'Host fourteen without renting chairs' — and let the best one become the headline over a single photograph that proves it, with the spec demoted to one plain proof line ('4 bed · west-facing terrace · two parking'). Keep the layout fixed across the set so the pack is generated by swapping act + photograph, and pick a CTA verb the category doesn't use.

entries.category: Modernism & identity / postwar Japanese graphic design
entries.tagline: Designed the Tokyo 1964 emblem and all four of its posters — the first Olympics run as one coordinated identity programme — and then built the institutions that made Japanese graphic design a profession.
entries.summary: Kamekura trained at the Institute of New Architecture and Industrial Arts (1935–37), the school that brought Bauhaus method to Japan, then learned art direction under the photojournalist and editor Yōnosuke Natori. Postwar he became the figure other designers called 'the Boss': marks for Nikon, NTT, Meiji and TDK, and in 1961 the Tokyo 1964 emblem — a red disc above gold Olympic rings and a single line of type — plus four posters that were the first in Olympic history to use photography. What makes him worth studying is less the artefacts than the apparatus: a written design policy agreed before any artwork, a committee under the critic Masaru Katsumi enforcing one typeface and one colour set across every touchpoint, and then the Japan Advertising Artists Club (1951), Nippon Design Center (1959), JAGDA (1978) and the bilingual magazine Creation (1989–93) — an infrastructure for the work, not just the work.
whatWorks: Write the rule sheet before the artwork: the 1960 committee agreed a short design policy — consistent Olympic colours, uniform typography (Helvetica, in its first big international outing) — so hundreds of pieces made by many hands over four years still read as one thing
Build the mark from two primitives at full contrast and stop: red disc, gold rings, one line of type. If you can describe the mark in a sentence, it will survive a lapel pin and a stadium banner

Decide out loud what a borrowed symbol means: Kamekura insisted his red circle was the sun and 'the passion and excitement of the Games', not the flag — the intent was stated, not left to the audience

Treat speed as evidence: the winning emblem was reportedly drawn in a couple of hours after he forgot the deadline, and chosen unanimously. A mark that needs weeks of nursing to read may not be the mark

Buy the decisive photograph with volume, not luck: for the Starting Line poster he had athletes and US servicemen stage roughly eighty false starts over three February evenings until one frame existed
Strip the photograph to a symbol: backgrounds blacked out at the plate stage (decades before compositing was easy) so a sprinter reads as a mark rather than a scene

Build the institution the work needs — an agency co-owned with major corporations (Nippon Design Center), a professional body, an association and a magazine — so the standard outlives any one commission

sections.name: How he begins
sections.notes: With the policy and the smallest use, not the sketch. Before artwork, the elements that must never vary are agreed and written down — the colour set, the single typeface, the format discipline — and the mark is tested at the sizes it will really live at: pin, ticket, flag, banner. Modernist method (Bauhaus training, plus Natori's photo-editorial rigour) is applied as a procedure, so a large programme can be delegated without drifting.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Split the system into two registers and let each do one job. The spine is geometric and reductive — compass-and-rule marks, flat colour, one typeface — carrying recognition and repeatability; the emotional register is photographic and dramatic, carrying heat. Neither contaminates the other: the emblem never becomes illustrative, the posters never become decorative.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Art-directing the 'impossible' photograph, then flattening it. He was first to put photography on an Olympic poster, which in 1962 meant a technical production problem: stage the action repeatedly (eighty false starts) until the split-second frame exists, then remove the surroundings so the figure reads as a symbol against colour. The photograph is directed like a mark, not captured like a moment.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Functional modernism warmed by Japanese lyricism — geometry and grid for structure, light and colour for feeling — judged by whether every touchpoint still reads as one system ('total design'). Consistency is a written rule the committee enforces rather than a taste the designer defends, and the profession itself is part of the design job: clubs, an agency, an association and a bilingual magazine so the standard is shared, taught and exportable.

principle.title: Write the one-page rule sheet before you make anything
principle.explanation: A multi-piece programme drifts not because anyone designs badly but because each piece is decided fresh. Kamekura's Tokyo 1964 held together across four years and hundreds of artefacts because a short policy — these colours, this one typeface, this format discipline — existed before the first poster and was enforced by a committee. Fixing the invariants up front is also what makes delegation and volume safe: the decisions that matter are already made, so the remaining work is craft.
principle.howToApply: Before starting an Aperture pack, write the policy on one page and keep it in the order folder: one typeface with its two roles (display / labels), one accent colour and where it is allowed, fixed crop ratios for hero, detail and portrait, the address and price format, where the logo and legal line sit on every piece, and the caption rule for photographs. Then build the magazine, flyer, bifold, postcard and web page against that page rather than against each other — and when a piece wants to break a rule, change the page or drop the piece.

entries.tagline: A cause homepage built as one continuous argument, where every headline emphasises its own operative words in a heavier weight instead of shouting the whole line.
entries.summary: The Ocean Cleanup's homepage is a single descending scroll rather than a stack of sections: the aerial hero photograph dissolves into a deep navy field, and mission, problem and goal are three statements set on that same field with enormous vertical air between them. The typographic system is the whole design — one geometric sans, used light for the sentence and bold-plus-cyan for the words that carry the claim, so “WE AIM TO CLEAN UP 90% OF FLOATING OCEAN PLASTIC POLLUTION BY 2040” reads twice: once as a skim of bold fragments, once as a sentence. Everything else is deliberately plain — a single cyan circular-arrow link component reused from hero to news card, text-only testimonials, numbers instead of adjectives. The honest caveat: the long navy stretch leaves half the viewport empty and leans on scroll-linked imagery that a static capture flattens, so the top third is better live than in a screenshot.
whatWorks: Prove scale by shrinking the subject: the hero is an aerial where the cleanup barrier is a hairline arc and the two support vessels are specks — the ocean is the hero, the hardware is the evidence.
Emphasis lives inside the headline. Operative words go bold (and cyan), the rest stays light, at the same size on the same line — so the argument is scannable without a deck, kicker or callout box.

One link component everywhere: a small cyan circle with a white arrow plus a short label, used as the hero CTA, the three card link rows and the news card “Read the update”. The nav's navy DONATE NOW pill is the only thing allowed to look different.
Sections dissolve instead of stacking: the hero photograph fades into the navy field it sits on, so mission, problem and goal read as one continuous dive rather than three slabs with edges.
Numbers do the arguing — 100,000,000 kg, 1000 rivers, 80% of riverine pollution, 90% by 2040 — and each sits in the bold/cyan emphasis, so the figure is what the eye lands on.
Testimonials are text-only: a sentence and a small attribution line (Chris Martin, Coldplay; NBC Nightly News; Marc Benioff), with no headshots, logo lockups or star ratings.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Full-bleed aerial drone photograph of System 002 in the Great Pacific Garbage Patch, shot from high enough that the U-shaped barrier is a thin white curve and the vessels are dots. “JOIN THE LARGEST CLEANUP IN HISTORY” sits low-left in light-weight all-caps; the only CTA is a small cyan circular arrow labelled “Help clean” — quieter than the DONATE NOW pill in the sticky white nav, which lets the photograph carry the fold.

sections.name: The argument scroll: mission → problem → goal
sections.notes: Three statements on one uninterrupted navy field, each introduced by a short cyan rule, each headline mixing bold-cyan and light-white words in the same line (“A PLANET-SIZED PROBLEM”), each followed by one paragraph held to roughly a 45-character measure in the left column. The vertical gaps are enormous and the right half stays empty — restraint that reads as confidence on desktop, though it is where the page leans hardest on live scroll imagery.

sections.name: Two systems, given equal weight
sections.notes: A 50/50 full-bleed split — “CLEANING THE OCEAN” and “INTERCEPTING IN RIVERS” — with identical centred type, one paragraph carrying one hard number each (100,000,000 kg of plastic; 1000 rivers, 80% of riverine pollution), and one cyan LEARN MORE button apiece. Because the treatment is identical, the two programmes read as equal halves of one strategy rather than a flagship and a footnote.

sections.name: Join the cleanup
sections.notes: The palette inverts to a full cyan band holding three white cards — Help remove plastic / Work with purpose / Stay in the loop — each with a circular icon medallion straddling the card's top edge. Card links are bottom-aligned above a hairline rule so unequal copy lengths never break the row, and every link is the same cyan circle-arrow used in the hero.

sections.name: Partners and endorsements
sections.notes: White ground, four partner logos under “GLOBAL MISSION PARTNERS” with one line of plain framing copy, then a horizontal card carousel of quotes attributed by name and role. No portraits, no publication logos, no pull-quote decoration — just the sentence and a small navy attribution — which keeps famous names from turning the section into a celebrity wall.

sections.name: The latest news
sections.notes: Four dark cards, each a photograph with a bottom gradient scrim carrying a small date, a two-line headline, and “Read the update” with the same circle-arrow pinned to the card bottom on a hairline. It works as live proof of operation — dated, specific, refreshed — rather than a static “impact” section.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Navy, four link columns (Projects and updates / About us / Help / Legal), social icons as outlined circles, and a newsletter field whose only persuasion is a proof line: “Join our 80,000+ strong community”. Trademark and reCAPTCHA notices sit in small type at the base.

principle.title: Emphasise inside the headline, not around it
principle.explanation: Most pages add hierarchy by adding elements — a deck, a kicker, a highlighted stat block, a callout. The Ocean Cleanup gets two reading speeds out of one line instead: the operative words are set in the bold weight and the accent colour while the rest of the sentence stays light, at the same size on the same baseline. A skimmer collects the bold fragments (“PLANET-SIZED”, “90%”, “OCEAN PLASTIC”) and already has the argument; a reader gets a proper sentence. Nothing extra had to be drawn to achieve it, which is why the page can afford so much empty space.
principle.howToApply: On the next Aperture or listing page, delete the deck and the stat chips and rewrite the section headline as one full sentence, then bold only the two or three words that are the claim — “Sold in 11 days at 4% over ask in Highland Park”. One typeface, two weights, one accent colour used only on the bolded words; then squint at the page until only the bold reads, and confirm that skim is still the pitch.

site.name: Toyota — ‘Please Hilux Responsibly’ (film: cinema → TV / digital / social)

entries.category: Still from a 60-second video ad (pan-European film with digital and social cutdowns)
entries.tagline: The endline is a compliance warning — “PLEASE HILUX RESPONSIBLY” — so the safety notice and the durability brag are the same sentence.
entries.when: Launched Summer 2026 across Europe, anchored by a 60-second spot in UK cinemas; published on Ads of the World in August 2026
entries.summary: T&P and Toyota built the new Hilux launch around a mock public-service announcement aimed at the truck's own overconfident owners, who have spent years posting extreme feats online. The line borrows the exact grammar of “please drink responsibly” — a sentence European audiences have read a thousand times on labels and end-cards — and drops the product name into the verb slot, so the format's borrowed authority does the work a durability claim would otherwise have to argue. Directed by Martin Werner via Papaya Films, the film runs eight scenarios (a jungle river crossing past a hazard sign, snow peaks, a lava field, a dust storm rolling through a wind farm) shot with the handheld and drone grammar of owner footage rather than car-commercial gloss. It closes without a claim card: the Toyota wordmark simply appears over a live sunset landscape above the clouds where the truck has parked.
whatWorks: Borrow a sentence people already obey. “Please [X] responsibly” arrives pre-understood, so the joke and the product claim land in a single read with no setup line.
Use the brand name as a verb. Putting “Hilux” in the verb slot asserts category ownership grammatically — you don't drive it, you Hilux it — which no adjective could claim as cheaply.
Cast the customer's actual behaviour as the insight: the ad is about owners filming reckless feats, and the logged frame is exactly that — a passenger standing in the bed filming an erupting volcano.
Put the brand mark in the scene before it appears as a logo: the TOYOTA tailgate wordmark fills the lower third of the frame as part of the truck, not as an overlay.
Show the claim as consequence, not capability — a hazard warning sign standing beside the truck at the river crossing does more for “indestructible” than a spec line would.
End on the world, not a black slate: the wordmark dissolves over the live location, so the last image is still the story rather than a packshot.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: Opens mid-jeopardy with no product beauty shot — a dust storm barrelling across a wind farm with the truck a speck on a track below, framed from behind rocks as if the camera were hiding. Jeopardy first, brand later.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: “PLEASE HILUX RESPONSIBLY” — a regulatory formula with the brand as the verb. Because the audience can complete the sentence pattern before it finishes, the line reads simultaneously as a warning, a joke and a boast about durability, and it scales down cleanly to a social caption or a display end-frame.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Eight distinct scenarios — jungle river, snow peaks, volcano lava field, desert dust — shot handheld and by drone in the visual language of the owner clips the campaign is teasing. The still logged here is the campaign in one frame: the yellow tailgate reading TOYOTA across the lower third, a passenger standing in the bed filming, an eruption at frame left.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: There isn't one, and that is the discipline: no URL, no offer, no configurator card. The film resolves on the Toyota wordmark superimposed over the live mountaintop above the clouds, letting the endline be the only thing the viewer carries away.

principle.title: Put your brand in the slot of a sentence people already obey
principle.explanation: Borrowed formats arrive pre-installed in the audience's head. “Please drink responsibly”, “terms and conditions apply”, “not suitable for children under three” — each carries an authority and a tone the viewer accepts without checking, and each is short enough to survive as a caption, an end-frame or a text-only story. Dropping the brand into the verb slot of one of those sentences buys three things in five words: instant comprehension, a joke, and a claim you never had to defend, because the format itself implies the product is potent enough to need a warning.
principle.howToApply: Before writing a headline, list the fixed sentences your audience already reads without resistance — “subject to inspection”, “open house, all welcome”, “terms apply”, “please drink responsibly” — and try the brand or the offer in the verb or object slot. Keep only the version that still says something true (Toyota's warning is a durability claim); reject the ones where the joke and the claim point in different directions. Test it as a caption on a phone with no image attached.

entries.category: Polish Poster School / conceptual poster design
entries.tagline: The father of the Polish Poster School, who taught design as philosophy rather than formula — the brief restated as a phrase to interpret, answered with one hand-made image.
entries.summary: Tomaszewski trained at the Warsaw Academy of Fine Arts (1934–39) and from 1947 designed film posters for Poland's state film agency, where postwar shortages of ink, paper and star photography pushed him away from Western-style product advertising and toward flat colour, abstract shape and wit. That scarcity became a school: his conceptual posters eluded both Soviet socialist realism and Western advertising convention, won five gold medals in Vienna in 1948 and first prize at the São Paulo Biennial in 1963, and made him the acknowledged father of the Polish Poster School. As a professor at the Warsaw Academy from 1952 to 1985 he shaped three decades of designers by refusing to teach technique — he set assignments as aphorisms (“Always the other”, “Life is but a span”, “Interpret”, “Yesterday/Today/Tomorrow”) and asked students to surprise the viewer. Lettering was never a delivery mechanism for him: text was drawn, not set — deformed, rescaled and composed as a parallel means of expression, as in his celebrated Henry Moore exhibition poster.
whatWorks: Restate the brief as a phrase you must interpret, not a product you must promote — an aphorism generates images, a spec generates layouts.
Set the bar at surprise, not clarity: the test is whether the viewer has to complete the image, not whether they were told the facts.
Draw the words. Treat lettering as a second image — scaled, deformed, hand-made — rather than choosing a typeface at the end.
Let scarcity choose the medium: when photography and inks were unavailable, flat colour and abstraction became the style rather than the compromise.
Refuse formula, including your own — his output is recognisable by intelligence rather than by a signature look, which is why it never dated into a style.
Keep judging separate from making: three decades of studio crits were about the thinking behind the image, not its execution.

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: Not with the product, the poster size or the type. He begins with a sentence — in the studio, literally an aphorism handed to students in place of a client brief (“Always the other”, “Interpret”, “Yesterday/Today/Tomorrow”). The first move is to translate the commission into a phrase open enough to be interpreted, so the work starts as a question about meaning rather than a request for arrangement.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Reduce the interpretation to one metaphor, then find the simplest hand-made mark that carries it. Because the postwar Polish poster could not lean on star portraits or process photography, the image had to be invented — a synthetic shape, a gesture, a joke — and the limit of two or three flat colours forced the idea to be legible as pure form before anything was rendered.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Hand-drawn lettering used as a parallel image: letters scaled against each other, deformed, positioned disruptively, composed asymmetrically alongside a simplified figure — the Henry Moore poster being the canonical example, where the monumentality of the drawn letters answers the sculpture. Text is never applied to a finished picture; it is drawn as part of it.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Does it surprise? Does the viewer have to finish it? Is it a formula — anyone's, including mine? Wit and metaphor are the currency and explanation is failure. He judged students on the intellect behind the image rather than on depictive skill, on the belief that a competent creative practitioner is made by thinking, not by technique.

principle.title: Rewrite the brief as a phrase you have to interpret
principle.explanation: A brief written as a specification (“four-page flyer, three photos, price, agent headshot, QR code”) can only be arranged, and arranging produces layouts that look like everyone else's. Tomaszewski's studio method was to convert the task into a short phrase with room in it — an aphorism — because a phrase demands interpretation and interpretation produces images. The phrase is not decoration: it becomes the thing you judge the work against, so you can tell at a glance whether a rough is an idea or just a tidy arrangement of the required parts.
principle.howToApply: Before opening the template on the next listing or campaign, write the job as one interpretable phrase on a sheet of paper — “the last house on the hill”, “sold before the sign went up”, “a room that only works at 4pm” — and make three roughs that answer the phrase rather than the asset list. Pin them beside a straight version built from the spec; if the straight version wins you have lost nothing, and if a phrase-driven one wins you now have the one image the listing will be remembered by. Keep the phrase visible on the artboard as the acceptance test.

entries.tagline: The whole site is one ~720px column on a violet field — desktop gets no extra layout, just the toy sold at toy scale.
entries.summary: Panic sells a $229 black-and-white handheld by refusing to behave like a hardware brand. The entire page is a single narrow column that never widens on desktop, stacked as coloured blocks — grey hero, yellow feature essays, black Season Two, light-grey Catalog, teal education, violet pricing, near-black specs, violet footer — so hue is the only chapter marker you get: no dividers, no sticky section labels, no eyebrows. Headings are two-word noun phrases with a full stop ("The System." "The Design." "The Crank." "The Season." "The Idea."), and the body copy argues with a sceptic in plain speech ("Yes, the crank. Is it a gimmick? Nah.") instead of listing capabilities. One caveat: the Season One block is a 3-up grid of 24 image-only game covers, so that section says nothing at all until the art loads.
whatWorks: One column, one width, every viewport — the desktop page IS the mobile page, so there is no second layout to design, test or keep in sync.

Section = colour block. Six full-bleed grounds (grey, yellow, black, teal, violet, near-black) do all the wayfinding; the only element allowed to break the column is one edge-to-edge marquee of game art in the Catalog block.
Two-word headings with a full stop. "The System." "The Crank." "The Idea." The period makes each one land as a statement, and skimming the set gives you the table of contents the page never prints.
Copy names the objection before making the claim: "Yes, the crank. Is it a gimmick? Nah. Does it charge Playdate's battery? Nope. Is it really fun? Yes yes yes."

One CTA component — a pill with a tiny icon — recoloured to sit on whatever block it lands in (violet on grey, yellow on violet, teal on teal), always with the number in the label: "Order now for $229.", "Order now for $34."

Credibility is drawn, not tabulated: the spec panel pairs hand-drawn category icons with orthographic technical wireframes of the device bleeding off both edges, and the footer runs front/side/back product views instead of a logo wall.
Every gallery image carries real written alt text ("Hands holding a Playdate and opening its cover.", "Playdate resting on a wooden tray next to some dice.") — accessibility handled as copywriting.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Grey ground; small nav (Games / Dev / Education / Help / Sign In) with a "Buy Now!!" pill. The device floats in three-quarter view with "Hello." on its screen, then three short lines of plain sentence — "It's a new, tiny handheld game system with a bunch of brand-new games. We made Playdate just for fun." — then the giant yellow "play / date" wordmark stacked in two lines, then one violet pill: "Order now for $229." The price is on the fold and the wordmark is used as the graphic, not the logo.

sections.name: The System. / The Design. / The Crank.
sections.notes: Yellow ground, three short prose essays rather than feature cards; each is two tight paragraphs with only the operative phrase set bold inline ("very special black and white screen", "an analog controller that flips out from the side"). The Design credits Teenage Engineering in the copy. The crank essay embeds the device photo with a "Watch the game!" button sitting on its screen, so the demo lives inside the product shot instead of beside it.

sections.name: The Season. → Season Two → Catalog
sections.notes: The actual proposition in plain numbers — two new games a week for 12 weeks, 24 free games — followed by a 3-up grid of 24 covers guarded by a speech-bubble aside: "Wait! No spoilers, please!" The ground then flips to black for the Season 2 badge and a fanned pile of covers, then to light grey for Catalog, whose full-bleed scrolling strip of game art is the only thing on the page that leaves the column.

sections.name: Playdate for education
sections.notes: Teal ground and an alternate lockup ("playdate for education"), three short paragraphs on project-based learning, the 15% institutional discount stated as a sentence rather than a badge, and a teal-on-teal pill. A separate audience gets its own colour and its own lockup instead of its own page.

sections.name: All for just $229. + Playdate Cover
sections.notes: Violet block. Price as the heading, then what's included ("the full Season One of games – 24 original Playdate games, delivered weekly, at no extra charge") and, unusually, what isn't ("Does not include shipping. But you do get a very nice yellow USB-C to USB-A cable."). The $34 Cover gets the same treatment and its own pill — accessory upsell without a second template.

sections.name: The Specs.
sections.notes: Near-black panel, two columns of icon → label → value (battery, CPU, storage, size, wireless, sound, display, inputs, included, cost) with ghosted orthographic engineering drawings bleeding off the left and right edges. The nerd detail is quarantined here so the nine sections above it can stay conversational.

sections.name: The Idea. / Who Made It? / Footer
sections.notes: The founding question is set inside a grey thought-bubble — "If we made hardware, and built a tiny little game system that came with lots of surprise games, would that make people happy?" — then Panic's credits (Firewatch, Untitled Goose Game), a bare email field with a yellow "Notify Me!" pill, and a help pill. The footer returns to violet with three orthographic device views, the Panic mark, the Portland address, EU responsible party and a four-column link list.

principle.title: Say the objection out loud, then answer it in three words
principle.explanation: A product page's real reader is arguing with it — about price, about whether the thing is a gimmick, about what's missing. Printing their doubt in their own words costs one line and buys the claim that follows: you stop sounding like a brochure and start sounding like someone who has heard the question before. Playdate does it structurally ("Is it a gimmick? Nah." / "Does not include shipping. But you do get…"), which is also how it gets away with a 720px page and no comparison table.
principle.howToApply: Before laying out a listing or spec section, write the two questions a buyer would ask a friend rather than the agent — "Is that terrace real or a ledge?", "Is the HOA a dealbreaker?", "Why has it been listed twice?" — set them at body size in the section's own voice, answer each in one short sentence directly beneath, and only then place the photograph. Same move for the price block: state what the number does not include in the same breath as the number.

entries.when: Launched summer 2020 (June–July, UK and global) — AMV BBDO, directed by Nisha Ganatra, animation coordinated by Framestore
entries.tagline: Six interior lives, six different animation media — the material changes every time the narrator does.
entries.summary: AMV BBDO's film for Libresse/Bodyform opens and closes on a photoreal uterus lit like a nebula — pink tissue against a red-violet starfield — and in between cuts between live-action women and six animated "inner worlds", each built by a different team in a different medium (2D cel, stop-frame puppetry, oil paint on glass). First periods, endometriosis, IVF, miscarriage and menopause each get their own visual register, which is how one three-minute film moves between joy and grief without either flattening into a single brand mood. There is no product demo, no absorbency claim and no white trousers; the close is a hashtag, not an offer. It ran past 100M views and Bodyform UK reported a 200% lift in social following as people posted their own stories.
whatWorks: The hook is the taboo image itself, art-directed as landscape: the organ rendered photoreal and lit as a nebula reads as beautiful a beat before it reads as anatomy, which is what buys the next ten seconds.
One medium per story. Switching animation technique marks a change of narrator more clearly than any caption, name card or cut could.
Animation is used for exactly what live action can't show — pain, dread, longing — instead of for the usual euphemism (blue liquid, a poured beaker).
Category conventions are cut wholesale: no product in use, no performance claim, no smiling reassurance. The brand's absence for three minutes is the credibility.
The CTA is a participation prompt (#wombstories), so the proof of the ad is the replies it collects rather than a click-through.
Live-action faces are intercut at each emotional beat, anchoring the animated worlds to real people and stopping the film from reading as illustration.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A single uterus floating in a red-violet cloud of stars, photoreal and softly lit, with one tiny animated figure visible inside it. It is the one image the category never shows, made gorgeous — strange enough to stop a scroll without a caption, and it returns at the end as a field of uteri standing for the whole audience.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: No claim and no headline card until the last frame. The argument is the sequence itself — first period, endometriosis, IVF, miscarriage, menopause — and the only line asked to carry it is the hashtag that names all of them at once. The film argues by accumulation rather than by proposition.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Six animated interior worlds, each in a different medium and by a different team, intercut with live action; the medium switch IS the transition device, so the viewer feels a new narrator arrive before they understand the story. Framestore's invisible VFX keeps the live-action passages continuous with the animated ones.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: #wombstories — an invitation to post, not to buy — with the Libresse/Bodyform lockup held back to the final frame, so the piece never declares itself a spot until it has already been watched.

principle.title: Change the medium when the speaker changes
principle.explanation: When one piece has to carry several voices or several very different feelings, a single unified visual language flattens them into one mood — and it averages to the safest one. Giving each voice its own material (a different animation technique, a film-vs-flat-illustration split, a type-only card) lets a piece travel from joy to grief without the whole thing having to compromise, and the switch itself does the labelling work that captions usually do.
principle.howToApply: On any multi-voice deliverable — a mixed-use listing with very different units, a set of client testimonials, the Magazine's caption spreads — assign each voice its own register (one shot on film, one flat illustration, one type-only card) and keep the frame constant: same ratio, same margins, same logo position, same typeface. The consistency lives in the chassis so the switch reads as intent rather than as an inconsistent set.

entries.category: Institutional design / American International Typographic Style
entries.tagline: Ran MIT's design office for three decades and turned lecture notices — the least glamorous brief there is — into a museum-collected poster system.
entries.summary: Casey joined MIT's Office of Publications in 1955 and directed it (later Design Services) from 1972 to 1989, producing posters for department lectures, symposia and exhibitions with Swiss discipline and an American appetite for the visual pun. Her posters run at two speeds: one arresting or puzzling image to stop a student walking past, then the whole message in small type for whoever stopped. She worked from the International Typographic Style — Müller-Brockmann, Hofmann, Gerstner — alongside Ralph Coburn and Dietmar Winkler, and built MIT's visual character out of announcements nobody was obliged to read. RIT holds 99 of her posters at her own request; more are at MoMA and the Library of Congress.
whatWorks: Interview the expert before designing: she sat with faculty to understand the lecture or the research, treating each job as something to learn rather than something to style.
Treat the glance and the read as two separate jobs in one artefact — a big element that carries no information, and small type that carries all of it and is never enlarged to compete.
Hunt for the pun in the subject's own language: a typographic wordplay can't be detached from the words, so the idea and the information stay the same object.
Design against the corridor, not the client: the test is whether someone with no reason to stop, stops.
Run the output as one continuing series — same office, same formats, decades of it — so consistency comes from volume and each new poster is read against the last.

Hold both halves to account. Her own formulation: the "American interest in visual metaphor" plus the "Swiss fascination with planning, fastidiousness, and control over technical execution" — a clever idea sloppily made fails, and so does an immaculate grid with nothing to notice.

sections.name: How she begins
sections.notes: With the subject rather than the format. Early in her MIT years she interviewed the faculty whose lecture or research she was announcing, treating every poster as an education in a field she didn't know — so the visual idea came out of one specific true thing about that talk, not a generic notion of "science" or "architecture".

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: A two-speed hierarchy, stated by her outright: "My job is to stop anyone I can with an arresting or puzzling image, and entice the viewer to read the message in small type." The big element is bait and deliberately withholds information; the informational type stays small, complete and calm. Nothing in the middle is allowed to blur that split.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Typographic wordplay in Swiss dress — letters cropped, repeated, mirrored, rotated or made into the thing they name — set on a strict grid in a tightly limited palette, so the pun reads as inevitable rather than as a joke. The visual metaphor is built out of the announcement's own words instead of an illustration placed beside them.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Judged against the passer-by and against craft simultaneously: if it doesn't arrest, it has failed regardless of how well it's made; if it arrests but the execution is loose, it has also failed. Working inside an institution for 34 years, she also judged each piece as part of a series — does it belong to, and extend, everything this office has already put on the wall?

principle.title: Go learn the subject before you style it
principle.explanation: The arresting image can't be invented out of the brief — it comes from one specific fact you had to go and get. Casey's puzzles work because she interviewed the faculty first, which is also why three decades of lecture posters never repeat themselves: the research supplied the variety that a house style can't. Design is downstream of finding out.
principle.howToApply: Before designing a listing, spend fifteen minutes with the agent or the owner and write down five facts you could not have guessed from the MLS sheet — the architect's name, what the odd back room was built for, the neighbour's fig tree, who the previous owner was. Pick the one thing only this property has, make it the arresting image, and put every other fact in small type underneath at a size you never enlarge.

entries.tagline: Sells a rack of server hardware with the visual manners of a lab manual — numbered figures, mono captions, and real console screenshots instead of abstract tech illustration.
entries.summary: Oxide is selling something almost nobody can see in person — a whole cloud computer in a rack — so the site is built to read as documentation rather than marketing. The ground is near-black, there is exactly one accent (a signal green borrowed from the rack's own status LEDs), the display type is a plain neutral grotesque in sentence case, and every piece of micro-labelling is uppercase mono: "POWERING THE BEST TEAMS", "ELASTIC COMPUTE ▸", "FIG. 1 OXIDE CLOUD COMPUTER". The result is a page where each claim sits next to a numbered artefact — a terminal mid-login, a console table of running instances, a draggable compute sled — so the tone is engineering evidence rather than adjectives. One caveat: it is a long page and the payoff sections repeat the same dark card at similar contrast, so the middle third can blur on a fast scroll; the numbered figures are what keep your place. (Note: the full-page capture stops at the management section — the closing CTA and four-column footer are below the crop.)
whatWorks: One accent, sourced from the product: the only saturated colour on the page is the same green as the rack's status LEDs, so buttons, state chips and code highlights all feel like readouts rather than decoration
Uppercase mono is used exclusively for labels, eyebrows and captions, and never for reading copy — it does the work of a second typeface without adding one
Every product image is a real interface at real density: instance names, vCPU counts, RUNNING/STOPPED chips, actual firewall rules — no lorem dashboards, no floating glass cards
Figures are numbered and captioned (FIG. 1 rack, FIG. 2 web console, FIG. 3 compute sled), which turns a long scroll into a spec sheet you can navigate by evidence
Hierarchy inside a single paragraph: the claim is white, the enumeration greys back, the payoff line returns to white — three levels with no kicker, no stat chips, no rules

The hero pairs the abstract promise with two concrete artefacts side by side — a live CLI card and the photographed rack, joined by a thin connector line — so "on-prem that feels like cloud" is illustrated, not asserted

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Headline "On-prem that feels like the public cloud" set in two calm sentence-case lines on the left, while the right half is filled by a photographed rack whose green LED columns bleed off the edge. Above it, a small terminal card (tabs: CLI / API / CONSOLE) runs `oxide auth login`, wired to the rack by a single hairline. The label FIG. 1 OXIDE CLOUD COMPUTER sits top-right in mono. The fold therefore carries the promise, the hardware and the developer surface at once.

sections.name: Proof band
sections.notes: A low-contrast strip — "POWERING THE BEST TEAMS" in mono small caps over monochrome logos (Switch, Stoke Space, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, Jump Trading). Deliberately quiet: the logos are all reduced to one ink so the band reads as a fact rather than a trophy case, and the two national-lab names do the credibility work.

sections.name: "One integrated platform" + photo triptych
sections.notes: A single paragraph does the whole positioning job by colour alone: "One integrated platform." in white, "Compute, storage, networking, software…" greyed, then "The cloud you own." back in white. Beneath it, a full-bleed three-image band — a sign-in console, racks in a row, an empty machine room — gives the product physical scale before any feature is named.

sections.name: Capability row + the two-option argument
sections.notes: Four mono-labelled columns (ELASTIC COMPUTE ▸ / ELASTIC NETWORKING ▸ / EFFICIENT POWER DESIGN ▸ / ELASTIC STORAGE ▸), each with a cropped screenshot of the actual UI that delivers it, and hard numbers where they exist (12× cooling efficiency, 55% less total power). It then frames the market as a forced choice — traditional on-prem (8+ vendors) versus public cloud (no ownership, unpredictable bills) — so the product arrives as the third option rather than a better version of either.

sections.name: Four proof cards
sections.notes: Secure by default / API-driven developer velocity / Predictable, lower costs / 2-hour setup, as dark hairline-bordered cards. What makes them work is that each card's illustration is the evidence for that specific claim: a root-of-trust panel, a Terraform snippet, an itemised included/not-included list, a terminal provisioning a rack. The claim and its proof are the same element.

sections.name: FIG. 2 — the web console, at full width
sections.notes: "The biggest forward leap in on-prem in decades" over one large, unretouched console screenshot with a modal open mid-task. This is the page's centre of gravity: it shows the thing you actually buy the product to use, at a density that implies it is finished software. A one-line newsletter strip (field + green SUBSCRIBE) closes the band without a full-width interruption.

sections.name: Workloads grid → 3D explorer → CTA & footer
sections.notes: "Purpose-built for frontier workloads" fans out into six named use cases (cloud repatriation, VMware exit, AI/ML, HPC, sovereign cloud, CI/CD) and three industry cards with schematic illustrations. Then the one true toy on the page: a draggable "2nd Gen platform" explorer labelled FIG. 3 OXIDE COMPUTE SLED, with numbered hardware specs beside it — interaction spent on inspection, not on scroll effects. The close is plain: "Modernize your infrastructure / Talk to our team", two buttons, and a four-column footer that repeats the tagline "The cloud you own".

principle.title: Number your evidence like a manual
principle.explanation: Oxide's page feels rigorous before you read a word of it, and the mechanism is small: each significant image carries a mono caption in the form FIG. n — WHAT IT IS, numbered in order down the page. Numbering does two things at once. It implies the images were chosen as evidence for specific claims rather than dropped in for texture, and it gives a very long page a spine you can skim by artefact instead of by heading. It also disciplines the author: if a figure can't be captioned with a concrete noun, it probably shouldn't be on the page.
principle.howToApply: On the next property or product page, caption every image in a small mono label — "FIG. 1 — SOUTH TERRACE, 4PM", "FIG. 2 — FLOOR PLATE, UNIT 401D", "FIG. 3 — BUILDING SECTION" — numbered sequentially top to bottom, and use one accent colour for the label only. Then read the captions alone: if that list doesn't tell the whole story of the property, the images are wrong, not the copy.

site.name: Surreal — 'Serena Williams eats our cereal*' (digital OOH + social)

entries.category: Digital OOH panel / social key visual
entries.tagline: Buys the celebrity endorsement it can't afford by finding a non-famous person with the same name — and puts the confession in the asterisk.
entries.when: March 2023 (UK); the fake-endorsement idea ran in waves through 2022–2023
entries.summary: A bus-stop digital panel in Surreal's brand cyan: four lines of heavy black caps reading "SERENA WILLIAMS EATS OUR CEREAL*", and beneath it, in a quiet light weight, "*She's a student from London and we paid her to eat it but the point still stands." The headline borrows all the borrowed-fame mechanics of a real endorsement ad, and the footnote hands it straight back — which is the joke, and also the reason it's legally clean and endlessly repeatable (Dwayne Johnson the bus driver, Michael Jordan from St Albans). There is no URL, no QR code and no CTA; the only branding is the pack itself, shot straight on a white sweep in the lower third. It works because the format is honest about being a stunt while still delivering the two things the ad needs: a famous name and a photograph of the product.
whatWorks: The hook is a name, set at maximum size with nothing competing — no logo lockup at the top, no strapline, no badge
The reveal lives in the asterisk line, in the smallest type on the panel, so the reader has to lean in and finish the joke themselves
Type does all the design work: one heavy grotesque in caps for the claim, one light weight for the confession, no third style anywhere
One flat brand colour edge to edge; the only imagery is the pack and the product, lit plainly, so the panel still functions as a product ad
Zero CTA — no URL, no QR, no discount code. The pack shot is the call to action, which is the right call for a supermarket impulse buy
The structure is a template, not a one-off: swap the name and the footnote and you have the next twenty executions with no new design

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A celebrity name at billboard scale on flat cyan. It exploits the two seconds of recognition you'd give a real endorsement poster — and the asterisk hanging off "CEREAL*" is the only hint that something is off.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: "SERENA WILLIAMS EATS OUR CEREAL*" — a complete sentence, present tense, no adjectives about the product. Then the footnote: "*She's a student from London and we paid her to eat it but the point still stands." The gag and the disclosure are the same sentence, so the brand reads as cheeky rather than deceptive.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Lower third: the pack (SURREAL wordmark, cocoa variant, high-protein claim down the side) beside a bowl of cereal with chocolate chunks spilling onto a white sweep. Deliberately plain packshot photography — the surrounding copy is doing the entertaining, so the product only has to be legible and appetising.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: None, and that's the point: no site, no code, no QR. The panel spends its whole budget on being remembered and recognised at shelf. Distribution does the rest — the format is screenshot-shaped, so the digital OOH panel becomes the social post for free.

principle.title: Put the twist in the small print
principle.explanation: Most ads bury the caveat because they assume it weakens the claim. Surreal inverts it: the headline makes the biggest claim it can honestly make, and the footnote — the smallest type in the layout — delivers the reveal. That does three jobs at once. It earns trust (nothing is hidden), it makes the reader an accomplice (they complete the joke), and it turns the disclaimer into the most-read line on the panel. The mechanic only works if the small print is written in the same voice as the headline, not in legal language.
principle.howToApply: Whenever a claim needs a qualifier, stop hiding it. Write the strongest true version as the headline, then write the qualifier as one plain, human sentence in the smallest type, in the brand's own voice — "*Two of the four bedrooms are on the lower level", "*The roof terrace is shared with three other units". Set it directly under the headline rather than in the footer, and give it the same margins so it reads as part of the sentence.

entries.tagline: A two-founder studio that runs on a stated quality bar — "it'll do, won't do" — and a publicly numbered archive of everything it has ever looked at.
entries.summary: Build (Studio.Build) was founded in 2001 by Michael C. Place and Nicola Place, after Michael left a decade at The Designers Republic — where he helped shape the visual language of 1990s electronica, including Warp Records sleeves and Sony's WipEout — went travelling, and came back wanting to work differently. The studio stayed deliberately small while working for Google, Nike, Instagram, RIBA and the British Film Commission, and its output is typographic, systematic and production-obsessed: identity toolkits, custom type, flexible graphic devices built to be extended rather than reissued. What makes it worth studying as a model is that almost all of its process is visible from the outside — the work is filed, numbered and tagged in public.
whatWorks: Questions before aesthetics: "we'll always ask questions and delve deeper first", on the stated basis that "how something looks is just one piece of the puzzle"
A single spoken quality bar — "it'll do, won't do" — short enough that anyone in the studio can apply it out loud to a piece of work
A numbered, coded archive ("Scraps": #00001 onward, tagged SB-WRK, SB-TYP, INSP, ART, ARC, READ, SYS) that keeps their own output and their references in one retrievable system
Build systems that extend: for Nike Track & Field they added one new flexible device — the "acceleration graphic" — to an existing identity instead of restarting it
One long-term production partner (a decade-plus with Generation Press) so ideas can be tested in real print without re-explaining the studio's standards each time
Deliberately small: clients speak to the designer doing the work, and hiring weighs personality fit alongside craft — "we're a small studio, we need to make sure your personality fits too"
Public honesty about pace: Michael Place left the industry's it's-all-rosy pose behind after burnout, and says so — the studio is run to be survivable

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: With the client's world, not the moodboard. They go in with "no preconceived idea of the outcome", learn the business, and try to "see the world through their eyes"; the first work is questions and writing, not marks. Because the studio is small, the person asking the questions is the person who will design the answer, so nothing is lost in a handover.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Design the system, then prove it. Their deliverable is typically a robust identity toolkit — visual and verbal, often with custom type — rather than a set of finished artefacts, and they judge it by whether someone else can extend it. The Nike Track & Field work is the pattern: don't replace what exists, add one flexible device that lets the existing system reach new configurations.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: The archive as a working tool. "Scraps" is a running, numbered file (#00001, #00002 …) where every entry is coded by type — SB-WRK for their own work, SB-TYP for type experiments, INSP / ART / ARC / READ / SYS for what they're looking at, from Otl Aicher to Donald Judd. It is inspiration turned into a retrievable index instead of an unsorted feed, and it doubles as the studio's public evidence of taste. Michael's Letraset catalogue collecting is the same instinct: study the source material, then apply it.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: "It'll do, won't do" — a bar inherited from The Designers Republic and stated as studio motto: work that would merely pass is rejected out loud. Alongside it, two beliefs about judgement itself: that a piece can't be fairly judged on its visual outcome alone (critics "are not privy to the discussions with the client"), and that the point is "doing great work, with great people" — meaning the client relationship and the studio's own health are treated as part of the quality of the work, not overheads outside it.

principle.title: Number and tag your references so they can be found again
principle.explanation: Build keeps a public archive where every input and output is given a serial number and a type code — their own work, their type experiments, architecture, artists, reading. That single act converts "inspiration" from a scroll you can't search into a library you can cite. It also raises the standard of what gets saved: assigning a code forces you to decide what kind of thing this is and why it earned a number, which is exactly the decision most saved images never survive.
principle.howToApply: Start one file for the Design Journal's own inputs and give every item a number and a three-letter code — REF for a site or campaign, TYP for a type pairing, PHO for a photography approach, SYS for a layout or grid system, OWN for your own past work. Add one sentence per entry saying what the borrowable move is. When a new listing or build starts, search the codes instead of the memory: pull three numbered entries and design against those, so the reference is cited rather than half-remembered.

entries.tagline: A very long retail-bank homepage that stays readable because every claim carries its own qualifier and every statistic carries its own date.
entries.summary: Monzo sells eight product families on one page — current accounts, savings, investments, credit, travel, mortgages, pensions, business — and survives the length by never letting a section improvise: one white ground, Hot Coral as the only saturated accent, a rounded-card chassis in coral or near-navy, and short two-register headlines ('Payday, the Monzo way', 'Humans on hand, 24/7'). Depth is folded into tabbed modules rather than added as more scroll — 'Free features / Paid features' in one block, 'Save / Invest / Retire' in another — so the page reads as three or four decisions instead of twenty pitches. What raises it above a competent marketing page is the proof layer: a 'Did you know?' row of oddly specific numbers (£131 extra saved a year on roundups, £8.5bn in Instant Access Pots, £4.56m cashback in 2024, ~1,000 fraud attempts caught a month) each stamped 'Published August 2026', and below it the independent service-quality survey printed as a bar chart that names Starling, Nationwide, First Direct and Chase with their scores next to Monzo's 79%. The caveat is honest: past the accounts grid the page keeps going, and the regulatory blocks at the bottom are read by almost no one.
whatWorks: One accent, used as a surface not a highlight: Hot Coral appears as whole card grounds alternating with near-navy, so the palette is two filled shapes rather than coloured text and buttons scattered over white

Every card wears a small grey label chip above its sentence ('24/7 support', 'No hidden fees', 'FSCS protected', 'Deposit cash and cheques') — the chip is the scannable layer and the sentence is the proof

Fine print sits inside the block it qualifies, at one line: '£500 minimum deposit', 'You could get back less than you invest', the rate dropping to 2.60% after two withdrawals — no footnote pile at the bottom of the page
Statistics are un-round and dated: £131, £4.56m, ~1,000 a month, all under 'Published August 2026', which makes them read as an audited figure rather than a marketing number
Third-party proof is printed as a chart with competitors named and scored, not as a badge — Monzo 79%, Starling 76%, Nationwide and First Direct 75%, Chase 68%
Depth is tabbed, not stacked: 'Free features / Paid features' and 'Save / Invest / Retire' keep three product families inside one section chassis so the visitor compares instead of scrolling

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: 'Monzo for all your money' over a lifestyle frame of someone on a sofa holding the Hot Coral card, one primary CTA ('Open a free bank account'), and immediately beneath it three regulatory trust marks — Which? Recommended Provider, Current Account Switch Guarantee, FSCS. A bank's fold has to answer 'is my money safe' before 'is this nice', and putting the three seals in the fold retires that question in one row.

sections.name: Rate offer + 'Tell me about…' topic row
sections.notes: A single savings rate gets its own block ('Earn up to 3.65% AER (variable) with Select Access') with the deposit minimum in one line under the CTA, then the nav problem is solved sideways: a row of seven cards named as the visitor's own request — Bank accounts, Savings and ISAs, Investments, Credit, Travel, Mortgages, Pensions — each with a flat custom icon (coral card, piggy bank, umbrella, plane, house). Entry points are labelled by what the visitor wants to ask, not by how the product line is filed.

sections.name: 'Manage your money today' (tabbed free / paid)
sections.notes: One module with a Free features / Paid features toggle: four benefits per tab, each a short headline plus a sentence plus either app UI or a hand paying with the coral card. Tabs are doing real work here — the paywall becomes a comparison the visitor performs themselves instead of a pricing table argument, and the section stays one screen tall no matter how many features exist.

sections.name: 'Build your money for tomorrow' (Save / Invest / Retire tabs)
sections.notes: The same chassis reused for the three long-horizon products, with the risk language sitting in the block that earns it ('You could get back less than you invest', '18+, Monzo current account required'). Imagery switches to still-life props — a watering can, a tilted coin, a coin jar with leaves — which keeps three abstract financial products visually distinct without three new layouts.

sections.name: Trust block: 'A regulated bank with 24/7 support'
sections.notes: A four-card grid, coral and navy alternating diagonally, with the headline and one CTA centred in the gap between them; each card is a label chip plus two lines of plain fact (in-app chat, no monthly fees, PayPoint/Post Office cash deposits at £1, FSCS to £120,000). The centred headline in a hole in the grid is the page's one structural flourish, and it works because the cards around it are all the same size.

sections.name: Accounts grid + Which? recognition
sections.notes: Eight account cards carrying name, one value sentence, the fee or APR spelled out (Perks £9/mo, Extra £3/mo, Max £19/mo, Flex 29% APR representative) and a 'Learn more' link — type only, no imagery, so price comparison is the whole job of the section. It is immediately followed by 'Which? recommended 2 years in a row' with both dated badges and '16 million people already banking with Monzo'.

sections.name: 'Did you know?' stats + independent service quality survey
sections.notes: The proof floor of the page: six stat cards with un-round numbers and small illustrated icons, stamped 'Published August 2026', then the FCA-mandated service-quality charts for Great Britain and Northern Ireland with named competitors and percentages, stamped 'Published February 2026', plus the APP fraud rankings and a link to the PSR report. A block most brands would treat as compliance is used as the strongest evidence on the page.

sections.name: App download, web fallback, footer
sections.notes: Conversion ends practically rather than emotionally — literal install instructions with both store badges, then 'No phone? No problem.' explaining laptop login if the phone is lost, over a warm orange-to-red gradient. The footer is five honest columns (Products / Company / Using Monzo / Help & Security / Site & App Info) with the FCA registration number, company number and registered address set plainly rather than hidden.

principle.title: Date-stamp your numbers and keep them un-round
principle.explanation: A statistic with no date and a suspiciously tidy value ('over 500 homes sold', 'thousands of happy clients') reads as a claim; the same fact given to the pound or the day, with the month it was calculated, reads as a record someone could audit. Monzo's proof row works because £131 and £4.56m and '~1,000 a month' are obviously counted rather than composed, and because 'Published August 2026' tells you when they were true — which also gives the number a shelf life, so it gets refreshed instead of quietly ageing on the page.
principle.howToApply: On Aperture pages and collateral, replace every round brag with a counted one and stamp it: '112 days average time on market in Lakewood, Jan–Jun 2026', 'list-to-sale 98.4% across 37 closings in 2025', 'photographed within 6 days of signing, last 12 listings'. Put the source in the same small line, keep the stat block to one row, and set a quarterly reminder to re-date it — an un-refreshed stamp is worse than no stamp.

site.name: PlayStation — 'It Happens on PS5' (hero film + global social, digital and OOH)

entries.tagline: A campaign of impossible worlds whose payoff frame is a normal living room seen through a door standing alone in a desert.
entries.when: Launched 17 August 2026, global — Sony Interactive Entertainment with adam&eve\TBWA; a hero film plus social, digital, out-of-home, creator partnerships and local installations (Marvel's Wolverine challenge pods in France, Berserker Mode in Australia, Sentinel head installations in the UK, Canada and Spain), timed to the Wolverine launch on 15 September
entries.summary: The film is a run of large, expensive, obviously impossible images — cars hanging in mid-air over a plaza in front of a stadium built in the shape of the PlayStation logo, classical statues at golden hour holding a book embossed with the four PlayStation symbols, a high-speed jet ski chase — but the frame the campaign keeps returning to is a wooden door standing on its own in a purple dune field under a starfield, opened onto a warm, ordinary living room where someone is sitting with a controller. The spectacle is the promise; the small lit rectangle is the product. It also hides its branding in the world rather than locking it up in a corner: the mark is a building, an embossed cover, a shape in the architecture, so the logo is discovered rather than presented.
whatWorks: One aperture, two temperatures: a warm tungsten interior rectangle set inside a cold purple-blue exterior — the colour contrast alone tells you which side you are meant to want
The impossible object is boring in construction (a plain panelled door, hinges, a handle) so the surrounding surrealism reads as real rather than rendered
The product moment is deliberately unglamorous — a normal room, a rug, a wall shelf, a person seen from behind — so the fantasy resolves into something the viewer can actually occupy
No logo lockup in the frame: the brand appears as world-building (a stadium in the shape of the mark, the four symbols embossed on a statue's book), which survives cropping to any social ratio
Sightline composition: the door is off-centre and the light spills toward the camera, so the eye lands on the screen inside the room, which is the only detail small enough to require a second look
The line does the CTA's job by naming the place rather than the action — 'It Happens on PS5' — and the game slate carries the urgency instead of an offer

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A door with nothing attached to it, standing in an empty dune field under a Milky Way sky. The scroll stops on the impossibility of an interior object in an exterior with no building — and unlike a big action frame, it poses a question ('a door to where?') that only resolves if you keep watching.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'It Happens on PS5' — a locative, not a claim: no adjective, no comparison, no spec. It lets an anthology of unrelated worlds (Wolverine, 007, God of War, GTA VI) sit under one line, and it puts the emphasis on the room the console is in rather than on the hardware.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: The composition is a warm rectangle inside a cold field. Interior light does the pointing, the door frame does the cropping, and the human is small, seen from behind, and doing nothing photogenic. Branding is embedded in the world elsewhere in the campaign — the mark as a stadium, the four symbols embossed on a book held by a statue — so the frame never needs a lockup.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: There is no button; the release calendar is the call to action (Marvel's Wolverine on 15 September, then the rest of the slate), extended physically by local installations — challenge pods, a Berserker Mode activation, Sentinel heads — so the ask is 'come and stand in it' rather than 'click'.

principle.title: Make the ordinary room the payoff, framed by the spectacle
principle.explanation: Aspirational imagery fails when the viewer cannot find themselves in it: a perfect frame with no ordinary detail is admired and forgotten. Putting the mundane, occupiable thing at the end of a spectacular setup gives the fantasy somewhere to land — the vastness is the promise, the small warm rectangle is the thing being sold, and the contrast between them is what makes the ordinary thing feel earned rather than modest.
principle.howToApply: Shoot the listing hero at dusk from the dark side: stand outside in the cool blue of the garden, terrace or street and frame the warm lit interior through a doorway, window or arch, with one lamp on and a person or two seated inside doing nothing staged. Let the aperture crop the room instead of shooting the room wide, keep the exterior deliberately empty and cold, and skip the logo in the frame — the caption can carry it.

entries.category: American mid-century modernism / book jackets, interiors, identity
entries.tagline: Designed over seventy New Directions jackets by reading each book and restating its feeling as one abstract mark — and, once blind, by dictating the layouts in picas.
entries.summary: Lustig was the American designer who refused to stay in one medium: book jackets for New Directions' New Classics series, interiors, a chair, textiles, signage, magazine art direction (visual research director at Look in 1944, work for Fortune), taught by nobody in particular and shaped instead by three months at Frank Lloyd Wright's Taliesin in 1935 and a print shop he ran at the back of a Brentwood drugstore. His jacket method was to read the text, take the author's private, subjective drive and objectify it — sometimes as an obvious symbol lifted from the subject, sometimes as a purely atmospheric characterisation of the book's emotional content — and each jacket commits to one or the other. Diabetes left him effectively blind by 1954 and he kept working by dictating layouts to assistants in exact measurements ('indent 12 picas, flush left'), with Ivan Chermayeff apprenticing beside him; he died at 40 in December 1955, and Elaine Lustig Cohen carried the practice on. Pictured is his cover for Perspektiven no. 5 (S. Fischer Verlag) rather than a portrait — there is no freely licensed photograph of him.
whatWorks: Read the actual content before designing: his stated method was to get the feel of the author's creative drive, then restate it in graphic terms — not to illustrate the plot
Decide per piece whether it needs a literal symbol taken from the subject or an atmospheric equivalent of its feeling, and commit to one

Build the image from the material already on hand — his first New Directions jacket was assembled from pieces of type metal pulled from the cases of his own print shop, not from commissioned illustration
Make every decision nameable in measurements, so the design can be dictated, handed to someone else's hands, and reproduced exactly
Treat a jacket, a room, a chair and a letterhead as the same problem at different scales — the same visual argument should survive the change of medium
Refuse to design down: assume the audience can read an abstract mark, and let the small type carry the literal information

sections.name: How he begins
sections.notes: With the text, not the format. He read the book, looked for the author's creative drive rather than the story's events, and named the feeling he was going to translate. The brief was therefore always about equivalence — what does this book feel like, and what shape is that — which is why seventy-odd jackets in one series never settle into a formula.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Objectify the subjective: take the private, internal content and project it outward as one visual statement. He was explicit that the symbols were sometimes obvious and taken straight from the subject, and sometimes evasive, characterising the emotional content instead — a fork in the road he chose on purpose each time rather than blending both into one crowded cover.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Making pictures out of typographic material. Working from his own experimental print shop (1937–1944, much of it for Ward Ritchie Press) he composed non-representational images from standard geometric type ornaments and pieces of type metal, which gave him abstraction that a letterpress could actually print. The constraint was the style: shapes limited to what sat in the cases, colour limited to what the press could hold.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: A design should be specifiable, not gestural — the proof is that from 1954, blind, he kept producing work by dictating instructions in picas and alignments. He held that the audience did not need designing down to, so the arresting element could be genuinely abstract while the small type stayed complete and legible. And he judged the work across media: if the idea only survived as a jacket, it was decoration rather than an idea.

principle.title: Choose a symbol or an atmosphere — never both
principle.explanation: Most weak layouts are two designs fighting: a literal emblem of the thing (the arch, the key, the coastline) sitting on top of a mood (the gradient, the film grain, the golden light), each halving the other's force. Lustig's jackets are decisive because he picked the register first — this one is a symbol taken from the subject, that one is a characterisation of its feeling — and then spent the whole surface on that one choice. Naming the register before you start also gives you a test you can apply to every element afterwards: does this serve the symbol, or does it serve the mood?
principle.howToApply: Before laying out a cover, flyer or ad, write one word on the artboard: SYMBOL or ATMOSPHERE. If SYMBOL, find the one object only this property has (the spiral stair, the olive terrace, the arched window), shoot or draw it clean against a flat ground, and forbid yourself any mood treatment — no gradient, no vignette, no warm filter. If ATMOSPHERE, commit to light and colour (the 5pm room, the fog off the water) and forbid any emblem or icon, letting the small type carry every fact. Then check each element against the word and delete what serves the other one.

entries.tagline: A homepage with no house display face: six full-bleed panels, each one wearing the artwork's own lettering, held together by an identical outline button.
entries.summary: Criterion sells three things off one page — a disc store, a streaming channel and a film magazine — and it never asks its own brand typography to compete with the art it licenses. Each panel is a full-bleed still with the title set in that film or series' own lettering (Little Odessa in red condensed stencil, 'Rock Biopics That Don't Suck' in comic bold plus script, The Complete Kubrick in wide grotesk), so the page reads like a stack of posters rather than a template. What makes it cohere is not a typeface but a set of invariants: the same panel proportion, the same centred stack, and the same white 1px outline button at the same width and vertical position, every single time.
