The one house typographic decision left on the page is a quiet one — the nav sets 'Current', the editorial arm, in italic serif while the two commercial destinations stay roman.
whatWorks: No single hero: six stacked full-bleed panels of roughly equal weight, each a complete offer (image + title lockup + exactly one button), so any scroll position is a valid entry point.

Every CTA is the identical white 1px outline button — same width, same centred position, same small letterspaced caps — which is the invariant that makes six wildly different artworks read as one page.
Each panel's title is set in the content's own lettering, not a house display face; the site's brand voice is the frame, not the font.
'THE CRITERION COLLECTION' runs vertically up the hero's left edge, exactly where a disc spine would sit — the physical product's spine carried into the layout.

One type switch encodes the change of register: 'Current' is italic serif in both nav and footer while 'Shop the Collection' and 'The Criterion Channel' stay roman — you know it's reading, not shopping, before you click.
The new-release panel tilts the cover art into an overlapping collage rather than a tidy grid, so twelve covers become one texture with room for a centred headline on top.
The footer is deliberately image-free — serif column headings over uppercase sans links — so nothing competes with the six panels above it.

sections.name: Hero (rotating title panel)
sections.notes: Full-bleed key art for Little Odessa with the film's own red condensed stencil title, a single 'SHOP NOW' outline button, five dot indicators bottom-left and a down-chevron. The dots say it rotates and the chevron says the page continues — two tiny affordances instead of a scroll hint animation. The vertical 'THE CRITERION COLLECTION' rail on the left edge is the only place the brand name appears in the fold.

sections.name: Channel promo — 'Adventures in Moviegoing'
sections.notes: A documentary photograph of Fred Armisen and Carrie Brownstein mid-conversation, title in chunky white display, and a small yellow ticket-stub graphic tucked into the lockup as the one hit of colour. 'WATCH NOW ON THE CHANNEL' — same button, different destination, so the streaming service gets equal billing with the store without a separate nav level.

sections.name: New releases — 'November Titles Announced!'
sections.notes: Instead of a product grid, a dozen cover artworks are scaled up and tilted into an overlapping collage; the covers themselves are the brand asset, so the section's job is to show range (Harold and Maude, Marie Antoinette, Wild at Heart, The Right Stuff, K-Pop Demon Hunters) rather than list SKUs. Centred serif headline plus 'PREORDER NOW'.

sections.name: Editorial programming — 'Rock Biopics That Don't Suck'
sections.notes: A black-and-white still carries a comic-red display headline with a script kicker — tonally the loudest panel on the page, and it works because the chassis around it hasn't changed. This is the panel that proves the system: swap in a completely different type voice and the page still reads as Criterion.

sections.name: Box set — 'The Complete Kubrick'
sections.notes: A 2001 spacesuit still with the title in a wide, tightly-tracked grotesk stacked over three lines, dropped low-centre so the figures read either side of it. 'PREORDER NOW' sits at the same y-position as every other button on the page.

sections.name: Criterion Closet Picks
sections.notes: A 4-up video-store portrait strip of guests holding discs, with the only interrogative copy on the page — 'Which movies did your favorite filmmakers, actors, and artists take home?' — in a friendly geometric sans beneath the title, then 'WATCH & SHOP'. The single CTA that admits it's doing two jobs at once, which is the whole business model in two words.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Near-black ground, the 'C' mark alone at top-left, then a four-column sitemap: serif headings (Shop the Collection / Current / The Criterion Channel / Our Mission / My Criterion / Terms of Use / FAQ) over small uppercase sans links, with 'Current' still italic. Newsletter field with one line of plain copy, four social glyphs, and the Janus Films lockup as a co-brand at bottom-right — no imagery, no repeated CTA, no back-to-top gimmick.

principle.title: Mark your editorial arm with a type style, not a separate site
principle.explanation: When one brand runs a store and a publication, the usual moves are a subdomain, a dropdown, or a visually different second site — all of which cost traffic and make the reading feel like a side project. Criterion keeps all three businesses in one nav and distinguishes the editorial one with a single typographic switch: 'Current' in italic serif, 'Shop the Collection' and 'The Criterion Channel' in roman. Style change is enough to reset the reader's expectation of register, and it costs one CSS rule instead of an architecture.
principle.howToApply: On Aperture, put the journal / market notes in the same top-level nav as Listings and Services, but set that one item in the italic of the house serif, and carry the same italic through to its section headings, card titles and footer column. Nothing else changes — same grid, same cards, same footer — so readers register 'this is reading, not shopping' before they click, and the traffic and SEO stay on one domain.

site.name: The New Zealand Herpes Foundation — 'The Best Place in the World to Have Herpes'

entries.category: Social / digital campaign key visual + gamified index
entries.tagline: It says the stigmatised word at full display size, in the exact typographic costume of a New Zealand tourism poster — and then turns the ask into a national leaderboard.
entries.when: Launched 13 October 2024 (Global Herpes Awareness Day), New Zealand; Cannes Lions Grand Prix winner 2025. Agencies: FINCH (Sydney) and Motion Sickness (Auckland).
entries.summary: The key visual is a sun-faded pastoral landscape — snow-capped range, sheep in a green paddock — with a fat rounded-gothic headline knitted into the photograph: 'Make New Zealand the best place in the world to have herpes.' Every craft decision is borrowed from tourism advertising rather than health advertising: the retro drop-shadowed type, the faded Kodachrome grade, the civic 'Make New Zealand…' construction. Behind it sat the actual mechanic — a Herpes Stigma Index that publicly ranked OECD countries and a six-part destigmatisation course fronted by recognisable New Zealanders — so the campaign gave the country a score to move rather than a message to agree with. It climbed from 9th to 1st in eight weeks, with 12.7 million social impressions and 69% of participants reporting reduced stigma.
whatWorks: The taboo word is set at full display size in the headline — no euphemism, no 'HSV-1', no clinical hedge — which is what makes the friendly typography read as confidence instead of avoidance.

Type is interlocked with the photograph: 'Make' and 'the best place in the world to have' drop to small weight and tuck into the negative space between the big words, so a 40-character sentence still reads as one shape.
The whole palette comes from the landscape — sky blue, paddock green, one mustard yellow for the two secondary lines — so nothing on the frame looks like a brand overlay.
The construction is civic, not personal: 'Make New Zealand the best place…' asks for a national achievement rather than asking an individual to feel better, which is why strangers shared it.

The proof was built as a public scoreboard (the Herpes Stigma Index, ranked against other OECD countries) — a thing that can visibly move, so the campaign had a reason to be posted about again in week six.
Authority was cast rather than asserted: a former Director-General of Health and an All Blacks coach hosting the course did the credibility work that a logo and a statistic cannot.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: For about a second it is indistinguishable from a 1970s '100% Pure' tourism poster — mountains, sheep, faded film grade. The scroll stops because the visual promises one thing and the last word of the headline delivers another; the surprise is carried by the typography's warmth, not by shock imagery.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'Make New Zealand the best place in the world to have herpes.' The operative words — New Zealand / herpes — are the two largest, and the connective tissue shrinks to fit between them, so the skim reads as a country plus a condition. It is an invitation to a national ranking, not a plea for sympathy.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: A wide, unpeopled landscape doing the emotional work: the subject of the ad is the country, not a patient, which sidesteps every stock-photo cliché of health advertising. Rounded slab-gothic with a hard drop shadow places it in the era of civic pride posters, and the type sits *in* the photograph's depth rather than on a scrim above it.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: The ask is not 'learn more' but 'take the course' — a six-part video series — with the Herpes Stigma Index as the running scoreboard that reported back on progress. The action is measurable, public and repeatable, which is why the campaign kept generating posts after launch week instead of decaying.

principle.title: Give the audience a scoreboard, not a message
principle.explanation: A campaign that asks people to believe something has one moment of attention and then decays. A campaign that publishes a number the audience can move has a reason to be checked, shared and re-posted every time the number changes — and it converts a soft attitude brief into something with a visible before and after. The creative's job becomes recruiting people onto a team rather than persuading them of a position.
principle.howToApply: Pick one number Aperture can publish and genuinely move, and put it somewhere public with a date and a rank: 'Lakewood: 112 days average time on market — 4th of 9 districts we track, August 2026.' Post the standings monthly, name the districts, and let the movement be the content — the listing is what people click after they've come back to check the table.

entries.tagline: Ran CBS's entire visual output for four decades on two deliberately different rulebooks — loose and idea-led for the advertising, absolutely locked for anything permanent.
entries.summary: Dorfsman joined CBS in 1946, took over from William Golden as creative director in 1959, and stayed until 1991 — roughly 45 years with authority over advertising, on-air promotion, news set design, packaging, annual reports, signage and the building itself. He is the best argument in the canon for the in-house designer: not a supplier executing briefs, but someone who learned the business well enough to invent the assignments. His masterwork, the Gastrotypographicalassemblage — a 35-foot hand-milled wood-type wall for the Black Rock cafeteria, made with Herb Lubalin and Tom Carnase — is also the clearest statement of his method: 'enthusiastic excess and clinical precision' in the same object.
whatWorks: Learn the client's business from the inside before designing: he sat with the CBS Radio sales force and read the audience research, then made hundreds of small-space ads each arguing one specific point about the medium.
Run two rulebooks — eclectic and idea-first for campaign work, obsessively systematised for anything permanent — and never let one standard leak into the other.
Invent the assignment nobody asked for when the business needs it (the 132-page 'Field of Vision' book on CBS's seven-game NFL broadcast; a commemorative volume on the 1969 moon-landing coverage).

Commission the typeface rather than choose one — CBS Didot and CBS Sans from Freeman Craw — then push it down to the surfaces nobody briefs: door numbers, elevator buttons, wall clocks, cafeteria menus.
Write the ad as an argument, not a description: 'This program is so beautiful it has to die' saved The Waltons by making the audience the appeal's mechanism.
Treat the small, unglamorous, permanent artefacts as the real identity — the campaign is temporary, the door number is forever.

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: By minding the client's business, in his own framing — he went to the CBS Radio sales meetings, learned what the reps were actually up against and how the audiences differed, and only then designed. The output of that phase was volume, not a concept: hundreds of small print ads, each one making a single compelling case for radio as a medium. The immersion, not a portfolio, is what got him Golden's job when Golden died in 1959.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Two explicitly different standards depending on the artefact's lifespan. Outward-facing advertising was eclectic — whatever typography, illustration or photography the idea demanded, changing execution to execution, image-driven and fast where the industry was still text-heavy. Everything permanent — the headquarters, the stationery, the signage, the on-air identity — was governed with near-fanatical rigour. Same designer, same decade, two rulebooks, held apart on purpose.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Proprietary type applied to the surfaces nobody thinks to specify. Rather than pick a face for Black Rock, he had Freeman Craw cut CBS Didot and CBS Sans, then specified them everywhere in the building — elevator buttons, door numbers, clock faces, cafeteria signage. The Gastrotypographicalassemblage (1966) is the extreme case: the cafeteria's food list rendered as a wall of hand-milled wood type, dense to the point of excess yet set with the precision of a title sequence.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Design defines the company's character, which makes every un-designed surface a leak. Corollaries he acted on: it is the designer's job to identify the opportunity, not to wait for the brief; and to take responsibility for the thing being sold, not just its presentation — he built news sets, convention booths and commemorative books because they were needed. He extended Golden's conceptual clarity rather than replacing it, and he judged work by whether it argued something, wittily and quickly.

principle.title: Run two rulebooks: loose for campaigns, locked for the permanent surfaces
principle.explanation: Most brand programmes fail in one of two ways — they systematise the campaign work until every ad looks like the last one, or they leave the permanent surfaces unspecified so the identity dissolves in the places people encounter it daily. Dorfsman's answer was to sort artefacts by lifespan and apply opposite standards: a one-off persuasion piece is allowed to invent its own typography every time, while anything that sits in the world for years gets no discretion at all. Consistency lives where it compounds; freedom lives where it converts.
principle.howToApply: Split the Aperture inventory into two lists. Temporary — carousels, story units, single-property key visuals: fixed logo position and legal line, everything else negotiable per property. Permanent — business cards, yard signs, email signature, the magazine masthead and folio, listing-page templates, PDF covers: one typeface pair, one accent, exact sizes and positions, and a written rule that they are never redesigned for a single job. Then find the permanent surfaces currently unspecified (the email footer, the PDF filename convention, the sign rider, the closing-gift card) and lock those next.

entries.tagline: A two-market estate agency that sells its taste before its inventory — the fold is one villa with its architect credited, and the dual-market claim is proved by two clocks that keep running.
entries.summary: Domus Nova sells design-led homes in London and Ibiza, and the homepage is built so that the properties, not the agency, do the talking: no slogan above the fold, no search box, just one featured villa in a wide frame with the neighbouring slides peeking in at both edges. Everything below reuses a single card template for rentals and sales alike, scoped by All / Ibiza / London chips so one page serves two geographies instead of splitting into two sites. Warm off-white grounds, a quiet transitional serif for headings, tiny sans for every piece of metadata, and photography allowed to be the only saturated thing on the page. The caveat: it is a long scroll that repeats its carousel pattern several times and several modules lazy-load late, so the middle of the page can feel like it is still arriving.
whatWorks: The fold carries no slogan at all — one villa, its name ('Villa Aria'), its market ('Ibiza Sales'), and a right-aligned one-line dek that credits the architect by name ('a striking new-build villa for sale by award-winning Fran Silvestre Arquitectos'). The property is the headline and the architect is the proof.

Two live local clocks — 'LDN 15:22:31' and 'IBZ 16:22:31' in tiny mono — sit directly above the positioning paragraph, so 'London and Ibiza' is demonstrated by something that keeps ticking rather than asserted in a sentence.

One card template does rentals and sales: photo (a second image on hover), an overline badge that says why this one is notable ('New Listing – Architect Designed', 'Under Offer', 'Designed by Romano Arquitectos'), then two tight lines — name and location on the left, price and beds/lettings term hard right.
Market chips (All / Ibiza / London) sit at the top right of each carousel and scope the module rather than the navigation, keeping both markets in one brand and one page.

The journal block deliberately breaks the photo rhythm: flat colour panels (sage, deep teal) carrying a city-and-date stamp ('LDN · 03 Aug 2026'), a headline and topic chips — dated, attributable, and no image needed.

Conversion is one centred sentence — 'Thoughtful design is the foundation for a life lived well' — and one outlined 'Request appraisal' button in acres of white; the printed magazine (Issue 08) and a photograph of the actual shopfront do the credibility work instead of badges.

sections.name: Hero — featured listing carousel
sections.notes: A wide landscape frame holds one villa, with the previous and next slides cropped in at both edges so you can feel the queue without a dot nav. Caption sits below the image in two columns: property name and market lower-left, a single descriptive line lower-right that names the architect. No headline, no CTA, no search — the first thing the site says is 'here is a house worth looking at'.

sections.name: Positioning + dual clocks
sections.notes: On a warm off-white panel: two running local times labelled LDN and IBZ, then a three-line serif statement ('An independent estate agency specialising in London and Ibiza's design-led homes.'), a short paragraph with the only hard numbers on the page ('More than 20 years' experience'), a small 'Find out more' with a square bullet, a hairline rule, and the BARNES International lockup as borrowed credibility. Right half: one architectural interior. This is the whole About page compressed into one screen.

sections.name: Featured Rentals & Featured Sales
sections.notes: Two horizontally scrolling carousels using the identical card, one for lettings and one for sales, each with 'View all' and All/Ibiza/London chips. Giving rentals the same visual weight as sales is a positioning choice — it says the taste, not the transaction size, is the brand. The badges carry the editorial judgement ('Architect Designed', 'Sea Views'), which is what makes a grid of tiles scannable rather than uniform.

sections.name: Appraisal line
sections.notes: A single centred sentence and one outlined button, surrounded by more whitespace than any other block. The pitch is a belief ('Thoughtful design is the foundation for a life lived well') followed by the service in three verbs ('buy better, sell smarter and let with confidence') — the only place on the page the agency asks for anything.

sections.name: A new chapter / offices + the magazine
sections.notes: Left column of text explains the South Kensington office and the BARNES partnership; the right is a photograph of the real Notting Hill shopfront with someone walking past — premises as proof. Directly beneath, the printed 'Domus Ibiza Magazine 2026 – Issue 08' is shown as a rendered cover next to a lifestyle frame, with 'Read Now' and 'Browse our Editorial'. A physical artefact is harder to fake than a testimonial.

sections.name: Over in Ibiza + Our Journal
sections.notes: A three-image cluster (villa, owners, terrace) sets up the island arm with two buttons ('Find your escape', 'Explore Ibiza'), then the journal grid alternates flat colour cards with photo cards, every card stamped with market and date. The editorial sits inside the same page and the same nav as Buy and Rent rather than being exiled to a blog.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: 'Need some advice?' repeats the three verbs, then a newsletter field with explicit consent, both offices' phone numbers side by side, two separate social sets (London and Ibiza), and the unglamorous compliance links spelled out — Landlord Letting Fees, Tenant Letting Fees, CMP Certificate. The dual-market structure holds all the way to the last line.

principle.title: Prove the claim with something that keeps running, not a sentence
principle.explanation: Every agency says it is 'international' or 'local' or 'always on'. Those are adjectives, and a reader discounts adjectives automatically. A live artefact — a clock, a counter, a dated stamp, a last-updated time — cannot be written by a copywriter; it can only be true. Domus Nova spends two lines of 10px mono on London and Ibiza local time and gets more credibility from it than the paragraph underneath.
principle.howToApply: On Aperture's Europe collection page, put the local time of each market in a small mono row above the intro line (Dallas / Lisbon / Madrid), and stamp the listings grid with 'Updated 27 Aug 2026, 09:14' pulled from the build, not typed. On a single property page, the equivalent is a live 'Days on market: 6' or 'Last price change: none' — one running number beats a paragraph of positioning.

site.name: Dove — 'Real Beauty Redefined for the AI Era' (Pinterest takeover + paid social key visual)

entries.tagline: Two portraits at identical crop with the AI prompt left visible under each — the ad hands you the evidence and lets you draw the conclusion.
entries.when: Published in the US in June 2025 by Mindshare for Dove (Unilever) — the AI chapter of Real Beauty's 20th year, continuing the stance Dove took in 2024's 'The Code'.
entries.summary: Dove's argument is that generative AI has learned a narrow definition of beauty, and rather than say so, the creative shows it: two vertical feed-shaped frames, same crop, same scale, same golden light, one generated from a generic prompt and one from Dove's Real Beauty prompt, with the prompt chips still sitting at the bottom of each image. The right third is almost empty — a navy question, a four-line stat, the wordmark with '20 years changing beauty', and a one-line CTA. The smallest type on the sheet is the honest part: AI was used here for the sole purpose of showing beauty bias in generative tools. In market it ran as a Pinterest homepage takeover plus paid social; the case study reports 787 million impressions and engagement 21.4% above Pinterest's norm for women.
whatWorks: The comparison is staged inside the tool's own interface: the prompt is left on the image as chips — 'imagine / a confident / woman' on the left, 'according to 🕊 Real Beauty Campaign' on the right — so the viewer can check exactly what was asked. The ad is self-verifying rather than self-congratulating.

The two frames are locked to the same crop, scale, focal length and warm light, so the only variable left in the composition is the thing being argued about. Any other difference would have let the viewer explain the result away.

The headline is a question nobody can answer with 'no' — 'What kind of beauty do we want AI to learn?' — set in three short lines of navy, which makes the brand the convener of the question rather than the owner of the answer.

The stat is deliberately un-round and attributed to a prediction, not to Dove ('By 2025, 90% of online content is predicted to be generated by Artificial Intelligence'), and it is set at roughly a third of the headline size — evidence in a supporting role.

A beauty ad with no product in it at all: no bottle, no pack shot, no swatch. The frames are portrait 9:16, i.e. already the shape of the feed they were built for, so nothing had to be re-cropped for placement.

The disclaimer works as craft, not compliance: admitting the ad used AI to demonstrate AI's bias closes the only hole a sceptic could put a finger in, and it is printed in the smallest type on the page rather than buried in a caption.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: Two phone-shaped rounded frames side by side, filling the left two-thirds. Before any words are read, the eye compares two faces at the same size and registers that one is uncannily smooth and one is a person laughing. The AI tell is left in on purpose — a melted patch on the left model's cheek and glassy plaid on her shirt.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'What kind of beauty do we want AI to learn?' in navy, three lines, centred in the right third. Beneath it, four short centred lines of grey: the 90% prediction, then 'Dove will keep committed to real beauty' and 'Learn more at: Dove.com' with only the domain in bold. Question first, position second, destination third — in that order.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: The prompt chips are the hero device. Bottom-left frame reads like an unfinished prompt bar ('imagine' with a cursor, then two white pills), bottom-right replaces the last pill with 'according to 🕊 Real Beauty Campaign' — the same interface, one input swapped. The dove mark appears inside the chip, so the logo does argumentative work instead of sitting in a corner.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: Deliberately soft: a domain in a sentence, then the wordmark with 'changing' bolded in '20 years changing beauty' — the only bold word in the block, and the one that carries the claim of continuity. Under it, the two-line asterisk about AI use. No button, no offer, no urgency.

principle.title: Stage the argument inside the interface, not next to it
principle.explanation: A claim about a system is easy to dismiss and hard to check. Rebuild the system's own interface — a prompt bar, a search field, a filter row, a results count — inside the creative, show the input you used, and the audience audits the claim themselves in about two seconds. It also solves the layout: the interface supplies the frame, the chips supply the caption, and you get to delete the explanatory paragraph.
principle.howToApply: For a listings ad, don't write 'more homes than the portals show'. Show two search-result panels side by side in your own UI at identical size, with the filter chips visible under each — 'Under €1M / 3+ beds / Portal' next to 'Under €1M / 3+ beds / Aperture' — and let the count and the photography differ. Same idea for a single property: put the real filter chips it satisfies along the bottom of the hero photograph instead of a bullet list.

entries.tagline: The compositor who made type into imagery — and who arrives at the composition with the wood letters in his hands and the press inked, not in a sketch.
entries.summary: Kitching was apprenticed at fifteen as a jobbing compositor, setting tickets, catalogues and posters by hand for six years, then spent decades in design studios — including Omnific with Derek Birdsall — before founding The Typography Workshop in Clerkenwell in 1989 and building a career out of a technology everyone else had abandoned. His letterpress work for The Guardian, the National Theatre, the British Library, Royal Mail and Dazed & Confused made words into pictures at large scale, printed by his own hand from wood and metal letter. He taught at the Royal College of Art from 1991 to 2006 and was made a Royal Designer for Industry in 1994. His line to students each morning is the whole method: 'I'm not interested in letterpress printing, I'm interested in what you can do with this stuff.'
whatWorks: Learn one craft from the inside before you art-direct it. Six years setting other people's tickets and catalogues gave him the vocabulary — sizes, spacing, lock-up, register — that he later broke on purpose. Fluency first, expression second.

Make the first version in the final material. The composition is arrived at by handling real type and pulling real proofs, so the true constraints (which sizes exist in the cabinet, how the ink sits, where the register drifts) shape the idea instead of being retrofitted to it.

Build the image out of the words themselves rather than adding illustration. In 'Rainforest' the Portuguese word descends through forest, trees, rain and earth so the setting depicts its own meaning — no picture required.
Hold every expressive move to a content test: 'I always try to have some logic to the job, to the work.' Scale, rotation and colour each have to be earned by what the words say.

Own the instrument. The workshop and its collections — including the 'Entertaining Types' theatrical wood type acquired in 1999 — are a competitive advantage no competitor can download; the studio's materials are part of its identity.

Make the artefact the master and the file the copy: prints are hand-set, hand-printed, then reproduced at the same size, so the ink texture and misregistration survive into the reproduction as evidence of how it was made.

sections.name: How he begins
sections.notes: With the words and the type cabinets, not a layout. He reads the commission looking for the one thought that can be carried by letterforms alone, then goes to see what actually exists — which faces, which sizes, how many of each sort. Availability is treated as part of the brief rather than an obstacle, which is why his solutions look inevitable rather than styled.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Composition by proofing. Set, lock up, ink by hand, pull a proof, look at it, change it, print again over the top. Because colour arrives as successive transparent layers rather than as a chosen palette, the final decisions are made with the sheet physically in front of him — the process is iterative in the material, not in a file, and each state is a real object he can judge.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Type as image: words scaled, rotated, overlapped and overprinted at poster scale from wood letter until the setting performs its own meaning. He leaves the marks of the method visible — ink texture, slight misregistration, the grain of the wood — so the piece reads as made rather than rendered, which is precisely what a vector version cannot fake.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Two rules do most of the work. First, the logic test: if a move can't be justified by the content, it comes out. Second, the medium is a means and never the subject — 'I'm not interested in letterpress printing, I'm interested in what you can do with this stuff' — which is the guard against nostalgia work, and the reason his commercial commissions never read as heritage pastiche.

principle.title: Make the first version in the final material
principle.explanation: Decisions taken in a sketch, a moodboard or an empty artboard are free, and free decisions are untested — the constraints that actually determine the outcome (the real photographs, the real address strings, the real column width, the real paper size, what the press or the template will actually do) are absent. Kitching never has that problem because his sketch *is* a print. Bringing the real material forward moves the hard discoveries to the beginning of the job instead of the end.
principle.howToApply: Build the first comp of any Aperture piece with the real assets in place: the actual selects at their actual crops, the real address and price strings at their real character counts, on the true print size — before any type refinement. For a page, do the first pass in the browser at the real breakpoint with the real listing data rather than in a design file. If a headline only works at a length the copy never is, you want to know that on day one.

entries.tagline: A spice shop that runs one four-claim spine down the entire page — named as a strip, argued as a comparison table, then evidenced with named farms and the people on them.
entries.summary: Underneath the loud palette this is one of the tightest argument structures in DTC: four claims — Single Origin, Fair Wages, Freshest Harvest, Highest Quality — are named once in a marigold strip near the top, then restated word-for-word as the four rows of a 'What Sets Us Apart' matrix two-thirds down, then evidenced a third time by a green full-bleed band of photographs from the farms themselves. The chassis is disciplined even where the brand is not: everything sits on a cream ground (#FFFDF3 / #FFFCEB), saturated colour is only ever allowed as a full-bleed band (magenta #D5137B, marigold #F58A23, green #007E00), and exactly two typefaces work with fixed jobs — the flared-serif P22 Mackinac Pro for every section heading and pull quote, Fustat sans for all UI, prices and body copy. The honest caveat: the middle of the page is still a conventional Shopify stack, and the carousel of star-rated product cards is the one place where four competing calls to action undo the clarity the rest of the page earns.
whatWorks: The same four claim labels appear twice in identical wording — as an icon strip near the top and as the row headings of the comparison table far below — so two modules read as one continuing argument instead of two pitches.

'What Sets Us Apart' is a 4-column × 5-row matrix (Diaspora Co. / Conventional Grocery Store / Other Spice Companies) with a mark per cell and a one-line qualifier under each — the 'why does this cost more' objection answered in a single scannable block rather than a paragraph.
Saturated colour is only ever a full-bleed band; cards, product tiles and photography always sit on cream, so no coloured container ever competes with a photograph.

Two typefaces with non-overlapping roles — P22 Mackinac Pro for headings and quotes, Fustat for every interface string — which is why a page carrying magenta, marigold and green still reads as one brand rather than a theme.
The sourcing claim is proved by a photograph of a named grower on the green band ('Sourced from 150+ farms across India & Sri Lanka'), not by a map graphic, a leaf icon or a certification badge.

Endorsement is split by job: one long pull quote at display size on its own magenta band does the persuading, while a small greyscale logo row (Wired, Bon Appétit) elsewhere does the reassuring — the two never share a block.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: A seasonal photograph — the Pumpkin Spice tin standing in a real still life of squash and pumpkin, not on seamless white — under one short sentence ('Your fall favorites are back!'), a single line of subcopy naming the two products, and exactly one magenta pill. No slider, no second CTA, no value props stacked in the fold.

sections.name: Claim strip
sections.notes: A marigold band directly under the hero naming the four claims — Single Origin, Fair Wages, Freshest Harvest, Highest Quality — as four small illustrated icons with two-word labels. It costs one screen-inch, sets the vocabulary for the rest of the page, and is the table of contents for the argument that follows.

sections.name: Cookbook + endorsement
sections.notes: The cookbook is sold editorially rather than as another product tile: a large P22 Mackinac pull quote attributed to Alice Waters, a second from Nik Sharma, and one 'Shop the cookbook' link — then a separate small greyscale press-logo row. Authority and reassurance are handled by two different components at two different scales.

sections.name: Most Popular grid
sections.notes: The commerce block: product cards with star rating, review count, badges (BESTSELLER, NEW), price and add-to-cart. It is the weakest section — every card shouts equally and the carousel arrows add a fifth thing to click — but it is quarantined in the middle of the page rather than interleaved through the argument.

sections.name: Sourcing band
sections.notes: A deep green (#007E00) full-bleed block, 'Sourced from 150+ farms across India & Sri Lanka', carrying two large photographs from the farms with real people in them and short caption copy naming the growers and the trade terms. This is the page's proof floor: the claim from the strip, now with a face and a place attached.

sections.name: What Sets Us Apart
sections.notes: A three-way comparison matrix on cream — Diaspora Co. against 'Conventional Grocery Store' and 'Other Spice Companies' — with the four claim labels as row headings and a one-line qualifier in each cell. It names the categories it is beating, which is what makes it feel like an argument rather than a brag; naming actual competitors would make it stronger still.

sections.name: FAQ, newsletter and footer
sections.notes: A marigold accordion answering the six questions the comparison table provokes ('How are your spices different?', 'How do you support your farm partners?'), then a magenta newsletter band with hand-drawn spice illustrations and a four-column link footer. The objection handling sits after the argument, not before it.

principle.title: Name four claims, then let the page prove each one twice
principle.explanation: Most pages make a claim once, in a strip of icons, and then move on to selling — so the claim is decoration. This page fixes four claims in a specific wording and then earns each of them at two further depths: a comparison matrix for the visitor who wants to argue, and named people and places for the visitor who wants to believe. Because the wording never drifts between the three passes, a skimmer, a comparer and a sceptic all leave having read the same four sentences at different resolutions — and the page reads as one argument rather than a stack of modules.
principle.howToApply: Before designing an Aperture listing or service page, write the four claims down as two-word labels and refuse to reword them afterwards. Place them once as a compact strip under the hero; restate the identical four as the row headings of a comparison block that names what you are being compared against (the portals, a conventional brokerage, a discount listing service); then prove each one with a specific artefact further down — the photographer by name, the actual days-on-market figure, the marketing pieces themselves. If a claim cannot survive all three passes, it was an adjective and belongs off the page.

entries.category: Creator-led social campaign with shoppable in-feed units
entries.tagline: Instead of policing 3.5 million unofficial 'Vaseline hacks', the brand lab-tested them and stamped the ones that passed with its own blue tick — so other people's videos became the advertising.
entries.when: Published May 2026 (South Africa and UK) — 2026 Clio Grand winner, by Ogilvy Singapore
entries.summary: People had been inventing uses for Vaseline for years and posting them — shoe polish, spice guard, teeth whitener, pomade, leather conditioner — with no involvement from the brand. Rather than issue a safety disclaimer or shoot a new film, Ogilvy Singapore built what the case calls a Social R&D Lab: scientists actually tested the viral hacks, and the brand then stitched into the original creators' videos to verify or debunk them, marking the survivors with a hand-drawn 'Vaseline Verified' tick. Verified hacks were made shoppable inside the same feed unit and the creators earned commission on tubs sold through them. Treat the numbers as the entrant's own — +43% underlying e-commerce sales growth, 63.3M interactions — but the structural move stands on its own.
whatWorks: The hook is not a brand asset at all — it is a stranger's existing video, already carrying its own audience, with the brand entering as a small badge dropped into the corner of the frame.

One reusable device does all the work: a hand-drawn white speech-bubble outline holding an iridescent check, with 'Verified' set as a bitmap/geometric hybrid — small enough to overlay any 9:16 frame without covering a face, and identical across hundreds of posts.
The verdict is binary and public — verify or debunk — so the badge carries information; a mark that can never say no is decoration.
Proof is shown as procedure rather than adjective: a lab bench, gloved hands, a gloss-meter reading going from 0.0 to 7.0 on screen, instead of the words 'dermatologically proven'.

The conversion step lives in the same frame as the proof — verified hack, then a tagged product card (£4.50, Vaseline Petroleum Jelly 250ml, Sold by UnileverUK, Add to basket / Buy now) — so the demonstration, the shelf and the creator's payout are one unit rather than three campaigns.

The whole system is one Vaseline blue with white type, which means the only colour, texture and lighting variety on screen comes from the creators' own footage — the brand layer never competes with the content it is certifying.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A face the viewer may already follow, in their own bedroom or workshop, mid-hack — a leather bag being conditioned, a shoe being buffed, cuticles being sealed. Nothing about the first second reads as an ad, because the first second is not the brand's footage.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: One word, 'Verified', carrying the entire argument: it concedes that the audience invented the use, and claims only the right to adjudicate it. The pixel-lettered V and d graft the language of a platform badge onto the brand's own wordmark, so the meaning is understood before the copy is read.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: The lab: gloved hands, pipettes, a gloss meter, before-and-after readings on screen. It is the only part of the campaign the brand shot, and it exists purely to make the badge cost something — the certification is credible because the testing is visible.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: The badge itself becomes the buy button: the verified frame carries a tagged product card with a real price and 'Buy now', and commission flows back to the creator whose hack it was. The call to action is the same object as the proof, which is why nothing has to be re-explained at the point of sale.

principle.title: Certify what your audience already made instead of shooting something new
principle.explanation: When people are already producing content about you, a new brand asset has to buy attention that their content already has. Adjudicating it — publicly, with a pass/fail that can genuinely fail — converts that existing reach into your media, gives your mark real information value, and makes the audience the author while you stay the authority. The discipline is that the mark must be refusable: a badge that is only ever awarded is a sticker, and viewers price it accordingly.
principle.howToApply: Buyers and sellers already circulate rules of thumb — 'never list in December', 'repaint the front door', 'the Zestimate is close enough', 'stage every room'. Run those against Aperture's own closing data and publish a standing series with one fixed overlay device — VERIFIED or BUSTED, the number, the sample size and the month — laid over the original post format rather than a new template, and let it say BUSTED often enough that VERIFIED means something. Same badge, same position, one claim per post.

entries.category: Communication design / brand systems and exhibition curation
entries.tagline: Muji's art director, who works by re-designing what everyone already knows and by building empty vessels rather than sending messages.
entries.summary: Hara joined Nippon Design Center in 1983 and has been Muji's art director since 2001 and a professor at Musashino Art University since 2003. He designed the programmes for the 1998 Nagano Winter Olympics ceremonies and the Expo 2005 Aichi posters, and curated the exhibitions that are really his method made public — Re-Design (2000), Haptic (2004), Senseware — alongside the books Designing Design, White and Ex-formation. The through-line is a refusal of novelty as the goal: design's job, in his account, is not to make things but to make things understood, and the strongest communication is often an empty container that the audience fills with their own meaning.
whatWorks: Set the brief as a re-design of an object everyone already knows — a toilet roll, a tea bag, a box of matches — so the audience carries the original in their head and the idea can be judged rather than merely admired.
Run 'ex-formation': take one subject and make it unknown again through several parallel studies, treating an increase in curiosity as the deliverable rather than a solution.
Write the brief in a sense other than sight — how it should feel in the hand, its weight, the sound it makes — and let the visual answer follow from that.

Design a vessel, not a message: the Muji 'Horizon' poster is a salt flat, a hairline horizon, one small figure and the logo, with no product and no copy, precisely so the brand can hold whatever the customer brings.
Judge by sufficiency instead of maximum: Muji's 'kore de ii' ('this will do') rather than 'kore ga ii' ('this is the one') — a standard that rules out the extra flourish by definition.
Treat white and emptiness as capacity rather than absence, and protect that space in the layout the way you would protect a headline.

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: Not with a search for a new form, but by choosing something already universal and re-designing it. Re-Design (2000) handed 32 designers everyday objects — toilet paper, tea bags, matches, immigration stamps — precisely because the familiar version acts as a control: every decision is visible against it, so the exhibition doubles as a critique of the designer's thinking rather than a display of their taste.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Ex-formation, the inverse of information. Where information makes something known, ex-formation makes the known unknown again: pick one subject (a river, the Shinano; a resort; the nose) and run many parallel studies on it, each stripping away an assumption, until the subject is genuinely strange. He teaches it as a studio method — one subject, many attacks — and counts the increase in curiosity, not a finished artefact, as the result.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: The empty vessel. Muji under Hara does not broadcast a proposition; it offers a container. The 2003 'Horizon' campaign is an enormous photograph of the Uyuni salt flat with a figure the size of a full stop and the logo — no product, no headline — and the brand's whole meaning is what the viewer supplies. The companion move is Haptic (2004): briefing designers to design for touch, weight and temperature, so the concept arrives through a sense that cannot be faked in a rendering.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: 'Design is not about making things, it is about making things understood.' The practical tests: is this a message or a vessel? Can more be removed without the thing breaking? Is 'this will do' honestly true, or am I still adding to impress? And does the piece communicate through a sense other than sight — because if it only works as an image, it will not survive being an object, a shop or a room.

principle.title: Redesign the artefact your audience already knows by heart
principle.explanation: A newly invented format has to be learned before it can be judged, which is why new formats get admired and then quietly ignored. A re-design of something familiar is legible on sight: the audience holds the original in their head, so every change you made is visible, arguable and measurable, and you are forced to edit where you might otherwise have invented. It also protects you from the trap of proving your value with novelty rather than with improvement.
principle.howToApply: List the ten artefacts an Aperture buyer has already seen a hundred times — the yard sign, the open-house sign-in sheet, the one-page flyer, the 'just listed' post, the price-drop email, the key tag, the appointment text, the business card, the MLS photo order, the closing gift. Rank them by impressions per year, take the one with the most impressions and the least design, and redesign only that one thing. Present it as old-and-new at the same size on one sheet so the improvement is the argument, and do one a month instead of inventing a new format.

entries.tagline: A textile company that holds every piece of interface in greyscale so the only colour anywhere on the page comes out of a photograph.
entries.summary: Kvadrat sells fabric to architects, and the homepage is built so that nothing on screen can compete with the fabric. The wordmark, nav, headings, body copy, buttons and footer are all white, off-white, near-black and one mid-grey — so the blue sky through the weave in the hero, the green and blue curtains in the second card, and the oxblood chair further down are the only saturated colour a visitor ever sees. Type is never set over an image: every photograph runs clean and the title, two lines of copy and a dark pill CTA sit centred beneath it in a narrow measure, which makes the page read like catalogue spreads rather than a website. The honest caveat is that the discipline is total — every block gets the identical card and the identical pill, so nothing is louder than anything else and the page gives no steer on what matters most; it is a beautifully set shelf rather than an argument.
whatWorks: The UI palette is white, off-white, near-black and one mid-grey, with zero brand accent colour — every saturated pixel on the page is inside a photograph, so the products supply the entire colour story and nothing has to be re-picked when the season changes.
No type is ever set over an image. Photographs run clean edge to edge within the margin, and the title, two lines of copy and the CTA sit centred underneath in a measure about half the image width.

Four different photographic registers — a macro shot of the weave against sky, product on a warm seamless, an in-situ interior with curtains and furniture, and three chairs on a studio floor — all lit in the same soft daylight with no grade, so the variety reads as one shoot instead of a stock mix.

Images are inset by exactly the same left/right margin as the text and never bleed to the viewport edge, which frames the whole page like paper and keeps the white ground continuous from masthead to footer.
One CTA component, repeated: a dark near-black pill with a white one-word label, the same size everywhere. There is no primary/secondary button system to maintain and no colour spent on buttons.

A sub-brand tab strip (kvadrat / shade / acoustics / Raf Simons / really) sits in 11px grey above the masthead, so a visitor picks the business before the product and the main nav stays seven plain words.
Product names are set in italic inside running copy — ‘discover Waves’, ‘two textiles, Ria and Field’ — a magazine convention that identifies a SKU without a chip, badge or coloured tag.

sections.name: Brand strip & masthead
sections.notes: Two stacked bars do different jobs. The top one is a tiny grey tab strip of the five sub-brands with the active one underlined, plus search, a colour tool, language and account pushed hard right. Beneath it the masthead is almost empty: lowercase ‘kvadrat’ wordmark at left, seven plain nav words at right (Products, Brands, Sustainability strategy, Designers, Inspiration, Contact, Events). Splitting business-selection from page-navigation is what lets a company with five sub-brands keep a seven-item menu.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: An extreme macro of an open weave shot against blue sky — you can see through the fabric. It fills the column width but stops at the page margin, and carries no overlay type at all. The proposition (‘THREE presents textiles as sensual, spatial and sculptural forms’) sits below it, centred, at body size, with an ‘Explore’ pill under that. Because the image is a texture rather than a scene, it works as both a photograph and a brand pattern.

sections.name: Two-up: events
sections.notes: 3daysofdesign and Fulton Market Design Days share a row: a black mesh textile sculpture floating on warm off-white next to a real interior with green and blue curtains, a sofa and a paper lamp. One is object-on-seamless, one is in-situ — the pairing shows the material abstract and applied in a single glance. Identical card structure under both: centred title, two lines, pill.

sections.name: Full-width feature: Our recycled polyester
sections.notes: The sustainability story is not a badge or an icon row — it is three chairs in navy, oxblood and olive on a grey seamless floor, with the headline ‘Our recycled polyester’ set large and light beneath the photo. The claim is made in the one place a specifier actually judges it: how the recycled fabric looks upholstered. One line of copy handles longevity and performance; there is no percentage graphic anywhere.

sections.name: Two-up: collaboration & proof
sections.notes: The last content row pairs cultural credibility with commercial proof — Klára Hosnedlová's textile commission at the New Museum next to opera-house seating at the Nanchang Poly Grand Theatre. The CTAs differentiate the two intents in words rather than styling: ‘Discover our collaborations’ and ‘Discover our projects’. Named textiles (Ria, Field) appear in italic inside the copy, so the art story and the spec story both end in a product.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: The only tinted panel on the page — a light grey block that signals end-of-document without a rule or a divider. Three columns, each headed in near-black bold with links beneath in mid-grey: Downloads (product downloads, image bank, catalogues, care and maintenance), Company info, and Contact us with the full Ebeltoft address, CVR number, email and phone. The download column is placed first, which tells you the real user is a specifier who came for a file.

principle.title: Spend the colour budget on the photograph, never on the interface
principle.explanation: Most brand pages spend colour twice — an accent on buttons, badges and headings, plus whatever is inside the imagery — and the two fight. Every coloured chip near a photograph competes with the thing it is pointing at, and it commits you to a palette that has to be reconciled with each new shoot. Holding the interface to one near-black, one grey and a white ground means the imagery can change completely, season to season or listing to listing, without a single UI decision being revisited, and it makes any photograph look more expensive than it is because nothing on screen is brighter than it.
principle.howToApply: On the next Aperture page, set the whole interface — nav, headings, body, buttons, footer — in one near-black (#1A1A1A), one mid-grey for secondary text, and white, and delete every accent: no gold price chips, no coloured ‘Just Listed’ badges, no tinted section bands, no coloured icons. Use a single dark pill for every call to action at the same size, and let the words differ instead of the colour (‘See the home’ vs ‘Book a viewing’). Then screenshot the page and desaturate everything except the photographs — if anything outside a photo changes, it was spending colour it did not need.

site.name: Jacquemus — ‘Bags on Wheels’ (vertical social film, Instagram/TikTok)

entries.when: Launched 5 April 2023 on Jacquemus’ Instagram, captioned ‘I THINK I LIKE PARIS NOW’; 3D by Ian Padgham. Reported ~20M views inside 24 hours.
entries.tagline: A product ad with no headline, no logo lockup and no call to action — just the bag, at bus scale, rolling through real Paris traffic.
entries.summary: Jacquemus posted a 9:16 clip of giant burgundy Le Bambino handbags on wheels driving down the bus lane past the Palais Garnier. It is entirely CGI, but every production decision is aimed at hiding that: real location, real midday sun and hard shadows, a handheld camera held low at pavement height, no colour grade and no cut to a product shot. The debate about whether it was real is what carried it — people stopped to verify a photograph rather than to read an ad, and the thing they stared at while verifying was the silhouette of the product. The only branding in frame is the small gold foil logo that is on the actual bag.
whatWorks: The hook is a scale error inside a place the audience can name. Palais Garnier and a painted Paris bus lane are unambiguous, so the one impossible element — a handbag the size of a bus — forces the viewer to check the image instead of skipping it.

It is shot in the grammar of a bystander, not a brand: vertical, handheld with visible wobble, slightly low, uncorrected daylight. The format is the disguise — it looks like something a passer-by filmed, which is the only kind of footage the feed does not pre-filter as advertising.
One product, one colourway, no cast, no props, no copy. Nothing in the frame competes with the outline of the bag, which is what a handbag campaign actually has to sell.
Branding is diegetic: the gold JACQUEMUS foil appears because it is physically on the bag. No lockup, no end card, no logo bug — so nothing in frame reads as a paid unit.
The words live in the caption (‘I THINK I LIKE PARIS NOW’), not on the image, which keeps the creative clean and lets the brand’s voice do the work in the one place people expect voice.

There is no CTA at all. The intended action is the argument in the comments about whether it is real — the ad is designed to be described to someone else, which is cheaper distribution than any button.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: First frame is already the whole idea: a bus-sized Le Bambino rolling in the bus lane in front of the Opéra. No build-up, no logo intro, no title card — the contradiction lands inside the first half-second, which is all a vertical feed gives you.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: There is none in the frame. The message is carried entirely by the caption, and it is a mood rather than a claim — ‘I THINK I LIKE PARIS NOW’. No product name, no price, no collection reference. Withholding the copy is what keeps the clip readable as footage rather than as an ad.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: The product is the hero at architectural scale, in real light. The craft is in the imperfections that were deliberately kept: the camera drifts, the sun is harsh and unflattering, the bag is slightly soft with motion, pedestrians and bollards partially occlude it. A clean, graded, tripod-steady version of the same render would have read instantly as CGI and died.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: Absent, and that is the design. No swipe-up, no shop link, no end card. The conversion event is the share and the ‘is this real?’ comment; the product page is left for the people who go looking. It works because the silhouette is memorable enough to be searched for by shape.

principle.title: Break the scale of the one thing you’re selling, in a place your audience can name
principle.explanation: In a feed, people verify before they read. An adjective can be skipped; a photograph containing a real, recognisable location and one impossible measurement cannot, because the brain has to resolve the contradiction before it can move on — and the thing it stares at while resolving is your product. The recognisable place is the load-bearing half: the same object at the wrong size against a neutral background is just a render, and gets scrolled past. Shooting it in bystander grammar (vertical, handheld, unpolished daylight) is what stops the feed from filing it as advertising before the idea lands.
principle.howToApply: For a listing, pick the single element that IS the property — the arched window, the roofline, the pool shape, the front door — and build one asset where it appears at the wrong size in a street the local audience can name. It does not need CGI: chalk or tape the window outline full-size on the sidewalk at a named intersection, lay the floor plan out at 1:1 in the neighbourhood park, or prop a door-sized print of the front door against a landmark. Film it vertically, handheld, at eye level in ordinary daylight, keep every headline out of the frame and put the line in the caption instead, and let the only branding be the sign that would genuinely be standing there.

entries.category: Graphic design studio — Amsterdam / late modernism
entries.when: Founded 1997 · Amsterdam, Netherlands · Marieke Stolk, Erwin Brinkers, Danny van den Dungen
entries.tagline: Three people who have run the same studio for nearly thirty years by refusing to hire anyone, and who write the argument before they design it.
entries.summary: Stolk, Brinkers and Van den Dungen met at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie and started Experimental Jetset in Amsterdam in 1997. They have stayed exactly three people ever since — no employees, no departments, no named creative director — and describe the studio as a rock band rather than a firm: a unit small enough to share one artistic language, where everyone is invested in the outcome instead of executing someone else’s. The work is printed matter, museum identity and signage (the 2013 Whitney ‘responsive W’, the Stedelijk, a long shelf of books), almost always in a late-modernist vocabulary with the palette held near black, white, red and blue. Their monograph is called Statement and Counter-Statement, which is a fair description of the method: they write their way to a position, then set it.
whatWorks: Run the practice as a band, not a firm — cap it at the number of people who can share one visual language and all hold the whole job, and treat that cap as a design decision rather than a stage you grow out of.

Use ‘total football’ for roles: no fixed positions, any member can take any part of a job, and workload is distributed so all three keep every skill instead of specialising into a single point of failure. (They are honest that deadline pressure pushes them back into habitual roles — the rule is the intent, not a claim of perfection.)

Write before you design. Research and written argument come first, and writing is explicitly how they get enough distance to judge their own work — the essay is a working tool, not marketing afterwards.

Judge a commission by how much of your range it uses. They call a project satisfying when it needs writing, research, print and signage together, and treat one that exercises a single skill as a worse job regardless of the fee.

Choose each typeface for a stated reason rather than a house habit — Univers when the reference is historical, Futura when a logotype has to be embedded inside the letterform — and reject ‘we always use Helvetica’ as a description of the method even when the results look consistent.
Credit the studio, not the individual. They call the designer-as-rock-star framing repulsive and have gone out of their way to avoid appearing personally, which keeps the argument about the work.

sections.name: How the studio is structured
sections.notes: Three people since 1997, deliberately never more. Their stated model is a rock band — ‘a very tight socio-economic unit: just two, three or four people, sharing one collective artistic language’ — set explicitly against the boss/workers hierarchy and separated departments of a normal studio. Roles are run on Johan Cruijff’s total football: a player who moves out of position can be covered by any other player on the team, so no capability lives in one person.

sections.name: How they take on work
sections.notes: The selection test is range, not sector: the projects they describe as satisfying are the ones that require them to ‘function to our full abilities’ — writing, research, print, signage, sometimes sound and moving image in the same commission. That biases them toward long relationships with cultural institutions and museums, where one job legitimately contains a book, an identity, a wall and an essay, and away from single-deliverable work no matter how well it pays.

sections.name: Signature method
sections.notes: Argument first, form second. Extensive research and writing precede the visual work, and they keep writing afterwards because it ‘enables us to reflect on our own work, to look at our work from a bit of a distance’. The vocabulary is then deliberately narrow — late-modernist type, a palette mostly held to black, white, red and blue — which they defend not as a style but as their ‘authentic language, our mother tongue’, inherited from the Dutch late-modernist landscape they grew up in.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Every formal choice has to be answerable: a typeface is picked for a historical reference or a structural need, not because it is the house face. Growth is the thing they refuse — scaling would break the shared language the whole model depends on. And authorship stays collective: the studio is credited rather than the three of them, because a practice organised around one name starts optimising for that name.

principle.title: Size the practice so everyone can hold the whole job
principle.explanation: Experimental Jetset have stayed three people for nearly thirty years on purpose. At that size there is one shared visual language, no handoffs, and nobody working on a fragment they cannot see the end of — quality is a property of the group rather than a checkpoint someone else owns. The total-football rule is what keeps the cap from becoming a bottleneck: because any member can take any part of a job, capacity is elastic and no single skill is trapped in one head. The corollary is that the constraint has to be enforced on the intake side too — you protect the size by choosing fewer, wider projects, not by working faster.
principle.howToApply: Write down the largest number of people who could work on an Aperture campaign and still all have read the listing, seen the photographs and be able to finish each other’s pieces — for most of this work that is two or three. Treat that as a hard cap, and take fewer, wider jobs to stay under it: prefer the client who needs the CSVs, the magazine, the print pack and the page over four clients who each need one flyer. Then run total football inside it — rotate who writes the copy, who does the photo selects and who builds the layout across jobs, so no single part of the pipeline lives with only one person.

entries.tagline: A 15,000-pixel infrastructure homepage carried entirely by one illustrator's hand, where every drawing states a specific mechanic instead of decorating the section.
entries.summary: Fly.io sells hardware-isolated Linux machines for AI agents — a category where nearly every competitor's homepage is a dark gradient with a glowing terminal. Fly does the opposite: a white ground, pastel airbrushed panels with a halftone dot texture, a high-contrast old-style serif for two-to-four-word headings, and purple-and-mint marker-line characters (a tower PC with wings and a beak, a sprite asleep in a bed, a trench-coated sprite holding an ID card) that each explain one behaviour rather than filling a slot. The page alternates strictly between tinted panels for the argument and plain white for the technical claims, so the rhythm does the wayfinding with no dividers or eyebrow labels, and the proof at the bottom is deliberately unglamorous: four purple metrics and three long testimonials attributed only by role and company type. One honest weak spot — the small grey body copy inside the pastel cards is the lowest-contrast type on the page, and a few of the drawings (the hat, the planets) charm more than they explain.
whatWorks: One illustrator, one hand, one job per drawing: a sprite asleep in a bed = it sleeps when the agent stops; a trench-coated sprite holding an ID = the token never lands on the machine. The illustration is the explanation, so no diagram or jargon paragraph is needed.

Section containers carry the meaning: rounded full-bleed pastel panels with a halftone dot texture hold the persuasion, plain white holds the technical claims — alternating them is the only wayfinding device on a page with no section dividers and no eyebrow labels.

Headlines are two-to-four-word states of mind in the serif (“Grow without drama”, “Nothing to Manage”, “Support that knows the stack”); every specific lives in a two-line sub-sentence set in the sans at body size, never in the headline.
Proof is four numbers, not a paragraph: 18+ regions, <1 second boot, 500ms typical deploy, 99.9% uptime — set in purple in a 2×2 grid with hairline dividers, directly beside the claim they support.

Testimonials are attributed by role and company type only — “Platform Engineer / Series B startup”, “Staff Engineer / Fintech”, “Founder / AI-first product” — with no names, no headshots and no logo wall, and the quotes left long and un-trimmed.

The disqualifying condition sits inside the block that makes the promise: “Sprites Block Device is currently in private beta” in small grey directly under the durable-filesystem claims, rather than in a footnote.

sections.name: Hero — “Computers for agents”
sections.notes: Full-bleed pastel airbrush (mint → pink → lavender) with wandering hand-drawn ribbon lines and a stack of winged purple tower-PC characters at the right. Two serif lines of headline, then two short declarative sub-lines that do the positioning by negation — “Sandboxes aren't enough. / Give your agent a real computer and get back to building.” — and exactly one purple pill. No logo strip, no secondary CTA, no product screenshot in the fold.

sections.name: Use-case carousel — “Machines that Remember”
sections.notes: The first tinted panel restates the offer in one sentence (“Real hardware-isolated Linux computers for agents, evals, and tools. The bill goes to zero when nobody's home.”) then runs a horizontal card set — Coding Agents, Personal agents, MCP servers — each a small drawing plus three lines of plain prose. Naming actual tools by name (Claude, Codex, MCP) does the qualifying that an audience selector usually does.

sections.name: Capability blocks — “A Real Durable Filesystem” / “Nothing to Manage”
sections.notes: White section: serif head and two short claim lines on the left, three hand-drawn checkmarks with one-line benefits on the right, then the private-beta disclosure in small grey. Then straight back into a tinted panel of three drawn cards (No disk sizing, Automatic checkpointing, Sprites Connectors). The alternation is the structure; the white sections read as facts and the coloured ones as pitch.

sections.name: Product disambiguation — “Sprites: where your agent runs. Machines: where you run what it builds.”
sections.notes: Instead of a comparison table, one centred serif sentence resolves which product is which, over a wide drawn cityscape, with two calm cards beneath (Sprites / Machines) each ending in a text link rather than a button. A two-product problem solved with a sentence.

sections.name: Scale proof — “Grow without drama”
sections.notes: Left column argues the migration fear away in two short paragraphs (“The API you start with is the API you keep”); right column answers it with the four-metric grid. The claim and its evidence are on the same horizontal band, so the numbers read as the answer to that specific worry rather than as a stat band bolted onto the page.

sections.name: Credentials, logos and support
sections.notes: “A Connection to Everything” opens with an italic lead-in that states the risk in the brand's voice (“Sprites are social creatures. Your credentials shouldn't be.”) and closes on a single centred pill. Eleven customer wordmarks then sit in two centred grey rows with no “trusted by” headline at all, followed by “Support that knows the stack” — “Our support team writes code” — and the three role-attributed quotes.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: The only dark surface on the site: deep indigo, wordmark, five short link columns (Company / Articles / Resources / Contact / Legal) that include Status and Support Metrics as first-class links, then a newsletter row whose pitch is written like a person — “What we shipped, what we learned, like … stuff you put in a newsletter. Get it monthly.”

principle.title: Draw the mechanism you can't photograph
principle.explanation: The most persuasive parts of an offer are usually the invisible ones — what happens while nobody is watching, what you no longer have to do, where the risk is being held. There is nothing to photograph, so most pages reach for a stock image or a generic icon set, and the claim stays an adjective. A commissioned drawn vocabulary in a single recognisable hand fixes both problems at once: each drawing can state one specific behaviour, and because the hand is unique to you it can't be bought by a competitor the way a photo library or an icon pack can.
principle.howToApply: List the parts of the Aperture offer that have no photograph — the pre-list timeline, what happens between signing and the photo shoot, how an off-market listing reaches a buyer, what's actually in the print pack — and give each one small drawing in a single hand, drawn once and reused across the page, the magazine and the pitch deck. Caption each with the behaviour it states (“photography booked before the sign goes up”), keep the set to one line weight and two colours so it reads as a system, and reserve photography for the properties themselves so drawings and photographs never compete for the same job.

site.name: Pedigree — ‘Adoptable’ (programmatic display, social and digital OOH)

entries.tagline: Every Pedigree ad becomes an ad for a real shelter dog that is available near the person seeing it — and the dog is pulled from the media the moment it's adopted.
entries.when: Launched 10 April 2024 in New Zealand as a test market (Colenso BBDO Auckland with Nexus Studios), published June 2024 and rolled out internationally through 2024–25; Cannes Lions 2024 and Clio 2025 winner
entries.summary: Colenso BBDO turned Pedigree's entire media buy into a distribution channel for shelter dogs: a plain shelter snapshot is rebuilt as a studio-quality image — a digital double supplies the pose, a machine-learning model refines it back to the specific real dog — and then dropped into Pedigree's own ad units, geo-targeted so the animal shown is genuinely local and genuinely available, and withdrawn from circulation as soon as it is adopted. The key visual explains the whole product in one frame: a single dog's face split down the middle, untextured grey CG mesh on the left, finished warm studio portrait on the right, on flat Pedigree yellow, under an ‘Adoptable’ wordmark whose paw-in-a-house dingbat is the offer. The one line of copy describes the media model rather than a benefit — “Turning every PEDIGREE ad into an ad for a shelter dog.” — and the result is counted in animals rather than impressions: 50% of featured dogs were homed within two weeks of appearing. Worth naming honestly: this is AI-enhanced imagery of a living animal, and it only stays honest because the dog is real, local and reachable, and disappears when it's gone.
whatWorks: The hook is a single image that explains the mechanic with no diagram: one face, split on the centre line, raw mesh against finished portrait — process and payoff in the same frame.
Flat brand yellow, one subject, no environment: at feed size the split is the only thing competing for attention, which is why it survives a 3-inch screen.
The wordmark carries the offer — ‘Adoptable’ in a warm slab-serif with a paw-in-a-house mark replacing the accent — so the campaign is named, not described.
The support line states the media model in plain words (“Turning every PEDIGREE ad into an ad for a shelter dog.”) rather than a product benefit, which is what makes a brand ad worth watching.

The buy is the deliverable: geo-targeting and first-party data mean the dog shown is nearby and actually available, and a standing rule pulls it the moment it's adopted, so the creative can never go stale or lie.
The result is countable in the unit that matters — 50% of featured dogs adopted within two weeks — not in reach.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The split face. The left half is deliberately unfinished — grey, untextured, visibly computer-generated — so the eye is forced to read left-to-right as a transformation rather than as a portrait. It works because the seam sits exactly on the animal's centre line, where a viewer already expects symmetry.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: One word doing the naming (‘Adoptable’, with the house-and-paw dingbat), one sentence doing the explaining, set small and centred beneath it. No benefit claim, no product shot, no dog food anywhere in the frame — the brand appears once, as the rosette logo in the corner.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: The finished half is lit like a pedigree studio portrait — catchlight in the eye, warm brown coat against saturated yellow — which is the actual argument of the campaign: shelter dogs lose adoptions to bad photography, so the fix is to give them the photography that sells purebreds.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: The key visual carries no button; the conversion lives in the live units it explains, where the dog shown links through to that animal's shelter profile. The call to action is inventory, not a verb — and the campaign's honesty rests on the retirement rule behind it.

principle.title: Spend the media on live inventory, not on a brand image
principle.explanation: Most brand advertising spends its whole budget on a picture of the idea of the thing, then asks the audience to go find the actual thing themselves. If the ad unit instead carries a real, currently available item chosen by the viewer's location, three things happen at once: the creative can never be stale, the click has somewhere specific to land, and the campaign becomes countable in units moved rather than impressions served. The rule that makes it credible is the retirement rule — the item leaves the media the moment it converts, so nobody is ever shown something they can't have.
principle.howToApply: Make the standing Aperture social and display unit a feed rather than a key visual: one fixed frame — photograph, street, price, days on market, small ‘Available today’ stamp — filled automatically with the nearest currently-available listing to the viewer, and pulled the same day it goes under contract. Keep one designed chassis so the only thing that changes is the property, and report the campaign in listings shown and tours booked rather than reach.

entries.tagline: The Black Panther Party's Minister of Culture, who ran a national weekly visual language off paste-up tables, transfer tints and the cheapest press available.
entries.summary: Douglas learned commercial printing basics at 13 in a juvenile correctional facility, studied graphic design at City College of San Francisco from 1960, and joined the Black Panther Party in 1967 as its Revolutionary Artist and later Minister of Culture. He redesigned The Black Panther, moved it onto a web press so it could carry colour and graphics, and art-directed it weekly to a peak circulation of 300,000–400,000 in 1970 — then adapted his strongest drawings across posters, flyers, pamphlets and greeting cards.
