What makes him a process study rather than a style study is that almost every visual decision was a production decision: the thick woodcut-weight outlines exist because a cheap newspaper press misregisters, and the tints exist because a second colour was affordable and a fourth was not.
whatWorks: Decide the reproduction before the drawing: the heavy black marker outline was chosen because it hides the registration drift of a cheap web press — the style is a specification for the press, not a preference.
Buy texture instead of colour: most issues ran black plus one colour, with transfer film patterns and tints supplying shading, depth and greys that a halftone budget wouldn't cover.
Keep a repeatable weekly kit rather than a studio: “regular tables, regular lights, Elmer's glue, rubber cement. We cut and pasted. We made up our own layout sheets. Non-repro blue markers.”

Choose tools by what protects the deadline — he preferred Formatt transfer lettering to Letraset because the sheet had a line under the alphabet, so words could be set straight without rubbing letters off.
One drawing, many surfaces: the images that worked were re-cut for the newspaper cover, the poster, the flyer and the greeting card instead of commissioning new art per format.

Test legibility against a named person, not a peer: “You have to draw in a way that even a child can understand to reach your broadest audience without losing the substance or insight of what is represented.”

sections.name: How he begins
sections.notes: From the distribution end, not the artboard. The first question is which press, which paper, how many colours and what day it ships — he upgraded the paper itself to a web press to unlock colour and graphics before worrying about individual layouts. The brief also arrives as a real audience with a real reading distance: papers sold on street corners, posters taped in windows, read by people with no design vocabulary and no patience.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Weekly paste-up on a fixed, cheap kit — self-made layout sheets, rubber cement, non-repro blue, transfer lettering, photostats — with drawing, collage and re-collage of his own earlier drawings and found photographs as the way to make volume possible. The system is designed so that a full-colour national visual identity can be produced every seven days by a handful of people with no budget.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Woodcut-weight black contour, flat areas of one spot colour, and transfer-film tints for everything in between. It reads at a glance across a street, survives being folded, photocopied and reprinted, and is forgiving of the exact printing faults it was designed around — which is why the same artwork works as a cover, a placard and a card.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: The image has to be understood instantly by the broadest possible audience without losing its substance — comprehension is the acceptance test, not sophistication. And the work is judged on what it does: the drawings serve specific, nameable purposes (the survival programmes, free breakfasts, clinics, legal aid, recruitment), so any image that can't say which job it is doing doesn't run.

principle.title: Design for the worst surface in the chain, then run everything off the same artwork
principle.explanation: Every piece has a most-degraded destination — a thumbnail in a feed, a black-and-white office copy of a flyer, a 200-pixel card in an email, a sign read from a moving car — and that destination, not the retina mockup, is what decides line weight, contrast, crop and type size. Designing for it first has a second payoff: an image tough enough for the worst surface is usually good enough for all the others, so one piece of artwork can serve every format instead of each format getting its own art and its own drift.
principle.howToApply: Before designing an Aperture piece, write down the roughest place it will actually land — usually a 400px card on a phone or a photocopied open-house handout — and build the first version at that size in greyscale: one image, one heavy-enough type weight, the address and price legible, nothing that depends on fine tint or a hairline rule. Then produce the flyer, the story ad, the email card and the postcard off that same artwork by re-cropping, not redrawing, and check each one by printing it on the office copier: whatever disappears there was never load-bearing.

entries.tagline: A museum homepage set almost entirely in one heavy grotesque on plain white, where the artwork supplies the whole palette — and the only two colour panels on the page are both asks.
entries.summary: MoMA's homepage is a stack of near-identical rows built from one custom grotesque (MoMA Sans, drawn by Christian Schwartz with the museum's design team and Made Thought in 2017, a refined Franklin Gothic — the museum's face since the 1930s) on white: a two-line bold section heading with a one-line purpose and a single arrow link in the left rail, content in the well to its right. Nothing is tinted, bordered or badged, so the art supplies the entire palette — a turquoise installation wall, Warhol's Flowers, van Gogh's Starry Night — and the two saturated bands on the page (lime for the Modern Fund, cyan for UNIQLO Friday Nights) are the only places the museum asks for something. The quiet masterstroke is the collection grid: each work sits uncropped at its own proportions, with the captions rather than the picture edges doing the aligning. The honest caveat is length — at roughly 16,000px with eight rows in the same rhythm, the middle of the page flattens, and only the two colour panels break the tie.
whatWorks: One typeface doing two jobs: heavy MoMA Sans for every heading (two lines, tight, sentence case) and the same family at body size for all copy — no serif, no italic, no display face anywhere on the page.

The welcome line and the operational fact share one row: 'Welcome / Explore art and ideas at MoMA.' on the left, 'The museum is open 10:30 a.m.–5:30 p.m. today.' plus a black 'Plan your visit' button on the right, closed by a single black rule.

Uncropped artwork: the collection grid lets each work keep its native aspect (Warhol's Flowers tall, Man Ray's Chess Set wide) and aligns the two-line caption — artist in bold, title in italic — instead of the image edges.

Only two saturated panels on a 16,000px page, and both are asks — lime for 'Support experimentation, learning, and creativity → Donate to the Modern Fund', cyan for 'Free admission during UNIQLO Friday Nights'.
Carousels bleed off the right edge — the third exhibition card is deliberately cut by the viewport — so 'there is more' is shown by the crop instead of being said by a label.
Editorial cards carry a small cyan kicker naming the strand (UNIQLO ArtSpeaks, Art for All) above the headline, so a sponsored series and an in-house one run through the identical card.

sections.name: Utility header & nav
sections.notes: The wordmark sits far left at display size; Membership, a grey Donate and a cyan Tickets sit top-right; a second row carries five plain nouns (Visit, Exhibitions and events, Art and artists, Store, search). The two money actions are the only elements on the page with a filled background, and they are separated from browsing by living on their own row.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: A single full-bleed installation photograph, edge to edge, with no type on it at all and no slider controls. Because the hero carries no words, the first typography a visitor meets is the Welcome block, which means the greeting can be quiet rather than shouting over an image.

sections.name: Welcome
sections.notes: 'Welcome' as an H1 with a one-line purpose beneath, and on the same row, right-aligned, today's actual opening hours plus a black 'Plan your visit' button; a black rule closes the block. The emotional line and the operational fact are given equal billing in one row — the most useful thing a museum homepage can do.

sections.name: Exhibitions
sections.notes: A 3-up carousel that bleeds past the right edge, arrows aligned to the heading. Each card is image, bold title, then a small kicker where there is news ('Member Last Look, Sep 13') and a closing date ('Through Nov 29') — so urgency is carried by dates, not by badges.

sections.name: Art and artists in our collection
sections.notes: The left rail holds the two-line heading, a one-sentence dek ('Discover artworks that speak to you, from the 1880s to today.') and one arrow link; the right well holds a three-column grid of works at their true proportions, each captioned with artist in bold and title in italic. Rows are ragged in height and read as ordered because the labels line up.

sections.name: Events, visit services & the two colour ask panels
sections.notes: 'Events for everyone' and 'Your day at MoMA' reuse the identical left-rail contract — heading, one-line dek, one arrow link — with a large event card plus four small square category tiles (Films, Families, Members, Talks), then the visit-services cards (Digital Visitor Guide, Design Store, cafés). The two flat panels that interrupt this rhythm are the only asks on the page: lime for the Modern Fund, cyan for free Friday nights, each set heading-left, copy-and-arrow-right.

sections.name: MoMA PS1, partners & footer
sections.notes: The affiliate gets a black band — heading, two-line description, arrow link, photograph right — which is the only ground change in the page and does the work a nav item would have done badly. Beneath it a grey strip credits major partners ('MoMA would like to thank our major partners.' + one logo), then a dark footer repeats both addresses with 'Open today, 10:30 a.m.–5:30 p.m.', socials, the wordmark and the legal line.

principle.title: Let each image keep its own proportions, and align the captions instead of the crops
principle.explanation: A grid usually picks one aspect ratio and crops everything into it. That is fine for interchangeable stock and destructive for objects whose shape is information — a painting, a floorplan, a magazine spread, a product silhouette. MoMA's collection grid pins the column width and the caption position, then lets the height float, so a tall Warhol and a wide Man Ray sit in the same row at their true proportions; the row still reads as ordered because the labels line up, not because the pictures do. You get variation for free and never have to explain why the work was cut.
principle.howToApply: On the Aperture pages where an object's shape carries meaning — floorplans, magazine spreads, the printed pack, elevation drawings, a client logo strip — set the grid by column width and caption baseline only, let each image find its own height, and put a two-line caption under it (name bold, detail in grey italic). Keep uniform crops where scanning matters (listing cards, unit tiles) so the ragged-height grid reads as a deliberate second register rather than a broken layout.

site.name: Heineken — 'The Pub That Refused to Die' (campaign key visual + social/digital rollout)

entries.category: Branded documentary — key visual for social, digital and cinema
entries.tagline: Twenty-six real villagers packed until the frame runs out of room — the headcount is the whole argument, and the number is never printed.
entries.when: Premiered 28 February 2026 at the Dublin International Film Festival, with an Irish roadshow and digital rollout through 2026
entries.summary: LePub Milan and Publicis Dublin built the campaign around a documentary (directed by Gar O'Rourke, produced by Antidote Films Dublin) about the residents of Kilteely who bought, reopened and renamed their village's last pub. The key visual does not illustrate the story, it counts it: every face is a real local, packed so tightly that there is no background left — no floor, no ceiling, no pub. The title runs across the frame in three keylined boxes of wide-tracked all-caps serif, 'THE PUB / THAT REFUSED / TO DIE', a six-word line carrying subject, threat and outcome. Heineken appears only as two glasses raised in the crowd, one of them a 0.0, with no logo lockup anywhere in frame.
whatWorks: The crowd IS the background: faces are cut off at all four edges, so the image reads as 'more people than fit' rather than as a posed group shot.

Nobody is cast — hard hat, hi-vis, beanie, flat cap, ear defenders, a fleece, a printed scarf: the wardrobe is what the village actually wears, and half the faces are mid-laugh or looking off-camera instead of smiling to lens.
The title is a story in six words (subject, threat, outcome) and needs no supporting copy on the visual; the past tense promises the ending is good.
Type is split into three staggered keylined boxes rather than one block, so it threads between heads instead of covering any face.
Branding is a product in a hand, not a lockup — two Heineken glasses inside the mass, one of them 0.0, which also does the responsible-drinking note quietly.
The number itself is nowhere on the artwork: the count is something you do with your eyes, not a statistic you are asked to believe.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: Faces at scale. No establishing shot of the pub, no landscape, no logo — just a wall of people cropped on every edge. At feed size you register the crowd before you read a word, and the crop is what creates the sense of overflow.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'THE PUB THAT REFUSED TO DIE' in wide-tracked all-caps serif inside thin white keylines, staggered top / middle / bottom. The personification does the work — a building that refuses is a character — and the boxes let big type sit in a dense image without masking anyone.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: The actual owners, in their own clothes, in mixed uncorrected light, arranged rather than styled. It is the same casting logic as the documentary: the proof of a community story is that everyone in the picture is from the community.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: There is no button and no URL on the key visual. The ask is 'come and see the film', delivered by the festival premiere, the roadshow and the social rollout, with the brand carried by the product in frame — which sits under a wider Heineken commitment to Irish pub culture, so the film functions as evidence rather than as the whole ad.

principle.title: Cast the whole number and let the frame run out of room
principle.explanation: The instinct with a number worth bragging about is to set it large — '26 locals', '500+ agents', '37 closings'. A printed number is a claim the viewer has to accept; the same number staged as bodies filling the frame with no background left is a fact they count for themselves. Crowding is also what makes it read as true: real wardrobe, mixed light, faces cut by the edges, some people looking away. Leave tidy breathing room around the group and it becomes a corporate team photo, at which point the count stops mattering.
principle.howToApply: When the proof is a headcount, photograph the headcount. For Aperture: one frame of every agent in the district office packed to all four edges in whatever they wore that day, or every past client from a single street, cropped so people are cut off at the border — with the line set small in two or three keylined boxes threaded between heads ('THE STREET / THAT SOLD / ITSELF'). Keep the brand to something physically in someone's hand, a sign rider or a key tag, and leave the number out of the copy entirely. If the frame still has empty space, there aren't enough people in it yet.

entries.category: Graphic design, design writing & pedagogy / British post-war modernism
entries.tagline: The designer who wrote down what design was for — First Things First (1964) — and then ran a practice by it for forty-seven years.
entries.summary: Garland trained at the Central School of Arts and Crafts alongside Alan Fletcher and Derek Birdsall, art-directed Design magazine from 1956 to 1962, then ran Ken Garland & Associates from 1962 to 2009. In 1964 he stood up at an ICA meeting and read out First Things First, a one-page manifesto arguing for 'the more useful and more lasting forms of communication' against a culture where 'the high pitched scream of consumer selling is no more than sheer noise'; twenty-three designers signed it, and it was re-signed as First Things First 2000. His best-known body of work — Galt Toys, plus Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament material — came out of the same habit: settle in writing what the work is for, then test it on the people who will actually use it.
whatWorks: Write the position down and publish it: one page stating what work you take and what you refuse is a filter you can point at, not a mood board.
Test with the real user before you style anything — he handed an unfinished Galt puzzle to friends' children and one of them solved a design problem he was stuck on.
Photograph the real thing: the Galt catalogues ran close-ups of his own kids and their friends actually playing, so the marketing imagery was documentation of the testing.

Take the whole surface area, not the poster — he insisted on designing every visual manifestation of Galt (packaging, catalogues, factory graphics, the London store), so consistency came from scope rather than from policing.
Turn the practice into a handbook: Graphics Handbook (1966) and Illustrated Graphics Glossary (1980) codified what he knew so it could be handed on, and he taught at Reading for nearly thirty years.
Credit the team — he refused the single-author story and described the work as a flexible group effort, which is part of why the studio lasted forty-seven years.

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: With language, not layout. Garland had been a magazine art editor before he was a studio principal, and he treated a brief as a piece of writing to be argued with and corrected — what is this for, who is it useful to, how long should it last. First Things First exists because he wrote the whole argument out at full length before expecting anyone to act on it.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Define the terms, then take the whole system. On Galt he treated toys, packaging, catalogue, factory signage and the London shop as one job, so nothing had to be reconciled later; the identity was coherent because the scope was, not because a rulebook enforced it. He also kept the work explicitly collaborative — a flexible team, credited as one.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Play as research. He put unfinished games in front of real children, watched what they did, and let their solutions change the design — then photographed those same children using the products, so the persuasion material was a by-product of the testing rather than a separate shoot.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Usefulness and longevity over persuasion: 'the more useful and more lasting forms of communication' is the test, and work whose only job is to raise the volume of selling fails it. Because the work was a team's, the question was never 'is this my best idea' but 'is this the clearest solution we have'.

principle.title: Write your position before you take the work, and let it do the refusing
principle.explanation: Most practices work out what they stand for retroactively, from whatever portfolio they happen to accumulate. Garland did it in the other order: a written, published, one-page position that told him — and everyone else — which jobs were his. It costs nothing, it turns 'no' into a two-sentence email instead of an argument, and it compounds, because over a few years the work starts to look like the position rather than like the last client.
principle.howToApply: Write one page of numbered lines on what your design work is for: what you will always do (photograph the real property, name the photographer, one price format, breathing room before every image), what you will not (fabricated twilight skies, virtual staging without a label, copy a fair-housing reviewer would flag), and the test a piece has to pass before it ships. Keep it in the repo next to the templates, read it before quoting a new job, and revise it once a year rather than once per project.

entries.tagline: A hotel group that sells the neighbourhood before the room — every card carries a sentence you couldn't move to another card.
entries.summary: The Hoxton sells cities, not rooms. The hero is a documentary photograph of two staff pulling coffee — no made bed, no styled suite — and everything below it is built out of place: a carousel of city photographs, then nineteen hotel cards where each one gets a sentence of specific local detail instead of a label. The whole page sits on a warm cream ground with a near-black charcoal footer, and exactly one element is allowed to be loud: the coral 'Find a Room' button. The honest weak spot is the very top, where three stacked promotional messages (flexible cancellation, a 15%-off referral, a Lacoste capsule) fire before you reach any content.
whatWorks: One filled button on the entire page — the coral 'Find a Room', in the header and again as the last cell of the booking bar. Every other action is an outlined button ('View offer', 'Learn more') or an underlined text link ('View hotel'), so nothing competes with booking.

Property cards carry a sentence, not a label: 'Our 10th Hox is in a leafy corner of Rome, a stone's throw from Villa Borghese'; 'Our Florence hotel near the beautiful Piazza della Libertà celebrates both Renaissance and Postmodern interiors across two spectacular buildings'. The reason to click sits in the card rather than behind it.
The hero photograph is of people working — an espresso machine, two staff, a stack of saucers — so the first image sells the feeling of the place and the room shots are saved for the property page.

The booking bar butts flat against the bottom edge of the hero photo: square corners, hairline dividers, no drop shadow, no float. It reads as part of the same composition instead of a widget parked on top of one.

Carousel images are matted — each photograph sits inset in its cell with cream margin on all sides and a full-height hairline between cells — which makes an ordinary row of city photos scan like a gallery wall.
Tiny uppercase field labels (LOCATION, CHECK IN / CHECK OUT, GUESTS, GOT A CODE?) sit above larger placeholder text, so a five-field booking form stays readable without a single input outline.

sections.name: Utility strip & header
sections.notes: A black strip carries one rotating promotional line ('Travel uncertain? We've got you with flexible cancellation — EXPLORE MORE'), then a cream header band: the lowercase serif wordmark 'the hoxton' hard left, a short sans nav right, and the coral FIND A ROOM button pinned to the corner as the only filled control on the page. A second, lighter row holds just '+ Select Location'. Splitting brand from booking across two rows keeps the nav short, but stacking three promo messages here is the page's one real cost — it spends the visitor's first scroll on offers rather than places.

sections.name: Hero + booking bar
sections.notes: Full-bleed documentary photograph of two staff making coffee, warm and slightly grainy, with 'Welcome to The Hoxton' set large in white sans at lower left. The five-cell white booking bar sits flush on the photo's bottom edge — Location, Check in / Check out, Guests, Got a code?, then the coral submit as the terminal cell. Choosing craft-in-progress over an empty suite is the whole positioning in one frame: you are buying the place, not the bed.

sections.name: Trending destinations
sections.notes: Centred heading with a single conversational line under it ('Thinking about your next city break? These are the places our Hox community can't get enough of'), then a horizontal carousel of portrait-format city photographs — Amsterdam, London, Florence, Rome — each matted inside its cell with vertical hairlines between and small circular chevrons at the edges. It answers 'where' before 'which hotel', which is the order a traveller actually thinks in.

sections.name: Explore all our Hotel locations
sections.notes: The workhorse block: region tabs (Europe / UK & Ireland / USA / All) filtering a grid of nineteen property cards. Each card is photograph, name, one sentence of genuinely specific detail, and an underlined 'View hotel' link — no button, no price, no star rating. Tabs rather than a second page keep every property one click away, and the sentence does the qualifying that a 'Learn more' can't.

sections.name: Best Rate? Book Here / Referral Scheme
sections.notes: Two conversion panels side by side, split by a single vertical hairline, both with outlined buttons rather than filled ones. The copy is plain-spoken and in the same voice as everything above it — 'Here's the inside scoop: book direct on thehoxton.com and you'll unlock our best rates, plus a few extra perks we keep just for you.' Direct-booking persuasion sits after the browsing, not in front of it.

sections.name: Newsletter & footer
sections.notes: 'Get the Inside Scoop' is a centred two-field form on cream with underline-only inputs — no boxes, no card, no shadow. Then the ground drops to near-black charcoal for a deliberately short footer: three columns (Links / Social / Language), cream text, a hairline, and a bottom bar with the Ennismore parent mark and copyright. No repeated newsletter, no sitemap dump, no oversized logo lockup.

principle.title: Put the reason to click inside the card, not behind it
principle.explanation: A grid of place names is a grid of unanswered questions: the visitor has to open each one to find out whether it's the one they want, so most of them open none. One sentence of specific, non-interchangeable detail per card does that qualifying up front — 'a leafy corner of Rome, a stone's throw from Villa Borghese' cannot be swapped onto another card, which is exactly why it earns reading. It also lets the card's link stay a quiet underlined 'View hotel' instead of a button, because the sentence has already done the selling and the page's one loud button can stay reserved for the action that matters.
principle.howToApply: On the Aperture Europe collection page, give every property card one sentence true of that property only — the street, the view, the age of the building, the thing you'd notice walking in — and never a category line like 'Luxury villa in Spain'. Write the sentence before choosing the photograph, and test it by trying to move it to another card: if it still fits, it isn't specific enough. Then demote the per-card CTA to an underlined text link and keep exactly one filled button on the page for the single action you actually want.

site.name: The Ordinary — 'The Truth Should Be Ordinary' (Truth Drop key visual, paid social & display)

entries.when: Launched 11 February 2025 — Uncommon Creative Studio for The Ordinary (DECIEM)
entries.tagline: A blackened, rotting tomato under a headline that corrects the beauty industry — the frame is spent on the argument and the bottle is left in the corner.
entries.summary: Uncommon built The Ordinary a campaign that doesn't sell a product. Each 'Truth Drop' takes one widely believed beauty myth and corrects it — in black and white, on white space — and points at a free public archive of research papers, including myths in categories The Ordinary doesn't even sell into. This execution pairs a blackened, decaying tomato with 'Firms. Tones. Corrects the myth that parabens in skincare are dangerous.' — the category's own claim grammar hijacked so the third verb lands on the truth instead of the skin. The creative rule was stated plainly by the team: truth doesn't need a thousand colours or fonts or crazy imagery, it just needs space. Honest 2026 footnote: thetruthshouldbeordinary.com no longer resolves, which is its own lesson about an ad whose whole payload is a URL.
whatWorks: The hook is the category's own iconography turned against it — 'natural' represented by a rotting tomato, lit and shot like a lab specimen, so the image has made the argument before the headline is read.

The headline borrows the product-claim format every skincare ad uses ('Firms. Tones.') and then completes the list with a fact rather than a benefit — you read two lines of advertising and land in a correction.
No colour at all. Black, white and grey read as clinical and unbiased; one accent would have filed it back under advertising.
The bottle is small, low and near the edge; roughly nine tenths of the frame is argument and empty ground. The product is the footnote to the claim, not the subject.
Numbering the executions (#TruthDrop 4) turns a campaign into a series an audience can follow and a brand can keep extending without redesigning anything.
The call to action sends people to a free research archive instead of a product page — giving the evidence away is what makes the claim believable.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A single black-and-white object, isolated on white: a tomato collapsing in on itself, stem still attached, photographed with the flat clarity of a specimen shot. It stops the scroll because it is grotesque in a category that only ever shows dewy skin and glass bottles — and because 'natural' rotting is the exact counter-image to the myth being corrected.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'Firms. Tones. Corrects the myth that parabens in skincare are dangerous.' The first two words are the category's stock claim rhythm, so the eye reads them as an ordinary product ad; the third clause swaps the object of the sentence from your face to the industry. A short paragraph of body copy underneath states what the drop is and where the evidence lives — small, unhurried, no bold, no exclamation.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: One object left, type right, everything on white with generous margins and a lot of nothing between them. Monochrome across the whole set (the OOH run and the shredder film share the same rules), which makes the campaign recognisable at a glance and signals 'evidence' rather than 'beauty'. The typography is the brand's own plain sans at a modest size — the restraint is the credibility.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: '#TruthDrop 4' and the archive URL, both set tiny, with the 'The Ordinary.' lockup in the bottom corner. There is no shop link, no discount, no urgency device: the ad's destination is a library of research papers the brand doesn't monetise. The generosity is the proof — and the risk, since a campaign that lives at a URL dies when the URL does.

principle.title: Make the ad an argument, not an announcement
principle.explanation: Most category advertising announces — here is the product, here is the adjective, here is the button — and every competitor's announcement looks identical, so the audience files them all in the same place without reading. An argument behaves differently: it has a claim someone could disagree with, evidence you can go and check, and a shape that borrows the category's own grammar so it gets read before it gets recognised. It also inverts the frame — the claim is the hero, the product is the footnote — which buys attention that no amount of shouting the offer can.
principle.howToApply: On a Just Listed or collection post, pick the one claim a buyer would actually challenge — 'the third bedroom is a real bedroom, not an office'; 'south-facing here means sun on the terrace until 7pm in June' — and give the entire frame to proving that single claim, with address, price and agent block small at the bottom. Point the CTA at the evidence (the floorplan, the full photo set, the days-on-market page), not at the contact form, and host that evidence on a page you control and will keep, so the campaign doesn't outlive its own link.

entries.category: Album art, identity & art direction / British post-punk modernism
entries.tagline: The art director who mostly didn't draw — he found an existing image and moved it into a room where it didn't belong.
entries.summary: Saville studied graphic design at Manchester Polytechnic (1975–78), where Malcolm Garrett showed him Jan Tschichold's New Typography — which he used almost immediately on FAC 1, the poster for Tony Wilson's Factory club. He co-founded Factory Records in 1978 with Wilson and Alan Erasmus and became the label's visual author: Joy Division's Unknown Pleasures (a plot of the pulsar CP 1919 lifted from an astronomy reference book), Closer (Bernard Pierre Wolff's photograph of a tomb in Genoa's Staglieno cemetery), New Order's Power, Corruption & Lies (Fantin-Latour's A Basket of Roses from the National Gallery, paired with a colour-coded alphabet) and Blue Monday's die-cut floppy-disk sleeve. Later came Manchester's city identity and Metrolink, Manchester International Festival, work for Dior, Stella McCartney and Pringle, and Burberry's 2018 logo; CBE in 2020, Royal Designer for Industry. He is also famously, comically late — a running joke in 24 Hour Party People — which is part of the method's honest cost.
whatWorks: Source instead of originate: keep a standing library of images you didn't make — scientific plates, museum paintings, archival photography — and open a brief by asking which existing image, moved into this context, says the thing.
Withhold the obvious. Unknown Pleasures carries no band name and no title on the front; refusing to introduce itself is precisely what makes people look longer and remember it.
Encode rather than state: the colour wheel on Power, Corruption & Lies spells the title only if you decode it, so the meaning is available to anyone who wants it and delivered to nobody.

Let the object carry what the image can't — Blue Monday's sleeve was die-cut as a 5.25-inch floppy disk, so the format itself is the argument. It also famously cost more to make than the record earned: craft that ignores unit economics is a decision, not an accident.
Borrow authority from another register — a 19th-century still life or an astronomy diagram on a pop record imports credibility the category cannot manufacture for itself.
Art-direct rather than execute: the moves are select, crop, colour and place. Almost nothing on a Saville sleeve was drawn by Saville, and the work is no less authored for it.

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: Not with a sketch — with a search. Saville's first move on a brief is to go looking through what already exists (books, museum collections, scientific reference, other people's photography) until something reframes the subject, and the design job becomes choosing and placing rather than inventing. The origin story is the method in miniature: a friend hands him Tschichold's New Typography, and it goes straight onto a live job as FAC 1. The corollary is that the library has to be built before the brief arrives, because you cannot search a collection you don't have.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Transposition. Take an image with a settled meaning in one world and set it down, largely unaltered, in another — a pulsar plot from astronomy onto a post-punk record, a Victorian flower painting onto a synth-pop sleeve — and let the friction between the two contexts do the work. As critic Alice Twemlow put it, he would irreverently lift an image from one genre and recontextualise it in another. The discipline is restraint: the borrowed image is not decorated, it's cropped, coloured and framed, and the design lives in what surrounds it.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: The withheld cover plus the private system. Strip the identifying information off the front (no name, no title) so the object has to be approached rather than read, then build a system underneath it that rewards the people who come closer — the colour-coded alphabet, the silver ink, the die-cut. Two registers running at once: an immediate image anyone can respond to, and a coded layer for whoever decides to look twice.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: He designs for an audience assumed to be as curious as he is — the test is whether the piece earns a second look, not whether it explains itself on the first. Beauty and rightness are allowed to be reasons on their own: if the image is right, it doesn't need to shout, and adding a lockup or an explanation would only file it back under advertising. The honest limits are visible in the record too — chronic lateness, and sleeves that cost more than they made — so the method needs someone counting, which at Factory was somebody else.

principle.title: Find the image before you make one
principle.explanation: The default reflex on a brief is to commission or generate something new, which is expensive, slow and usually lands on whatever the category already looks like. Searching first is faster and produces stranger, more specific results, because the world is full of images made with total conviction for some other purpose — scientific diagrams, archival maps, botanical plates, municipal photography — and the meaning they carry from their first life is something you could never manufacture. The design work then moves to selection, crop, colour and placement, which is where authorship actually lives.
principle.howToApply: Before commissioning any graphic for a European listing, spend an hour in the archives of the place: the town's cadastral map, a botanical plate of the tree in the garden, the entry-hall tile pattern photographed flat, a page from the region's 1930s tourist brochure. Give the best one a full page in the magazine — unaltered, uncredited on the page, credited in the index — and let it carry the section that has nothing to photograph. Start the standing library now, one folder per region, so the search is possible when the brief is live and not just when there is time.

entries.tagline: A luxury product homepage where every tile is an editorial sentence that ends in the exact model name, and no type is ever allowed to land on a photograph.
entries.summary: NOMOS sells €2,000–€4,000 mechanical watches on a page that reads like a magazine contents list rather than a shop. Each block is one photograph on white or pale grey with its headline set above it — 'The very definition of a dress watch: Orion gold neomatik new black' — and the same tiny 'Discover now ›' link underneath, so the images stay uncropped, unscrimmed and untinted while the sentences do the persuading. One light grotesque at two weights, near-black on white, means the only saturated pixels on 12,500px of page live inside the watches themselves: gold cases, navy dials, and one orange highlight in a live stock-exchange ticker. The one lapse is a floating 'Do you have any questions?' chat bubble parked directly on the hero watch — the single element permitted to cover product photography.
whatWorks: Headlines sit above the image, never on it — no gradient scrim, no dead-space crop, no text-safe area, so every photograph can be chosen as the best photograph rather than the most overlay-friendly one

Each tile's headline is a full sentence that ends in the specific model ('In real time, worldwide: Club Sport neomatik Worldtimer – Edition Handelsblatt') — the claim and the SKU are inseparable, which forces the claim to be true of one object instead of the catalogue
One identical micro-link ('Discover now ›') on every tile instead of a differently-worded button per block — the headline carries the difference, the CTA never competes

Under the world-time watch runs a live marquee of exchange codes and UTC offsets (HKEX +7, TSE +8, SYD +9, NOU +10, AKL +11, PPG ±12, HNL −11) with the currently open markets in orange — the feature is demonstrated, not described
Numbers are the copy: '13 model families, 13 mechanical calibers', and each family in the picker is labelled with its own inventory ('TANGENTE / 37 watches'), so navigation doubles as a stock report
Provenance is a four-tile row whose first tile is a drone shot of the actual town of Glashütte, followed by hands, a caliber under a press and a bare movement — location, R&D, production, part
Social proof is one oversized pull-quote in German guillemets »…« attributed simply 'Hodinkee', set in the page's own headline face at headline size rather than boxed in a testimonial card
The footer leads with the newsletter field and sets 'Withdraw from Contract ›' in bold among the legal links — consumer rights treated as a trust signal instead of fine print

sections.name: Header
sections.notes: Wordmark centred and stacked (NOMOS over letterspaced GLASHÜTTE), the three content routes pushed left — Watches, Watchmaking, Topics — and commerce pushed to the far right (Shop, Find retailer, account, search). The nav order tells you the site thinks of itself as a publication with a shop attached, not the reverse.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Two lines of headline and a 'Discover now ›' link sit on white ABOVE a full-width photograph of one watch on pale grey. No price, no button, no badge, nothing overlaid. The generous line spacing and the light weight of the grotesque do the luxury signalling that a serif or a gold accent would usually be asked to do.

sections.name: Two-up feature row
sections.notes: Two products, two editorial sentences, one shared link style: the Worldtimer on white with its live exchange ticker beneath, and 'No two pairs are alike: Twice Unique offers individual design in stainless steel and gold' shot on navy leather. The grounds differ (studio white vs. material close-up) so the pair reads as two registers of the same system rather than a repeated card.

sections.name: Model families / Watchfinder
sections.notes: A small left-set paragraph of facts ('13 model families, 13 mechanical calibers—high-precision watches crafted by an independent Glashütte manufacture') with an outlined 'Watchfinder' button hard right, then a five-up carousel of watches on white, each with a tiny all-caps family name and its live count. This is the whole catalogue compressed into one scannable row — no filters, no price grid.

sections.name: Manufactory / provenance
sections.notes: 'Made in Glashütte: In our manufactory films, the smallest parts of the watch are the stars' with a 'Watch Season 7 now' button, over a full-bleed macro of a single component so shallow in focus it reads as landscape. Then a short paragraph and the four provenance tiles. Making the film series a numbered 'Season' commits the brand to publishing rather than to one brand video.

sections.name: Pull quote
sections.notes: One quote from Hodinkee at headline scale on white, with the German »quotation marks« kept rather than converted — a small piece of national grammar left in place. The attribution is one word, no logo wall, no star rating, no carousel of five.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Pale grey ground. Newsletter first with an inline email field, then four columns of ~10px all-caps labels (Useful information / Watches / Shop / About NOMOS / Follow / Legal information), a bolded 'Withdraw from Contract ›', and a bottom rule carrying 'Location: International ›' and 'Language: English ›'. Every item is a plain text link; there is not one icon button in it.

principle.title: End the tile headline with the thing's own name
principle.explanation: Most product and listing tiles split into two texts — a marketing line on top and a model or address label underneath — so the visitor reads an adjective first and only learns what they are looking at on the second read. Collapsing both into one sentence that finishes on the specific object ('The very definition of a dress watch: Orion gold neomatik new black') makes the claim inseparable from the thing, which quietly forbids any claim that is only true of the category.
principle.howToApply: On Aperture collection grids and the magazine contents page, write every card as '<one-sentence claim>: <the actual address or unit>', cap it at two lines, and delete the separate name label underneath. Keep one identical micro-link on every card and set the sentence above the photograph so the image never needs a scrim. Test: if the claim still reads fine when you swap in a different address, it is a category adjective and has to be rewritten.

site.name: German Rail (Deutsche Bahn) — 'No Need to Fly' (Facebook / Instagram dynamic feed ads)

entries.category: Meta feed ad — data-driven dynamic creative
entries.tagline: Two photographs the viewer cannot tell apart, with two prices under them that are impossible to confuse.
entries.summary: Ogilvy built an ad whose argument is a visual near-match: an algorithm read the foreign destinations Germans were searching to book, found German locations that look almost identical in stock imagery, and generated the pair as a single feed unit carrying the day's real flight price against a €19 rail fare — roughly 10,000 personalised variants from one layout. The unit here pairs paddleboarders in Santos, Brazil with paddleboarders on the Spree in Berlin, labelled 'Frankfurt → Santos / Plane: 1,154 Euros' and 'Frankfurt → Berlin / Train: 19 Euros'. No train appears anywhere in the creative; the product is the trip, and the persuasion is arithmetic the viewer performs themselves. The agency reports a 24% revenue lift off the campaign.
whatWorks: The hook is a near-match, not a headline — two photographs split by a hairline gutter, close enough that the eye checks one against the other before reading a word
The two price chips are mirrored to the outer edges (left chip flush left, right chip flush right) so the comparison resolves as two numbers at the frame's far corners: 1,154 against 19
Each chip is exactly two lines in tight bold sans on DB crimson — route with an arrow glyph, then mode and price — and carries no other information

The body copy concedes the fantasy before undercutting it: 'You could fly to Brazil for a sightseeing tour in the water. Or simply to go Berlin. #noneedtofly' — the hashtag rides the joke, not the offer
The CTA repeats the number instead of the brand ('Discover Germany. For just 19 Euros.' + 'Book Now'), so the ad still lands if the image is scrolled past half-shown
No model, no lifestyle gloss, no logo lockup inside the frame — the only branding is the DB avatar in the post header, which is why the pair reads as evidence rather than art direction
One layout, thousands of variants: the creative is a template whose content is data (search demand → lookalike location → live fare), so relevance scales without a redesign

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: Two square photographs edge to edge with a hairline gutter, shot from similar heights in similar light — paddleboarders on flat water, low buildings behind. The comparison is doing the work a headline usually does: you look twice to check whether it is the same place, and by then you have read both prices in the outer corners.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: The in-feed copy is one sentence of concession and one of substitution: 'You could fly to Brazil for a sightseeing tour in the water. Or simply to go Berlin.' It never argues that Berlin is better, only that the experience pictured is available closer and cheaper — and #noneedtofly compresses the entire positioning into one word.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Neither half is a product shot; there is no train, no interior, no staff. What is pictured is the thing the customer already wanted, twice. The images are ordinary feed-resolution photography rather than retouched campaign stills, which is exactly why the equivalence is believable.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: 'Discover Germany. For just 19 Euros.' set as a two-line link block with a quiet outlined 'Book Now' at the right. The price appears three times in the unit — in the right-hand chip, in the CTA, and in the offer — because the number is the whole campaign.

sections.name: The system behind it
sections.notes: An algorithm matched trending searched-for destinations to German lookalikes and pulled live flight and rail fares at serve time, producing ~10,000 generated pairs targeted by the traveller's own intent. The layout was designed once; every subsequent 'idea' was a new row of data.

principle.title: Make the comparison the creative, and let data write the copy
principle.explanation: A claim of equivalence — you can get this same thing here, for less — is weak as a sentence and unarguable as two photographs the viewer cannot separate. And once the layout is a fixed comparison frame with two image slots and two number slots, relevance stops being a creative problem: speaking to a different desire means a different row of data, not a new design.
principle.howToApply: Build one fixed side-by-side frame for Aperture — identical crop both sides, hairline gutter, label chips pinned to the outer corners — and fill it from a CSV: the aspirational comparison on the left (Amalfi, Provence, Lake Como with its real €/m² or nightly rate) and the equivalent Aperture listing on the right with its actual price. One layout, one sheet, one post per pairing, so the series runs for months without new art direction. The gate: if the left and right photographs are clearly distinguishable at a glance, the pairing is not ready to post.

entries.tagline: The designer who imported Ulm's method to Brazil and renamed the job: not graphic art, but visual programming.
entries.summary: The son of Yugoslav immigrants who grew up around his father's typography workshop, Wollner was picked by Max Bill for the first intake at the Hochschule für Gestaltung Ulm and trained there from 1954 to 1958. He came home to São Paulo and, with Geraldo de Barros and Ruben Martins, opened Forminform in 1958 — one of the first design offices in Brazil — building identities for Eucatex, Klabin, Ultragaz, Santista, Coqueiro and the original Banco Itaú mark, all drawn with compass, ruler and set square from geometric programmes. In 1963 he helped found ESDI in Rio on the Ulm model and taught there for years, because his real product was not a logo but a transferable method. He is generally credited as the father of modern Brazilian design, and he insisted on the term 'programação visual' — visual programming — over 'graphic art'.
whatWorks: Rename the deliverable to change it: refusing 'graphic artist' for 'visual programmer' turns the output from a picture that is composed into a system that is programmed, and the client's expectations move with the word
Draw with instruments, not with the hand — every mark derived from circles, squares and a grid module, so it can be rebuilt from its own construction at any size by anyone
Write the reasoning before the drawing (the Ulm habit), so the mark arrives as the conclusion of an argument that someone else can check rather than a preference to be defended

Take the entire visual output as one commission — interiors, signage, packaging, typefaces, advertising, employee clothing — so coherence comes from scope rather than from a brand manual policing separate vendors
Grid first, ornament last: anything decorative that could not be defended as communication was removed, which is how the marks end up describable in a single sentence
Institutionalise the process instead of protecting it — he built a school to teach the method, which is the only version of a working process that outlives the practitioner

sections.name: How he begins
sections.notes: With a definition rather than a sketch. Wollner treats a brief as a request for a programme: what the company actually makes, at what scales its marks will appear, on which surfaces, and which of those surfaces will still exist in ten years. The Ulm training means the written rationale comes first, so nothing gets drawn that cannot be explained.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Programação visual — the identity as a rule set covering everything the company emits, delivered as one job. For his corporate clients that meant the complete visual communication: office interiors, signage systems, typefaces, packaging, advertising media, even what staff wore. The system is the deliverable; each artefact is an instance of it.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Instrument-built geometry. Marks constructed with compass, ruler, triangle and square out of circles, squares and grid modules, with the tangents and centres implied in the finished form — the primacy of the grid, structural rigour, and a mark whose logic survives being redrawn by a signwriter, an embroiderer or a printer who never sees the original artwork.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Function outranks flourish: if a shape cannot be justified as communication it comes off, however pleasant. A solution should be reproducible from instructions, not from a file. And a method is only real if it can be taught — hence ESDI, and hence a career spent giving away the process rather than mystifying it.

principle.title: Ship the construction, not just the artwork
principle.explanation: A mark handed over as a finished file gets rebuilt wrongly the first time somebody needs it at 12mm on a sign, embroidered on a jacket, or re-set inside a template you do not control. A mark derived from a geometric construction can be redrawn from its own instructions — and the discipline of having to construct it in the first place kills every shape that was only ever a nice gesture.
principle.howToApply: For any Aperture mark or recurring device — collection badge, magazine folio, unit-number plate, the carousel slug — deliver a one-page construction sheet beside the SVG: the circles and squares it is built from, the grid module, minimum size, clear space, and the two-sentence reason it looks like that. Require the same sheet for anything a vendor will re-set (print, signage, embroidery, a Canva template someone else fills in). If a piece cannot be drawn from its sheet, it is not finished.

entries.tagline: The headline sets one of its own words inside a Notion inline chip, so the sentence is already a screenshot of the product.
entries.summary: Notion's homepage argues almost entirely in product stills. The fold reads “Where teams and agents ● Think together.” — and the word “Think” is not styled text, it is drawn as a Notion inline chip with the little blue dot, so the claim about working inside Notion is demonstrated inside the claim. Everything below is the same discipline: a real workspace (“Ramp HQ”) rather than an abstract UI, feature sections whose eyebrow states the job and whose headline states the outcome, and a five-chip row of literal tasks. The page is near-monochrome — near-black type on off-white, one blue reserved for the primary action — and spends its entire colour budget on three saturated testimonial cards near the bottom, which is exactly where a skimmer needs a stop.
whatWorks: Hero headline contains a live UI element: “Think” is set in the product's own inline chip (rounded pill, blue dot), same size and baseline as the surrounding words — no callout, no annotation.

The fold's product shot is a named, plausible workspace (“Ramp HQ” with real-looking sidebar items and task rows), not a sanitised demo — and hand-drawn line-art characters peek in from the margins so the screenshot doesn't sit in a vacuum.
Logo wall carries a caption that converts it from decoration into a statistic: “Trusted by 98% of the Forbes Cloud 100”, set small and grey directly beneath.

Feature cards use a two-line stack — a small grey eyebrow naming the job (“Capture knowledge”, “Find answers”) over a bold sentence naming the outcome (“Bring everything into one system of record.”) — so the skim reads as job → result.
“See what Notion can do” is a row of five plain task chips (“Resolve support tickets in Slack”, “Respond to security alerts faster”) — verbs a buyer already has on their list, not capabilities.

Colour is rationed: the whole page is near-black on off-white with one blue for the primary button, and the only saturated blocks on the page are the three quote cards — so colour marks the one section that is pure opinion.
Every headline is a complete sentence ending in a full stop (“AI where your team works.”, “Trusted by teams that ship.”, “Get started today.”), which reads as statement rather than menu label.

sections.name: Nav
sections.notes: Five items only — Product, Resources, Pricing, Request a demo on the left cluster; Log in and a single blue “Get Notion free” pill on the right. One filled button in the entire header, so the primary action is unambiguous on every screen.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Centred, three lines of tight-tracked bold sans: “Where teams and agents ● Think together.” with “Think” drawn as a Notion inline chip. One grey subhead line (“Capture context, find answers, and automate tasks with AI built for your team.”) and a two-button pair — solid blue primary, ghost secondary. Nothing else competes above the fold.

sections.name: Product proof + logo wall
sections.notes: A wide, softly-shadowed screenshot of an actual workspace sits directly under the CTAs, with doodle characters breaking its edges to keep it from reading as stock UI. Two rows of client logos follow at low contrast, closed by the grey line “Trusted by 98% of the Forbes Cloud 100” — the caption is what makes the logos evidence.

sections.name: “AI where your team works.”
sections.notes: Left-aligned section head, then a 2-up then 1-up card grid on very light grey. Each card: grey eyebrow (the job) → bold sentence (the outcome) → a circular arrow button → a product still cropped so it bleeds off the card. The stills carry the explanation, so the copy stays at one sentence.

sections.name: “See what Notion can do”
sections.notes: A five-across strip of small bordered chips, each with one coloured icon and a two-line task written as an imperative (“Triage product feedback →”). It functions as a use-case index without a heavy tab component — the cheapest possible way to let five different buyers self-identify.

sections.name: “Trusted by teams that ship.” + stat bar
sections.notes: Three tall cards in saturated red, blue and amber gradients — the only strong colour on the page — each holding a serif-italic pull quote with attribution set small at the bottom left. Beneath them, a single thin row of five stats with tiny icons (“100M users in over 50 countries”, “Over 50% of YC companies”, “62% of Fortune 100 use Notion”), which keeps the numbers out of the emotional block.

sections.name: Closing CTA
sections.notes: “Get started today.” centred on a light grey band with the exact two buttons from the hero, same order, same styling — the page ends by repeating its opening offer verbatim rather than inventing a new one.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Four link columns (Product, Resources, Company, Notion for) beside the logo and, unusually, a Marshall McLuhan quote — “We shape our tools, and thereafter our tools shape us.” — credited in small grey type. One line of belief in the coldest part of the page, where a manifesto costs nothing and is found by the people who scroll all the way.

principle.title: Set one word of the headline in the product's own interface
principle.explanation: Notion doesn't write “works the way you already work” — it renders the word “Think” as the exact inline chip you'd see in the app, at the same size and baseline as the rest of the sentence. The claim and its evidence occupy the same three centimetres, so there is nothing to believe: a reader who has used the product recognises the component, and one who hasn't has just been shown it. It works because the element is real and restrained — one word, no callout arrow, no annotation.
principle.howToApply: On an Aperture hero or a listing page, take the single word in the headline that names something the buyer will actually meet and set it as that thing: render “$1.2M” in the same price chip used on the cards, put the street name inside the map-pin label, set “11 days” in the days-on-market stamp. One word only, inline, same size and baseline as its neighbours — if it needs a caption explaining the joke, it's decoration and should come out.

site.name: Guide Dogs — ‘Life Unleashed’ (integrated: film, digital, print, radio)

entries.when: Launched 28 August 2026 in the UK; running through September with legacy-giving activity into October
entries.tagline: A sight-loss charity stops asking for pity and starts filming first times — and ships a bespoke typeface drawn for the people it serves as part of the same campaign.
entries.summary: Fold7's debut work for Guide Dogs is built on ‘firsts’: a 2:45 film, ‘First Steps’, directed by Tom Green with voiceover by Maxine Peake, in which every person on screen is a real Guide Dogs service user rather than an actor — a teenager walking back into school after losing their sight, a fan returning to the stands, a toddler learning a cane. The reframe is the whole idea: the charity's product is not the dog, it's the first time. What lifts it past a well-shot fundraising film is that the agency's studio also drew Guide Dogs a bespoke typeface tuned for readers with vision impairment, so the accessibility argument is made by the artwork itself and not only by the script. The still here is a poster frame from the film; the campaign is best judged with sound, since the radio leg is built from real thank-you voice notes.
whatWorks: The category reframe is one word: ‘firsts’. It converts a deficit story (what someone lost) into an achievement story (what they just did) without softening the fundraising ask.
Casting is the proof — real service users, not actors, and vignettes small enough to be credible (a cane, a school corridor, a stadium seat) rather than a single triumphant set piece.
Cinematography stays undramatic: available daylight, shallow depth, mid-shot at the subject's height, no swelling reveal — so the achievement carries the emotion instead of the grade.
The typeface commissioned for low-vision readers means the campaign's headline asset is also its accessibility asset — the medium is not exempt from the message.

Each channel is cast for what it does best: film for the moment, radio for real voice notes from service users thanking staff, social (‘Behind every first’) for the unglamorous partnership work behind it.
The ask is written as a mechanism, not a mood — ‘Your donation helps make life-changing firsts possible for people with sight loss’ names the unit your money buys.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: An ordinary frame of someone about to do something ordinary — a woman standing still in a field holding a cane, eyes closed, sun on her face. No logo, no super, nothing announcing a charity. The scroll stops because you can't yet tell what it is, and the answer is a person mid-achievement rather than mid-hardship.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: ‘Life Unleashed’ as the platform, with the running argument that Guide Dogs exists for life-changing firsts, not just for dogs. Maxine Peake's voiceover stays low and unsentimental, letting the service users' own moments carry the claim; the donation line arrives as a plain statement of what a gift produces.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Documentary grammar throughout — real locations, real people, daylight, handheld-adjacent framing, and the guide dog or cane treated as an everyday tool in shot rather than a symbol placed in shot. Typography across the print and digital cutdowns uses the bespoke vision-impairment typeface, so the identity reads as designed-for rather than designed-about.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: A donation ask tied to the unit the campaign spent two minutes defining — the ‘first’ — rather than a generic ‘support us’. Legacy-giving activity runs behind it into October, so the same emotional frame is reused for the longest-horizon ask instead of getting its own separate campaign.

principle.title: Put the accessibility into the brand asset, not into a compliance pass
principle.explanation: Guide Dogs didn't caption an existing typeface as accessible — the studio drew a new one for people with vision impairment and made it the campaign's own voice. That inverts the usual order, where the design is made and then checked against a contrast ratio at the end. When the accessible choice is the brand asset, every future piece inherits it for free and nobody has to argue for it per-job; when it's a checklist, it is the first thing dropped under deadline.
principle.howToApply: Decide the accessibility rules at the template layer of the Aperture Power Pack and Magazine rather than per order: set the floor body size for print collateral and never go under it to fit copy, fix a minimum text-on-photograph contrast and require a solid panel rather than a scrim when a caption can't clear it, and check the house typeface's numerals and unit abbreviations at the smallest size a spec line is ever set. Write those three into the template's construction sheet so the constraint arrives with the file, not with the review.

entries.category: Brand consultancy / corporate identity — London, New York, San Francisco, Los Angeles (image: co-founder Wally Olins)
entries.when: Founded 1965, Camden Town, London · Michael Wolff (designer) & Wally Olins (business); ≈150 people today
entries.tagline: The studio that invented the modern brand consultancy by putting a designer and a business mind in the room as equal authors — and defined identity as ‘strategy made visible’.
entries.summary: Wolff Olins was founded in 1965 by Michael Wolff, a designer, and Wally Olins, who came from advertising and business — a deliberate two-headed practice at a time when corporate identity meant a draughtsman tidying a logo. Olins's definition of the job, ‘strategy made visible’, is still the clearest description of what an identity is for: not decoration applied afterwards, but the organisation's intent made legible. The work runs from BOC (1967) and Apple Records (1968) through Orange (1994), Tata, NBC Universal and London 2012 to the BBC's Reith blocks. They are also worth studying for the failures — the 2012 Olympic mark was savaged at reveal and then worked in motion and application, while abrdn was ridiculed and reverted in 2025 — which together make the honest case that an identity has to be judged in use, and that a name nobody can say is not saved by a good system.
whatWorks: Put a maker and a business mind in the room as equal authors from the first meeting — not strategy first, then design, but both arguing over the same decision.
Write the strategy as a sentence before drawing anything, then treat every visual decision as an attempt to make that sentence visible; anything that can't cite it is decoration.
Design for the organisation the client is becoming, not the one that walked in — Orange in 1994 had no telecom cues at all because the brief was about a future behaviour.
Be willing to invent the name and the whole language, not just the mark — naming is where most of the strategy actually gets fixed.
Judge the identity in application over a year (motion, signage, small sizes, templates) rather than at the reveal, where it is being judged as a picture.
Pair evidence with a leap — the house phrase is ‘maths and magic’: research narrows the options, but somebody still has to choose the one nobody asked for.
Know the honest limit: the reveal-backlash defence only holds when the idea is sound. If the thing is unsayable or unspellable, application won't rescue it.

sections.name: How it's structured
sections.notes: Founded as a partnership of opposites — Wolff the designer, Olins the business and advertising side — and built out into a consultancy that keeps strategists, writers, designers and now culture and experience specialists on the same team rather than in a relay. Today the practice organises itself around three linked pillars (brand, culture, experience) precisely so an identity can't be delivered without also changing how the organisation behaves internally.

sections.name: How it takes on work
sections.notes: The engagement starts with the client's ambition rather than their asset list: what is this organisation trying to become, and what would have to be true for people to believe it. That framing is why so much of the output is a name, a proposition and a behaviour set, with the mark arriving late — the deliverable is the argument, and the logo is its most compressed form.

sections.name: Signature method
sections.notes: ‘Strategy made visible.’ Olins's phrase is an actual working test: for each element you are proposing, state which line of the strategy it makes visible. Executed in the extreme by Orange — an invented name with no category reference, a square of one colour, and a line (‘The future's bright’) that describes a posture rather than a service — which is what let it act as a challenger from launch instead of growing into one.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Judge the work in use, not at reveal: London 2012 was dismissed at reveal (Stephen Bayley called it ‘a puerile mess’) and then earned itself back through motion, colour and application across a whole games. The counterweight is abrdn — ridiculed, never recovered, reverted in 2025 — which sets the limit honestly: application rescues a mark that is merely unfamiliar, never one that is unusable. Today they state the bias plainly — ‘optimisation won't ensure success’ — preferring a defensible leap to a safe increment.

principle.title: Make a maker and a business mind co-authors from the first meeting
principle.explanation: Wolff Olins exists because Michael Wolff and Wally Olins were partners, not a sequence — a designer and a business head deciding together, which is the only arrangement in which ‘strategy made visible’ is a method rather than a slogan. When strategy is handed over finished, the designer spends the job decorating someone else's conclusion; when the maker is in the room while the conclusion forms, the visual idea and the commercial idea end up being the same idea.
principle.howToApply: Before laying out any Aperture order, take twenty minutes with the agent — the business head on that property — and leave with one written sentence naming who this piece is for and what it must make them do (‘make out-of-state buyers book a tour before the open house’). Put that sentence at the top of the working file. Every later choice — which photograph opens, whether the price leads, how much copy survives — has to cite it, and anything that can't gets cut at the first pass instead of the third.

entries.tagline: A shop built as a stack of flat-colour posters, where the hero's feature list is two hand-drawn arrows scribbled onto the product photograph.
entries.summary: Tony's sells personalised chocolate bars and an argument about forced labour in cocoa on the same page, and never changes voice between the two. Every section is a full-bleed slab of one flat brand colour — royal blue, then red, then white — with its title set in the house woodblock display face at full viewport width, so scrolling reads as turning over posters rather than moving through a template. Yellow appears nowhere except buttons and article tags, which is what keeps a very loud page navigable. The cost of that commitment: there is almost no quiet type on the page — everything is bold, hierarchy comes only from size, and the centred body copy gets tiring once a paragraph runs past three lines.
whatWorks: The hero replaces a feature list with annotation — two hand-drawn arrows and handwritten labels ('fully customizable wrapper', 'Fairtrade cocoa') point straight at the bar a hand is holding, so the claims sit on the product instead of in a column beside it
Section breaks are colour changes, not rules or whitespace: each block runs edge to edge in one flat hue, with no gradient, drop shadow or rounded card anywhere on the page

Section titles ('CHOCO SHOP', 'CUSTOMIZE YOUR WRAPPER', 'OUR WALL OF PRAISE') are set in the woodblock display face at full page width, one line, tracked to fill the measure — the headline is the section's only ornament
One hue is quarantined for action: yellow is used for every button and news tag and for absolutely nothing else, so the next step is findable inside any colour block

Testimonials are drawn as tilted speech bubbles with tails and attributed by role and organisation ('Senior Manager of Retail & Merchandising'), so proof reads as people talking rather than as a review widget
The mission block sits mid-page between two commerce sections in plain centred copy — the argument is inside the shop, not quarantined on an About page
The product photography lets the wrapper carry the design: bars are shot flat on saturated grounds so each customised label reads as its own poster in the grid

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: Royal-blue slab. Right half: 'CHOCOLATE THAT MAKES AN IMPACT' in three lines of the chunky house display face, one line of supporting copy, one small yellow 'shop now' button. Left half: a hand holding a customised bar, annotated with two hand-drawn arrows. No slider, no video, no second CTA.

sections.name: Choco shop
sections.notes: White ground, and the words 'CHOCO SHOP' in red at full viewport width — the section label is the graphic. Under it, three lines of centred copy and a carousel of wrapper designs, each bar shot flat on its own saturated ground so the personalisation is legible at thumbnail size.

sections.name: Wedding favours split block
sections.notes: The page's only quiet moment: white ground, copy left, one styled photograph right of stacked pink bars on a wedding table with Polaroids. It works because it is the one section that isn't shouting — the contrast buys it attention.

sections.name: Customize your wrapper
sections.notes: Red slab, full-width title, then the decision split into two literal buttons — 'choose a template' or 'start from scratch' — with the carousel below showing both routes. Two doors instead of one vague CTA.

sections.name: Corporate gifting
sections.notes: Blue slab holding three white cards (image, heading, two lines, yellow button): 'irresistible Belgian chocolate', 'customization for any occasion', 'ditch the dull merch'. The cards are the only place on the page where content sits on a panel, which is what marks this block as the B2B lane.

sections.name: Mission
sections.notes: White ground, centred copy left and a video right: 'We exist to end exploitation in cocoa. Not just the cocoa in our chocolate, but in all chocolate worldwide… The choice is yours, are you in?' Placed between two selling sections, with a plain 'read more' — the ethics are load-bearing merchandising, not a separate page.

sections.name: Wall of praise / What's new / Footer
sections.notes: Red slab of four tilted speech-bubble testimonials, each with role and organisation; then a white news row of four dated cards with coloured category tags ('news', 'new products', 'serious stuff') so the campaign log is date-stamped; then a red footer, 'LET'S BE SERIOUS FRIENDS' email capture, five link columns and a self-deprecating 'website footer joke generator' with a 'meh..' button.

principle.title: Annotate the hero photograph instead of listing its features
principle.explanation: A bullet list asks the reader to hold the claim in one place and the thing in another, and to trust that they match. An arrow drawn onto the photograph does the matching for them: the claim is pinned to the pixels that prove it, the eye never leaves the product, and the handwriting reads as a person pointing rather than as marketing copy. It also enforces brevity — you can only fit three words on an arrow.
principle.howToApply: On a listing hero or the front of a flyer, drop the feature bullets and annotate the photograph instead: two or three short handwritten labels with curved arrows, in one consistent hand, pointing at the actual evidence — 'original 1920s casement windows', 'south-facing all afternoon', 'garage fits two'. Cap it at three, keep them on the empty parts of the frame and never over a face or the roofline, and use the same hand across the whole pack so the annotation reads as a house device rather than a one-off sticker.

entries.tagline: Sends the same résumé to 100 job ads under two names, one female and one male, and lets the callback gap be the whole ad.
entries.summary: Spain has more than 450,000 professional truck drivers and around 30,000 unfilled seats, but only about 2% of large-vehicle drivers are women — and many of those women had learned to blur the photograph and hide the name on their CV to get an interview at all. Midas built CV Visible, a platform where drivers send their full identity, kilometres and licences straight to hiring companies, and proved the need with a controlled experiment: 100 job ads, 200 applications, identical qualifications, one variable changed — Andrea Flores Gil vs Andrés Flores Gil. The male profile drew 66.7% more opportunities; 13 companies called only the man, 3 only the woman. The craft is in the restraint: black frames, one statistic at a time in Midas yellow, documentary footage of real drivers on either side of the data.
whatWorks: The central image is the audience's own workaround — a real CV with the identity block blacked out — rather than a metaphor for bias
The method is shown before the result: '100 OFERTAS DE EMPLEO / 200 candidaturas enviadas / 100 Andrea — 100 Andrés' on a flat yellow card, so the finding is auditable when it arrives
One statistic per frame, set as the only yellow element on black — 66.7%, then 13, then 3 — so no number has to compete with another
The figures are un-round and small-sample-honest, which reads as an experiment rather than as a rounded marketing claim
Documentary footage of named working drivers bookends the data, so the statistics have faces before and after the graphics
The call to action is a working platform (CV Visible) plus one line, 'Únete al cambio' — the campaign leaves something running behind it

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: Women driving — a cab window, a port, a hand on the wheel — shot flat and documentary, then a hard cut to a CV whose name and photograph are covered by a black bar. The blacked-out bar is the stop-scroll image, and it is a real artefact, not an illustration.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: Statistics stated one per frame in white and Midas yellow on black: '3 de cada 4 españoles creen que siguen existiendo barreras de género en el acceso al mercado laboral de la automoción.' Bold weight only on the clause that carries the claim.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: The experiment card: flat yellow ground, black rules, '100 OFERTAS DE EMPLEO' over '200 candidaturas enviadas', two identical CVs with a female and male pictogram, '100 Andrea' and '100 Andrés' pinned at the outer edges. The whole mechanic reads in one still — which is why it also works as the social frame.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: The black bar lifts off the CV to reveal 'Andrea Flores Gil' in full, then the endcard: 'Cv Invisible' becomes CV Visible, 'Únete al cambio', #EllasConducen — a live platform where drivers submit name, face, kilometres, years and licences directly to hiring companies.

principle.title: Build the opposite of the workaround your audience invented
principle.explanation: When people quietly hack around a problem — blurring a name, cropping a photo, leaving a field blank — the hack is a finished piece of research: it names the barrier, the emotion and the exact artefact to put on screen.
