Ghost splits proof into three labelled rows for the three audiences it actually serves, gives each row four named real customers as photographs, and captions each with the number that segment is chasing: members for publishers, monthly revenue for creators, category for brands. The visitor finds their row in one scan, and the metric tells them what success looks like in units they already use.
principle.howToApply: On an Aperture services or seller page, replace the mixed testimonial carousel with three labelled rows of four — Sellers, Developers, Relocating buyers — each tile a real photograph of the actual property with the client or building name over the image, and one metric underneath in that segment's own units: 'sold 6 days, 4% over ask', '38 units absorbed in 9 months', 'closed remotely from Lisbon'. If a row can't be filled with four real ones, it isn't a segment you serve yet — cut the row rather than padding it.

site.name: The Economist — 'Raising Eyebrows and Subscriptions' (programmatic display)

entries.category: Programmatic display banner — contextual, in-article mobile
entries.tagline: A redacted headline in Economist red, served deliberately inside the news story that completes it.
entries.when: Launched 2015 (Proximity London with UM London; Gold at Cannes Lions and the DMA Grand Prix that year)
entries.summary: The unit is four elements: a field of Economist red, a headline that has been redacted with black censor bars so only 'CIA' and 'torture.' survive, the small red Economist logo box bottom-left, and a black button reading 'DON'T CLICK HERE ▸'. What makes it work is where it ran — served programmatically into a CNN mobile article headlined 'CIA Director responds to torture report', so the surrounding editorial supplies the half of the sentence the bars are hiding. The line and the media buy were built as one idea rather than in sequence, which is why the copy can be two words long. The campaign ran a portfolio of these lines against matched contexts and pushed readers to free Economist articles rather than straight to a paywall.
whatWorks: The brand's own red fills the unit edge to edge, so it separates instantly from the grey-and-white news page it is placed in and is identifiable before a single word is read.
The headline is a redaction, not a sentence: black bars cover everything except 'CIA' and 'torture.', so the reader has to finish it — one second of work, and that second is the engagement.

The placement is the punchline. Served against a CNN story about the CIA torture report, the ad and the article around it become one message; the targeting is doing the job a longer headline would otherwise do.

The CTA inverts the standard imperative — 'DON'T CLICK HERE' — while keeping the arrow pointing the way and staying a single plain black button; the contrarian line reads as the brand's voice, not a trick.
The logo is a footnote, not the lead: the red Economist box sits small in the bottom-left corner with its pointer, so the ad closes with the brand instead of opening with it.
Total element count is four — field, redacted line, logo, button. No product shot, no offer, no price, no stock photography.
The click goes to a free, related Economist article rather than a subscription form, so the first thing the provocation delivers is the actual product.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: Pure colour plus censorship. A flat red rectangle inside a page of neutral news UI stops the scroll on contrast alone, and the black bars read as 'something is being withheld from you' before any word is parsed — an information-shaped tease for an information brand.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: Two surviving words, 'CIA' and 'torture.', set in the Economist's own type, white on red and black on red. The sentence is unreadable and that is the copy: the redaction device is both the joke and a claim about what the paper covers. The full stop after 'torture.' keeps it a statement rather than a headline fragment.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: There is no image. The visual idea is a typographic device — censor bars sized and positioned like real redaction over real words — which means the unit weighs nothing, renders identically at every banner size, and can be re-written for a new context in minutes. That reproducibility is what let the campaign run hundreds of context-matched variants programmatically.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: A small black pill, bottom-right, reading 'DON'T CLICK HERE ▸'. It does three things at once: it's a legible button in the expected place, it's in the paper's contrarian register, and it dares rather than asks. The Economist logo sits opposite it bottom-left, so the bottom edge reads as signature-then-invitation.

principle.title: Build the creative and the placement as one idea, not in that order
principle.explanation: Most display is written first and targeted afterwards, so it says the same thing everywhere and gets read as wallpaper. The Economist wrote lines that only detonate in a specific context — a redacted 'CIA … torture.' running inside a CNN story about the CIA torture report — so the article around the unit supplies the missing half. The reader experiences it as relevance rather than advertising, and the creative can be radically shorter because the page is doing half the work.
principle.howToApply: For the next Aperture digital-ad flight, write one line per placement context instead of one line for the whole flight, and build the variants before the media plan is locked: the unit running beside a school-ratings page reads differently from the one beside a relocation or interest-rate article, and different again on a neighbourhood guide. Keep the layout identical across all of them so only the line changes. The test is simple — if a line still makes sense on any page, it isn't using its placement and should be rewritten or cut.

entries.tagline: Wrote his typefaces with a pen before he ever drew them — Palatino, Optima, Zapf Dingbats, Zapfino — then spent his second career teaching computers to set type properly.
entries.summary: Zapf was essentially self-taught: in 1935 he saw an exhibition honouring Rudolf Koch in Nuremberg, bought two books, and taught himself calligraphy from them. Everything after that began with the written hand — Palatino (1948), Melior, Optima (released 1958) and eventually Zapfino (1998) all started as pen strokes and were only then refined into type, cut in metal alongside punchcutter August Rosenberger at the Stempel foundry. The second half of his career ran in the opposite direction: he lectured on computerised typesetting from the 1960s, consulted for Hallmark on a lettering style manual, held the first professorship in typographic computer programming at RIT from 1977 to 1987, and wrote the hz-program to fix justification and spacing systematically rather than page by page.
whatWorks: Start with the tool that makes the form, not the outline: write the alphabet with a broad-nib pen first, so stress, thick/thin distribution and the natural joins fall out of the pen's physics — the drawing then refines something that already moves, instead of inventing movement from scratch.

Work from one named source you can point at, not a mood: Palatino takes its name and its logic from the Renaissance writing master Giambattista Palatino; Optima came out of flared Florentine stone letters. A specific historical document beats a board of references.

Sit beside whoever makes the final object. Zapf worked directly with Rosenberger at the punchcutting bench rather than sending drawings over a wall, so the constraints of the production step reached him while the design was still moving.

Design the connective tissue too, not only the stars — companion italics, a text-weight partner (Aldus to Palatino), a whole family of symbols (Zapf Dingbats). The useful thing is often the supporting piece nobody briefs.

Learn the next production technology roughly a decade before you need it: he was lecturing on computer typesetting long before desktop publishing arrived, so the upheaval found him fluent rather than defensive.
When you catch yourself fixing the same thing by hand repeatedly, fix the system instead — rather than hand-adjusting justification forever, he wrote the hz-program so every page got better.

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: With a pen and a real source. Zapf's first move on a face was calligraphic — sheets of written letters with a broad nib, at large size, to find the skeleton and the rhythm before any outline existed — and his starting reference was usually one identifiable historical hand or inscription rather than a general period feel. The self-taught route matters here: he learned by copying named exemplars out of two books and a library, so 'go study a specific artefact closely' was the method he had, and it stayed the method.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Written form first, drawn refinement second, production collaboration third. He iterated between the pen and the drawing board, then took the drawings to August Rosenberger to be cut in metal at Stempel, refining against what the punchcutter and the press revealed. The loop is the point: each pass moved the design closer to the material it would finally exist in, and the person who handled that material was in the room.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: The humanist compromise — letters that carry calligraphic stress without obvious calligraphic decoration. Optima is the clearest case: a sans serif whose strokes flare at the terminals, so it reads with the warmth and the thick/thin modulation of a written or carved letter while having no serifs at all. The move is to keep the evidence of the hand in the proportions and the stroke, and strip the ornament that usually advertises it.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Judge a text face in a paragraph at reading size, never in a display showing — the test is the even grey of a block of text and how the letters behave next to each other, not how handsome a single 'a' looks blown up. And treat spacing as a system problem: his late work (the hz-program, the Hallmark style manual, the RIT professorship) is all the same instinct applied at a larger scale — if the rule can be written down, write it down so it runs everywhere, and reserve the hand for the things a rule can't reach.

principle.title: Judge the face in a paragraph at reading size, never in the specimen
principle.explanation: A display showing flatters everything — at 120pt any typeface looks characterful, and you end up choosing letterforms rather than texture. Zapf's judgement was made on the block: set real text at real size and look at the evenness of the grey, how the letters space against each other, where a pair collides, which characters go soft. Almost everything that decides whether type works in the wild — the 8pt disclaimer, the caption, the MLS thumbnail — lives at sizes the specimen never shows you.
principle.howToApply: Before locking a typeface for an Aperture piece, print one sheet with nothing but the real smalls: a full property description paragraph at its actual size, the spec line with real digits, the fair-housing disclaimer at its true 7–8pt, the agent block with a real long email address, and a price string with commas — then look at it at arm's length, not on screen. If the numerals go soft, the paragraph turns patchy, or the disclaimer fills in, the face is wrong regardless of how the address looks at hero size.

entries.tagline: A 24/7 radio station whose homepage puts what is on air right now in a strip above its own navigation, sets the entire page in one condensed typeface at 13–24px, and spends its single red on nothing but the word 'live'.
entries.summary: NTS is a London internet radio station with two always-on channels, and the homepage is built as a broadcast chassis rather than a marketing page: before the logo row there is a live strip — red dot, channel 1 and 2, the show playing now, the city it is coming from — so the first thing the page says is what is happening this second. Everything below it is set in Univers Condensed, uppercase, one bold weight, between 13px and 24px, on pure black; there is no display type, no hero headline and no brand accent anywhere except a single alarm red (#E81717) that is only ever the live indicator. Hierarchy is done with position, black-and-white inversion and genre chips instead of size, which is how a page carrying eight shows, a shop rail, a supporter pitch, a collections rail and a news row stays under 3,500px and still reads as calm. The honest caveat: the type is small and dense everywhere, so this restraint depends on an audience that arrives to browse rather than to be persuaded.
whatWorks: Two live channel rows sit above the nav, not inside it — red dot, channel number in a white box, show title in 14px uppercase bold, origin city right-aligned — so the schedule outranks the menu and the page is never a snapshot.
One typeface (Univers Condensed), one voice (uppercase), one weight family, 13–24px for literally everything from nav to show titles to footer; no display size appears on the page at all.
The single saturated colour in the chassis is the red live circle. Desaturate the page and nothing changes except the show artwork — which is the only place colour is allowed to live.

Every show is the same card: 4:3 artwork, a metadata line (date · SUPPORTER RADIO · CHICAGO), the uppercase title, then genre chips (HOUSE / EURO HOUSE / ELECTROCLASH) that are the site's real taxonomy rather than decoration.

Exactly one conversion moment in the whole page — a full-bleed dark photographic band with 'BUILT FOR MUSIC LOVERS, BY MUSIC LOVERS' and one outlined button — so the ask reads as a membership, not a banner.
The product promise is five words in the footer: 'FREE. NO ADS. 24/7.' It is never restated in a hero, because the live strip has already demonstrated it.

sections.name: Live strip & nav
sections.notes: A black bar above everything: 'LIVE NOW' with a red dot, then two numbered channel rows each carrying a play triangle, the show title in uppercase bold and the city (LONDON) right-aligned, with a small waveform and time controls at the right end. The nav row beneath it is seven uppercase words (RADIO, LATEST, EXPLORE, INFINITE MIXTAPES, SHOP, NTS SUPPORTERS) plus search and account. Putting state above navigation means the page answers 'what's on?' before it answers 'where can I go?'.

sections.name: Hero: In Focus + Infinite Mixtapes rail
sections.notes: A full-bleed editorial photograph (this week: John Martyn) with a small black caption card set into the bottom-left — genre tags, title, two lines of dek, a play triangle — and carousel arrows tucked in the bottom-right corner rather than overlaid on the face. To its right, a fixed rail of Infinite Mixtapes: stacked colour-coded tiles (POOLSIDE, SLOW FOCUS, LOW KEY) each with its own artwork and play button. The hero sells one editorial pick; the rail sells the always-on alternative. No headline, no CTA button, no brand statement anywhere in the fold.

sections.name: NTS Picks
sections.notes: Eight identical cards in a 4×2 grid under a small 'NTS PICKS ›' label and a one-line dek ('Recent radio highlights hand picked by NTS'). Each card: artwork, a grey metadata line with date and station/city, the title in uppercase bold, then genre chips. Uniform crop and identical card weight mean the artwork — which ranges from a blurred portrait to a red text-only cover to a classical painting — does all the visual variety, and the eye can still scan the column of titles.

sections.name: NTS Shop
sections.notes: A horizontal rail of product cards on plain white grounds (radio player, jacket, tee, earphone case) with name and price set in exactly the same condensed caps as the show titles. Commerce is given no special styling, no badges and no coloured buttons — it is another content type in the same system, which is why a shop row inside an editorial page doesn't feel like an interruption.

sections.name: Supporter band
sections.notes: The only persuasion block on the page: a full-bleed, dark, out-of-focus club photograph with two centred lines — 'BUILT FOR MUSIC LOVERS, BY MUSIC LOVERS' — and a single white-outlined 'BECOME AN NTS SUPPORTER' button. It appears after the visitor has already seen forty shows for free, so the ask arrives as a consequence of the page rather than a condition of it.

sections.name: Collections & News
sections.notes: Two more rails using the same card, differentiated only by label and by where the title sits: Collections overlays the title on the artwork with a play button (they are playable), News & Events keeps the title below (they are readable). One component, two behaviours, no new styling.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Three columns of plain uppercase links — NTS (About, Careers, Help, Support, Gift), Stay up to date (email field, an explicit consent checkbox, SUBSCRIBE), Listen on the NTS app (App Store / Google Play badges) — then the NTS mark centred, 'FREE. NO ADS. 24/7.' beneath it, and a row of social icons. The strongest claim on the site is given the smallest type and the last position.

principle.title: Let your one accent colour mean one state, not the brand
principle.explanation: An accent used for emphasis is decoration and the eye stops reading it within a screen or two. An accent bound to a single condition — on air now, open today, taken — is information: its presence anywhere on the page tells you something true, and its absence tells you something too. NTS can run a black-and-white interface at 13px and still be instantly scannable because the only red on screen always means one thing.
principle.howToApply: Pick the one accent in the Aperture palette and write down the single condition under which it is allowed to appear — 'open house today', 'just listed this week', 'under offer' — then ban it from headings, buttons, hovers, chips and section bands. On a collection page that means the accent appears on three cards out of thirty and a visitor can find what's happening today without reading a word; if you find yourself wanting it on a button, use a black pill and change the label instead.

site.name: Domino's — social film series & key visual (France)

entries.category: Reactive social campaign (short films + key visual)
entries.when: September 2026 — released in France within days of Apple's foldable phone reveal, by agency Foolish for Domino's Pizza France
entries.tagline: Shoots a cardboard pizza box with the exact production grammar of a phone launch — seamless sweep, macro folding shots, sentence-case grotesque — and lets the mismatch make the argument.
entries.summary: Apple unveiled a foldable phone; days later Domino's France published a series of short films that introduce its pizza box using the visual codes of a tech keynote — precision macro shots of the folding, the product floating alone on an off-white infinite sweep, and a launch lockup reading 'Domino's / The Original Foldable'. The joke only survives because the craft is real: the lighting, the retouching, the contact shadow and the typography are all at the level of the thing being spoofed, so it reads as a campaign rather than a meme. It is also true — the box has always arrived flat, folded, opened and closed — which is what separates this from a topical gag: the claim is a product fact that was sitting there the whole time. Apple is never named; the week's news supplies the reference for free.
whatWorks: The staging is the hook, not the copy: off-white seamless, soft top light, two boxes at a three-quarter float with a contact shadow — a device-launch frame your eye decodes before you read a word.

Typography does the borrowing — small brand name above, large sentence-case product name below, set in a neutral grotesque with a wide empty margin to the right. No food typography, no italic, no burst.
The boxes are art-directed as hardware: blue and red lids read as colourways, 'comes in multiple sizes' becomes a spec line, the die-cut vents become a product detail.
Everything an ordinary pizza ad would carry is absent — no price, no offer, no appetite macro, no corner logo lockup, no 'order now'. The restraint is the parody.
It is reactive by design: published in the slipstream of someone else's launch, so the audience arrives already holding the reference, and the ad never has to explain the comparison.
The claim is literally true, so the campaign lands as a fact about the product rather than a joke at a competitor's expense — nothing to retract, and it can be repeated at the next launch.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: Format mimicry in the first frame: in a feed full of phone-launch footage, a shot that looks exactly like phone-launch footage — until the object resolves as a pizza box. The scroll stop costs nothing in copy because the audience's eye is already tuned to this frame that week.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: 'The Original Foldable', three words, with 'Domino's' set small above it in the keynote position. It is unreadable as a joke on any other week and perfectly readable this one — the placement in time is doing half the writing. 'Original' quietly does the competitive work without naming anyone.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Two boxes, one closed and one part-opened, floating on an off-white sweep with the brand's blue and red lids as the only colour. The films extend the same grammar into precision macro: the crease, the fold, the click of the tab — shot with the loving slow-motion normally reserved for a hinge mechanism.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: There isn't one, and that's the discipline — no price, no promo code, no 'order now' end-card. The payoff is the product reveal itself. Honest caveat: a no-CTA brand film only works on top of an ordering habit that's already frictionless; it buys fame, not this week's orders, and shouldn't be the whole plan.

principle.title: If you borrow another category's format, buy its production values too
principle.explanation: Parody only reads as confidence when the craft matches the thing being parodied. The moment the lighting, the retouching, the type or the timing falls below the borrowed format's standard, the audience reclassifies the work from campaign to meme and the brand loses the authority the borrowing was meant to steal. The comedy lives in the straight face — which is expensive to hold.
principle.howToApply: When an Aperture piece borrows a format — a spec sheet for a house, a keynote reveal for a new development, a gallery wall label for a renovation — commit to that format's real standards: its exact typographic register, its lighting, its white space, its absence of sales furniture. Then delete every element the borrowed format would never contain (the price flash, the agent headshot, the QR burst). If you can't afford to execute the parody to the standard of the original, run the plain version instead.

entries.category: Advertising & editorial art direction — the New York 'Creative Revolution'
entries.tagline: Ninety-two Esquire covers in ten years, each a single image that argues — and the strongest working model for arriving with one idea instead of three options.
entries.summary: Lois came out of Doyle Dane Bernbach, co-founded Papert Koenig Lois, and between 1962 and 1972 art-directed 92 covers for Esquire under editor Harold Hayes — Muhammad Ali as St. Sebastian pierced with arrows, Andy Warhol drowning in a can of soup, Sonny Liston as Santa Claus — work now held by MoMA. His method was the 'Big Idea': one image and one line, fused so tightly that neither survives alone, produced fast and then defended at length. He is also the cautionary half of his own story — a relentless self-mythologiser whose authorship claims were disputed — but the process he practised is unusually teachable, and the discipline underneath it (one idea, presented with its argument, executed under your own eye) is the part worth stealing.
whatWorks: Reduce the brief to a single sentence that can be argued with. If you can't say what the piece is claiming in one line, there is no idea yet, only a layout.
Test for the one-image rule: if the point needs two pictures, a diagram or a build, the idea isn't finished. Lois's covers are all single frames.
Fuse word and image so neither works alone — the line should be meaningless without the picture and the picture unreadable without the line.
Present one idea, not a menu. Options are a way of handing the decision to the client; an argument is a way of making it.
Sketch in minutes, sell for months. He treated the selling of the idea — not its generation — as the long and skilled part of the job: if you can't sell it, you didn't have an idea.
Stay on the floor: he cast the shoot, directed the talent and stood behind the camera. The idea is not handed off to production, because the execution is where it is usually lost.

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: Not with references or thumbnails, but with the argument. Lois read the story or the sales problem and reduced it to one provoking sentence — Ali is being martyred by the establishment; nobody believes the Democratic ticket — and only then looked for the single picture that would make a stranger think it. He worked fast on purpose: the first idea that passes the one-sentence and one-image tests is taken seriously rather than diluted by a week of alternatives.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: The 'Big Idea': one image plus a handful of words, fused. He designed the cover as an argument aimed at a person walking past a newsstand at four feet, not at an editor holding a proof at reading distance. The corollary is brutal editing — no secondary cover lines fighting the picture, no explanatory dek, no second subject. Everything that isn't the argument is removed before it's presented, which is why the presentation is a single board.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Casting the real person into the borrowed image. Rather than illustrate a metaphor, he staged it with the actual subject and made them perform it: Ali as Mantegna's St. Sebastian, Nixon being made up by four hands, Warhol going under in a Campbell's can. Because the subject is real and the frame is borrowed from something the audience already knows, the picture needs no caption to be decoded — and it is impossible to mistake for stock.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: One idea per problem; no options. Research reports what has already happened, so it can't validate something new. The idea must be defensible in one sentence to a hostile room — and if it can't be sold, it wasn't strong enough to begin with. He judged work by whether it would be remembered and repeated, not by whether it was liked in the meeting; the whole method assumes a client relationship (Hayes at Esquire gave him control) in which the art director is allowed to be right, which is the precondition most people skip.

principle.title: Bring one idea and the sentence that sells it — never a menu
principle.explanation: Presenting three options hands the decision to whoever has the least context, and guarantees the result is the safest of the three. Arriving with one direction plus a one-line argument moves the conversation from taste ('which do you prefer?') to reasoning ('is this the right claim?') — which is the only conversation in which good work survives. It also forces the editing to happen before the meeting, where it's cheap, rather than in it.
principle.howToApply: For the next Aperture deliverable, write the one-sentence claim before opening the template ('this house is bought for the light in the mornings, not the square footage'), build the single direction that makes that claim, and present it alone with the sentence on the first slide. Keep the alternates in a folder for when the claim itself is rejected — not as a tasting menu. If you can't write the sentence, the piece isn't ready to show, however finished the layout looks.

entries.tagline: A shop homepage that opens not with a hero shot but with twenty-four small material crops, and where the biggest type on the page is about 32px — all the scale is carried by photography.
entries.summary: Vipp sells kitchens, cabinets, chairs and a handful of guesthouses and co-owned houses, and the homepage refuses the usual e-commerce grammar: no carousel of offers, no badge rows, no filled buttons above the fold. Instead the page alternates two states — a full-bleed photograph with three lines of white serif set over its calmest area, then a white "rest" block holding a letterspaced caps label, one sentence and an underlined text link — and repeats that rhythm nine times down the page. Colour is used as an index rather than decoration: one sand field (#CCBCA2) for the cabinet system, one terracotta field (#804A2E) for the Residences co-ownership business, charcoal for the footer, and white everywhere else, so every saturated pixel between them comes out of a photograph. The caveat is length: the page runs past 15,000px with several editorial blocks competing for the same "read more" slot, and a first-time visitor looking for a price has a long scroll ahead. (The capture covers the page down through the outdoor collections; the kitchen grid, guesthouse cards and footer sit below it.)
whatWorks: Open on material, not on a room: the fold is a sand field with an italic serif fragment ("From lightness…") small in the top-left and a 3×8 mosaic of twenty-four tight crops — oak end-grain, fluted metal, a marble edge, an open drawer, a ceramic bowl — so the product is introduced as a set of surfaces before it is ever shown whole.

Cap the headline size and let the photograph do the scaling. Nothing on this page is set much above ~32px; the emotional volume comes from full-bleed imagery, which means the type never has to shout over it.
Alternate full-bleed image with a short white rest block — caps label, one 2–3 line sentence, one underlined link — so no section is asked to carry both maximum image and maximum copy.
Place overlay copy in the calm zone of the photograph (sky, plaster wall, empty floor) at a narrow centred measure, never across the busy subject; no scrim is needed anywhere on the page.
Let a craft photograph do the selling: the new swivel chairs are argued with a close shot of hands and callipers on the shell, not with a feature list — the making is the proof.

Credit the photographer inside the headline ("Scottish photographer Richard Gaston has spent a spring weekend at the Vipp Montafon") so the block reads as reportage with an author rather than as brand copy.

Give each business line its own colour field. Sand means the cabinet system; terracotta means Residences — a different offer with a different transaction — and the change of ground announces that before a word is read.
Keep conversion quiet where the page is editorial: caret + underlined text links throughout, with the only real form (newsletter, country selector) parked in the charcoal footer.

sections.name: Hero — cabinet mosaic
sections.notes: Sand ground, italic serif fragment small in the top-left corner, and a 3×8 grid of tight material crops that animates in place. It does the job a hero image would do — establish register, palette and material — while also functioning as a contact sheet: the visitor scans twenty-four surfaces in the time one wide shot would have taken.

sections.name: Statement block
sections.notes: White, centred, with a tiny letterspaced caps eyebrow ("A CABINET OF MATERIAL CURIOSITY") over three lines explaining the eight modular units, then an underlined text link. The eyebrow names the thing, the sentence explains the system, and the whole block is roughly one-eighth the height of the section above it — a deliberate rest.

sections.name: Vipp Apartment editorial
sections.notes: Full-bleed interior with a three-line white serif headline centred over the middle of the frame and a small bold link beneath. The copy is a piece of news ("Vipp returns to its hometown of Copenhagen with a city apartment"), not a product claim, which is what lets an image this quiet hold a whole screen.

sections.name: Swivel Chair product story
sections.notes: Asymmetric two-column: a wide lifestyle shot on the left, a tight process photograph on the right — hands measuring the moulded shell with callipers — with caps eyebrow and four lines of body under it. Then a single full-bleed scene, a centred one-line sentence ("Configurable in multiple ways to suit any space") and a four-up row of variants (Vipp452–455) with hairline rules and caret affordances.

sections.name: Montafon photo essay
sections.notes: Full-bleed alpine hütte with the photographer named in the headline. The move is editorial attribution: a third party has spent time in the place, which converts the property from inventory into a story someone chose to tell.

sections.name: Residences — Mallorca
sections.notes: The only coloured section on the page: terracotta ground, a tall exterior on the left, copy on the right, a second interior lower right. Colour marks a different business (co-ownership, an external site) so the reader knows the offer has changed before reading the eyebrow "CO-OWN THIS HOUSE IN MALLORCA".

sections.name: Outdoor, kitchens, guesthouses, Inspiration
sections.notes: The lower page settles into four-up card rows — four kitchens (V1–V4), four guesthouses (Cold Hawaii, Todos Santos, Lagrasse, Bruny Island), three Inspiration stories with small category labels. Identical card geometry throughout, so the shift from editorial to catalogue is legible without a heading change.

sections.name: Footer
sections.notes: Charcoal ground, three link columns (Company / Customer Service / Professionals), then the newsletter field with a country selector, the CVR number and social icons. All the transactional furniture the top of the page refuses to carry is collected in one place at the end.

principle.title: Open with the material, not the room
principle.explanation: A single wide hero shot asks the visitor to judge a whole space in one glance, and every competitor's hero looks the same because the frame is the same. A mosaic of tight material crops — grain, join, edge, handle, tile — sells the thing photographs of rooms are worst at conveying (what it is made of and how well it is made), and it reads as a contact sheet, which flatters both the property and the photographer.
principle.howToApply: On the next property page or Power Pack opener, build the fold from 18–24 square detail crops shot at the same session and the same light — casement hardware, stone edge, timber grain, tap, tile join, stair nosing — laid in a tight grid on one warm ground, with the address line small above and one underlined text link beneath. Keep the wide room shots for the sections below: the mosaic establishes quality, the wides establish plan.

site.name: Club Med — 'The Art of Free Time' (key visuals, social & digital OOH)

entries.category: Campaign key visuals — paid social / digital OOH (film-led integrated campaign)
entries.tagline: Three frames, no headline doing any explaining: the whole idea is carried by one absurd human gesture staged inside the real resort.
entries.when: Launched 6 September 2026, international (Europe, US, Latin America, Asia) — BETC Paris, film directed by Fleur Fortuné
entries.summary: BETC's platform for Club Med reframes idleness as a skill — free time as the ultimate luxury — and the key visuals argue it without a single line of body copy. A woman in a bathrobe and towel turban balances horizontally on a man's upturned feet above an alpine pool, sipping from an espresso cup; two skiers ride a chairlift in white ski suits with face-mask cream and cucumber slices on; a mother and two children walk a beach carrying stacked towers of pool rings. Each frame is a one-second read, shot on location in real Club Med settings rather than composited, and the only type is a four-word lockup — "The Art of free time" in a high-contrast serif with the two key words in italic — pinned in the same top-right corner of every frame beside the trident. Because the wardrobe is white in all three and the grounds are sky-blue, snow and sand, a summer beach ad and a winter ski ad read as the same campaign without any shared graphic device beyond the lockup.
whatWorks: One gesture per frame, legible before any word is read: the acroyoga espresso, the cucumber slices on a chairlift, the tower of pool rings. Each is a single tableau, not a sequence or a build.

The location is the product and the joke is staged inside it — real Alps, real beach, real chairlift — so the setting sells while the gesture entertains; nothing is fabricated on top of the photograph.
The lockup never moves. Same corner, same size, same white across all three frames, so the set reads as one campaign at feed scale where nothing else is shared.

Copy is four words and it reframes rather than describes: 'The Art of free time' makes doing nothing a discipline you can be good at — which is the entire strategy compressed into a headline that never has to appear anywhere else.
One wardrobe rule (all white) carries the campaign across two opposite seasons, letting beach and ski creative run in the same flight without looking like two brands.
No CTA, no price, no offer strip. The unit is asking for recognition, not a click, and it does not pretend otherwise — the ask lives later in the funnel.

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: A physical impossibility played entirely straight — a person horizontal in mid-air in a bathrobe, or skiers in full spa treatment on a moving chairlift. The absurdity is in the behaviour, not in the retouching, so the eye stops without feeling sold to.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: Four words in a high-contrast serif with 'free time' in italic: a reframe, not a description. It categorises leisure as a craft, which quietly flatters the buyer and licenses every silly scenario in the campaign.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: Real resort locations shot in flat bright daylight, deep-focus, with the subject small enough that the landscape still reads. The gag occupies the lower two-thirds and the lockup takes the empty sky at the top right — composition planned around where the type would go.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: There isn't one, beyond the brand lockup. The key visual's job is to re-position the brand; the booking ask is left to the performance units, which is why the frame can stay this clean.

principle.title: Direct one gesture, and let it carry what a headline would have said
principle.explanation: In a feed the image is decoded before the words are, so a picture that needs its caption to make sense has already lost the scroll. A single staged human action — one frame, no build, no second element — is understood pre-language, and it lets the copy stop describing and start reframing, which is the only job left worth doing in four words.
principle.howToApply: For a listing campaign, name the benefit in one sentence, then direct a single human gesture inside the actual property that dramatises it — dinner laid on the dock instead of in the dining room, a child's bike parked at the bottom of the stairs, coffee on the roof terrace at 7am — shot on location with no compositing. Keep the campaign lockup (address or campaign line plus mark) in the same corner at the same size across every frame in the flight, cap the copy at five words, and let the price, specs and CTA live in the performance unit that follows.

entries.category: Photographic modernism — photomontage, advertising and identity
entries.tagline: The designer who made his own raw material: trained as a painter, worked as a photographer, and built posters by pairing two photographs at wildly different scales.
entries.summary: Matter studied painting in Geneva and at the Académie Moderne in Paris under Léger and Ozenfant, then worked around Cassandre, Le Corbusier and the type foundry Deberny & Peignot before returning to Zurich in 1932 to make the Swiss National Tourist Office posters that changed what a photograph could do on a sheet of paper. He emigrated in 1936, worked for Alexey Brodovitch at Harper's Bazaar, was design consultant to Knoll from 1946 to 1966, designed the 1954 New Haven Railroad identity and its NH monogram, consulted for the Guggenheim, filmed Alexander Calder at work, and taught photography at Yale from 1952 to 1976. What makes him worth studying as process rather than style is the order of his operations: he shot first and designed second, which meant his compositions could use images no picture library would ever have held.
whatWorks: Make the raw material before you make the layout. Matter photographed the mountains, faces, boots and objects himself, so the composition was never limited to frames someone else had already chosen to shoot.

Build the frame from two elements at violently different scales — a head filling the sheet, a skier at a fiftieth of its size behind it. Scale contrast produces depth and hierarchy without any grid at all.
Assemble in the medium that will print it: Matter's layouts were made photographically, in the darkroom, so what he approved and what came off press were the same object.
Treat type as an element inside the image, overprinted in a second colour and locked into the composition, rather than as a caption zone under it.
One photographic idea per surface. His posters never carry two arguments; the second idea becomes a second poster.
Keep your own picture library and keep shooting between jobs — his Knoll advertising, the Calder films and the Yale teaching all fed off the same continuous photographic practice.

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: With a camera rather than a sketch. Matter's first move on a tourism brief was to go and photograph the place, the equipment and the people, generating raw material that didn't exist yet — which is why his posters could do things his contemporaries' drawn posters couldn't. The painting training (Léger, Ozenfant) supplied the sense of flat picture construction; the camera supplied the parts.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: The darkroom as the layout table. For the Swiss National Tourist Office posters of 1934–36 he montaged: enlarge one photographic element until it fills the sheet, drop a second at a fraction of the size, overprint type in one flat colour, and resolve the whole thing photographically rather than by pasting artwork. The technique fused photograph and typography into one surface — the move that later became the house grammar of Swiss design.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: Extreme scale jumps between two photographic elements in a single frame — a foreground head or hand ten times the size of the figure behind it — creating depth, reading order and drama without perspective tricks or illustration. The 1941 'America Calling' poster shows the same logic in wartime form: one enormous eagle photographed as an object, type bitten into the image, three flat colours.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: Image first, type as part of the image, one idea per surface, and consistency across media — the New Haven Railroad work is a mark plus a rule for how everything gets photographed and repainted, not just a logo. He judged work as a photographer does: does the frame hold at a glance, and is anything in it doing nothing? Everything else — Knoll ads, museum graphics, film titles — ran off the same photographic instinct.

principle.title: Commission the raw material, not the finished picture
principle.explanation: A layout can only be as good as the frames that exist. If every photograph in the delivery is a well-made wide shot of a room, every layout will be a well-made grid of well-made wide shots — there is nothing to build scale contrast from. Matter could pair a giant foreground element with a tiny distant one because he had shot both himself, on purpose, knowing what the sheet needed.
principle.howToApply: Write the shot list as pairs, and send it before the shoot: for every wide (façade, living room, garden), one extreme close of something in that same frame — the door handle, the plaster, the tap, the tile join, the casement catch — shot at the same session in the same light. Then build the opener by pairing one of those closes enlarged to full bleed with the wide dropped in small, and set the address line into the image rather than beneath it. Anything the layout can't do later is usually a frame nobody asked for on the day.

entries.tagline: A luxury commerce homepage with one button on the entire page — everything else is a tiny underlined caps link, and every category is represented by a still commissioned for it rather than a catalogue shot.
entries.summary: RIMOWA sells hard-cased aluminium luggage on a page that behaves like a print catalogue: a transparent header over a full-bleed shoreline photograph, then alternating bands of near-white product ground and full-bleed lifestyle, separated by unusually deep white space. Type is a light, widely letterspaced sans used at two registers only — tiny caps for labels and micro-CTAs, large and low-contrast for the one brand sentence — and there is no accent colour anywhere, so the grooved silver, sand and black of the products are the only saturated things on screen. The most instructive part is the 2x2 category grid: each tile is a purpose-built still (a case standing in a model-railway landscape, a bag suspended mid-air against grey), not a reused product photo. One honest caveat — the pale grey type on near-white in the brand statement and the smallest caps labels sit right at the edge of readable, and would fail a contrast check.
whatWorks: Exactly one button on the page (the hero's outlined 'DISCOVER THE SELECTION'); every other action is a small letterspaced caps word with a hairline underline, so the single button is unmissable

The 2x2 category grid uses four commissioned stills — trio on an olive backdrop, bag and case suspended against grey, a case in a miniature model landscape, the Faber-Castell pencil case open — each on a ground built for it, all at one crop ratio and one caption treatment

Every category tile is captioned with the same construction ('SEE ALL LUGGAGE', 'SEE ALL BAGS', 'SEE ALL ACCESSORIES', 'SEE ALL SPECIALTIES') so the grid reads as one series even though the four images share nothing

The brand sentence is a single claim with a dated eyebrow above it — 'A GERMAN LEGACY OF OVER 125 YEARS' / 'RIMOWA has placed quality and innovation at its core to create functional tools for a lifetime of movement' — and no supporting paragraph

A four-icon band sells what happens after the purchase, not the purchase: Lifetime Guarantee, Worldwide Repairs ('over 120 repair points'), Free Returns ('prepaid label within 30 days'), RIMOWA Unique (customise)
Product photography is all one light and one ground: each item floats on a pale gradient with a soft reflection, so a carousel of four different silhouettes still looks like one shoot

sections.name: Utility bar + transparent nav
sections.notes: 'Ship to United States | English' sits top-left, the wordmark is centred, search / account / wishlist / bag are right, and the nav row of ten letterspaced caps words floats directly on the hero photograph with no bar behind it. The header only gains a solid ground once you scroll off the image, so the fold is a photograph rather than a photograph with furniture on it.

sections.name: Hero
sections.notes: A full-bleed shoreline frame — a leather flap backpack stacked on a grooved aluminium cabin case at the water's edge — with 'Built for Business' centred in light-weight type and one outlined ghost button beneath. The headline is three words and makes a use claim, not a product claim; the product is the whole picture rather than a cut-out pasted onto a scene.

sections.name: Iconic products carousel
sections.notes: A tiny 'ICONIC PRODUCTS' eyebrow, then four items on a pale gradient ground with soft reflections, each labelled with its real product name (Original Cabin, Never Still - Leather Flap Backpack Large, Distinct Cabin, Hybrid Check-In L) and a row of 8px colourway swatches. No prices, no badges, no 'Shop now' — the name and the swatch row are the whole card.

sections.name: Category grid — 'Find a match for every kind of journey'
sections.notes: Four square stills in a 2x2, each shot on a ground constructed for that category, each captioned with an identical underlined caps link. This is the page's real argument: a category grid built from commissioned images stays true when the inventory turns over, where one built from the current best listing photo dates the moment that item sells.

sections.name: Brand statement
sections.notes: Centred, generous, no image: a 10px letterspaced eyebrow dating the company, one sentence set large in pale grey, and a single underlined 'LEARN MORE ABOUT RIMOWA'. The whole band is three lines of text in a screenful of white — the page spends its most expensive real estate on one claim.

sections.name: Video band + service reassurance
sections.notes: A full-bleed retail-interior still ('RIMOWA VIDEO SERIES' / 'Discover our staples for daily commuters' / 'WATCH NOW') is followed immediately by a pale grey band of four line-drawn diamond icons covering guarantee, repairs, returns and customisation. The sequence is deliberate: aspiration, then the ownership terms, in that order.

sections.name: Stories carousel + footer
sections.notes: 'STORIES / Our latest news and views' runs as a horizontal editorial carousel with circular arrow buttons, then a four-column footer (About RIMOWA / Support / Services / Legal) with the newsletter sign-up in the left column and a bottom bar carrying locale, socials and copyright. The editorial content is placed after the commerce, not instead of it.

principle.title: Commission one built image per category, not the prettiest listing photo
principle.explanation: A category or collection grid assembled from current inventory photos is obsolete the day that inventory sells, and it teaches the visitor nothing about what the category means — four rooms shot four ways just look like four rooms. RIMOWA instead stages one deliberate still per category on a ground built for it, and holds crop ratio, subject scale and caption construction identical across all four, so images that share no subject still read as one commissioned series and stay usable for years.
principle.howToApply: For a collection or services page, shoot four stills yourself in one session — one object that means each category (a mooring cleat for Waterfront, a gate latch for Ranches, keys on rolled drawings for New Construction, a stack of lease folders for Rentals) — each on its own plain ground, all at the same square crop, same subject scale, same caption construction ('SEE ALL WATERFRONT'). Keep them in the repo and reuse them for years; never let a live listing photo stand in for a category.

site.name: Louis Vuitton — LV By The Pool (digital campaign)

entries.category: Luxury digital / paid social campaign key visual
entries.tagline: A luxury ad with no headline, no logo lockup and no CTA in frame, where every object brought to the shoot is already one of the location's three colours.
entries.when: Launched May 2024 (summer 2024 'LV By The Pool' collection, shot by Ethan James Green, art direction Michella Rossetti, in-house at Louis Vuitton)
entries.summary: The creative is a single photograph: a model on the stern of a white launch at the water's edge, a sand-coloured Capucines bag held loose at hand height, surfboards and kayaks stacked along the bottom of the frame. There is no type in the image at all — the collection name, the offer ('a selection of pieces available exclusively online') and the click live entirely in the caption and the placement, so the same file runs in every market and language. What makes it more than a pretty holiday picture is the colour discipline: the sea, sky, hull and sand give three colours, and everything brought into frame — the printed trousers, the knit, the hat, the bag, the bracelets — is one of them. The product looks discovered on the boat rather than placed on it.
whatWorks: Zero copy in the frame: name, offer and CTA sit in the caption and placement, so one master image ships to every market unchanged
The bag is small, half-turned and held at hand height — treated as luggage someone is carrying, not as a hero object lit on a plinth
The location supplies the palette (sea blue, sand, white hull) and every styled element repeats it; the floral trousers are the sea's blues, the bag is the sand, the knit is the hull

Props are functional and plural — a stack of surfboards and kayaks in orange, teal, mustard and green across the bottom edge — the only saturated colour in the frame, and it sits away from the product
The horizon is dropped to roughly a third, so two-thirds of the frame is soft water and pale sky and the figure reads instantly at feed scale
Two rock outcrops on the far horizon, left and right, quietly frame the figure without any compositional device in the foreground

sections.name: Hook
sections.notes: The scroll-stopper is atmospheric, not graphic: a wide, low-saturation field of tropical water and pale sky with one figure standing at the exact centre. At feed size it reads as a place before it reads as an ad, which buys the extra half-second.

sections.name: Message / headline
sections.notes: There is no headline. The message is carried by the situation — you have arrived somewhere by boat and the bag came with you — and the only words ('a carefree holiday spirit', 'available exclusively online') live in the post copy. Removing type from the frame is what lets one shot serve global paid social.

sections.name: Visual / hero
sections.notes: The Capucines is in the lower third, held down and away from the body so its shape reads against the white hull; the model's pose (weight back, elbow on the boat) makes the product incidental to the scene. The bag is the smallest element in the frame and still the first thing a buyer of this category will find.

sections.name: CTA
sections.notes: None in the image. The commercial mechanism is 'exclusively online' stated in the caption, which makes the click the only way to get the thing rather than a button asking for it.

principle.title: Cast the wardrobe and the props from the location's own palette
principle.explanation: On location, anything you carry into frame that isn't already one of the place's colours reads as a prop, and the eye separates it from the setting — which is exactly what you don't want when the whole argument is that the product belongs here. Pulling three colours off the real location first and requiring every brought-in element to be one of them makes the frame look found rather than styled, and has the side benefit of a coherent palette for the type and chips that go around the image later.
principle.howToApply: Before a property shoot, photograph the fixed materials (the terracotta floor, the brass window furniture, the sea or the stone outside) and pull three hex values off them. Require every staging object, throw, book, flower and vase to be one of those three, and pull anything that isn't out of frame — a staging kit brought in wholesale will always fight the house. Use the same three values for the chips, rules and section grounds in the collateral so the printed piece and the photograph share one palette.

entries.category: Italian modernism / optical and kinetic graphics
entries.tagline: An architect who ran graphic design as a perceptual laboratory, made roughly 14,000 experiments with no client attached, and drew his commissions out of that archive.
entries.summary: Grignani trained as an architect in Turin (1929–33) and came up through Italy's second Futurist and Constructivist circles, but spent his working life on one question: what makes the eye move. He built an apparatus-based practice — rephotographing images through industrial textured glass, reflecting them off curved chrome, solarising and pushing line film to extreme contrast, then twisting, rotating and splitting the results — and accumulated something like 14,000 experimental sheets. The commissions came out of that body of research rather than out of blank-page ideation: over 150 posters and a full identity for the printer Alfieri & Lacroix, 26 years art-directing the Pubblicità in Italia annuals, the 1969–70 Penguin Science Fiction covers pictured here, and the Woolmark mark of 1963–64 — a skein rendered as one continuous optical ribbon, eventually applied to some five billion products.
whatWorks: Separate generation from judgment: build a mechanical process that produces variants you did not imagine, then switch roles and select

Keep the apparatus fixed and the input variable — one operation (one sheet of textured glass, one chrome curve, one exposure) applied across many images, so results are comparable rather than one-off accidents
Do the research without a client attached, date and file everything, and treat the archive as the raw material a live brief is answered from
Start from a correct, resolved image and then interfere with it — distortion applied to something already working, not used to rescue something that isn't
Judge by physical effect on the viewer (does the eye move, does the surface vibrate) rather than by taste or by whether it looks current
Stay in black and white while researching form; introduce colour only once the structure is settled — the Penguin covers are one flat ink over black

sections.name: How they begin
sections.notes: Not with sketches of the finished piece. Grignani began by making an image — a photogram, a photomontage, a clean line drawing — and then putting it through a physical process to see what came back. His architectural training showed up as method rather than style: define the operation, apply it systematically, record the result, compare.

sections.name: Core method
sections.notes: Optical interference at industrial scale. He rephotographed artwork through sheets of textured industrial glass to break the form into vibration, reflected images in distorting chrome surfaces, re-shot line film to introduce blur and movement, and used darkroom high contrast and solarisation. He then intervened directly on the image — rotations, twists, splits, plastic deformations — building a personal vocabulary of 'virtual forms'. Roughly 14,000 works came out of this, nearly all of them unpaid research.

sections.name: Signature technique
sections.notes: The continuous ribbon that reads as a solid object because the eye supplies the volume. The Woolmark (1963–64) is the pure case: a skein of wool drawn as one unbroken optical band, no outline, no gradient, that holds at a millimetre on a garment label and at building scale. The Penguin Science Fiction covers do the same trick with photographic source — a single flat fluorescent ink over black, the image distorted until the subject is felt before it is identified.

sections.name: Decision rules / philosophy
sections.notes: He judged work by whether it acted on perception, not by whether it was handsome: the test was a measurable reaction in the viewer's eye. That gave him a hard filter — anything that merely looked stylish got archived rather than used. He called drawing a mark the most exciting assignment a designer gets, and he treated a logo the same way as a research sheet: one form, tested for what it does to a person looking at it.

principle.title: Run a standing experiment file, then design by choosing from it
principle.explanation: Inventing at the deadline means inventing from whatever you already know, which is why work converges on the same three layouts. Grignani inverted it: the exploration happened continuously, with no client, using fixed mechanical operations that produced results he could not have pictured, and the brief was then answered by selecting and cropping from that corpus. Two practical consequences — the strange options exist before anyone is paying for them, and generation and judgment never happen in the same hour, so nothing gets defended for being hard to make.
principle.howToApply: Keep a dated, numbered experiments folder with no job attached to it, and spend one short session a week filling it with one fixed operation applied across many inputs — the same listing photograph through six treatments at one export setting, one price string set at eight scales in the house serif, one floorplan redrawn at three line weights, a hero crop at every ratio the templates use. Never judge on the day you generate. When a brief lands, open the folder first and look for what is already there before opening a blank artboard.
